title: China Uneasy Leaving Yuan to 'Market Forces' -- Market Talk
text:
15:22 EDT - The People's Bank of China has been purchasing foreign currencies "at a frantic rate in recent weeks," says Capital Economics. Firm estimates the PBOC purchased roughly $70B last month, and notes that the PBOC was stepping in to keep the yuan weak in 3Q when other emerging-market central banks were working to shore up their currencies. CapEcon says the PBOCinterventions may have been aimed at limiting yuan gains against other emerging-market currencies in August and September. But ultimately, "China's policymakers remain deeply uncomfortable with allowing market forces a say in determining the exchange rate at times of uncertainty," CapEcon adds. (erin.mccarthy@wsj.com)

13:36 EDT - USD/PEN has a natural ceiling of around PEN2.80 to PEN2.83 per US dollar, and if that is tested, HSBC says the Central Reserve Bank of Peru is expected to intervene to rein in sol weakness. Firm sees the sol strengthening to PEN2.75 a dollar, from its current 2.77 level. Upbeat data out of China and new investment projects in Peru should support the currency, it adds, though too much strength could also stir up central-bank action. "The central bank will likely manage the currency within a relatively narrow range, preventing too much PEN strength to maintain export competitiveness, and restrict excessive PEN weakness to protect businesses with (unhedged) USD-denominated liabilities," HSBC says. (robert.kozak@wsj.com)

0000 GMT (Dow Jones) Goldman Sachs is bearish on HUF versus EUR as discussions in the government on a foreign currency debt relief plan and pre-election news could lead to more short-term weakness and volatility.

EUR/HUF is relatively low at 294.81 vs 295.12 late Friday, as a more cautious tone from the the country's rate setters, still-positive real interest rates, a current account surplus, and a more dovish U.S. Fed have recently helped anchor the Hungarian currency, Goldman Sach says.

However, the structural drivers of the currency remain unchanged, and HUF will likely continue to suffer from foreign currency deleveraging and lower potential economic growth in the longer term. The rate differential has narrowed further on the back of more cuts this year and higher U.S. rates, which could also start to erode demand for Hungarian assets. So far, HUF strength has been boosted by the high carry, but the key policy rate has dropped to 3.60% after a series of gradual cuts enacted over the last year or so.

Goldman notes however that HUF weakness appears to be one of the policy objectives for the future - but the government and the central bank aren't willing to allow HUF to depreciate just yet. They first need to reduce foreign currency sensitivity, and are also constrained by the upcoming general elections in spring 2014.

Average yield on Polish two-year bonds is down to 3.07% from 3.13% late Friday, five-year is down to 3.66% from 3.74% and the ten-year paper yields 4.37% today, from 4.42%. Thus, "with inflation now falling, there may be room for modest rate cuts in the next six months," Capital Economics says. It expects the first move to ease policy to happen by the end of this year, and sees a cumulative 75 bps cut over the next half of the year. (andrey.ostroukh@dowjones.com)

13:22 EDT - Of the crazy mortgages issued during the housing bubble, possibly the most egregious was pick-a-pay. Such loans allowed borrowers to decide how much to pay monthly (of course not paying the full minimum increased the loan balance). That California-based favorite helped push Wachovia--which inherited such loans through a top-of-the-market aquisition--into Wells Fargo's (WFC) arms. The bank breaks out some numbers for such mortgages in its quarterly results, and the picture continues to brighten. WFC's pick-a-pay balances were $29.4B as of Sept. 30, down from $32B to start 2013; the total topped $120B under Wachovia. And loan-to-value levels keep falling, with such California borrowers on average having 2% equity in their home versus being 13% underwater at year's end. Thanks, rebounding house prices. title: DJ  Peru 's  Central Bank  Seen Continuing With  Intervention  To Defend Sol
text:
LIMA, Peru--With the sol coming under heavy depreciation pressures, the Central Reserve Bank of Peru is expected to continue to defend the local currency with spot market interventions to sell U.S. dollars.

Banks, private pension funds and foreign investors, among others, have dumped soles in recent weeks, prompting the central bank to increase efforts to ensure the sol doesn't weaken too much, which would run the risk of importing inflation and hurting borrowers who earn in soles but have debts in dollars.

So far this week the central bank has sold $950 million in spot market interventions. It has also placed dollar-indexed certificates of deposit, which help ease dollar gains.

Barclays said in a report Friday that despite an acceleration in inflation in Peru, its weakening economy is expected to make the central bank refrain from increasing interest rates.

"Meanwhile, we expect it (the central bank) to use strong intervention to contain the depreciation of the currency," it added.

The central bank has sold $4.2 billion since May. That is a sharp turnaround from the previous three years, in which the central bank bought a net total of $25.7 billion.

Last year the sol appreciated more than 5.0% against the greenback, despite purchases of $13.2 billion by the central bank in 2012.

But fears that the U.S. Federal Reserve could take the foot off the gas of its monetary easing, a decline in capital inflows, and poorer mineral prices that have cut into Peru's exports, are among the factors that have led to weaker demand for the sol.

So far this year through Thursday the sol has depreciated 10.19%.

"The central bank has been increasing the intervention in the exchange rate market to keep the sol limited, under pressure from a sizable current account deficit and the need to protect the financial sector from a rapid depreciation as well as to limit pass-through effects on inflation," BofA Merrill Lynch said in a report.

The central bank says it has no fixed rate for sol against the greenback, but intervenes to lessen volatility.

title: Peru 's  Central Bank Intervenes , Sells Record $600 Million
text:
LIMA, Peru--The Central Reserve Bank of Peruintervened in the foreign-exchange market on Wednesday to sell a record $600 million, aiming to control a clamor for U.S. dollars and ease depreciation pressures on the sol.

"There was demand from local clients, from foreign clients and from banks," said one foreign exchange market official.

The central bank intervened to sell $350 million on Tuesday.

The interventions Wednesday were done at an average of PEN2.8172 per U.S. dollar, helping the sol to end slightly stronger at PEN2.814. That's compared with PEN2.815 in the previous session.

The sol has depreciated 10.27% against the greenback so far this year.

Last year the sol appreciated more than 5.0% against the U.S. dollar, due in part to strong capital inflows into Peru.

Both the sol and the U.S. dollar are legal tender in Peru. The central bank says it has no fixed rate for sol against the greenback, but intervenes to lessen volatility.

title: FX  CHAT: Treasurys Not the Haven It Used to Be
text:
Treasurys are losing a bit of their safe-haven appeal. While we haven't seen the likes of Greece or Cyprus recently that could still spark a flight into Treasurys, Columbia Asset's Brian Weisman says the safety of this classic haven market is being defined differently now. He says investors are conscious of the damaging effects of rising rates, and that it's been a while since a client has asked to be invested in "pure safety" and with little regard for yield. In this environment, Weisman says the 10-year yield will have to get closer to 4% before "it would start to register on my radar" as an investment consideration for his clients. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; cynthialin_dj)

A confluence of forces are working against US Treasurys. Fed tapering fears have been the main driver, but traders say the technical break of Thursday's 2.823% peak triggered even more selling. Higher yields also spur more hedging from mortgage bond holders, traders say, which puts added pressure on Treasurys. This is all happening in thin August liquidity, which magnifies swings. "Clearly the momentum trade is in control," says Kevin Giddis, head of fixed income at Raymond James. And while rate strategists at JPMorgan say the market looks oversold with the 10-year yield reaching its 2.84%-2.915% target zone, the march higher in rates still looks intact. Ten-year notes down 25/32, yielding 2.858%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

When Treasury yields rise, riskier assets like stocks and emerging-market assets tend to shine as well. But not this time. As it is the prospect of Fed tapering that sparked a selloff in Treasury bonds, the higher yields have driven investors to sell US stocks as they prepare for a less generous Fed. No wonder the bond king has the blues. In a message Friday on Pimco's Twitter account, Bill Gross says that all asset markets are peaking and that without central bank check writing, or pumping money from QEs, "we only have ourselves [to] sell [to]." (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

In a survey of its members, one of Venezuela's largest private-sector groups, Conindustria, estimates that the countries' industries are working at little more than half capacity. Among the main reasons given for the stunted output were political uncertainty, the difficulty in obtaining foreign currency and raw materials, and power outages. President Nicolas Maduro, barely out of his first 100 days in office, began his term by reaching out to the private sector and naming cabinet members that promised more pragmatic policy. But political tension remains high and dollars are still scarce in the stalled economy. (ezequiel.minaya@dowjones.com)

Technical factors are coming into play on a thinned out Friday session, with few buyers around to stem the bleeding in US Treasurys. Benchmark 10-year yields just rose another 3bps, now at 2.851%, setting yet another 2-year high. Technical strategists have warned that breaching 2.75% would pave the way to faster selling. The next key support seen luring in buyers is just above 3%. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; cynthialin_dj)

Underscoring how sentiment toward bonds remains negative, Treasurys are getting hit with another round of selling after stabilizing this morning. The 10-year yield climbs as high as 2.829%, topping the 2-year high of 2.823% set Thursday. "The long-term trend is higher in Treasury yields," says Sean Simko, fixed-income manager at SEI Investments. "Anytime there is a strong move higher in Treasury yields, there will be certain investors that will reallocate assets out of bond funds." Simko says bond prices are looking more attractive in the short-term after this recent selloff. "If there is any inclination that the Fed may not taper in September, Treasury bonds could catch a strong bid," he adds. Ten-year notes down 16/32, yielding 2.825%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

Pimco senior rate strategist Tony Crescenzi writes in his August missive three policy takeaways that will influence the bond market in the years to come. 1) It takes cumulative data for the Fed to act. 2) Tapering is not tightening. In fact, Crescenzi notes the expected $10B reduction in monthly MBS purchases will actually be less than MBS originations because of the recent plunge in mortgage refinancing activity. That means at $30B a month, the Fed would actually be buying a bigger proportion of the market. 3) QE and the policy rate are two separate tools. As investors grow to understand this, Crescenzi says rates will be tied more to the latter. Pimco see the Fed funds rate unchanged until early 2016. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; cynthialin_dj)

Peru's central bank will likely continue to intervene in the foreign-exchange market to ease the depreciation on the country's currency against the US dollar, Banco de Credito said. The central bank has intervened regularly in recent sessions, selling dollars on the spot market. So far this week, it has sold $620M to prevent the sol from weakening further. The sol has depreciated 9.6% against the greenback so far this year, with the dollar recently trading at PEN2.797. (ryan.dube@wsj.com)

For the sixth-straight week, the amount of US Treasurys owned by foreign accounts stashed at the NY Fed fell. The $5.2B drop brings the total decline since early June to $58B. But RBS assures the streak shouldn't be interpreted as foreign investors losing confidence in US government bonds. Instead, the firm points out that these so-called custody holdings tend to track how Asian currencies perform. When these currencies strengthened amid growing Fed stimulus, dollars were bought to cap that strength, then often used to invest in US Treasurys. Now that EM currencies are weakening, the process is reversing. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; cynthialin_dj)

Peru's economic conditions are putting its policymakers between a rock and a hard place. The Central Reserve Bank of Peru faces decelerating economic growth, which points to a need for cut rates, while inflation and exchange-rate pressures may require a rate hike instead. "Facing these two opposite forces, we believe the most likely scenario is that the bank will remain on hold," Barclays said. "We think an initial stimulus to contain the slowdown could be provided through additional reductions in reserve requirements." Last week, Peru left its policy rate at 4.25%, where it has stood since May 2011. (ryan.dube@wsj.com)

Yet, the greenback is holding up against the yen, which shows how fervently markets believe an autumn tapering is coming. At this point, many market participants believe only a dismal August nonfarm payrolls number can derail a stimulus reduction. Dollar up 0.1% at Y97.48. text:
Peru's central bank will likely continue to intervene in the foreign-exchange market to ease the depreciation on the country's currency against the US dollar, Banco de Credito said. Of all data releases, surprises in monthly nonfarm payrolls move bonds and stocks most. Goldman Sachs finds that a 1-standard-deviation surprise--about a 80K swing--causes an average 5-basis-point move in the 10-year yield and 0.3% impact on the S&P 500. But when it comes to predictive powers for how the economy will actually fare in the months ahead, the investment bank finds payrolls has little. Instead, the Philly Fed and ISM manufacturing reports best illustrate the economy's strength and momentum. Those reports are both more timely (released shortly after surveys are taken) and subject to smaller revisions, says Goldman. The latest data from both were also surprisingly upbeat, contrasting the underwhelming July jobs. August Philly Fed comes Thursday. (cynthia.lin@dowjones.com; cynthialin_dj)

title: DJ Peru's Sol Seen Gaining After Hiccup That Weakened  Currency
text:
--Sol seen appreciating after period of weakness

--Peru's strong economic fundamentals seen helping currency

--Central bank interventions seen easing volatility

By Robert Kozak

LIMA, Peru--After weakening recently, Peru's sol appears set to regain its appreciation trend, as strong economic fundamentals again propel the currency.

The sol gained 5.4% against the U.S. dollar last year on strong capital inflows, despite heavy central bank intervention to purchase dollars.

Short-term factors weakened the sol in April and May, such as greater demand for greenbacks by companies to pay dividends outside of Peru. Political noise, tied in good part to the chance of greater government activity in the petroleum sector, also weakened the local currency.

"The fundamentals are there for the currency to continue to strengthen, but probably not at a pace in which it was happening in the past," Credicorp General Manager Walter Bayly said Tuesday in a conference call with analysts. Credicorp is the nation's largest financial-services company.

On Monday the sol closed slightly stronger at PEN2.614 per dollar, bringing the depreciation of the sol so far this year to 2.43%.

Scotiabank in Peru forecasts the sol will make up lost ground in coming days, "and continue appreciating at a moderate rhythm." That appreciation will be limited by central bank measures, it added.

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru, or BCRP, has shown its willingness to intervene to purchase dollars to ease volatility in the foreign exchange market, although it has been absent since April 19.

"We turn constructive on the sol given the political uncertainty, which had weighed on the sol the last two weeks, appears to be easing, and the risk of higher commodity price volatility should be limited by BCRP intervention," J.P. Morgan said in a report.

The central bank bought a net $13.2 billion in spot market interventions last year, and so far this year the central bank has purchased $5.21 billion.

The central bank has taken other measures, such as regularly increasing the amount that private pension funds can invest abroad. It has also increased commercial bank reserve requirements for U.S. dollars a number of times in order to choke off credit growth, and ease appreciation pressures.

Barclays Capital said Tuesday that some of the additional reserves bought by the BCRP are being sold to the treasury for the prepayment of debt with multilaterals and deposits in the stabilization fund.

Barclays says that with the treasury operations almost complete, the central bank intervention could decline in coming months, leaving space for some appreciation of the sol, although that could be limited due to other central bank measures.

"We expect the exchange rate to fluctuate around USD/PEN 2.60-2.55 range the rest of the year, breaking the appreciation trend of recent years," it said.

-Ryan Dube contributed to this article.

title: ANALYSIS-Spoonful of reforms helps Latin America capital flows go down
text:
* Foreign inflows high for third year running in 2012

* Short-term policy response skips over reforms

* 'Perfect storm' exit not seen for now

By Krista Hughes

MEXICO CITY, March 4 (Reuters) - B umper capital inflows to Latin America are putting the spotlight on shock-proofing policies to help economies digest the rush of investment - and guard against the inevitable exit.

Foreign investment inflows to Latin America were more than $280 billion in 2012, according to balance of payment data from countries covering 75 percent of the region's economic output, similar to the flows registered in 2011 as low interest rates in developed economies pushed investors to seek returns elsewhere.

According to the Institute of International Finance, Latin America outpaced other emerging market regions as a magnet for foreign capital in 2011 and 2012, taking the relative size of economies into account, a trend it expects to continue in 2013.

Rapid inflows can push up currencies, cause domestic demand to overheat, create asset price bubbles and fan inflation, but can be offset by tighter fiscal policy and reforms to boost economic efficiency. Peru and Chile have already done much of their homework, but reforms are pending in Mexico and Brazil.

"Currency appreciation pressures are a problem if they are too intense but it's also an opportunity to jump start structural reforms in order to improve productivity, which is one of the Achilles' heels of the region," said IIF Chief Latin America Economist Ramon Aracena.

Data show Peru and Chile are Latin America's foreign investment hotspots, with capital inflows, including banking, direct and portfolio investment, worth more than 10 percent of gross domestic product last year.

Mexico and Colombia follow, with inflows equivalent to around 7 percent of GDP, while Brazil - which has erected strict barriers to speculative financial investment - attracted inflows worth about 4 percent of GDP last year, down sharply.

SURGERY NOT PEPTO-BISMOL

Many countries have responded to the surge in investment with measures aimed at slowing inflows and preventing excessive currency appreciation, ranging from currency intervention to taxes on foreign investment.

But such short-term measures are the policy equivalent of taking Pepto-Bismol when what is really required is abdominal surgery - deep reforms to make economies better able to absorb such inflows without suffering indigestion.

Policies to encourage productivity, a prudent fiscal stance, currency flexibility and adequate foreign reserves also help shield against disruptions when money flows out, although this is not expected until developed economies start raising rates.

Peru and Chile, which undertook a round of structural reforms in the 1990s, score best on a checklist covering these five factors. Of the inflation-targeting countries, Mexico is in third place, followed by Colombia and Brazil.

Running tight fiscal policy can help offset the boost to domestic demand from excess money sloshing around an economy, and gives the central bank room to cut interest rates - making local assets less attractive to speculators.

Chile, the highest-rated sovereign issuer in Latin America, targets a structural budget balance, while Peru is the only major economy in the region that the International Monetary Fund expects to report an overall budget surplus in 2013.

A hands-off approach to currencies also allows the exchange rate to help balance the impact of inflows, dampening demand when inflows are high and providing a boost when flows reverse.

High levels of foreign reserves give countries a buffer against sudden capital reversals and room to intervene to shore up currencies if needed. Peru has the largest foreign reserves as a share of economic output at more than 30 percent of GDP, double the level of Brazil, Chile and Mexico.

High productivity is the ultimate mark of a flexible economy, but Latin America has lagged other emerging market regions - especially Asia - in improving output efficiency.

The Inter-American Development Bank estimates that if productivity in the region were as high as in the United States, per capita income would double.

PERFECT STORM?

Mexican Central Bank Governor Agustin Carstens, who has welcomed plans for structural reforms by the country's new government, warned last month that a "perfect storm" may be brewing as a result of the massive inflows to emerging markets, setting the stage for a painful reverse.

Thomson Reuters' Lipper service data show $495 million flowed out of U.S.-based Latin American equity funds last week, the biggest weekly fall since 2007, and emerging market debt also suffered as investors worried about Italy's deadlocked election result.

Funds tracker EPFR said stocks in Brazil, where the Bovespa index has slumped 10 percent since the start of the year, took the biggest hit in the recent outflow.

Many investors have been put off by Brazil's ad hoc capital controls and a failure to undertake deep reforms that would boost growth, although the country has recently started to unwind barriers to foreign investment, for example scrapping a 6 percent tax on purchases of real estate investment trusts.

Veteran emerging markets investor Mark Mobius, who oversees $51 billion in assets at funds manager Franklin Templeton, said he did not see bubbles at risk of bursting - yet.

"You'll know it when everyone is optimistic, everybody is buying and nobody is selling, and when the guy on the street says 'you should be buying stocks,' that's when you know you're in a bubble," he said during a visit to Mexico last week.

(Reporting by Krista Hughes; Editing by Maureen Bavdek)

title: Peru Central Bank  Pauses Dollar Buying  Interventions
text:
LIMA, Peru--The Central Reserve Bank of Peru has taken a pause in its daily purchases of U.S. dollars, without formally announcing any change to its policy.

In late August, the central bank began to purchase greenbacks every day, in part aiming to introduce uncertainty in what had become a one-way bet on sol appreciation.

The central bank has refrained from purchasing dollars on three separate trading sessions this year, but the latest pause has been the longest since it bought into effect its daily purchases.

Since purchasing $10 million on Feb. 25, the central bank hasn't bought any dollars.

"They haven't announced it, but the facts reflect the fact that the policy of dollar buying remains discretional," Scotiabank economist Mario Guerrero said Monday.

So far this year the central bank has purchased $3.36 billion, following a record-buying spree of $13.2 billion last year.

A central bank spokesman said there hasn't been any change in the bank's policy regarding buying dollars.

Strong inflows of capital into Peru last year helped the sol appreciate 5.4% against the dollar, despite the heavy interventions to purchase dollars.

The central bank has initiated a number of measures aimed at curbing the strength of the sol, including increasing commercial bank reserve requirements.

The strong local currency has raised the ire of exporters.

Following the introduction of various government measures the sol has depreciated 1.68% so far this year.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico yields see-saw ahead of cenbank minutes
text:
* Mexico minutes could reinforce views on rate cut possibility

 * Peru, Costa Rica move to limit hot money flows 

 By Michael O'Boyle

 MEXICO CITY, Jan 30 (Reuters) - Mexican yields were little changed on Thursday ahead of the release of central bank minutes that could either deepen or undermine bets that policymakers could soon cut interest rates.

 Mexican bond yields recently hit record lows, and interest rate swaps are pricing in a 25 basis point cut to the country's benchmark rate of 4.50 percent by September.

 In a policy U-turn at its January meeting, the central bank moved from warning of a potential rate hike to saying it could cut borrowing costs if inflation keeps cooling. Minutes from the meeting are due Friday at 0900 local time.

 The minutes "may show that there was no consensus, at least one director will highlight that it is not yet the time to (cut) and that we need these trends to consolidate," said Alberto Ramos, an economist at Goldman Sachs in New York.

 One reason to cut might be to discourage flows of hot money into the economy this year that could strengthen the peso currency to the point where it makes exports less competitive and crimps growth.

 The yield on Mexico's benchmark 10-year bond  fell 1 basis point to 5.03 percent after bidding up earlier in the session. The yield is trading just above record lows below 5 percent.

 The Mexican peso firmed 0.13 percent to 12.7105 per dollar. The peso has shed 1.2 percent since the central bank signaled it could cut rates. 

 Foreign investors have been piling into Mexican bonds;  foreign holdings of peso debt jumped 60 percent last year and are still rising. 

 "There is a element of preemptiveness to get ahead of the curve, with the steady flows into bonds," Ramos said. "They do not have an exchange rate problem yet, but they could have one down the road."

  An easing in the euro zone's debt crisis and new economic stimulus measures in Japan are seen fueling bumper investment flows into Latin America and other emerging markets in 2013 and policymakers are trying to ward off unwanted currency strength.

 Mexico has eschewed the types of direct intervention and capital controls that other countries have used.

Peru's sol currency finished bidding 0.31 percent weaker at 2.575 per dollar on Thursday, a day after the central bank tightened reserve requirements to soften the impact of heavy capital inflows. 

 The sol is near a 16-year high and the central bank has intervened in the currency market every day since late August to buy dollars, but it did not step in on Thursday.

 Meanwhile, Costa Rica said it will limit lending to limit the attractiveness of an interest rate gap that has sparked a credit boom and drawn in potentially destabilizing foreign capital. 

 The Brazilian real was little changed as the market eyed how far policymakers would let the currency firm.

 The real hit a seven-month high on Tuesday, breaking past the 2-per-dollar mark on bets the central bank will allow further gains as policymakers fret about a recent move higher in inflation.

 But its advance has stalled this week after Finance Minister Guido Mantega warned that the government was ready to correct any excessive moves in the exchange rate. 

 Brazil has used a series of measures to keep the real from gaining too much in recent years. The real  closed at 1.9885 per dollar, 0.05 percent weaker than Wednesday's close.

title: Peru Central Bank  Doesn't  Intervene  to Buy Dollars for First Time Since August
text:
LIMA, Peru--The Central Reserve Bank of Peru held off Thursday from purchasing U.S. dollars in the spot market for the first time in more than five months, as the sol depreciated almost 1% against the greenback in January.

In September, the central bank changed its policy for intervening in the foreign-exchange market by buying a fixed amount of dollars each day, regardless of whether the sol was appreciating or depreciating against the U.S. currency.

The change was aimed at curbing the appeal of dollar-denominated loans by creating more uncertainty for individuals who believed the sol would continue appreciating.

The central bank bought a net $13.2 billion in spot-market interventions last year, however the sol still appreciated 5.4% against the dollar in 2012.

The last time the central bank didn't buy dollars was on Aug. 24.

The central bank had maintained its intervention approach so far this year, even though the sol had been depreciating against the dollar in recent sessions.

The central bank bought about $1.8 billion so far this year in daily purchases that ranged between $10 million to $350 million.

A spokesman from the central bank wasn't immediately available to comment if the monetary authority was changing its intervention approach.

On Thursday, the sol closed at 2.576 soles per dollar, compared with PEN2.568 in the previous session. The sol depreciated 0.94% against the greenback in January.

title: Peru Expanding Efforts to Prevent  Currency  Appreciation
text:
--Government to buy up to $4 billion to stem currency gains

--Central bank likely to allow pension funds to invest more abroad

--Creation of a sovereign wealth fund is under consideration

Peru is planning to step up its efforts to stem the appreciation of its currency, the sol, as the country comes under increased pressure from capital flows leaving the developed world in search of more attractive emerging markets, according to interviews with top officials in the finance ministry and central bank.

The government is planning to spend up to $4 billion in the first half of this year to buy dollars that will be used to prepay debt owed to multilateral lenders and add funds to the country's fiscal stabilization fund, Finance Minister Luis Miguel Castilla said. The country also is considering the creation of a sovereign wealth fund to save more of its surpluses outside the country, delaying future dollar bond sales and increasing the amount private pension funds can invest abroad.

While Peru's mining-led economy is forecast to expand at an enviable pace of 6.3% this year, with relatively stable inflation and healthy government accounts, business owners are concerned that the rapid appreciation of the country's currency may sap competitiveness from its export sector, undercutting growth in the future.

Officials have taken steps to prevent a surge of capital inflows from overheating the economy and driving the sol even higher. Most aggressively, the Central Reserve Bank of Peru has intervened actively in currency markets, buying $13.2 billion in 2012 alone.

"What we've seen in the past few months is a faster rate of appreciation" in the sol, Mr. Castilla said in an interview in New York. "I think it's becoming too strong," though he said the currency's value isn't yet too far out of alignment with its fundamentals.

Peru is one of many emerging-market countries concerned about efforts to stimulate growth in the U.S. and Japan through bond buying, which floods the world market with dollars and yen, pushing up the value of foreign currencies. Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega first warned in 2010 that developing countries faced a "currency war," and the issue has resurfaced in recent months, as the Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan announced new plans to expand their bond-buying programs.

"I'm concerned about these very, very expansionary monetary policies, because they haven't taken into consideration the effect that this has on emerging markets," Mr. Castilla said. "We already had a trend towards capital inflows coming to emerging markets, but this has been exacerbated by the search for yield."

The sol has gain 4.8% in the past 12 months and is currently trading at PEN2.56 per dollar, near its strongest level in about 15 years. A stronger sol reduces the amount that the country earns, in local currency terms, from its substantial copper, gold, zinc and silver exports. It also cuts into profits for exporters of manufactured goods, which have to lower their prices to compete.

The government plans to prepay up to $2 billion in debt owed to the World Bank and Inter-American Development Bank in the first quarter of this year, Mr. Castilla said. The payment likely will be financed in part by issuing local currency debt that will be exchanged for dollars, augmenting efforts at the central bank to weaken the sol through interventions, Mr. Castilla said. The government also will use funds from the treasury, he said.

Peru is planning to buy another $2 billion to replenish the country's fiscal stabilization fund during the first half of the year and for debt servicing. In a separate effort to mitigate pressure on the sol, Mr. Castilla said he had asked state-owned companies, including wholesale bank Cofide, to delay international bond sales that would increase the flow of dollars into the country. Cofide had planned to sell up to $1.5 billion in dollar bonds this year, but it may issue local-currency debt in tranches instead, Mr. Castilla said.

In a separate interview, Central Reserve Bank of Peru Governor Julio Velarde said the sol was "slightly" overvalued at its current level and policymakers would keep a close watch on its strength.

He said he expects the central bank to continue to increase the amount of money that private pension funds can invest abroad by a rate of about two percentage points a quarter until it reaches the 50% legal limit, though the rate of increases will depend on how the economy and exchange rate evolve.

The central bank recently increased that limit to 32% from 30%.

Mr. Velarde also said that he expects inflation to fall to the central bank's 2% target by the end of 2013, which will make a rate cut possible this year, though he cautioned that any decision to loosen monetary policy will depend on how the economy performs going forward.

The central bank has kept its reference interest rate unchanged at 4.25% since May 2011.

Despite the challenges presented by the stronger sol, both Mr. Velarde and Mr. Castilla said they were broadly optimistic about the outlook, and the finance minister added that he may raise the country's growth forecast for this year.

"The numbers are going to be good" in the coming years, Mr. Velarde said. "Obviously, when the numbers are good, that's when we attract capital, which can then be a problem."

--Robert Kozak contributed to this article.

title: ANALYSIS-Latin America lays out defenses in  currency  war
text:
* Colombia joins Peru and Costa Rica in flows defense

* Pundits predict bumper year for emerging market assets

* Brazil seen on sidelines this time as inflation flares

By Krista Hughes

MEXICO CITY, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Latin American policymakers are manning their defenses ahead of what could be a new battle in the "currency wars" as flows of hot money put unwelcome upward pressure on their currencies.

Economists and investors predict that an easing in the euro zone's debt crisis, new economic stimulus measures in Japan and a return of risk appetite will fuel bumper investment flows into Latin America and other emerging markets in 2013.

Some policymakers are already at the barricades.

Colombia cut interest rates on Monday and said it would ramp up dollar purchases. Peru plans to pre-pay up to $1.5 billion in foreign debt this year and is intervening aggressively to curb currency gains. And tiny Costa Rica unveiled a steep hike in taxes on foreign investments this month.

Even Mexico, which has a hands-off approach to currency market intervention, is considering an interest rate cut that some economists believe reflects as much a desire for a weaker peso as it does concerns about growth.

"Much of the region is once again dealing with the impacts of currency wars and QE in the developed world," said Standard Chartered senior strategist Bret Rosen, referring to the extraordinary monetary easing measures undertaken by central banks known as quantitative easing.

Low interest rates in developed economies encourage investors to look for yield elsewhere, pushing up the currencies of countries at the receiving end of their attentions. Stronger currencies make exports less competitive, hurting economic growth.

It is a problem that has battered Brazilian manufacturers for several years. The government pushed back by slashing interest rates and intervening in the currency market to weaken the real, introducing capital controls and offering tax breaks for several industries.

But Brazil has less room for maneuver than other leading Latin American economies this year as policymakers are concerned about inflation, which rose above an annualized rate of 6 percent this month.

Latin American finance ministers complained last month about the impact of stimulus policies in developed economies, and Group of 20 economic policymakers are set to address the impact of monetary policy on currency valuations next month at a meeting in Russia.

Tools to combat appreciating currencies include buying dollars, as Colombia and Peru are doing; capital controls as in Costa Rica; and macroprudential measures, such as Peru's move to raise deposit requirements on dollar bank accounts.

Mark Mobius, who helps oversee $51 billion in emerging market assets at fund manager Franklin Templeton, expects a huge influx of funds into emerging markets this year as investors tire of low-yielding government bonds.

"I think it's going to be enormous, terrific, hundreds of billions. Investors have been penalized with so low rates that they are not making anywhere near what they need," he said.

Global stock markets are up 4 percent already this year, and fund tracker EPFR said it noted a clear preference for emerging market equities over bonds, which attracted most money in 2012. The VIX index, a gauge of investor stress, fell this month to its lowest levels since 2007.

The Institute of International Finance banking group predicts capital flows to Latin America will jump 5.6 percent this year from 2012 to a record $321 billion.

Inflows to the region in 2012, including foreign direct investment as well as stock and bond investment, were already estimated to be about 30 percent higher than the "hot money" period immediately before the global financial crisis in 2008.

WHAT'S HOT?

Brazil and Mexico, as the region's two biggest economies, are likely to attract the bulk of inflows in 2013, although Brazil has managed to deter a lot of speculative investors with capital controls introduced during 2010-2011, when a rush of capital pushed the real up 12 percent against the dollar.

Foreign portfolio inflows into Brazilian stocks and bonds totaled $16.5 billion last year, down from $67.8 billion in 2010.

In its January fund managers' survey, Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch said Brazil had the biggest share of "underweight" ratings in the history of the survey.

Mobius likes small to mid-cap companies in the region and firms exposed to the consumer sector, such as banks. Citigroup, which raised its stock ratings for Latin America to "overweight" as it cut back other emerging markets, likes industrials.

Mexico, for its part, is benefiting from optimism about tax and energy reforms being promised by its new government. That has helped propel stocks and bonds to record high levels.

Pacific Investment Management Co, the California-based firm known as PIMCO that operates the world's largest bond fund, sees opportunities to make money if Mexico's central bank cuts interest rates later this year, pushing up the price of bonds.

Mexico's central bank has made a U-turn from warning of rate hikes to warning of rate cuts, prompting many to suspect it is worried about the peso. The peso hit a 10-month high the day central bankers met to discuss rates, and it only came off those highs when policymakers warned the following morning that they could cut rates. Lower rates would make the peso less attractive to foreign investors.

"It's no surprise that with the peso being weaker in the second half of (last) year that they were a little bit more hawkish, and now we have had a very nice run in the peso year-to-date perhaps they would be more dovish," said Michael Gomez, co-head of emerging markets at PIMCO.

London-based Capital Economics sees Mexico's peso as the currency with the most upside this year, due mainly to the lower risk of intervention by laissez-faire policymakers, in contrast to the record $13.9 billion bought by Peru's central bank in 2012 as the sol hit a 16-year high.

Chile is likely to join Peru and Colombia in intervening to check gains in the peso while shunning capital controls, said Capital's Neal Shearing, while Brazil is in the unusual position of trying to strengthen its currency to fend off rising inflation. A stronger currency cuts the cost of imported goods.

"Inflation concerns are starting to creep back in Brazil, which now marks it out from Colombia, Chile and Peru who seem to be more worried about the strength of the currency and its impact on competitiveness," he said.

The central bank had intervened in the market in recent months to keep the real weaker than 2 per dollar, but this week rolled over currency swaps that mimic the sale of dollars in the futures market - a move with the opposite effect.

The real strengthened past the 2-per-dollar mark on Tuesday for the first time since July, and analysts said they believed policymakers would allow it to firm further if needed.

title: Peru's Strengthening Sol Sparks Debate Between Government, Business
text:
--Strength of Peruvian sol pits business sector against government

--Exporter group wants more government measures

--Exporters say strong sol is cutting into profit margins


 
   By Robert Kozak 
 

LIMA, Peru--The strength of Peru's sol has sparked a heated debate between the government and business sector about what should be done, with exporters leading protests after the sol gained 5.3% against the U.S. dollar last year on strong capital inflows.

The local currency has made further gains early this year, and former prime minister Pedro Pablo Kuczynski, an investment banker, recently forecast that the sol could reach PEN2.30 to the U.S. dollar this year from around MXN2.55 at present, damaging the business sector.

The government has taken a number of indirect measures, such as increasing reserve requirements, most recently at the start of this year, in order to weaken credit growth.

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru has intervened strongly, buying $1.5 billion so far this year and helping to turn back some of the sol's gains.

In all of 2012, the central bank bought $13.2 billion in the exchange market, and the central bank's chief economist said recently there is no limit on how many dollars the bank can purchase.

On Friday, the central bank increased to 32% from 30% the maximum amount of assets under management that private pension funds can invest outside of Peru in what Credit Suisse called "an attempt to counter large currency inflows into the country."

The business sector wants more, however, pointing out that the strong sol means imports are growing much faster than exports.

The main private-sector association of Peruvian exporters, known as ADEX, wants the finance ministry to prepay external debt, something the finance minister has said could take place this year.

ADEX's chief economist, Carlos Gonzalez, told Dow Jones Newswires Monday that profits for companies that export manufactured products fall sharply as the sol appreciates. The association says lower profits damp corporate investments.

The exporters want a series of new measures, including a government crackdown on illegal activities, such as illegal gold mining and narcotics trafficking, which create greater inflows of cash and demand for the sol. Money laundering in Peru is estimated to be worth from $6.5 billion to $7.0 billion a year.

The government has responded by pointing to strong export growth in recent years, adding that exporters must become more efficient.

Finance Minister Luis Miguel Castilla said that in the last decade the sol has appreciated by about 30%, while nontraditional exports, such as manufactured products, have increased fivefold, government agency Andina reported.

According to Andina, Mr. Castilla said that if inflationary pressures trend lower then it might be a good idea to eventually debate whether there should be a decline in the reference interest rate, which has been at 4.25% since May 2011. That would help weaken capital inflows.

title: DJ  Peru 's  Central Bank  to Keep  Intervening  to Buy U.S. Dollars as Needed
text:
LIMA, Peru--The Central Reserve Bank of Peru will keep intervening as long as necessary to buy as many U.S. dollars as needed, aiming to avoid any extreme volatility in the foreign exchange market, the central bank's chief economist said.

Adrian Armas said Friday in a conference call with reporters that accumulating U.S. dollars will help prepare Peru in the case of any future capital outflows.

Peru attracted large amounts of capital last year, leading the central bank to purchase $13.2 billion in its attempt to moderate the appreciation of the sol. So far this year the central bank has bought another net $420 million in its daily purchases.

"The central bank has no problem in continuing to intervene to buy dollars. It is accumulating foreign currency and it is prepared to keep accumulating," Mr. Armas said.

The sol gained about 5.4% against the U.S. dollar last year.

Mr. Armas said that the central bank doesn't have any target for the local currency, the sol.

"There is no floor or ceiling," he added.

He said that the value of the sol going forward will depend largely on external factors.

"The exchange rate is a variable that is difficult to forecast," he added.

Mr. Armas said that the central bank has no plans at present to introduce any currency controls, although he says the central bank in principle doesn't rule out using any measures.

The central bank has been more recently increasing commercial bank reserve requirements, especially in U.S. dollars, aiming to limit credit growth.

LIMA, Dec 28 (Reuters) - Peru's sol closed at 2.552 per U.S. dollar on Friday, ending the year with gains of 5.72 percent despite record intervention by the central bank, which purchased $13.85 billion in U.S. dollars to curb the local currency's advances to a 16-year high.

Analysts polled by Reuters at the start of the year predicted the sol would remain nearly unchanged at around 2.68, while a few predicted a gain of as much as 3 percent to 2.60.

Peru's strong economy and the U.S. Federal Reserve's stimulus helped stoke the sol's advances, leaving Peru's central bank trying to soak up excess liquidity.

The monetary authority bought dollars in the local spot market every day since Aug. 27 but only managed to slow the pace of the currency's appreciation, not stop it.

This year, the central bank also restricted the ability of banks to make bets in the currency market and tightened reserve requirements several times to stem the inflow of speculative capital as the sol reached levels not seen since 1996.

The sol ended bidding at 2.546 per dollar on Thursday - its strongest level in more than 16 years - but finished the year slightly weaker after the central bank bought $40 million on Friday.

A Reuters analysis after the Federal Reserve announced its third round of financial easing in September said the sol would finish bidding this year at 2.55 per dollar.

Meanwhile, performance in the stock market turned out to be less robust than analysts predicted.

At the start of 2012, equity analysts surveyed by Reuters said Lima's main stock index would finish the year with gains of between 15 percent and 30 percent.

Though the index did rise 23.5 percent through April, it then retreated on a host of worries - from the slowdown in China, to debt woes in Europe, to a sluggish U.S. economy.

As of Friday, Lima's bourse was on track to finish the year at around 20,400 points, a rise of just 4 percent. It will be open for limited trade on Monday.

text:

* High opportunity cost for $135 billion dollar purchases

* Policymakers fret about new round of currency pressure

By Krista Hughes

MEXICO CITY, Dec 17 (Reuters) - Currency market intervention has cost South America's central banks more than $13 billion in the last 2-1/2 years but they are likely to maintain their defenses against hot money inflows if a fresh rush of cheap money sparks another round of currency wars.

Latin American finance ministers meeting in Chile on Friday said monetary easing in developed countries could hurt their export competitiveness by pushing up currencies in the region - a problem they have been wrestling with since the global financial crisis.

Bank of England Governor Mervyn King warned last week that a 2013 might see a growing number of countries deliberately weakening their currencies to offset the impact of a slow global economy.

Central bank data shows Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Peru have bought $135 billion in dollars to help keep a lid on their currencies since mid-2010, just before the U.S. Federal Reserve announced its last round of monetary easing, dubbed QE2.

The Fed is now well into QE3, and Chilean Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said Wednesday's decision to further bolster U.S. asset purchases was a "source of worry" for all emerging markets with healthy growth and floating exchange rates.

Low interest rates in advanced economies encourage investors to seek higher returns in faster-growing emerging markets such as Latin America, but accelerating capital inflows put unwelcome upward pressure on currencies, making exports more expensive.

"This is the third round of QE and we are starting at a level where the FX rates are a lot stronger," said Jefferies Latin America strategist Siobhan Morden, who sees central bank intervention as the biggest concern for investors in local debt.

"It clearly places more stress on policymakers in how to manage this liquidity."

Low inflation in Peru, Chile and Colombia and healthy budget balances give central banks plenty of leeway to keep buying dollars, adding to already-swollen reserves, analysts said - a contrast to the last round of QE, when many countries were struggling with inflation fanned by a V-shaped recovery.

Most dollar purchases so far have been offset by market operations, such as issuing bonds, to mop up or sterilize excess liquidity - but these operations have a high cost due to the gap between very low U.S. yields and higher local interest rates.

Calculations by Thomson Reuters put the accumulated opportunity cost of currency purchases from mid-2010 to November 2012 at about $13.9 billion, more than $11 billion in Brazil alone, without taking currency fluctuations into account.

Brazil's cost reflects benchmark interest rates which were as high as 12.5 percent in mid-2011, before an aggressive easing cycle which slashed them to a record low 7.25 percent, while U.S. official rates were - and are - close to zero.

Intervention has cost Chile, Peru and Colombia between $500 million and $1 billion each, according to estimates based on central bank data on reserve asset returns, or local and U.S. market interest rates where not.

DIFFERENT STROKES

Officials attending the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC) meeting in Chile did not come up with a joint solution on how best to handle hot money flows, but agreed they were a major challenge to the region.

Brazil has slapped strict controls on foreign investment and intervened heavily in markets, while the Andean nations have largely eschewed capital controls and analysts expect they will continue to rely on market intervention in the future.

While Brazil and Chile have scaled back or paused their interventions this year, Peru and Colombia remain very active in the market - despite having an even higher interest rate gap with the United States than they did in mid-2010.

Colombia has picked up the pace of currency interventions, buying 18.5 percent more dollars in the 11 months to November than in all of 2011, and traders are also wary of Chile, where the peso has appreciated 9.5 percent this year.

Peru has bought a record $13 billion so far in 2012 and has also limited banks' ability to make big bets in the currency market with tighter rules on forwards.

Subdued inflation in Peru, Colombia and Chile means those central banks have less reason to worry about the impact of liquidity created by currency market intervention, which depends on demand for local paper to mop up the extra funds.

"Peru will likely increase its intervention and it has the scope to do so," said Nomura Securities economist Benito Berber.

Compared to August 2010, just before the Fed flagged its QE2 easing, the Peruvian sol is up 9 percent, the Chilean peso up 5 percent and the Colombian peso up 1 percent, although Brazil's real is weaker thanks to concerted official efforts.

Brazil confused many by intervening to strengthen the currency in December after a sharp weakening when third quarter growth came in well below expectations.

Policymakers have indicated the central bank wants the currency to stabilize somewhere between 2.0 and 2.1 per dollar, and it is unlikely to tolerate a sharp strengthening.

Economist Intelligence Unit analyst Anna Szterenfeld said Brazil was likely to face less upward currency pressure given recent rate cuts there, compared with rate increases during the Fed's QE2 period. "Some yield-seeking investors - Brazil would call them speculators - won't find Brazil as attractive as they did then," she said.

AREQUIPA, Peru--Former Trade Minister Alfredo Ferrero said Thursday the strength of Peru's sol, which has appreciated 4.45% so far this year against the U.S. dollar, doesn't appear to be harming exports from the Andean nation.

"Exports would be affected by keeping the sol too strong, and it is also the case that fixing the sol in an arbitrary manner would be a risk for the nation. The sol is strong because the dollar is weak on a global level, and that doesn't depend on Peru," he said on the sidelines of a business conference being held in this southern Peruvian city.

"I would say the central bank should continue with its policies, and there is no reason for that to affect the exchange rate," he added.

Peru manages its floating currency, intervening on a daily basis in the foreign exchange market to purchase greenbacks. It has purchased some $12 billion so far this year.

Mr. Ferrero was Trade and Tourism Minister in the administration of former President Alejandro Toledo and helped negotiate free-trade pacts with other nations.

title: Capital Inflows Into Peru Seen Driving Sol's Continuing Appreciation
text:
--Appreciation of Peru's sol should continue next year

--Fundamental reason for gains shifts to capital inflows

--Foreign direct investment may hit $10 billion for 2012

By Robert Kozak

LIMA, Peru--Strength in Peru's sol is expected to continue next year, though it will be capital inflows driving most of the gains this time, say currency investors.

Among those forecasting more gains is Scotiabank, the third-largest bank in Peru, which said low interest rates abroad, abundant liquidity and an improvement in Peru's risk profile are helping to attract capital. The bank forecasts record foreign direct investment this year of close to $10 billion as well as increased corporate and financial sector long-term loans and bond placements.

Drivers of previous rallies had been a positive trade balance and the process of domestic dedollarization.

"External noise is having less of an impact on the national currency than it did in the past. This shift, from being a high-risk currency to a low-risk one, is structural," the bank said.

Already this year, the sol has appreciated 3.82% against the U.S. dollar, ending Wednesday at PEN2.594 per dollar. Scotiabank forecasts the sol will end 2013 at PEN2.49 per dollar.

Other forecasters seeing gains are Capital Economics and UBS. UBS said it expects the Peruvian economy will expand by about 6.0% next year, while inflation is seen slowing toward 2.0%.

"We think the sol has room to strengthen but at a more-moderate pace," UBS said.

One risk to further gains, however, is the prospect of foreign-exchange intervention by the country's central bank to purchase dollars. The Central Reserve Bank of Peruintervenes regularly to purchase U.S. dollars, having bought about $12 billion so far this year as part of its efforts to manage the currency.

Another potential hit to the currency would be if the government allows local private pension funds to invest more abroad.

Unlike other central banks around the world, which have moved aggressively to stem a drop in their home countries' economic prospects, Peru's central bank has avoided changing its reference interest rate since May, 2011. It has even aimed to tighten credit this year by increasing reserve requirements.

"The central bank's main objective seems to be to maintain credibility in the context of ongoing strong intervention in the FX spot market to lean against sol appreciation," J.P. Morgan said in a report, while adding that, "We remain of the view that the central bank will keep the policy rate on hold for the foreseeable future."

title: Peru's Sol Depreciates Following Regulatory Proposals -Nomura
text:
LIMA, Peru--Peru's sol has been giving up strength against the U.S. dollar in recent sessions following changes to regulations made by a government regulator, and that depreciation may continue.

In recent sessions, the sol has appreciated about 1.0% against the greenback, ending Friday at PEN2.599 per dollar, compared to PEN2.590 in the previous session. The sol has appreciated 3.63% against the dollar this year.

Nomura strategist Benito Berber wrote in a report Friday that the sol could "actually depreciate a bit more given the changes in regulation."

He noted that the banking regulator will limit the net short U.S. dollar global position in both spot and nondelivery forwards of local financial intermediaries to 10% from 15% of their liquid assets, forcing the financial institutions to increase their dollar positions.

The regulator will also limit the nondelivery forwards position of financial institutions to 20% from 25% of their liquid asset position or below 300 million soles, ($115 million) whichever is a larger sum, aiming to reduce the exposure of local institutions to foreign flows, Nomura said.

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru has also been intervening to purchase greenbacks in each trading session, whether the sol has been appreciating or depreciating. The goal is to take some of the certainty out of what had become a one-way bet on sol gains.

The central bank has purchased about $11.8 billion this year, driving Peru's net international reserves to a record $62.18 billion as of Oct. 23.

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  up on US data, Peru sol at 16-year high
text:

 * US retail sales come in stronger than expected

 * Peru buys $130 mln in biggest daily move since August

 * Mexican peso firms 0.43 pct, Brazil real up 0.32 pct 

 By Jean Arce and Ursula Scollo

 MEXICO CITY/LIMA, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies firmed on Monday after U.S. retail sales data eased concerns about the outlook of the world's top economy, driving Peru's sol to a nearly 16-year high despite market intervention by the central bank.

 Data showed U.S. retail sales in rose a higher-than-expected 1.1 percent last month, improving economic prospects for the United States, the main destination of Mexican exports.

 "You can start to see the recovery in the United States and that is what is encouraging markets a bit," said Jose Curiel, a currency trader at Intercam brokerage in Mexico City.

 The Mexican peso  gained 0.43 percent to 12.8075 per U.S. dollar while in Brazil, the real   bid 0.32 percent stronger at 2.0340 per greenback at the local close.

 Analysts said the region's currencies could remain stuck in recent trading ranges as the markets await a solution to Europe's debt crisis.

 Investors are watching closely for signs that Spain is ready to formally request financial aid, a step seen as crucial to curb the spread of the euro zone crisis.

 Madrid could finally ask for financial aid from the euro zone next month, officials said. 

 "We have this situation with the United States growing, but slowly. And Europe continues with its problems," said Ures Folchini, a treasury vice president at WestLB bank in Sao Paulo. "It's not an optimistic scenario, it's a scenario where you want to protect your capital and wait."

 A central bank survey of economists showed on Monday that Brazil will likely hold its benchmark interest rate at its current level of 7.25 percent through the end of this year, ending a year-long cycle of rate cuts. 

 Last week, the central bank of Latin America's biggest economy cut its key interest rate to 7.25 percent, an all-time low.

 Monetary stimulus programs in the United States and Europe are expected to keep driving investors toward higher-yielding emerging market assets.

 Brazil, Peru and Colombia have been intervening in currency markets to fight the appreciation of their currencies and protect local manufacturers from cheaper imports.

 Markets in Colombia and Chile were closed for the Columbus Day holiday.

 Peru's sol currency firmed to its strongest in nearly 16 years against the dollar even as the country's central bank bought $130 million - its biggest daily dollar purchase since the end of August.

 "The central bank intervened, as it routinely does in the market, but its (dollar) purchases lack the force to even cause a hiccup in the exchange rate," a trader said.

Peru's central bank has bought a record of nearly $11.6 billion so far this year, but the sol has still advanced more than 4 percent against the dollar.

--Peru's sol has strengthened more than 6% in last 12 months

LIMA, Peru--The ongoing appreciation of the sol is causing concerns for the government by cutting into the revenue of Peru's exporters, a high-level government official said Thursday.

Trade and Tourism Minister Jose Luis Silva said in a meeting with the Foreign Press Association of Peru that the government has to take a broad, multisector view of the sol's gains. He didn't, however, mention any new government measures.

The sol has gained 3.8% so far this year against the greenback, despite intervention by the Central Reserve Bank of Peru to purchase more than $10 billion this year.

"We are concerned that the exchange rate could strengthen more, and that this would continue to affect revenues for exporters," Mr. Silva said.

Peru's sol ended Wednesday at PEN2.595 per U.S. dollar, 6.4% stronger than 12 months earlier.

Economists continue to forecast a strong sol.

"The average exchange rate at the end of year will be PEN2.58 per dollar," said Elmer Cuba, managing partner with consultant Macroconsult, adding that the sol could end 2013 at PEN2.55 per dollar or stronger, depending in good part on monetary-policy decisions in the United States.

Peru's central bank recently outlined a new intervention plan in which it will buy dollars whether the sol is appreciating or depreciating in order to introduce some uncertainty in the foreign-exchange market.

"The currency will continue trading with very little volatility given active intervention by the central bank. We remain neutral on the currency," BofA Merrill Lynch Global Research said in a report.

Peru's economy is heavily dependant on exports, especially of minerals such as gold, copper, zinc and silver.

At the same meeting, Trade Minister Silva said Peru is expected to end this year with a trade surplus, although the trade balance will be weakened by a decline in the prices for minerals, expected to be overcome to some extent by rising export volumes.

"With its high levels of FX reserves (at $59.8 billion, or 18 months of imports), and still comfortable initial current account deficit of only 1.9% and fiscal surplus of 0.9% of GDP as of 2011, Peru has room to withstand some deterioration of its external balance without provoking a sudden adjustment," BofA Merrill Lynch Global Research said.

"Yet the fact that macro policies are conflicting with the pursuit of external balance seems worthy of concern, particularly as policy makers are not conveying awareness of this inconsistency," it added.

Peru Central Bank  Governor:  FX Interventions  Aim at Reducing Volatility
text:
NEW YORK--Routine interventions by the Central Reserve Bank of Peru in its currency market is aimed at reducing volatility in the exchange rate, not a commitment to guiding the Peruvian sol in a specific direction, the central bank's president said Wednesday.

At an annual investment forum in New York, central bank chief Julio Velarde said the bank's efforts, along with Peru's "solid" fiscal position, have helped to stabilize the country's currency.

So far this year, the central bank has purchased more than $10 billion through interventions, actions that effectively rein in the strength of the sol. The latest move came Tuesday, with a $60 million purchase of U.S. dollars at an average rate of PEN2.5962 per dollar.

The greenback has weakened 3.8% against the Peruvian sol since the beginning of the year.

Mr. Velarde explained Wednesday that the central bank has left its policy rate unchanged at 4.25% since May 2011 as he believes the economy is growing in line with its potential. "We've been keeping the same rate because we don't see much change in that scenario," he said, adding that Peru's inflation has been steady around the bank's 3% upper target and is among the lowest within Latin America.

Earlier this month, the central bank increased its forecast for growth in gross domestic product for 2012 to 6% from a previous forecast of 5.8%. The governor said Wednesday he sees growth accelerating to 6.3% in 2014.

Demand from a growing middle class is seen driving this growth, as well as a push in exports beyond Peru's core commodity sector. Mr. Velarde said "non-traditional" exports have nearly tripled in the past decade. Meanwhile, the country's demographics continue to improve.

"Only China can compete with us in the reduction of poverty," Mr. Velarde said, noting that the poverty rate has fallen to 28% last year from 55% in 2001.

Mid-August, Moody's Investors Service upgraded its ratings on Peru to Baa2, citing the South American country's robust economic growth and sound fiscal performance. Mr. Velarde expects the government to post a fiscal surplus of 1.5% this year.

As a byproduct of strong growth, Mr. Velarde said credit has been expanding. Banks are a "main source of financing" in Peru, he said, which is one reason why the central bank has moved to tighten reserve requirements.

It increased the average reserve requirements in domestic and foreign currencies by 0.5 of a percentage point earlier this month. The average requirement for banking sector companies in June was 16% in the local currency, while it was 39.8% for foreign currencies.

"Credit continues growing, maybe even more than what we like," Mr. Velarde said. "But it's also a sign of our dynamics as we're growing in pretty good fashion."

title: As Fed Readies QE3, Foreign Governments Brace for  Currency  Onslaught
text:
--As with QE2, a weaker dollar is predicted for QE3

--Emerging market central banks might retaliate by weakening their currencies, but that could stoke inflation

--The risk is that this descends into an-out race to the bottom with tit-for-tat currency depreciations

The Federal Reserve's plan to embark on an open-ended round of asset purchases to bolster the U.S. economy has put financial authorities in other countries on high alert.

Looking back to the last time the Fed printed dollars to finance bond buying, which sent the U.S. currency on a year-long decline against most of its counterparts, officials are bracing for an unwanted flood of speculative money into their markets and a possible cycle of tit-for-tat retaliatory measures. The biggest fear is that it triggers a self-reinforcing and self-destructive race to the bottom in which monetary policy and direct interventions are used to prevent other countries from gaining a competitive advantage through weaker exchange rates.

The Bank of Japan provided fodder for such concerns Wednesday. Just six days after the Fed said it would purchase an additional $40 billion in mortgage bonds a month for an indefinite period, Japan's central bank announced it would add another 10 trillion yen ($127 billion) to its asset-buying program and extend it out to the end of 2013. Although the BOJ didn't explicitly cite the yen's strength as a motivating factor, Japan's currency immediately fell to a one-month low versus the dollar. Last Friday, following the Fed's announcement a day earlier, Finance Minister Jun Azumi forcefully complained that the strong yen was hurting the Japanese economy and hinted at direct intervention by vowing to "take decisive steps when it is deemed necessary."

Some emerging market governments have also taken matters into their own hands this past week. Brazil has conducted so-called "reverse dollar swaps" to prevent its currency, the real, from appreciating; Peru adjusted its intervention strategy toward weakening the Peruvian sol; and Turkey cut interest rates by more than expected.

Others have been notably more muted in their response. Officials in South Korea, Thailand, Singapore and the Philippines took a cautiously sanguine view of the uptick in their currencies, though they all asserted a readiness to smooth out market movement if capital inflows become excessive.

The moves from the Fed and BOJ come after the European Central Bank announced its own plan to buy bonds, in its case those of struggling governments in the periphery of the euro zone, in a bid to contain the region's debt crisis. Unlike the Fed and BOJ's actions, which will result in a net addition of fresh currency into global financial markets and are widely described as "quantitative easing," or QE, the ECB will "sterilize" its transactions by selling certificates that mop up the additional euros. Nonetheless, the moves are seen boosting the willingness of investors to take on risky investments generally, which typically results in large-scale transfers of funds out of dollars and into other currencies.

"All of this cash generated by the Federal Reserve is going to be entering foreign shores," said Komal Sri-Kumar, chief global strategist at TCW. "Emerging markets are going to be tempted to cut interest rates...to offset their currencies appreciating too much."

Emerging market currencies are in the crosshairs of speculators during such times because their interest rates tend to be higher than those in the U.S., European countries and Japan, allowing investors to book a profit on the difference between the two. But such countries often depend heavily on exports, which become more expensive when exchange rates rise. The dilemma for their central banks at times when global liquidity is rising is that they also face inflationary pressures from rising commodity prices and inflows into their real estate and other markets. If they were to combat those rising prices with higher rates, it would only further increase the appeal of their currencies.

In the previous round of Fed quantitative easing, which was dubbed "QE2," the dollar weakened significantly. In the 13 months from June 2010, when expectations of more Fed stimulus first began to rise, until the $600 billion bond-buying program wound up the following summer, the Wall Street Journal Dollar Index, a measure of the dollar's value against a basket of major currencies, lost 18% of its value. It dropped 20% against the Brazilian real over the same period and 18% versus the Korean won.

The dollar followed a similar, but slower path leading up to the QE3 announcement last week. The WSJ Dollar Index hit a 22-month high in July and then started to slide gradually before dropping sharply once Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke signaled the central bank's plans at his speech in Jackson Hole, Wyo, on Aug. 31. The index is now nearly 6% off its July high.

The fallout during QE2 in 2010 and 2011 prompted an especially bellicose response from a few foreign officials, with Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega famously declaring that the world had entered a "currency war," an allusion to the highly damaging competitive-depreciation policies that undermined world trade during the Great Depression. This time around, Mr. Mantega has been less bellicose, though he remains critical of Fed policy. Speaking in Paris on Tuesday, he said, "I don't believe that the new monetary easing will resolve many problems for the U.S., but it could cause several problems for emerging market countries."

The Fed declined to comment Wednesday. In the past, Fed officials have defended their actions by saying that efforts to strengthen the U.S. recovery help the global economy. Mr. Bernanke said in 2010 that different monetary policies may be appropriate for different groups of countries, drawing a distinction between advanced economies and countries with emerging markets that may see more inflation pressure. But he also noted that disparities between exchange rate policies had led to global spending imbalances as "those countries that have allowed their exchange rates to be determined primarily by market forces have seen their competitiveness erode relative to countries that have intervened more aggressively."

In general, the latest response from other emerging market governments has been muted. That may be because those countries' currencies are already well down from their 2011 highs, a function in part of the interventionist actions many undertook in the wake of QE2, with Brazil in particular resorting both to dollar purchases and taxes on short-term foreign investment.

Yet this hands-off response could merely embolden foreign investors. Paresh Upadhyaya, director of currencies at Pioneer Investments with $200 billion under management, said his firm has increased bets on the Korean won, Indian rupee, and Turkish lira over the past week, on expectations they'll benefit from monetary easing in the U.S, Japan, U.K. and euro zone. He says he doesn't expect as much of a backlash from emerging markets as there was during QE2.

The stakes may even be higher this time around. A much slower global growth environment and weakening international trade will make export-driven emerging market countries more protective of market share. And unlike the time limits that were placed on previous such programs, the Fed's new QE plan is open-ended, allowing the central bank to effectively print money until the employment picture in the U.S. meaningfully improves.

Meanwhile, other major central banks beyond the Fed, ECB and BOJ have programs in place that tend to steer money away from their currencies. The Swiss National Bank has been regularly entering the market to buy euros and sell francs since September 2011, setting a floor on the pair. And the Bank of England has conducted Fed-style "unsterilized" bond-buying that pumps extra pounds into financial markets.

Faced with such barriers, investors will tend to go for higher-yielding currencies that are allowed to float more freely.

"Within the EM universe there clearly are going to be relative value trades," said Jonathon Griggs, global chief investment officer of the currency group at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. In choosing currencies from "laissez-faire" countries over those that are more interventionist, Mr. Griggs said one interesting trade is the Mexican peso against the Korean won. Other investors cite the Polish zloty, Norwegian krone and Canadian dollar.

The problem for policy makers in such countries, however, is that with so many other currencies off limits, theirs could end up bearing an even bigger burden from exchange rate appreciation.

And if China, the world's biggest goods exporter, gets into the currency devaluation game--either through direct moves to weaken the yuan or through a more aggressive round of monetary easing--the temptation for other countries to retaliate with their own actions could become even more intense.

"Three of the four major central banks have now acted and the last shoe to drop will be China," said James Rickards, partner at JAC Capital and author of the 2011 book "Currency Wars: The Making of the Next Global Crisis."

--Matthew Walter and Kristina Peterson contributed to this article.
