title: Peru 's  Central Bank  Changes  Intervention  Approach to Buying Dollars
text:
--Central bank changes approach to foreign-exchange interventions

--Aims to increase uncertainty in exchange market

--Central bank may purchase dollars even if sol is weakening


 
   By Robert Kozak 
 

LIMA, Peru---The Central Reserve Bank of Peru has changed its approach to intervening to buy U.S. dollars, aiming to make it less of a one-way bet.

The central bank may now buy a fixed amount of dollars regardless of whether the dollar is depreciating against the sol, a central bank spokesman said.

The central back has purchased about $10 billion so far this year, mainly by buying varying amounts in each trading session depending on the appreciation pressures on the sol, aiming to reduce volatility.

On Monday, for example, the central bank purchased $40 million, and the sol closed slightly weaker at PEN2.603 to the dollar compared with PEN2.595 on Friday.

Despite the interventions that have helped drive up Peru's net international reserves to a record $60 billion so far this year, the sol has appreciated by 3.5% against the dollar.

Peru's bustling economy--gross domestic product expanded by 7.2% in July--and strong debt ratings, among other factors, have helped boost inflows of capital.

The central bank's aim now is in part to add some uncertainty for those taking out dollar-denominated loans for things like cars or houses, trying to ensure that there is no excessive debt burden in dollars that could hurt borrowers who earn in soles, should the dollar appreciate sharply against the sol.

"I think it is an error for those who earn in soles to be taking out loans in dollars," Central Reserve Bank of Peru President Julio Velarde said at a news conference late last week.

"Before, the sentiment that some [market participants] had is that when it [the sol] starts to depreciate, we stopped buying," he said, adding that, "If we are buying the same amount it will lead to some volatility. We are going to see how it works."

Both the U.S. dollar and the Peruvian sol are legal tender in Peru and are widely used. Most real-estate purchases are made in dollars.

Mr. Velarde added that the office of the Superintendent of Banking, Insurance and AFPs is seeking to turn around the trend of having more and more loans being made in dollars in Peru.

"They are trying to establish some additional provisions and to increase risks in mortgage loans in dollars, and will do the same with vehicle loans afterwards. It is a process," Mr. Velarde said.

Vehicle loans rose 22% in July over the same month last year, with 73% denominated in dollars, a 9-percentage-point increase in dollar-denominated loans over the same month a year earlier.

-Ryan Dube contributed to this article.

title: Rising sol: Peru's  currency  at year-high after shaking off protest impact
text:
LIMA, May 11 (Reuters) - In a country shaken by years of political volatility, Peru's national currency has emerged as a mainstay of relative stability among Latin American foreign exchange markets, reaching its strongest level in a year this week.

After taking a hit during the nearly two-year presidency of Pedro Castillo, the Peruvian sol is bouncing back just months after his removal and subsequent protests that briefly stifled the economy of the world's second largest copper producer.

For the third straight day Thursday, the sol had its best showing since May 2022, trading at 3.665 soles per dollar, data from the central bank and traders showed.

Latin America's main currencies have strengthened sharply in recent months, like Mexico's peso, which hit a five-year high this week.

Peru's currency, however, has not deviated much in value since 2000 and it is up some 3% so far in 2023 from its closing price at the end of December.

"Since the beginning of the century, we have depreciated something like 6% (...) while other currencies have depreciated by 50%, 100% or 150%," the head of Peru's central bank Julio Velarde said Wednesday at an event launching a commemorative coin.

In this context, "the sol is one of the most stable currencies in the region among large and medium-sized countries," Velarde said.

Of Peru's ten presidents this century, most have respected free market policies with rigid fiscal discipline. This allowed the economy to enjoy record growth rates for years, accumulate large net reserves and have a currency market that moves freely with supply and demand.

In this context, Peru's central bank has only intervened in the market by buying or selling dollars or financial instruments to mitigate the sol's volatility.

"What has been shown in 20 or 30 years is that the sol is a currency that guarantees value recovery, which is why Peru has more or less 40% of its debt in soles," Economy Minister Alex Contreras said at a recent event.

(Reporting by Marco Aquino; Additional reporting by Hernan Nessi in Buenos Aires Editing by Alistair Bell)

title: What does the one dollar bill that can be worth US$ 150,000 look like to collectors?
text:
Do you have a dollar stashed among your things? Find out what are the characteristics of these bills for which they can be worth up to US$ 150,000 today.

What are the rivets on the corners of jeans pockets used for?Why was the singer Marco Antonio Guerrero fired from Grupo 5 in the middle of a concert?Numismatics is a passion that has united thousands of people, so it is not surprising that collectors are willing to pay exorbitant sums of money for a banknote that has defects or anomalies, since some have a great monetary value due to certain curious characteristics.

An example of this is the 2014 one dollar bill, which for having a simple printing error, can currently be worth up to US$ 150,000. Find out, below, how this flaw was generated and how you can identify it.

Since 1876, the U.S. dollar bill has been the smallest denomination of U.S. paper money.

One-dollar bills worth up to US$ 150,000 In 2014, the U.S. Federal Reserve, the government agency in charge of printing U.S. dollars, mistakenly issued two equal runs of 6.4 million one-dollar bills

. That same year, the first batch of dollars with error was distributed in the state of New York and, curiously, two years later another group exactly the same arrived in Washington.

This mistake caused 6.4 million "even bills" of one dollar with the same serial number to be distributed around the world, although only 9 of these pairs have been found so far. Due to their rarity and the difficulty of finding them, some collectors offer up to US$ 150,000 for them.

How to identify these dollar bills? To know if your dollar bill is worth thousands of dollars, you should check its serial number, which should be between B00000001 and B00250000 or B03200001 and B09600000.

In addition to this feature you should make sure that the bill has a Federal Reserve stamp with the letter "B" on it. Also, the serial number should end with a star.

This bill can be worth thousands of dollars. Photo: El Universo

What are the one dollar bills sold for US$ 200 like? The United States Federal Reserve issued in 1969 a series of one dollar bills, which have an error in the "Gutter note", reason why there are many collectors willing to pay a fortune for them.

Dollar of 1969. Photo: eBay

A copy of these bills sells for US$ 200 (approximately S/. 783) on eBay. However, it is worth clarifying that to know how much money would be paid for these it is necessary to consult an interested buyer, although they are sold at that price on the aforementioned website.

Ladder dollar bills Ladder dollar bills are the rarest in history. This is formed in the serial number of the bill and bears the numbers one through eight in ascending or descending order (12345678 or 87654321). Because it is very difficult to find its value in the collector's market is around US$ 5,000.

Variations of the ladder pattern include numbers in order that do not start with one, such as 00123456 or 034567. These may also be in reverse order; however, both variations are more common on one dollar bills and less valuable than the authentic ones.

Ladder dollar bills are worth up to $5,000 in the collectors' market. Photo: TyC Sports

What are the dollar denominations that exist? The U.S. Federal Reserve Board currently issues seven denominations of dollar bills. These are:

US$ 1 billUS$ 2 billUS$ 5 billUS$ 10 billUS$ 20 billUS$ 50 billUS$ 100 bill. The US Federal Reserve Board currently issues seven denominations of dollar bills. Photo: AFP

How many 1 dollar bills worth up to US$ 150,000 have been sold today? So far, only nine pairs of one-dollar bills have been found that were duplicated by errors, which means that there are millions of them circulating in the United States and around the world. To confirm that you have a bill of this denomination and that it belongs to the group of the most sought after by buyers, you should consult a specialist.

When did the first dollar bill appear? The history of U.S. banknotes is one of the main aspects that determine the value of dollars. Therefore, it is necessary to have a certain amount of knowledge on the subject. For example, the first one dollar bill was printed on May 10, 1775, during the colonial period. This happened during the American Revolutionary War, so there were many obstacles in the process of printing the bill.

This is how the first 1 dollar bill was printed. Photo: capture Old money prices

How to know if a dollar is real or fake? Just as a dollar can cost an exorbitant amount of money, there is also the possibility that it is a fake. Below, we share some tips to identify if a dollar is a fake:

Dollars have high image quality, so you should check if yours has a clear design.The numbers on dollars are sharper, so you will be able to tell if it is a fake or not by the resolution of the digits.Real dollars have amber tones in their presentation, while counterfeit dollars have light colors.Counterfeit dollars have a tendency to be rougher.If you hold a real dollar up against the light, you will notice the watermark with Benjamin Franklin's image. On the other hand, on counterfeit dollars, the watermark can be seen with the naked eye and has an almost yellowish hue.The edges of the real dollars are sharp, while the fake ones are usually blurred. Who was George Washington, the character that appears on the dollar bill? Since 1869, George Washington, who is considered the Father of the Nation and was also the first president of the United States, has appeared on the lowest denomination bill.

George Washington achieved the independence of the United States and was the only one of the founding fathers who wrote a clause to free his slaves in his will. Photo: Difusión

Who are the characters appearing on the dollar bills? The characters appearing on the different denominations of dollar bills are:

US$ 1 bill: George WashingtonUS$ 2 bill: Thomas JeffersonUS$ 5 bill: Abraham Lincoln10 US$ bill: Alexander Hamilton20 US Dollar Bill: Andrew Jackson50 US Dollar Bill: Ulysses S. GrantUS$ 100 bill: Benjamin Franklin. What is the mystery of the two-dollar bill? The US$ 2 bill features the image of Thomas Jefferson, as well as a vignette depicting the signing of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Its mystery lies in the fact that due to its lack of use, this bill was discontinued in 1966 until it was reprinted in 1976 for the bicentennial of the American Revolution.

What is the mystery behind the two-dollar bill? Photo: El heraldo de México

How to know if a US$ 2 bill is real? The paper of the two-dollar bill will allow a person to know if it is real or fake. When handling the bill, it should have a crisp sound, as it is made of one quarter of linen and three quarters of cotton.

Why do we use the dollar as an international currency? In recent years, according to Diego Marrero on the AFP Habitat website, 61% of the world's central bank reserves are in US dollars. The U.S. currency is used for 60% of world trade.

The U.S. dollar is one of the world's main currencies, along with the euro, the pound, the yen and the renminbi, and is included in the International Monetary Fund's basket of Special Drawing Rights currencies. How did its importance come about?

It all goes back to the end of World War II, when the United States became the major hegemonic superpower. Before the end of the war, the Bretton Woods agreement (the United Nations monetary and financial settlement in 1944) established an international monetary system where the dollar became the main reference currency for trade around the world.

The last 500 dollar bill with the image of President McKinley was printed in 1945. Photo: Public domain / Investopedia

What is the dollar made of? Interestingly, a dollar bill is not made of paper. The formula to make them stronger involves a composition of cotton and linen.

Why is it called a dollar? In the 16th century, coins were minted in St. Joachimsthal, a town in Bohemia, as the place was considered to have the purest silver in the world. Thus, the coins were christened Joachmisthaler, from which the popular name Thaler was derived.

Gradually, some regions of Europe began to call the coins Daler. In addition, this was the name Spain used as the official currency in the American colonies. Until, finally, with the independence of the United States, came the issuance of coins and bills in 1985, so Congress decided to call these as dollar and dollars.

What does it mean to be given a dollar? As a sort of tradition, carrying a dollar in your wallet or purse is a sign of good fortune and wealth, so it is usual to give or receive a specific dollar bill as a gift.

Where can I buy cheap dollars in Peru? Although the exchange rate of dollars to soles is constantly changing, the truth is that more and more people are in the need to acquire these bills, either for purchases abroad, etc.. The following is a list of places where you can buy dollars in Peru:

BanksExchange housesShopping mallsAirportsStreet money changers. What does US$ mean in money? Abbreviations such as US$ or USD mean that it refers to the US dollar, therefore, it is the legal currency of

the United States. How much is US$ 1 in S/ 1? The exchange rate from dollar to soles varies daily; however, today, the value of $1 converted S/ 1 appears within the values of S/ 3,890 the purchase and S/ 3,930 the sale in the parallel market, according to the website cuantoestaeldolar.pe

. Where is it advisable to change dollars in Lima? In Lima there are many places where you can exchange dollars. For this reason we leave you some options so that the currency exchange is favorable and safe for you.

The airport or terminalThe hotel where you are stayingFinancial institutionsExchange housesMoney changers on the street. What is the blue dollar and the official dollar? The blue dollar is the bill that is bought outside the formal circuit, mainly known as parallel dollar or informal dollar. It receives this name in Argentina and other regions. On the other hand, the official dollar is the one issued by banking entities.

The dollar has become the main reference currency for prices in Argentina. Photo: composition by Gerson Cardoso / La República / BCRA

Why is the price of the dollar important? The dollar is important because its market value has a direct impact on the global economy and politics, as well as on the fundamental decisions of governments, investors and businessmen, so it is also part of the public interest.

The dollar is part of the daily life of the most global cities. Photo: AFP

How many years does a dollar last? Approximately, a dollar bill lasts between 6 to 7 years. These are the years of life of each bill today, according to the U.S. Currency Education Program (CEP) website:

US$ 1 bill: 6 to 7 years.US$ 5 bill: 4 yearsUS$ 10 bill: 5 yearsUS$ 20 bill: 7 yearsUS$ 50 bill: 12 yearsUS$ 100 bill: 22 years. Other dollar bills that were issued Although the best known are the US$ 1, US$ 50 and US$ 100 bills, the truth is that in the past 3, 5, 10, 25 and 50 cent bills were also issued under the context of the American Civil War or Civil War in the 1860s, according to a report by the Midpoint website.

What is the phrase of the dollar? Since 1956, all dollar bills have the phrase "In God we trust", translated into English as "We trust in God". This is because President Dwight D. Eisenhower enacted a bill in which U.S. coins would be inscribed with the phrase, so Congress ordered it to be added to the bills as well.

The dollars are inscribed with the phrase 'In God we trust'. Photo: Pixabay

What is the Canadian dollar? The Canadian dollar is the official currency used in Canada. It was introduced in July 1858 and is symbolized by C$ or CAD

. U.S. dollar or Canadian dollar? Although both currencies have the denomination "dollar", in terms of exchange rate, it is the U.S. dollar that has a higher monetary value. This is because it is considered a strong currency, for economic and financial reasons.

How much is a Canadian dollar worth? At the exchange rate, the Canadian dollar is worth between 3.04 soles and 3.30 soles.

The Canadian dollar is the official currency of Canada. Photo: Hormigatv

Which other countries use the U.S. dollar as their official currency? The United States is not the only country that uses the US dollar as its official currency. Here are the other nations that use U.S. coins and banknotes.

EcuadorEl SalvadorMarshall IslandsZimbabweTimor LesteMicronesiaPalau. What is the largest dollar bill? Between 1934 and 1935, during the Great Depression, the U.S. Treasurer printed 42,000 of the US$100,000 bills. This was the largest denomination piece of paper money ever produced by the U.S.

Finding such a specimen is really difficult so counterfeits are relatively common. However, a handful of real US$100,000 bills, including an uncut sheet of 12 sample bills, are on display at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.

The US$100,000 bill is the highest denomination produced in the United States. Photo: Cambio Dólar

Who appears on the US$100,000 dollar? The bill is printed with the image of Woodrow Wilson, the 28th president of the United States, who took office from 1913 to 1921. It should be noted that this bill was only used for internal transactions between the Federal Reserve Banks.

100 dollar bill. Photo: Freepik.

The dollar bill that sells for US$ 95,000 dollars In 1977, the United States Federal Reserve issued a series of one-dollar bills, which although not in circulation, have a high value in the collectors' market: US$ 95,000. The reason for their high price is that these specimens have a misalignment error and are considered "rare".

In 1977, the U.S. Federal Reserve issued a series of 1 dollar bills worth up to US$ 95,000 in the collectors' market. Photo: TyCsports

How does the increase in the price of the dollar affect? The increase in the price of the dollar generates an increase in the cost of credit, not only in the United States, but also worldwide. In other words, borrowing money has become more expensive for countries, companies and individuals. As a result, activity becomes slower and recovery becomes more difficult.

Thousands of Peruvians exchange dollars for soles in the streets of Peru. Photo: EFE

Who determines the price of the dollar? In the first place, the price of the dollar is determined by the free market. This means two things: when there is a shortage of dollars, the exchange rate goes up; on the contrary, in times of abundance of dollars, it goes down. Secondly, the Central Reserve Bank (BCR), the entity in charge of exchange rate policy in Peru, intervenes to avoid abrupt fluctuations in the price of the dollar.

Learn how the price of the dollar is determined. Photo: AFP

What is the most expensive currency in the world? The most expensive currency in the world is the Kuwaiti dinar (KWD). Kuwait has the sixth largest oil reserves in the world, making it one of the richest Arab countries on the Asian continent. In theToday, its currency is the most expensive and most highly valued. One Kuwaiti dinar is equivalent to US$ 3.30.

The Kuwaiti dinar is the highest valued currency in the world. Photo: ANFRIX

What is the cheapest currency in the world? The most devalued currency is the Venezuelan Sovereign Bolivar (VES), which, after the crisis suffered in Venezuela, was devalued to the point of exchanging 1 dollar for 1,552,540 VES.

The Venezuelan Sovereign Bolivar is the currency with the lowest value worldwide. Photo: Cambio16

How many intis were equivalent to one dollar? The number of zeros was a main feature of the Peruvian currency in 1990. Thus, one dollar was worth 300,000 intis.

The inti is no longer in circulation in Peru. Photo: Banco de la Nación/Facebook

For how long did the Intis circulate? In May 1985 the first coins expressed in intis were put into circulation, while the first banknotes were put into circulation in December of the same year. The inti was valid as a monetary unit until June 30, 1991 (6 years).

The 1,000,000 Intis banknote was 140 x 65 millimeters in size and its colors were purple-pink. The obverse side showed Hipólito Unanue and the reverse side the San Fernando School of Medicine. Photo: La República/BCRP composition

Why are there 1 sol coins painted red? The phenomenon of red painted coins follows a common line: it is only those that have the design prior to the one incorporated in 2012 (the one that does not have the denomination in number).

When in doubt, Abraham de la Melena Ruiz, specialist in Analysis of the Circulating Currency of the Central Reserve Bank of Peru (BCRP), explained where these red spots came from.

The 1 sol coins painted red are not a coincidence. Photo: Archivo La República

According to what the specialist explained to La República in 2020, some gambling establishments did not use tokens for their slot machines, and opted instead to use one nuevo sol coins as tokens. The establishments painted these red for customers to redeem before leaving. This was a way to avoid running out of money.

Why are the S/ 1 coins from 2010 to 2016 worth more than 300 soles? According to the Peruvian tiktoker @numismaticainca, the coins that are part of the numismatic series Wealth and Pride of Peru, such as the case of Machu Picchu, have a high value due to the way they are presented and the small amount minted. The specialist also mentions that, since they are so sought after by collectors, the blister presentation of these coins can reach up to S/. 30 each.

title: Peruvian sol closes 2022 as one of the strongest  currencies  in the region, why is this?
text:
On the eve of entering a new year, it is important to highlight the performance of the Peruvian sol during 2022. In a scenario of high volatility for the economy due to international shocks and the country's internal collateral effects, our currency has consolidated itself as one of the strongest and most stable in Latin America.

According to the Central Reserve Bank of Peru (BCR), the US dollar closed this year 2022 slightly down at S/ 3.8070, registering a depreciation of 4.61% compared to the close of 2021 when it was quoted at S/ 3.991.

In view of this result, the local currency has positioned itself in a favorable position compared to the Chilean or Colombian peso. According to Bloomberg's ranking on the performance of the main Latin American currencies against the dollar, the Peruvian sol occupies a solid fourth position, surpassed only by the Uruguayan peso, the Brazilian real and the Mexican peso.

According to analysts, the Peruvian sol remains one of the most attractive currencies in the region due to the solid political and fiscal position of the country's economy, despite still high interest rates. It is also driven by its strong ties with its main trading partners, the United States and China.

Volatile exchange rate

Despite market volatility, Omar Azañedo, an economist at the Universidad del Pacífico, told Infobae that the Peruvian sol remains one of the strongest in the region against the dollar, having appreciated between 4% and 5% during 2022.

You may be interested in: Dollar in Peru: Its price closes lower at S/ 3.80 on New Year's Eve

"The greenback during this year has registered high volatility, but this has not only happened in Peru but also in the whole world. However, the Central Reserve Bank of Peru (BCR) has done an outstanding job in its monetary policy to prevent the dollar from continuing to rise," the expert pointed out.

Thus, the exchange rate in Peru reached a maximum level of S/ 4.00 at the end of October and a minimum of S/ 3.63 at the beginning of April 2022. However, analysts for 2023 expect a high dollar fluctuating between S/ 3.85 to S/ 3.95 due to the international scenario.

"The BCR has had a fairly good management of the monetary policy, but it is not enough, since in these times of global crisis is where more growth, investment, welfare and confidence should be generated, which is lacking in the country", emphasized Azañedo.

For his part, Diego Macera, general manager of the Peruvian Institute of Economics (IPE), stated that the good performance of the exchange rate in the country is due to the fact that it has a strong inertial component that provides certain expectations to the market. "We have the most stable exchange rate in the region in the last 20 years," he added.

BCR Intervention

Meanwhile, the president of the Central Reserve Bank (BCR), Julio Velarde, pointed out that, so far, in a context of social protests and political uncertainty, no major effect on the country's exchange market has been noticed.

"What has affected little is the exchange rate, and I think the perception has been that this is going to end, that is, it is a temporary thing, and in which case there would be no reason to be betting heavily against the sun. So far, no major effect has been noticed", explained the official during the presentation of the latest Inflation Report.

You may be interested in: Dollar in Peru: How the political crisis impacts the exchange rate

During 2022, Julio Velarde indicated that the BCR has made a net sale of USD 1,234 million in the exchange market. "The Central Bank has had a quite small intervention this year, the exchange pressures have not occurred. In fact, the sol has been appreciating, without major intervention by the BCR", he said.

The president of the BCR referred that some currencies in the region appreciated during 2022, in a context of rising interest rates, considering, in addition, that the dollar reached its highest value in 20 years.

"The few currencies in the world that are appreciating, which can be counted on the fingers of one hand, are those of Peru, Mexico, Brazil and Russia. These currencies have been strengthened this year, in a scenario where the dollar has been strong globally," Velarde noted.

Outlook for 2023

The Peruvian currency will show some weakness in 2023, in an environment of greater global risk perception and a decrease in the interest rate differential between soles and dollars, which will reduce the appetite for emerging economies' assets.

In this sense, BBVA Research projects that the exchange rate will end between S/ 4.00 and S/ 4.10 per dollar in 2023. "For the following months, we anticipate that the exchange rate dynamics will be more linked to external factors (monetary adjustment of the FED and lower appetite for risk will induce capital outflows from emerging economies)," the bank indicated.

You may be interested in: Dollar in Peru: How much could the exchange rate be worth for the New Year?

Meanwhile, Credicorp Capital anticipates that the exchange rate in 2023 would remain relatively stable, to end at S/ 3.85. However, Scotiabank estimates that the dollar could reach a higher value between S/ 3.85 to S/ 3.95.

"The country's exchange rate is well supported by the level of trade surplus, which is between USD 11 billion to USD 12 billion so far this year, as well as its high level of international reserves," said Mario Guerrero, assistant manager of Economics at Scotiabank's Economic Research Department.

Likewise, the expert affirmed that, in the context of a stronger dollar, the effects of the war between Russia and Ukraine, among other factors, could boost a higher U.S. currency that could reach a higher value at the beginning of 2023.

You may be interested in: What to expect for the Peruvian economy next year?

"When the dollar price approaches S/4 there is discomfort from the BCR because it increases the intervention pattern. Peru is working with a lateral pattern in the face of the international scenario", said the analyst.

Dollar still high in Peru

On the other hand, Azañedo pointed out that an average exchange rate of S/ 3.90 is high and a crisis scenario, since as we remember before the pandemic the dollar was quoted at S/ 3.30 or S/ 3.20.

title: What does the one dollar bill that can be worth US$ 150,000 look like to collectors?

One of these bills sells for US$ 200 (approximately S/. 783) on eBay. However, it is worth clarifying that in order to know how much money would be paid for them, it is necessary to consult an interested buyer, although they are sold at that price on the aforementioned website.

How much is a Canadian dollar worth?At the exchange rate, the Canadian dollar is worth between 3.04 soles and 3.30 soles.

What other countries use the U.S. dollar as their official currency?The United States is not the only country that uses the U.S. dollar as its official currency. Here are the other nations that use U.S. coins and bills.

EcuadorEl SalvadorMarshall IslandsZimbabweEast TimorMicronesiaPalau.What is the largest dollar bill?Between 1934 and 1935, during the Great Depression, the U.S. Treasurer printed 42,000 of the US$100,000 bills. This was the largest denomination piece of paper money ever produced by the US.

Finding such a specimen is really difficult so counterfeits are relatively common. However, a handful of real US$100,000 bills, including an uncut sheet of 12 sample bills, are on display at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.

Who is on the $100,000 dollar?The bill is imprinted with the image of Woodrow Wilson, the 28th president of the United States, who took office from 1913 to 1921. It should be noted that this bill was only used for internal transactions between the Federal Reserve Banks.

The reason for their high price is due to the fact that these issues have a misalignment error and are considered "rare".

In other words, borrowing money has become more expensive for countries, companies and individuals. As a result, activity slows down and recovery becomes more difficult.

This means two things: when there is a shortage of dollars, the exchange rate goes up; conversely, in times of dollar abundance, it goes down. Secondly, the Central Reserve Bank (BCR), the entity in charge of exchange rate policy in Peru, intervenes to avoid abrupt fluctuations in the price of the dollar.

Kuwait has the sixth largest oil reserves in the world, making it one of the richest Arab countries on the Asian continent. Currently its currency is the most expensive and valued currency. One Kuwaiti dinar is equivalent to US$ 3.30.

title: Price of the dollar in Peru LIVE: The exchange rate falls again and closes at S/3.97 this Thursday
text:
Credicorp Capital: dollar rise responds to higher interest rates in the world

The price of the dollar has been rising in the world as a safe haven currency in the face of global uncertainty and the rise in interest rates in the United States has caused this trend to be further enhanced, said the general manager of Credicorp Capital SAF, Rocio Coloma.

"The dollar has several components. This currency in the world has been rising as a safe haven currency and the high interest rates have caused the dollar to strengthen even more", commented the specialist.

In addition to this, in the local scenario, political instability also has an impact on the search for the U.S. currency, she said. In this sense, the price of the dollar in the country would close the year above four soles, projected the Credicorp Capital SAF executive.

This is how the U.S. currency has been performing this year

So far in 2022, as of October 24, the foreign currency appreciated 0.28%, taking into account that the price of the dollar closed last Monday at S/ 4.002, after having ended 2021 at S/ 3.991.

So far this year, as of October 21, the Central Reserve Bank (BCR) intervened directly in the market selling US$ 1,226 million, according to figures from the monetary authority.

It is worth mentioning that the price of the dollar dropped 0.18% at the end of the third quarter of this year, since it ended September 30 at 3.984 soles, according to BCR data.

The quotation of the US currency advanced 3.35% in September 2022 with respect to the previous month, after having ended last August 31 at 3.855 soles.

Analysts at FocusEconomics Consensus Forecast LatinFocus, in their October 2022 report, forecast that the dollar would be at 3.95 soles at the end of the year.

Price of the dollar in Peru fell again and closed at S/ 3.97 on Thursday.

On Thursday, October 27, the price of the U.S. dollar closed down again at S/ 3.9760, registering a 0.33% drop compared to Wednesday's closing price of S/ 3.9890, according to the Central Reserve Bank of Peru (BCRP).

So far in 2022, the U.S. currency accumulates a 0.38% retreat compared to the last quote of 2021, at S/ 3.991.

In the morning, the exchange rate in the parallel market was quoted at S/ 3.965 for buying and S/ 3.990 for selling. Meanwhile, at the main banks' windows it reached S/ 4.0060.

According to Bloomberg's ranking of the main Latin American currencies, during this year, the Peruvian currency against the dollar, despite having registered two consecutive days exceeding the barrier of S/ 4.00, still continues to appreciate by 0.3%, surpassed by the Mexican peso with 2.9%, the Brazilian real with 3.6%, the Uruguayan peso with 9.2%. While the Chilean peso recorded a depreciation of -10.4% and the Colombian peso -16.5%.

What to do in the face of the strengthening of the dollar?

According to Washington Lopez, CEO of Washington Capital, the strengthening of the dollar occurs due to external and macroeconomic factors, such as the contractionary monetary policy of the Federal Reserve in the United States, which seeks to counteract the blows of inflation not seen in the last 40 years.

As a result, currencies such as the euro, the pound sterling and the yen have also recorded historic lows. And this strengthening of the dollar affects Latin American currencies, which is why, this year alone, in May it was recorded at S/3.60, and now in October it reached S/4.00, with a perspective of being above this level in the coming months.

"It is important to warn, from now on, that the situation may worsen, our estimate is that the dollar will exceed the barrier of S/ 4.15 or even S/ 4.30, that is why, Peruvians are still in time to dollarize their surpluses or capital so as not to be affected by this depreciation of the exchange rate," said Lopez.

He added that this should be a medium-term view, for people who seek to dollarize their surpluses and not change them to soles in a long time because, if they return to the local currency in a year, they would be making a loss in case they need to make use of these soles.

Today's BCR intervention

At 11:05 a.m.: A S/ 200 million 3-month swap for sale (fixed rate) was placed, at an average rate of 3.71 percent.

At 10:20 am: The following auction was called: Swap Exchange Sale (fixed rate) for 3 months for S/ 200 million.

At 09:50 a.m.: S/ 300 million 3-month Swap Exchange Sale (fixed rate) at an average rate of 3.75 percent was placed.

At 09:20 am: The Central Reserve Bank (BCR) called for the following auction: Swap Exchange Sale (fixed rate) for 3 months for S/ 300 million.

The dollar opened slightly lower at the beginning of the session on Thursday, October 27th.

The price of the US dollar in Peru opened this Thursday, October 27 with a slight decline, after Standard & Poor's (S&P) ratified the country's credit rating and maintained it in stable outlook.

title: What does the one dollar bill worth up to $150,000 look like to collectors?
text:
Numismatics is a passion that has united thousands of people, so it is not surprising that collectors are willing to pay exorbitant sums of money for a banknote that has defects or anomalies, since some have a great monetary value due to certain curious characteristics.

An example of this is the 2004 one-dollar bill, which, due to a simple printing error, can be worth up to $150,000 today. Find out, below, how this flaw was generated and how you can identify it.

One-dollar bills worth up to $150,000In 2014, the U.S. Federal Reserve, the government agency in charge of printing U.S. dollars, mistakenly issued two equal runs of 6.4 million one-dollar bills.

That same year, the first batch of dollars with error was distributed in the state of New York and, curiously, two years later another group exactly the same arrived in Washington.

This mistake caused 6.4 million "even bills" of 1 dollar with the same serial number to be distributed around the world, although only 9 of these pairs have been found so far. Due to their rarity and the difficulty in finding them, some collectors are offering up to $150,000 for them.

How to identify these dollar bills?To know if your dollar bill is worth thousands of dollars, you should check its serial number, which should be between B00000001 and B00250000 or B03200001 and B09600000.

In addition to this feature you should make sure that the bill has a Federal Reserve stamp with the letter "B" on it. Also, the serial number should end with a star.

What do one dollar bills sold for $200 look like?The Federal Reserve of the United States issued in 1969 a series of 1 dollar bills, which have an error in the "Gutter note", reason why there are many collectors willing to pay a fortune for them.

One of these bills sells for $ 200 (approximately 783 soles) on eBay. However, it is worth clarifying that to know how much money would be paid for these it is necessary to consult with an interested buyer, although they are sold at that price on the aforementioned website.

Ladder dollar billsLadder dollar bills are the rarest in history. This is formed in the serial number of the bill and bears the numbers 1 to 8 in ascending or descending order (12345678 or 87654321). Because it is very difficult to find its value in the collector's market hovers around $5,000.

Variations of the ladder pattern include numbers in order that do not start with one, such as 00123456 or 034567. These can also be in reverse order; however, both variations are more common on one dollar bills and less valuable than the authentic ones.

What are the dollar denominations that exist?The U.S. Federal Reserve Board currently issues seven denominations of dollar bills. These are:

US$ 1 billUS$ 2 billUS$ 5 billUS$ 10 billUS$ 20 billUS$ 50 billUS$ 100 billHow many 1 dollar bills have been sold today?So far, only nine pairs of $1 bills have been found that were duplicated by errors, which means that there are millions of them circulating in the United States and around the world. To confirm that you have a bill of this denomination and that it belongs to the group of the most sought after by buyers, you should consult with a specialist.

When was the first $1 bill?The history of U.S. banknotes is one of the main aspects that determine the value of dollars. For this reason, it is necessary to have a certain amount of knowledge on the subject. For example, the first $1 bill was printed on May 10, 1775, during the colonial period. This happened during the American Revolutionary War, so there were many obstacles in the process of printing the bill.

How do you know if a dollar is real or counterfeit?Just as a dollar can cost an exorbitant amount of money, there is also the possibility that it is counterfeit. Below, we share some tips to identify if a dollar is counterfeit:

Dollars have high image quality, so you should check if yours has a clear design.The numbers on dollars are sharper, so you will be able to tell if it is a fake or not by the resolution of the digits.Real dollars have amber tones in their presentation, while counterfeit dollars have light colors.Counterfeit dollars have a tendency to be rougher.If you hold a real dollar up against the light, you will notice the watermark with Benjamin Franklin's image. On the other hand, on counterfeit dollars, the watermark can be seen with the naked eye and has an almost yellowish hue.The edges of the real dollars are sharp, while the counterfeit ones are usually blurred.Who appears on the dollar bill?Since 1869, George Washington, who is considered the Father of the Nation and was also the first president of the United States, appears on the lowest denomination bill.

Who are the characters that appear on the dollar bills?The characters that appear on the different denominations of dollar bills are:

US$ 1 bill: George WashingtonUS$ 2 bill: Thomas JeffersonUS$ 5 bill: Abraham Lincoln10 US$ bill: Alexander Hamilton20 US Dollar Bill: Andrew Jackson50 US Dollar Bill: Ulysses S. GrantUS$ 100 bill: Benjamin Franklin.What is the mystery of the two-dollar bill?The US$ 2 bill features the image of Thomas Jefferson, as well as a vignette depicting the signing of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Its mystery lies in the fact that due to its lack of use, this bill was discontinued in 1966 until it was reissued in 1976 for the bicentennial of the American Revolution.

How do you know if a two dollar bill is real?The paper of the two dollar bill will allow a person to tell if it is real or counterfeit. When handled, the bill should have a crisp sound, as it is made of one-quarter linen and three-quarters cotton.

Why do we use the dollar as an international currency?In recent years, according to Diego Marrero on the AFP Habitat website, 61% of the world's central bank reserves are in US dollars. The U.S. currency is used for 60% of world trade.

The U.S. dollar is one of the world's main currencies, along with the euro, the pound, the yen and the renminbi, and is included in the International Monetary Fund's basket of Special Drawing Rights currencies. How did its importance come about?

It all goes back to the end of World War II, when the United States became the major hegemonic superpower. Before the end of the war, the Bretton Woods agreement (the United Nations monetary and financial settlement in 1944) established an international monetary system where the dollar became the main reference currency for trade around the world.

What is the dollar made of?Interestingly, a dollar bill is not made of paper. The formula to make them stronger involves a composition of cotton and linen.

Why is it called a dollar?In the 16th century, coins were minted in St. Joachimsthal, a town in Bohemia, as the place was considered to have the purest silver in the world. Thus, the coins were christened Joachmisthaler, from which the popular name Thaler was derived.

Gradually, some regions of Europe began to call the coins Daler. In addition, this was the name Spain used as the official currency in the American colonies. Until, finally, with the independence of the United States, came the issuance of coins and bills in 1985, so Congress decided to call these as dollar and dollars.

What does it mean to be given a dollar?As a kind of tradition, carrying a dollar in your wallet or purse is a sign of good fortune and wealth, so it is usually given or received as a gift a specific dollar bill.

Where can I buy cheap dollars in Peru?Although the exchange rate of dollars to soles is constantly changing, the truth is that more and more people are in the need to acquire these bills, either for purchases abroad, etc.. The following is a list of places where you can buy dollars in Peru:

BanksExchange housesShopping mallsAirportsStreet money changers.What does US$ mean in money?Abbreviations such as US$ or USD mean that they refer to the U.S. dollar, thus the legal currency of the United States.

How much is $1 in S/ 1?The exchange rate from dollar to soles varies daily; however, today, the value of $1 converted S/ 1 appears within the values of S/ 3,890 the purchase and S/ 3,930 the sale in the parallel market, according to the website cuantoestaeldolar.pe.

Where is it advisable to exchange dollars in Lima?In Lima there are many places where you can exchange dollars. For this reason we leave you some options so that the exchange of foreign currency is favorable and safe for you.

The airport or terminalThe hotel where you are stayingFinancial institutionsExchange housesMoney changers in the street.What is the blue dollar and the official dollar?The blue dollar is the bill that is bought outside the formal circuit, mainly known as parallel dollar or informal dollar. It receives this name in Argentina and other regions. On the other hand, the official dollar is the one issued by banking entities.

Why is the price of the dollar important?The dollar is important because its market value has a direct impact on the global economy and politics, as well as on the fundamental decisions of governments, investors and businessmen, so it is also part of the public interest.

How many years does a dollar last?Approximately, a dollar bill lasts between 6 to 7 years. These are the years of life of each bill today, according to the U.S. Currency Education Program (CEP) website:

US$ 1 bill: 6 to 7 years.US$ 5 bill: 4 yearsUS$ 10 bill: 5 yearsUS$ 20 bill: 7 yearsUS$ 50 bill: 12 yearsUS$ 100 bill: 22 years.Other dollar bills that were issuedAlthough the best known are the US$ 1, US$ 50 and US$ 100 bills, the truth is that in the past 3, 5, 10, 25 and 50 cent bills were also issued under the context of the American Civil War or Civil War in the 1860s, according to a report by the Midpoint website.

What's the phrase on the dollar?Since 1956, all dollar bills have the phrase "In God we trust", translated into English as "We trust in God". This is because President Dwight D. Eisenhower enacted a bill in which U.S. coins would have the phrase inscribed on them, so Congress ordered it to be added to the bills as well.

What is the Canadian dollar?The Canadian dollar is the official currency used in Canada. It was introduced in July 1858 and is symbolized by C$ or CAD.

U.S. dollar or Canadian dollar?Although both currencies have the denomination "dollar", in terms of exchange rate, it is the U.S. dollar that has a higher monetary value. This is because it is considered a strong currency, for economic and financial reasons.

How much is a Canadian dollar worth?At the exchange rate, the Canadian dollar is worth between 3.04 soles and 3.30 soles.

What other countries use the U.S. dollar as their official currency?The United States is not the only country that uses the U.S. dollar as its official currency. Here are the other nations that use U.S. coins and bills.

EcuadorEl SalvadorMarshall IslandsZimbabweEast TimorMicronesiaPalauWhat is the largest dollar bill?Between 1934 and 1935, during the Great Depression, the U.S. Treasurer printed 42,000 of the US$100,000 bills. This was the largest denomination piece of paper money ever produced by the US.

Finding such a specimen is really difficult so counterfeits are relatively common. However, a handful of real US$100,000 bills, including an uncut sheet of twelve sample bills, are on display at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.

Who is on the $100,000 dollar?The bill is imprinted with the image of Woodrow Wilson, the 28th president of the United States, who held office from 1913 to 1921. It should be noted that this bill was only used for internal transactions between the Federal Reserve Banks.

The dollar bill that sells for $95,000 dollarsIn 1977, the U.S. Federal Reserve issued a series of 1 dollar bills, which although not in circulation, have a high value in the collectors' market: US$ 95 thousand. The reason for their high price is due to the fact that these specimens have a misalignment error and are considered "rare".

How does the increase in the price of the dollar affect them?The increase in the price of the dollar generates an increase in the cost of credit, not only in the United States, but also worldwide. In other words, borrowing money has become more expensive for countries, companies and individuals. As a result, activity slows down and recovery becomes more difficult.

Who determines the price of the dollar?First, the price of the dollar is determined by the free market. This means two things: when there is a shortage of dollars, the exchange rate goes up; conversely, in times of dollar abundance, it goes down. Secondly, the Central Reserve Bank (BCR), the entity in charge of exchange rate policy in Peru, intervenes to avoid sharp fluctuations in the price of the dollar.

What is the most expensive currency in the world?The most expensive currency in the world is the Kuwaiti dinar (KWD). Kuwait has the sixth largest oil reserves in the world, making it one of the richest Arab countries on the Asian continent. Currently its currency is the most expensive and valued currency. One Kuwaiti dinar is equivalent to 3.30 USD.

What is the cheapest currency in the world?The most devalued currency is the Venezuelan Sovereign Bolivar (VES), which, after the crisis suffered in Venezuela, was devalued to the point of exchanging 1 dollar for 1,552,540 VES.

How many intis were equivalent to one dollar?The number of zeros was a main characteristic of the Peruvian currency in 1990. Thus, one dollar was worth 300,000 intis.

How long did the Intis circulate?In May 1985 the first coins expressed in Intis were put into circulation, while the first banknotes were put into circulation in December of the same year. The Inti was valid as a monetary unit until June 30, 1991 (6 years).

title: Dirty flotation: what it is and how it helps the Peruvian  currency  to 'beat' the dollar
text:
Peru is currently facing what is probably its worst inflation in the last 30 years. We are talking about consumer prices rising 8.1 percent between May 2021 and May 2022, much higher than the targeted 2 percent. Despite this, the country preserves an important economic stability, which has to do with its dirty float monetary policies.

What is the dirty float all about? Peru has an atypical policy vis-à-vis the reference currency, which is the dollar. According to the BBC, this has allowed the Peruvian market to be one of the least volatile in Latin America, considering that there are other countries in the continent that suffer turbulences due to the increase of the dollar against their currencies.

The exchange rate with reference to the local currency is managed in different ways in several countries, according to their monetary policies with which they face one of the most influential currencies in the world.

First, there is the fixed exchange rate, in which central banks intervene to keep the dollar stable through buying and selling. This means that the central bank faces several challenges with respect to the markets and the growth of the dollar itself.

On the other hand, there is the floating model, which allows the exchange rate to move freely, since the central bank does not interfere directly with the exchange market. It is the one that is popularly implemented in European and American countries, and can give rise to large movements in the exchange rate due to external or conjunctural situations.

The Peruvian model is different, in this one there is also floating, but it is limited by the central bank itself, which 'stops' the Peruvian currency to prevent the dollar from going to the sky.

How does the dirty float work in Peru?According to Waldo Mendoza, from the Economics Department of the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Perú (PUCP), "the Central Reserve Bank of Peru (BCRP) rows against the current in the exchange market. It tends to buy dollars when the exchange rate goes down, and tends to sell when the exchange rate goes up".

This exchange rate is different from the fixed model in the aspect that there is a floating exchange rate. On the other hand, it is different from the floating model in the sense that the central bank itself is in charge of 'putting its hand' in the buying and selling of dollars to keep Peru's currency stable.

In the book Regímenes Cambiarios y Desempeño Macroeconómico written by Marco Vega and Erick Lahura, both from the BCRP's economic research team, Peru was the first economically large country in Latin America to implement the dirty float, this in the 1990s.

"The adoption of the floating exchange rate regime was part of a comprehensive macroeconomic stabilization plan that sought to reduce hyperinflation and get out of the deep recession in which the economy was in the early 1990s″, the book points out.

Countries such as Mexico, Brazil, Colombia and Chile also implemented this type of exchange rate, although they eventually abandoned it.

"In other countries, the timing and magnitude of the central bank's intervention could be known more clearly, making it possible to manipulate the system. The BCRP has more discretion, which allows it to be more effective in reducing volatility," Diego Macera, an expert at the Peruvian Institute of Economics and a member of the BCRP, told the BBC.

"There is no central bank that intervenes more in the exchange market than the Peruvian one," Waldo Mendoza told the BBC.

What will Peru do about inflation?The government needs to hand out cash, help communal kitchens and boost social programs while considering long-term reforms, said BCRP member Jose Tavara.

"The main problem is people's hunger, inflation hits the poorest households, because they spend a higher proportion of their income to buy food, Távara asserted. "In the cities, the poorest people are suffering, massive intervention is required from this government."

Peru has pledged to spend 3.2 billion soles ($845 million) on measures to contain inflation and soften its impact on the neediest. These plans include a tax exemption on diesel purchases, subsidies for fertilizers and aid for community kitchens. Together, the expenditures amount to four times the normal social program budget for a year, according to Economy Minister Oscar Graham.

With information from Bloomberg and BBC.

title: UPDATE 3-Peruvian markets retreat as President Castillo seeks new cabinet
text:
(Adds market intervention detail, Citi commentary)

LIMA, Feb 1 (Reuters) - Peru's currency and the Lima stock market fell on Tuesday amid uncertainty as President Pedro Castillo sought to form a new cabinet following the resignation of his prime minister, in a new crisis for his government.

Peru's currency, the sol , closed the day down 1.01% at 3.8810/3.8850 soles to the dollar, in the steepest daily decline since July 30, 2021, two days after President Castillo took office.

The sol's decline occurred despite the central bank placing some 1.1 billion soles in certificates of deposit and exchange swap, in an attempt to halt the depreciation.

The sol had been gaining ground since December and in the whole of January it rose 3.63%. Meanwhile, the Lima stock exchange benchmark yielded 1.0%, according to traders and market data.

"This base we had of 'no news, good news' was broken this week," a trader who asked not to be identified told Reuters.

Castillo, a rural school teacher who surprisingly won last year's presidential election, i announced on Monday that he decided to change his prime minister Mirtha Vasquez and reshuffle the cabinet, in what will be his third government team in just over half a year in office.

The now former head of the cabinet of ministers said, however, that she presented her resignation "due to the impossibility of reaching consensus for the benefit of the country".

The consulting firm J.P. Morgan said in a statement that Castillo's "lack of skills" to head a government would probably revive the idea that the opposition-dominated Congress would impeach the president again. "We now await the resolution of the political crisis to reassess our forecasts," J.P. Morgan analysts said in a note.

It was unclear whether Economy and Finance Minister Pedro Francke, who has given some calm to investors, would be changed or whether Castillo would ratify him in the post.

"If Francke stays and Castillo decides not to opt for more radical left-wing options for his cabinet, the negative market reaction may be short-lived," Citi said in a note on the Peruvian political conjuncture.

From the opposition-dominated Congress, mostly right-wing, there were calls to promote a new impeachment process against Castillo, who was spared from an impeachment trial in December that sought to remove him from office.

The promoter of the first attempt of "vacancia" of Castillo, legislator Patricia Chirinos of the right-wing Avanza País party, said that she will present to Congress a new legal initiative to remove the president, who took office in July.

The cabinet change will also take place in the midst of a climate of protests against the mining sector and fiscal investigations on alleged corruption in the government's environment.

(Reporting by Benjamín Mejias and Marco Aquino. Edited by Javier Leira and Daniela Desantis)

title: Peru's international reserves would rise 2.6% due to IMF allocation of US$ 1,800 million
text:
By Felipe Hernández

The special drawing rights (SDRs) allocated to Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Peru by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will strengthen their external balance sheets, but are unlikely to have any impact on fiscal or public sector debt figures. While a positive development, the assets do not significantly change the countries' challenging economic outlook.

The IMF allocated the SDRs last week. Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Peru received a combined total of 13.5 billion SDRs, equivalent to about US$19.1 billion. That represents about 1.1% of their aggregate GDP.

SDRs are likely to be used to increase international reserves. Current institutional frameworks make it difficult to use them to pay down debt, as proposed in Mexico, or to finance part of the budget deficit, as proposed in Colombia.

In Chile, the central bank aims to add US$12 billion to international reserves by May 2022. The allocations could reduce the amount of dollars the central bank still has to buy in the foreign exchange market by $2.4 billion.

Mexico gets biggest boost, Peru the smallest

Mexico was allocated SDR 8.5 billion, equivalent to about US$ 12.1 billion, the largest amount in the country sample in absolute terms and relative to international reserves, as of July 2021. Colombia was allocated the largest amount relative to GDP in 2020. Peru received 1.3 billion SDRs, or about US$1.8 billion, the smallest amount of the three counts.

Central banks decide fate of SDRs

SDRs have no significant IMF conditions. Countries use them according to their own laws and institutional arrangements. The allocations were conceived by the IMF to help countries fight the pandemic and support their economies. It was thought that they could help increase international reserves, limit excessive monetary tightening, add fiscal stimulus, and/or retire costly public debt.

SDRs are part of each country's international reserves. In Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Peru, they are included in the central bank's balance sheet. In all four countries, central banks are independent from the government, which implies that SDRs are managed by the monetary authorities.

Likely increase in international reserves

Barring a surprise, SDRs should generate higher international reserves in all four countries, with central bank assets and liabilities increasing by equal amounts. Mexico's reserves would rise 6.3% from their July level, the most among the countries in Bloomberg Intelligence's sample. They would rise 4.9% in Chile, 4.7% in Colombia and 2.6% in Peru. This would strengthen each country's external balance, but not significantly. Peru's international reserves would remain the highest relative to GDP.

The additional reserves would give central banks more ammunition to sell U.S. dollars if they wanted to. Bloomberg Intelligence does not expect any currency intervention now, but officials may consider it if currencies come under significant weakening pressure or spikes in exchange rate volatility.

This is more likely in Peru, where the central bank has a strong intervention bias and the currency remains under weakening pressure despite this year's sharp depreciation. It could happen in Colombia, where the exchange rate has weakened significantly since January. It seems less likely in Mexico; the currency has remained relatively stable and the central bank has a bias against intervention.

Chile's central bank is the outlier. It has been buying dollars since January, when it announced plans to buy US$12 billion over the next 15 months to boost international reserves. So far it has bought about US$6.2 billion through daily auctions. The SDRs could reduce the remaining dollars to be bought by $2.4 billion. That would mean that only $3.5 billion is needed to reach the target. Meanwhile, potentially lower demand could support the Chilean peso.

Institutions limit use of SDRs for fiscal and debt targets

Mexican President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador said there were discussions about using SDRs to pay off costly public debt. Colombian government officials floated the idea of using the allocation to finance part of this year's fiscal deficit.

Such plans seem highly unlikely because direct central bank financing of the government is illegal in Mexico, Chile and Peru. It is possible in Colombia, but requires the approval of all seven members of the central bank's board. This has been considered in the past, but was deemed unnecessary if Colombia still had access to external and/or domestic financial markets.

Even so, indirect financing-purchase of government bonds by the central bank in the secondary market-can be done without prior notice, except in Chile; special central bank authorization is needed, with the support of at least four of the five board members. In all four countries, the decision would be the central bank's, independent of the government. It would require the central bank to convert SDRs into dollars - or euros, sterling, yen or yuan - and then use them to buy external government debt, or sell them and use the local currency to buy local government bonds.

Both options would have a neutral monetary policy impact. They would not affect the level or cost of government debt, but would provide an additional source of demand in the secondary market. Purchases of local government bonds would imply a supply of dollars backing the currency. The swap of SDRs for government debt would increase the credit and foreign exchange risk on the central bank's balance sheet.

In Mexico, exchange rate policy is decided by the Foreign Exchange Commission. This committee is composed of the minister of finance and two of his or her alternates, plus the central bank governor and two of his or her alternates. The committee could decide to sell dollars to intervene in the foreign exchange market. This would have an impact on reserves, SDRs and the exchange rate, and would not provide financing for the government. Bloomberg Intelligence considers the scenario of the Foreign Exchange Committee making any changes to be highly unlikely.

Felipe Hernández covers Latin America for Bloomberg Economics in New York. He has more than 15 years of experience covering Latam at firms such as Banco Santander and Deutsche Bank.

title: Peru Central Bank Intervenes  in  FX  Market as Sol Depreciates -- Market Talk
text:
1526 ET - Peru's central bank sold $293M on the spot market as the sol currency depreciated to a historic low against the USD. The sol closed Friday at 4.07 per dollar, versus 3.928 in the previous session. The sol fell amid investor concerns about President Pedro Castillo's administration, which took power on Wednesday. Castillo appointed far-left politicians to his cabinet, including the prime minister and foreign minister, appearing to shun more moderate advisers. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1428 ET - The estimated 2.5% annualized advance in Canada's 2Q GDP is the latest in a series of positive surprises to the Bank of Canada 's forecasts, Bank of Nova Scotia economist Derek Holt says. Holt notes the economy outperformed the BoC's earlier forecasts for both 4Q 2020 and 1Q growth, and the latest data from Statistics Canada suggest it's now set to surpass the central bank's most recent forecast for 2Q, which called for 2% annualized growth. "Given the persistent upsides to the BoC's growth forecasts and to its inflation forecasts... there doesn't appear to be a need for emergency levels of monetary stimulus to persist," Holt says. (kim.mackrael@wsj.com; @kimmackrael)

1349 ET - Brazil's central bank will probably choose to pick up the pace of recent rate hikes and raise its benchmark lending rate, the Selic, by a full point to 5.25%, after three consecutive increases of 75 basis points apiece, according to Alberto Ramos, an economist at Goldman Sachs in New York. Since the previous rate hike in June, inflation has accelerated and industrial production, retail sales and services have all shown strength, he said. Policy makers, who will probably remain positive about the outlook for the economy, might also choose to eventually raise the Selic to a level higher than what would be considered neutral to help ground inflation expectations for 2022, said Ramos. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

1311 ET - Cryptocurrency traders from the US, UK and Turkey often list countries other than their real ones when posting about their trading on social media, according to a report released this morning. The report from data firm Inca Digital used the Twitter activity of traders on seven major crypto exchanges to analyze which countries they came from. It found hundreds of Americans trading on exchanges such as FTX, which are supposedly off-limits to US traders. "Most of the users that are supposed to reside in the United States, United Kingdom and Turkey are showing other locations in their bio," the report observes. ( alexo@wsj.com, @aosipovich)

1244 ET - A surge in inflation that St. Louis Fed leader James Bullard says Friday had outstripped central bank expectations doesn't seem to be leaking very much into underlying price pressures. The Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas says its Trimmed Mean PCE hit 2% in June from the same month a year ago, from a 1.9% annualized rise in May. The Trimmed Mean was at 1.7% at the start of 2021. The index strips out the biggest price movers in a given month to better gauge inflation trends. The June number compares to the 4% rise seen in the personal consumption expenditures price index for the same period. Fed officials expect inflation to ease over time and link the jump to pressures tied to the economic reopening process, although some worry high inflation might prove more persistent. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

1145 ET - Peru's sol currency weakened sharply on Friday against the USD, amid investor concerns over recently-inaugurated President Pedro Castillo. The sol depreciated to 4.02 against the dollar from about 3.92 the day before, an historic low. Castillo announced his cabinet yesterday, which includes several far-left members while shunning more moderate advisers. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1106 ET - MUFG Bank advises taking a short position in the euro against the pound, betting on the exchange rate to fall. It targets 0.8350 in EUR/GBP and places a stop loss at 0.8670. EUR/GBP last trades at 0.8528. "We have been encouraged by recent positive Covid-19 data from the U.K. suggesting that the risk of further pandemic-related disruption to the U.K. economic recovery has diminished," MUFG analysts say. The U.K.'s vaccine rollout and the number of people who have already had Covid-19 should dampen the severity of the current and any future waves of infections, preventing any fresh restrictions, they say. The economic recovery and rising inflation will pressure the Bank of England to scale back stimulus, they say. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1044 ET - The Norwegian krone could rise in coming days as risk appetite improves and oil prices recover but gains will be limited, ING says. Low summer liquidity, which is set to continue through August, will restrict the krone's appreciation, ING analysts say. "But with Norges Bank being the most hawkish G10 central bank--two [interest rate] hikes expected in the reminder of the year--and the liquidity expected to come back after the current summer lull, there is more upside to NOK in the latter part of the third quarter," they say. EUR/NOK last trades up 0.8% at 10.4645. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1039 ET - Brazil's fiscal situation is being helped by high commodity prices, high inflation and a recovering economy, but the stock of debt remains high and needs to come down, according to Alberto Ramos, an economist at Goldman Sachs in New York. Brazil's central bank said Friday that the country's public sector had a primary deficit of 65.5 billion reais, the equivalent of $12.8 billion, in June, down from 188.7 billion in the same month of 2020. The decline in the primary deficit from a year ago is a significant improvement, but the federal government needs to engineer a sustained declining trend in debt and reduce the deficit once the pandemic is under control, Ramos said. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

1021 ET - The prospect of higher inflation is driving capital to alternative asset classes, according to a survey that Vidrio, a provider of investment-management systems, conducted with investors that combined manage more than $100B in alternative assets. Eighty-percent of the respondents say they have made at least moderate adjustments to include more alternative assets in their portfolios in response to near-term inflation expectations. When asked which alternative asset classes are likely to see the largest inflation-driven capital inflow, with the option of choosing more than one, 44% of the respondents say private equity and an equal 44% point to commodity funds, while 33% and 22% select macro-hedge funds and private credit, respectively. (luis.garcia@wsj.com; @lhvgarcia)

1013 ET - Major foreign-exchange rates should trade sideways in coming weeks as the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve are unlikely to provide any fresh policy signals, Unicredit says. Further key communication from the Fed and the ECB will probably be delayed until Aug. 26-28, when Fed Chair Jerome Powell speaks at the annual Jackson Hole policy symposium, or Sept. 9, when the ECB holds its next policy decision, Unicreditforex strategist Roberto Mialich says. That will keep major currency pairs, including EUR/USD, GBP/USD and USD/JPY, trading in familiar ranges with the dollar maintaining the "bearish tone" that re-emerged after the Fed's cautious stance at Wednesday's policy meeting, he says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1012 ET - The Turkish lira will weaken even if the country's central bank holds off on cutting interest rates, UniCredit says. Data on Tuesday is likely to show continued high inflation in July, which could encourage Turkey's central bank to delay the start of easing monetary policy until later this year despite pressure from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to cut rates, UniCredit 's forex strategist Roberto Mialich says. "Yet, high inflation is set to erode further real rates [rates adjusted for inflation] in Turkey and to weigh on the TRY," he says. "We would not buy any TRY recovery attempt in the meantime." GENERAL INFORMATION

a)

Incorporation and operations

AENZA S.A.A., (hereinafter the 'Company') is the parent Company of the AENZA S.A.A. Corporation that includes the Company and its subsidiaries (hereinafter, the 'Corporation') and is mainly engaged in holding investments in Corporation companies. Additionally, the Company provides services of strategic and functional advice and office leases space to the Corporation companies.

The General Shareholder's Meeting on November 2, 2020 approved the modification of the Company's corporate name from Graña y Montero S.A.A. to AENZA S.A.A. which is effective as of February 4, 2021.

The Corporation is a conglomerate of companies with operations including different business activities, the most significant are engineering and construction, infrastructure (public concession ownership and operation) and real estate businesses. See details of operating segments in Note 7.

b)

Authorization for the issue of the financial statements

The condensed interim consolidated financial statements for the period ended June 30, 2021 were authorized by Management and Board of Directors on July 23, 2021.

The consolidated financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2020, have been prepared and issued with authorization of Management and the Board of Directors on March 5, 2021, and were approved on the General Shareholders' Meeting held on March 31, 2021.

Since the date the financial statements were submitted to our shareholders for their approval, until the date of presentation to the Securities and Exchange Commission of the financial information attached to the annual report 20F, subsequent events with material impact on our results occurred and as a result, and in compliance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), we have recorded such impacts herein. This was revealed through a relevant information communication on May 17, 2021. The events referred to previously, are related mainly to the considerable progress in the negotiations of the Company's plea bargain agreement, which allowed us to reassess our estimate of our exposure to the contingencies including within its scope. As a result, the amounts included in our financial statements were restructured.

After the filing of the Form 20-F, the Company signed an 'Acta de Acuerdo Preparatorio de Colaboracion y Beneficios' (the 'Agreement'), with the 'Procuraduria Publica ad Hoc'. who dedicate themselves exclusively to the knowledge of investigations related to Crimes of Corruption of Officials and related incurred by the company Odebrecht and others (the 'Prosecutor's Office' and with the ad hoc Public Prosecutor's Office for investigations and processes related to crimes of corruption of officials, money laundering and related assets incurred by the company Odebrecht and others (the 'Office of the Attorney General'). Pursuant to the Agreement, the Company assumed an obligation to pay a civil penalty, which is within the estimates included in such financial information. The effects of the Effective Collaboration Agreement will enter into force as of their judicial approval.

The consolidated restructured financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2020 have been prepared and issued with authorization of Management and the Board of Directors on June 9, 2021 to ensure consistency between the information presented to the markets in which the Company's securities are traded, and were approved on the General Mandatory Shareholder's Meeting held on July 6, 2021.

c)

Acta de Acuerdo Preparatorio de Colaboración y Beneficios - 'The Agreement'

Pursuant to the Agreement executed on May 21, 2021, AENZA S.A.A. accepts it was utilized by certain former executives to commit illicit acts until 2016, and commits to pay a civil penalty to the Peruvian State of S/321.9 million and US$40.7 million. The civil penalty is subject to (i) a repayment tenor of 12 years, (ii) the legal interest rate in domestic and foreign currency, (iii) a total collateral of S/197 million through a trust that includes shares issued by a subsidiary of AENZA, a mortgage on a real estate asset and debt service guaranty account. Among other conditions, the Agreement includes a restriction to participate in public construction and road maintenance contracts for 2 years. As of June 30, 2021, we registered the present value of the amounts described before, which amount to S/154 million and US$17.2 million (totaling S/220.5 million).

The civil penalty covers the total contingency to which the Company was exposed because of the investigations revealed in the notes to the financial statements since 2017. Nevertheless, the Agreement enforceability is subject to court approval and its terms and conditions are subject to confidentiality provisions in such agreement.

The Company is currently evaluating the changes to its Financial Plan approved on November 2, 2020 to repay the final amount of the civil penalty.

d)

Current situation of the Company

As of June 30, 2021, contingencies held by the Corporation are substantially the same as those existing as of December 31, 2020.

e)

New state of emergency due to COVID

On July 10, 2021, the Peruvian Government extended the State of National Emergency for a period of 30 days as a result of COVID-19. Likewise, certain economic activities are restricted, according to the alert level in each department of Peru, until August 31, 2021. Management considers that the measures taken by the national authorities have no impact on the continuity and development of the operations of the Company because the activities carried out by the Company are within the group of permitted activities and have not been significantly impacted by the pandemic.

The Company's Management continues to monitor the evolution of the situation and the guidance of the national and international authorities, since events beyond the control of Management may arise that require modifying the established business plan. A further spread of Covid-19 and the consequent measures taken to limit the spread of the disease could affect the ability to conduct business in the normal way and, therefore, affect the financial position and results of operations.

Citizen immobilization, the restriction of activities of strategic companies as well as the paralysis of public entities have affected the execution of investment projects as well as the performance of exploration activities, until the date of approval of the financial statements, it is not expected that operations and going concern will be affected.

Concerning to loans to related parties, the Corporation has measures in place to ensure the recovery of these loans through the controls maintained by the Corporate Finance Management and the performance evaluation conducted by the Board of Directors.
