title: Peru 's  Central Bank Intervenes  to Sell $335M -- Market Talk
text:
16:14 EST - Peru's central bank continues to intervene to sell U.S. dollars to ease deprecation pressures on the sol. On Thursday the central bank sold $335M. It had sold $303M on Monday. The sol has depreciated 10.5% against the greenback over the past 12 months, ending Thursday at PEN3.095 per dollar. (Robert.Kozak@wsj.com)

16:09 EST - Ukrainian gas behemoth Naftogaz could be split and partially privatized as early as this year, said the country's energy minister. Separating Naftogaz's oil and gas production arm from its pipeline network would bring Ukraine in line with EU competition rules. Volodymyr Demchyshyn said that the government was ready to put up minority stakes in the split-up company. Whether a deal could be closed in 2015 amid the war in the country's east is less clear. "There is no queue--unfortunately--standing outside," Mr. Demchyshyn said. (gabriele.steinhauser@wsj.com)

15:59 EST - Kiev could cut gas supplies to rebel-held regions in eastern Ukraine if continue to miss payments, Ukraine's energy minister said, highlighting another flashpoint with Moscow. Volodymyr Demchyshyn said local distributors in separatist territories have paid for just 20% of the gas they have received since August, at a great cost to state-owned Naftogaz. "If they are not paying I'm turning off" supplies, Mr. Demchyshyn said, a week after Russian President Putins said a gas cut-off "smells of genocide." Deliveries of eastern Ukraine were part of an EU-mediated gas deal between Ukraine and Russia that expires at the end of March and the Minsk peace plan. (gabriele.steinhauser@wsj.com)

15:58 EST - European companies could rent capacity in Ukraine's huge gas storage facilities to help fill them up to levels that could get the country through "worst case scenarios" over the next winter, Ukraine's energy minister said. Such a solution would be cheaper for everyone involved, as European companies have much lower capital costs than state-owned Naftogaz, said Volodymyr Demchyshyn. The European Commission, the EU executive, says Ukraine's storage needs to contain around 20 billion cubic meters of gas ahead of the winter, while Mr. Demchyshyn believes some 14-15 bcm should suffice. The issue could become a sticking point in upcoming gas talks between Ukraine, Kiev and the EU. (gabriele.steinhauser@wsj.com)

15:49 EST - While markets may be sensitive to news from New Zealand's central bank, ANZ says NZD/AUD remains very elevated, helped by tepid retail sales and a 10th-straight trade deficit in Australia. Thursday's NZ central-bank consultation paper was seen as the first step in allowing the entity to target the currency further when setting policy. But ANZ "still sees the threshold to RBNZ action as significant, seeing support for NZD remaining sound." The kiwi is at A$0.9626; ANZ expects a short-term range of A$0.9560-0.9660. (lucy.craymer@wsj.com; @lucy_craymer)

14:35 EST - February was another dismal month for farm equipment in Brazil, as factory volume sales of tractors to dealers and distributors fell 29% from a year ago. Harvesting combines were off 46%, based on Brazilian trade association figures. Brazil had been a key growth market for US farm equipment manufacturers Deere (DE); CNH Industrial (CNHI), the maker of Case IH brand equipment; and Agco, the maker of Massey Ferguson machinery. But lower prices for Brazilian soybeans and sugar and less attractive terms on government-subsidized equipment loans are discouraging farmers from buying machinery. Equipment "spending is likely to be curtailed in the near term," says JP Morgan in a note. Farm machinery stocks are mixed with DE up a touch, while Agco and CNHI are off 0.4% and 0.9% respectively. (robert.tita@wsj.com)

14:29 EST - The Mexico peso continues to surprise on the downside against the dollar, and Monex says it could break new levels of resistance in coming days. It's fallen some 19% since May to reach MXN15.2020. "The breaking of its principal resistance (MXN15.10) and the recent rise in the dollar index open the door for the exchange rate to put to test the next levels of resistance, first in the range of MXN15.28-33," says Monex. The brokerage recommends buying dollars in the medium-to-long term with an objective of MXN15.28 and a stop at MXN15.05. (laurence.iliff@wsj.com)

14:26 EST - The pace of labor market gains should remain steady in February despite severe snowstorms in parts of the country, says Deutsche Bank economist Joe LaVorgna. "February nonfarm payrolls may have dodged the worst of the recent weather disruptions because during the February employment survey week [the week through the 14th], jobless claims plunged." They were the lowest for the month then, while in the survey week for February 2014, jobless claims peaked (they haven't reached the same level since). Tax-receipt data also suggest employers are adding more jobs. The initial read for February 2014 was job growth of 175K; consensus for tomorrow is 240K. (jeffrey.sparshott@wsj.com)

13:12 EST - In what so far has been a repeat of last year's trend, economists are lowering economic-growth forecasts every couple weeks. It happened again at the end of February as the average 2015 GDP growth view of 35 economists is now 3.1%, versus 3.3% in January's Bank of Mexico survey. Expectations for next year also fall two-tenths, to 3.6%. The dismal scientists are also darken their views on the peso, predicting a year-end level of MXN14.54/dollar versus MXN14.18 previously. Last year, the GDP-growth consensus among economists started around 3.5% and slipped to around 2% year-end; growth ended up being 2.1%. (laurence.iliff@wsj.com)

13:05 EST - The bond market is in a tug of war today as conflicting factors spark volatile trading. Yields are ticking lower again, dragged down by falling rates in Europe amid Draghi's comments. But Treasurys are lagging European sovereigns as investors await Friday's jobs report. The yield on the 10-year Treasury is at 2.110% versus 2.121% Wednesday while the 10-year bund fell to 0.354%, near a record low. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

11:54 EST - The pace of potential job growth at small businesses declined in February as winter storms swept across the East Coast, according to the National Federation of Independent Business. A net 12% of 716 small businesses surveyed said they were planning to hire new workers, down 2 points from January, with gains more than offset by an uptick in the number of owners planning job cuts. Despite the declines, small-business hiring remains strong, according to William Dunkelberg, the Washington lobby group's chief economist. He anticipates "a firm number" in tomorrow's government report, though shy of the 300K average seen in recent months. (angus.loten@wsj.com)

11:40 EST - Currencies such as the dollar and the euro continue to move in accordance with central-bank news more so than economic fundamentals, says USForex's Lennon Sweeting. The euro has largely shrugged off recent upbeat data to trade lower leading into, during and following Draghi's press conference today. Meanwhile, "we've been seeing dollar strength while US fundamentals have been so-so." Investors are keying into the mid-month FOMC meeting, he notes. Still, tomorrow's jobs report should provide direction for the dollar--if only in relation to what the numbers mean for market expectations on the Fed and interest rates. The euro is down 0.5% at $1.1018 while the dollar rises 0.4% to Y120.20. (james.ramage@wsj.com)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: UBS Stays Bullish on Oilfield Majors -- Market Talk
text:
8:31 EST - UBS says oil prices should slowly move higher into 2016-7, to $65-70/barrel, as it defends its buy ratings on the world's four largest oilfield-services companies--Schlumberger (SLB), Halliburton (HAL), Baker Hughes (BHI) and Weatherford (WFT). It acknowledges pricing and oversupply will challenge the quartet and that oil prices are key. "As in every downcycle/recovery, EPS, rig count and multiples become less important as oil prices dictate the industry outlook and stock performance." Their stocks have fallen to varying degrees the past 6 months, with BHI off just 8% amid its pending purchase by HAL, which is down 35%. SLB has fallen 20% and WFT has slumped 48%. (dan.molinski@wsj.com; @dmwsj)

8:27 EST - Private payrolls added 212,000 in February, says ADP today, close to the 215,000 gain expected by economists. That suggests few or no forecasters will change their number for Friday's payrolls report. The consensus calls for the Labor Department to report a solid gain of 240,000 nonfarm jobs (which include government slots) and the February unemployment rate to fall to 5.6% from 5.7% in January. (kathleen.madigan@wsj.com)

8:27 EST - February may have proved to have been a yin-yang month for McDonald's (MCD) US sales, says Janney as it goes from 1% same-store-sales growth to a 1% decline ahead of Monday's report. "Clearly, part of the very-positive first half of February reflects favorable year-over-year weather. And just as clearly, part of the much-more-challenging second half of February reflects unfavorable year-over-year weather." (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com; @kevinkingsbury)

8:24 EST - Treasury prices perk up after the in-line ADP employment report, which admittedly hasn't been a stable predictor of the government's data. That print Friday will be the key release ahead of the FOMC meeting on March 17-8, the focus of which being whether patience is removed. The yield on the 10-year Treasury is 2.108%, versus 2.122% Tuesday. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

8:07 EST - As Abercrombie (ANF) continues to struggle, fellow teen-apparel retailer American Eagle (AEO) says F4Q EPS rose even more than anticipated as it gives an above-consensus 1Q forecast despite anticipated West Coast port impacts to the bottom line. Helping year-end results were "improved merchandise" and fewer promotions, says CEO Jay Schottenstein. AEO's same-store sales were flat in 4Q, which is actually decent considering how things have been in the space, and gross margin surged 3.2 percentage points to 35.1%. Inventory is also in check, down 5% from a year earlier on a cost/foot basis. AEO jumps 6.3% premarket to $15.75, which would be a 15-month high. ANF is now down 6.6% to what would be a fresh 6-year low. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com; @kevinkingsbury)

7:54 EST - Banco de Credito sees more volatility ahead for the Peruvian sol, saying it could take place in the gap between Peru's central bank meeting on March 12 and the following week's FOMC gathering. Peru's central bank has been actively intervening in the market by selling dollars (including $303M Monday) to ease volatility. Banco de Credito says the activity and an improved price for copper have eased depreciation pressures on the sol. (robert.kozak@wsj.com)

7:53 EST - Share buybacks have been a key source of stock gains and earning growth, and they look set to continue, analyst Ed Yardeni says, for the simple reason that it makes economic sense. Corporate bond yields have been and remain below the forward earnings yield for the S&P 500, he says, a phenomenon that has driven $2.1 trillion in buybacks from 2009 through 3Q 2014. Buybacks could mean 1H earnings growth for the index, now expected to be negative, could in fact turn in a positive reading. (andrew.dowell@dowjones.com; @drewdowell)

7:51 EST - Treasury prices are little changed after two days of selling as today's US data loom, starting in minutes with ADP's employment report. Still, the key one is Friday's nonfarm-jobs print, which should further shape expectations on the Fed's rate outlook. This week, Treasurys have been hit by a flurry of new corporate-bond sales. More are scheduled by week's end. The yield on the 10-year Treasury is at 2.12%, versus 2.122% Tuesday. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

7:45 EST - Weather hit the auto industry in February, but Morgan Stanley's Adam Jonas reflected other analysts in calling the softness a "minor hiccup." Volumes should come roaring back in March, as buyers come out of hibernation. The trend to watch? Transaction prices, which have increased eight straight months. Sales, Jonas says, "continue to punch above their weight on the value side. Disciplined use of incentives and demand for trucks and luxury are fueling this trend. But will it last? Don't be so sure. "Jumping forward to spring, we expect to see more accommodative/competitive financing. This will push volumes to 17M, but eventually there will be a "tab to pay when the string runs out." (john.stoll@wsj.com)

7:45 EST - Google (GOOGL) is losing its lock on location services. Uber's acquisition of deCarta, a mapping company, allows it to potentially distance itself from GOOGL. The two companies are on the one hand tied together--Google Ventures invests in Uber and a GOOGL executive sits on Uber's board. But on the other hand, GOOGL could become a competitor with self-driving cars. At the same time, Samsung (005930.SE) seems to be heavily promoting its own location services, says IHS Technology's Gerrit Schneemann. He notes the South Korean firm has prominently showed off its MirrorLink auto services and unveiled technology which would let a Samsung user tie together a phone, wearable device and car. (lisa.fleisher@wsj.com; @lisafleisher)

7:41 EST - Wondering how Tesla (TSLA) is doing this quarter? Finding a reliable answer will be tough. The company doesn't break out monthly volumes, but the situation is closely watched after TSLA reported disappointing 4Q volumes and said this quarter would benefit. Two firms which estimate the auto maker's sales have wildly different views. Autodata says TSLA's US sales were 1,200 last month, down 25%, with the estimated 2-month figure down 29% at 2,200. But while WardsAuto.com puts sales below Autodata, it says they've grown from year-earlier levels. WardsAuto estimates TSLA's February sales jumped 42% to 997 and are up 20% year-to-date at 1,793. (john.stoll@wsj.com)

7:37 EST - Abercrombie's (ANF) F4Q revenue fell even more than Wall Street feared, but EPS ended up being right in line with consensus as gross margin rose 1.9 percentage points to 60.9% on lower product costs. And at least inventories seem to be in check, down 13% from a year earlier at quarter-end. Meanwhile, "We expect the first half of 2015 to remain challenging," says Chairman Arthur Martinez between the ongoing sales hit from shrinking its logo business and currency impacts. "However, we believe that the benefits of all of the changes we have made will be reflected in improved performance in the second half of the year." Time will tell. ANF rises 0.7% in initial premarket trading to $24.16 after sliding 3% this week and 16% for 2015. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com; @kevinkingsbury)

"We have improved our performance during the half and we have again shown: the strength of our brands, which is driving our share gains; our strong innovation capability, which has enabled us to access new growth opportunities; and our focus on cost. We delivered the planned savings from our global efficiency programme together with procurement benefits in marketing spend which we have reinvested in our brands and we increased our investment in our routes to consumer while again expanding our margins.

We have already taken action to improve the performance of those brands and markets that have not performed as well as we would expect. This contributed to our stronger second quarter performance and I expect to maintain this momentum through the year.

The half saw Diageo acquire control of USL, putting us in the position to create an iconic leader in spirits in an attractive market. We have also reached agreement to acquire all of Don Julio, which will significantly strengthen our position in one of our fastest growing categories.

The quality of these results in a tough environment, with depletions ahead of shipments and improving cash flow, reinforce my confidence that Diageo can realise its full potential and deliver our performance ambition."

(d) Dividend

An interim dividend of 21.5 pence per share will be paid to holders of ordinary shares and ADRs on the register as of 27 February 2015. This represents an increase of 9% on last year's interim dividend. The interim dividend will be paid to shareholders on 7 April 2015. Payment to US ADR holders will be made on 10 April 2015. A dividend reinvestment plan is available to holders of ordinary shares in respect of the interim dividend and the plan notice date is 12 March 2015.

Diageo's dividend philosophy has been a consistent increase in the annual dividend payable while maintaining dividend cover between 1.8 and 2.2 times earnings per share. In recent years this has allowed the group to increase its dividend by 9% a year. Given the economic slowdown in emerging markets and the associated currency weakness expected in the future both of which had such a significant impact on Diageo's reported results in the year ended 30 June 2014, the group's dividend coverage ratio is now below the lower end of the range set. However cash flow is improving as these results show and the strength of the dollar is providing some offset to emerging market currency weakness. Therefore the interim dividend growth was maintained at 9%, but this will be reviewed for the full year and if necessary the rate of increase may be changed for the final dividend in order to maintain the coverage ratio, albeit at the lower end of the range.

1. Basis of preparation

This condensed set of financial statements has been prepared in accordance with IAS 34 Interim Financial Reporting as issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) and as adopted by the EU.

The annual financial statements of the group are prepared in accordance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRSs) as issued by the IASB and as adopted by the EU. As required by the Disclosure and Transparency Rules of the Financial Conduct Authority, the condensed set of financial statements has been prepared applying the accounting policies and presentation that were applied in the preparation of the company's published consolidated financial statements for the year ended 30 June 2014. IFRS is subject to ongoing review and endorsement by the EU or possible amendment by interpretative guidance and the issuance of new standards by the IASB.

The directors have a reasonable expectation that the group has adequate resources to continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future. Accordingly, they continue to adopt the going concern basis in preparing the condensed consolidated financial statements.

New accounting standards

The following amendments to the accounting standards, issued by the IASB or International Financial Reporting Interpretations Committee (IFRIC) and endorsed by the EU, have been adopted by the group from 1 July 2014 with no significant impact on the group's performance, financial position or disclosures:

IFRIC 21 - Levies

Amendment to IAS 19 - Defined benefit plans: Employee contributions

Amendment to IAS 32 - Offsetting financial assets and financial liabilities

Amendment to IAS 39 - Novation of derivatives and continuation of hedge accounting

Amendment to IFRS 2 - Share based payments - Definition of vesting conditions

Amendment to IFRS 3 - Accounting for contingent consideration in a business combination

Amendment to IFRS 3 - Scope exceptions for joint ventures

Amendment to IFRS 8 - Aggregation of operating segments and reconciliation of segment assets to entity's assets

Amendment to IFRS 13 - Short-term receivables and payables

The following standards issued by the IASB (not yet endorsed by the EU) have not yet been adopted by the group:

IFRS 9 - Financial instruments (effective in the year ending 30 June 2019, not yet endorsed by the EU) is ultimately intended to replace IAS 39 and covers the classification, measurement and derecognition of financial instruments together with a new hedge accounting model and new impairment methodology.

The group is currently considering the impact of IFRS 9 on its consolidated results and financial position.

IFRS 15 - Revenue from contracts with customers (effective in the year ending 30 June 2018, not yet endorsed by the EU) is based on the principle that revenue is recognised when control of goods or services is transferred to the customer and provides a single, principles based five-step model to be applied to all sales contracts. It replaces the separate models for goods, services and construction contracts under current IFRS.

Based on a preliminary assessment the group currently believes that the adoption of IFRS 15 will have no significant impact on its consolidated results or financial position. [ 29-01-15 0701GMT ]

2. Segmental information

The segmental information presented is consistent with management reporting provided to the executive committee (the chief operating decision maker).

The executive committee considers the business principally from a geographical perspective based on the location of third party sales and the business analysis is presented by geographical segment.

In the six months ended 31 December 2014 Diageo changed its internal reporting structure to reflect changes made to management responsibilities as announced on 30 July 2014. As a result of this change, Diageo reports the following geographical segments both for management reporting purposes and in the external financial statements: North America; Europe; Africa; Latin America and Caribbean; Asia Pacific and Corporate. As a consequence of this change, the financial information by geographical segments for comparative years has been amended and restated segmental information has been provided in the tables below.

Continuing operations also include the Corporate function. Corporate revenues and costs are in respect of central costs, including finance, corporate relations, human resources and legal, as well as certain information systems, facilities and employee costs that are not allocable to the geographical segments or to ISC. They also include rents receivable and payable in respect of properties not used by the group in the manufacture, sale or distribution of premium drinks and the results of Gleneagles Hotel.

Diageo uses shared services operations, including captive and outsourced centres, to deliver transaction processing activities for markets and operational entities. These centres are located in Hungary, Romania, Kenya, Colombia and the Philippines. The captive business service centre in Budapest also performs certain central finance activities, including elements of financial planning and reporting and treasury. The results of shared service operations are recharged to the regions.

The segmental information for net sales and operating profit before exceptional items is reported at budgeted exchange rates in line with management reporting. For management reporting purposes the group measures the current period at, and restates the prior period net sales and operating profit to, the current year's budgeted exchange rates. These exchange rates are set prior to the financial year as part of the financial planning process and provide a consistent exchange rate to measure the performance of the business throughout the year. The comparative segmental information, prior to retranslation, has not been restated at the current year's budgeted exchange rates but is presented at the budgeted rates for the year ended 30 June 2014.

In addition, for management reporting purposes Diageo presents separately the result of acquisitions and disposals completed in the current and prior year from the results of the geographical segments. 9. Financial instruments

Fair value measurements of financial instruments are presented through the use of a three-level fair value hierarchy that prioritises the valuation techniques used in fair value calculations.

The group maintains policies and procedures to value instruments using the most relevant data available. If multiple inputs that fall into different levels of the hierarchy are used in the valuation of an instrument, the instrument is categorised on the basis of the most subjective input.

Foreign currency forwards and swaps, cross currency swaps and interest rate swaps are valued using discounted cash flow techniques. These techniques incorporate inputs at levels 1 and 2, such as foreign exchange rates and interest rates. These market inputs are used in the discounted cash flow calculation incorporating the instrument's term, notional amount and discount rate, and taking credit risk into account. As significant inputs to the valuation are observable in active markets, these instruments are categorised as level 2 in the hierarchy.

13. Contingent liabilities and legal proceedings

(a) Guarantees

As of 31 December 2014 the group has no material guarantees or indemnities in respect of liabilities of third parties with the exception of a conditional back-stop guarantee issued by Diageo Holdings Netherlands B.V. (DHN) to Standard Chartered Bank (Standard Chartered), pursuant to a guarantee commitment agreement (the guarantee agreement) in respect of the liabilities of Watson Limited (Watson), a company affiliated with Dr Vijay Mallya, under a $135 million (GBP81 million) facility from Standard Chartered. The guarantee agreement was entered into as part of the arrangements put in place at closing of the USL transaction and announced by Diageo on 4 July 2013. The term of this facility and the DHN guarantee have since been renewed and extended to 2 March 2015, with the monetary limits of both the facility and the guarantee remaining unchanged. The terms of the guarantee continue to require that the right of Standard Chartered to call on the guarantee is subject to Standard Chartered having first taken certain agreed steps to recover from Watson, including defined steps towards enforcement of its security package. In addition, DHN has, in respect of its potential liability under this guarantee, the benefit of counter-indemnities from Watson and Dr Vijay Mallya as well as the security package put in place for the facility.

(b) Colombian litigation

An action was filed on 8 October 2004 in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York by the Republic of Colombia and a number of its local government entities against Diageo and other spirits companies, alleging several causes of action, including violations of the Federal RICO Act. This claim was dismissed in November 2012. The dismissal was without prejudice and as such, plaintiffs are not barred from bringing a similar action in future, although the company currently believes any such future action to be unlikely. Diageo remains committed to continued dialogue with the Colombian governmental entities to address the underlying issues.

(c) Korean customs dispute

On 5 January 2015, Diageo Korea accepted the Korean court recommendation to settle litigation against Korea customs regarding the transfer pricing methodology applicable to spirits imported between 2004 and 2010. For the six months period ended 31 December 2014 Diageo has charged GBP145 million before tax in respect of resolving this dispute as well as other related matters. Payments to be made pursuant to settlement of these related disputes will be reduced by GBP88 million which was paid to customs authorities prior to 30 June 2014 and was previously accounted for as a receivable from Korea customs.

(d) Thalidomide litigation

In June 2014, claims alleging product liability and negligence for injuries arising from the consumption of thalidomide were filed in the High Court in London against Distillers Company (Biochemicals) Limited, its parent Diageo Scotland Limited (formerly Distillers Company Limited), as well as against Gr nenthal GmbH, the developer of the drug (not a member of the group). The Particulars of Claim on behalf of ten claimants in these proceedings were served on Diageo on 6 December 2014. Diageo is unable to quantify meaningfully the possible loss or range of loss to which these lawsuits may give rise.

Distillers Company (Biochemicals) Limited distributed thalidomide in the United Kingdom for a period in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Diageo has worked voluntarily for many years with various thalidomide organisations and has provided significant financial support.

(e) Acquisition of USL shares from UBHL, winding-up petitions against UBHL and other proceedings in relation to the USL transaction

On 4 July 2013 Diageo completed its acquisition, under a share purchase agreement with United Breweries (Holdings) Limited (UBHL) and various other sellers (the SPA) of 21,767,749 shares (14.98%) in USL for a total consideration of INR 31.3 billion (GBP342 million), including 10,141,437 shares (6.98%) from UBHL. Through a series of further transactions, as of 2 July 2014, Diageo has a 54.78% investment in USL (excluding 2.38% owned by the USL Benefit Trust).

Prior to the acquisition from UBHL on 4 July 2013, the High Court of Karnataka (the High Court) had granted leave to UBHL under sections 536 and 537 of the Indian Companies Act (the Leave Order) to enable the sale by UBHL to Diageo to take place (the UBHL Share Sale) notwithstanding the continued existence of five winding-up petitions (the Original Petitions) that were pending against UBHL on 9 November 2012, being the date of the SPA. Additional winding-up petitions have been brought against UBHL since 9 November 2012, and the Leave Order did not extend to them. At the time of the completion of the UBHL Share Sale, the Leave Order remained subject to review on appeal. However, as stated by Diageo at the time of closing on 4 July 2013, it was considered unlikely that any appeal process in respect of the Leave Order would definitively conclude on a timely basis and, accordingly, Diageo waived the conditionality under the SPA relating to the absence of insolvency proceedings in relation to UBHL and acquired the 10,141,437 USL shares from UBHL at that time.

Following closing of the UBHL Share Sale, appeals were filed by various petitioners in respect of the Leave Order. On 20 December 2013, the division bench of the High Court set aside the Leave Order (the 20 December Order). Following the 20 December Order, Diageo filed special leave petitions (SLPs) in the Supreme Court of India against the 20 December Order.

On 10 February 2014, the Supreme Court of India issued an order admitting the SLPs and ordering that the status quo be maintained with regard to the UBHL Share Sale. The SLPs are scheduled for a next hearing date in the Supreme Court on 21 April 2015.

In separate proceedings, the various winding-up petitions against UBHL have been progressing through the High Court since closing of the UBHL Share Sale. In separate rulings issued by the High Court on 22 November 2013 and 13 December 2013, the High Court admitted two of the winding-up petitions against UBHL. An appeal filed by UBHL against the first ruling issued on 22 November 2013 was dismissed by a division bench of the High Court on 16 December 2013. That dismissal is now the subject of a further appeal by UBHL before the Supreme Court of India. On 6 February 2014, UBHL filed an appeal with a division bench of the High Court against the second ruling issued on 13 December 2013 and that appeal is still pending. The High Court admitted a further six winding-up petitions against UBHL on 2 January 2015 and ordered that notice of the petitions be published by the first week of February 2015, with the next hearing date scheduled for 26 February 2015.

Diageo continues to believe that the acquisition price of INR 1440 paid to UBHL for the USL shares is fair and reasonable as regards UBHL, UBHL's shareholders and UBHL's secured and unsecured creditors. However, adverse results for Diageo in the proceedings referred to above could, absent leave or relief in other proceedings, ultimately result in Diageo losing title to the 10,141,437 USL shares acquired from UBHL. Diageo believes it would remain in control of USL and be able to consolidate USL as a subsidiary regardless of the outcome of this litigation. There can be no certainty as to the outcome of the existing or any further related legal proceedings or the timeframe within which they would be concluded. [ 29-01-15 0701GMT ]

Diageo also has the benefit of certain contractual undertakings and commitments from the relevant sellers in relation to potential challenges to its unencumbered title to the USL shares acquired on 4 July 2013, including relating to the winding-up petitions described above and/or certain losses and costs that may be incurred in the event of third party actions relating to the acquisition of the USL shares.

Separately, Diageo continues to pursue completion of the acquisition of an additional 3,459,090 USL shares (representing 2.38% of the share capital of USL) under the SPA from the USL Benefit Trust. Definitions and reconciliation of non-GAAP measures to GAAP measures

Diageo's strategic planning process is based on the following non-GAAP measures. They are chosen for planning and reporting, and some of them are used for incentive purposes. Volume

Volume is a non-GAAP measure that is measured on an equivalent units basis to nine-litre cases of spirits. An equivalent unit represents one nine-litre case of spirits, which is approximately 272 servings. A serving comprises 33ml of spirits, 165ml of wine, or 330ml of ready to drink or beer. Therefore, to convert volume of products other than spirits to equivalent units, the following guide has been used: beer in hectolitres divide by 0.9; wine in nine-litre cases, divide by five; ready to drink in nine-litre cases, divide by 10; and certain pre-mixed products that are classified as ready to drink in nine-litre cases, divide by five.

Organic movements

In the discussion of the performance of the business, 'organic' information is presented using pounds sterling amounts on a constant currency basis excluding the impact of exceptional items and acquisitions and disposals. Organic measures enable users to focus on the performance of the business which is common to both periods and which represents those measures that local managers are most directly able to influence.

Calculation of organic movements

The organic movement percentage is the amount in the row headed 'Organic movement' in the tables below, expressed as a percentage of the amount in the row headed '2013 adjusted'. 'Exchange' in the organic movement calculation reflects the adjustment to recalculate the prior period results as if they had been generated at the current period's exchange rates.

Free cash flow

Free cash flow comprises the net cash flow from operating activities aggregated with the net movements in loans receivable and other investments and with the net purchase of property, plant and equipment and computer software that are included in net cash flow from investing activities.

The remaining components of net cash flow from investing activities that do not form part of free cash flow, as defined by the group's management, are in respect of the acquisition and sale of businesses.

The group's management regards the purchase and disposal of property, plant and equipment and computer software as ultimately non-discretionary since ongoing investment in plant, machinery and technology is required to support the day-to-day operations, whereas acquisitions and sales of businesses are discretionary. Return on average total invested capital

Return on average total invested capital is used by management to assess the return obtained from the group's asset base and is calculated to aid evaluation of the performance of the business.

The profit used in assessing the return on average total invested capital reflects operating profit before exceptional items plus share of after tax results of associates and joint ventures after applying the tax rate before exceptional items for the period. Average total invested capital is calculated using the average derived from the consolidated balance sheets at the beginning and end of the period. Average capital employed comprises average net assets for the period, excluding post employment benefit net liabilities (net of deferred tax) and average net borrowings. This average capital employed is then aggregated with the average restructuring and integration costs net of tax, and goodwill written off to reserves at 1 July 2004, the date of transition to IFRS, to obtain the average total invested capital.

RISK FACTORS

Diageo's products are sold in over 180 countries worldwide, which subjects Diageo to risks and uncertainties in multiple jurisdictions across developed and developing markets. The group's aim is to manage risk and control its business and financial activities cost-effectively and in a manner that enables it to: exploit profitable business opportunities in a disciplined way; avoid or reduce risks that can cause loss, reputational damage or business failure; manage and mitigate historic risks and exposures of the group; support operational effectiveness; and enhance resilience to external events. To achieve this, an ongoing process has been established for identifying, evaluating and managing risks faced by the group. A detailed description of the key risks and uncertainties facing the group are described in the 'Strategic report' section of the annual report for the year ended 30 June 2014 and under "Risk Factors" in the annual report on Form 20-F for the year ended 30 June 2014.

These key risks and uncertainties include: unfavourable economic conditions or political or other developments and risks in the countries in which Diageo operates; changes in consumer preferences and tastes and adverse impacts of a declining economy, among many factors, may adversely affect demand; litigation directed at the beverage alcohol industry and other litigation; climate change, or legal, regulatory or market measures to address climate change; water scarcity or poor quality; increased costs of raw materials or energy; regulatory decisions and changes in the legal and regulatory environment could increase Diageo's costs and liabilities or limit its business activities; increasing costs of monitoring and maintaining compliance with anti-corruption laws; failure to maintain Diageo's brand image and corporate reputation; competition may reduce Diageo's market share and margins; expected benefits may not be derived from Diageo's strategy focused on premium drinks or from its acquisitions or its cost-saving and restructuring programmes designed to enhance earnings; contamination, counterfeiting or other events could harm integrity of customer support for Diageo's brands and adversely affect the sales of those brands; increased costs or shortages of talent; disruption to production facilities, business service centres or information systems and change programs may not deliver the benefits intended; movements in the value of Diageo's pension funds, fluctuations [ 29-01-15 0701GMT ]

in exchange rates and interest rates; failure to maintain or renegotiate distribution, supply, manufacturing and licence agreements on favourable terms; inability to protect Diageo's intellectual property rights; and difficulty in effecting service of US process and enforcing US legal process against the directors of Diageo.

It notes that a rise in the global dairy prices in the overnight GlobalDairyTrade auction helped support NZD/USD although the fall in skim milk powder "was a poor sign." The pair is at 0.7788 and ANZ Bank tips a short-term range of 0.7730-0.7850. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com; @FarroHoward)

13:10 EST - With the US economy set to grow at a faster pace next year, helped along by the slump in oil prices, commodities markets must "fear a further strengthening" by the dollar, says Deutsche Bank. The Fed is likely to start raising rates in mid-2015, the firm says, even as Europe moves into QE mode to stave off falling prices. Deutsche Bank says precious metals and energy markets are likely to be worst off as the dollar gains. (matthew.cowley@wsj.com)

13:03 EST - The White House does not believe that Russia's ongoing currency troubles will have any major impact on the US economy. "If I was chairman of President Putin's Council of Economic Advisers, I would be extremely concerned. They are between a rock and a hard place in economic policy," Jason Furman, chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers, told reporters at the White House today. But he added: "In terms of the U.S. economy, we have enormous domestic strengths in terms of our consumers, their confidence, their increased spending, in terms of our businesses investing. Only 0.10 percent of the U.S. GDP is exports to Russia." (byron.tau@wsj.com)

12:59 EST - This year's grads are set to start work with a bang. Fifty-one percent of employers plan to offer signing bonuses to Class of 2015 college graduates--more than to any class in 5 years, according to a survey from the National Association of Colleges and Employers. Most of the signing bonuses will go to business, engineering or computer-science majors. Chemical-engineering majors are expected to receive the largest average signing bonuses at $5,250, followed by engineering without a sub-specialization at $5,107 and computer science at $4,364. (lindsay.gellman@wsj.com; @lindsaygellman)

12:56 EST - In the wake of last night's surprise rate hike in Russia and the continued slide of the ruble, Capital Economics' Andrew Kenningham says the "prospects for Russia's economy look even bleaker than they did a few days ago," declaring there's "now little doubt that Russia is heading for a deep recession." He acknowledges Russia's problems "will clearly have knock-on effects elsewhere," but cautions about blowing them out of proportion. "The economic links between Russia and the rest of the world are relatively small." (erik.holm@wsj.com; @erikholmwsj)

1632 GMT Greece is on track to meet its fiscal goals for a third straight year despite the political and economic uncertainty that has gripped the country for the last few weeks. The Bank of Greece, the country's central bank, says the budget target "is likely to be overachieved for the third year in a row, indicating that the improvement in fiscal aggregates is sustainable." Steep spending cuts have helped Greece's two-party coalition offset a drop in revenues in the first eleven months of the year. The latest data from the Finance Ministry shows that the central government's primary surplus--which doesn't take into account interest payments--rose to 3.53 billion euros for the January-to-November period, above the EUR2.9 billion target set by Greece's international creditors. (stelios.bouras@wsj.com)

On Tuesday, Newfoundland and Labrador said the projected budget deficit for FY14-15 would be C$916M, or nearly double the earlier forecast of C$538M. Mining, and oil-and-gas extraction account for nearly a third of Newfoundland's GDP, meaning the Atlantic province will be one of the big regional losers in Canada from the crude swoon. CIBC expects the Newfoundland economy to shrink 1% in 2015. (paul.vieira@wsj.com, @paulvieira).

11:06 EST - Treasurys are paring today's rally as safe-haven demand eases with oil trimming earlier declines and US stocks turn higher, encouraging some bond investors to book profits. David Ader of CRT Capital says Treasurys' gains have been "exaggerated" by year-end impacts. "Leading into year-end, investors are not wiling to take new risk" in things like the ruble, other EM assets or high-yield bonds. "They want to preserve capital and make fresh asset-allocation decisions in January." The 10-year Treasury is 10/32 higher, yielding 2.082%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

1603 GMT Denmark's central bank pencils in DKK75 billion in domestic government bond issuance in 2015, it says, broadly in line with the market's expectations. Next year's domestic issuance target is below this year's actual issuance of DKK102.64 billion, which slightly overshot the DKK100 billion target. Next year's strategy is to focus on the issuance of the 10-year nominal bond but also to build up the planned new two- and five-year debts, the central bank says. A new 2020-dated bond will be launched at the Feb. 4 auction, while a new 2018-dated two-year bond is planned in the first half of 2015, the central bank says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

markettalk@wsj.com

Given the scale of the savings, they downplay the idea that the fall indicates a softening of the global economy. Conversely, it's usually sharp oil-price spikes which touch off recessions. "There are no cases we know of when abundant, surplus crude-oil supplies and windfall savings for global consumers resulted in broad economic contractions." (anna.raff@wsj.com)

1548 GMT Law firm Linklaters says one side-effect of the plunging oil price might be a rise in Islamic finance capital markets activity. Neil Miller, global head of Islamic finance at Linklaters, says: "With the threat of a lower oil price landscape as we head into 2015, previous experience suggests that greater opportunities for the commercial financing of major projects may arise." Colleague, Jonathan Fried, Capital Markets partner at Linklaters in Dubai, adds "The flexibility and innovation seen in sukuk structures in 2014 will provide a strong foundation for the development of the sukuk market and its expansion into new sectors and geographies in 2015."(josie.cox@wsj.com)

title: CFTC Dollar Bulls Pull Back on Bets -- Market Talk
text:
16:45 EST - Investors grew less bullish on the dollar for the second straight week as growing fears over global growth and plunging oil prices sent investors in haven assets and prompted them to exit heavy strong-dollar bets. The net amount of investor cash wagering the greenback will rise against rivals fell 10.8% to $42.4B in the week ended Dec. 9, according to CFTC data. The moves unwound dollar gains on the back of robust US jobs data for November that had vaulted the greenback to fresh multi-year highs against the yen and euro just one trading session earlier. Accordingly, bearish euro and yen wagers thinned last week by 14.1% and 6.7%, respectively. Net bullish greenback positions should continue, as investors reduce risk and pull back on their largest bets, which include dollar-longs, ahead of next week's FOMC meeting. (james.ramage@wsj.com)

16:29 EST - Morningstar is lowering the rating for Actavis from triple-B to triple-B-minus, just one notch above junk, in response to the company's planned acquisition of Allergan for more than $65B. Morningstar notes that the cash portion of the deal will involve $27.5B of new term loans and bonds, and the company's debt to earnings ratio will rise to the mid-to-high 4s, up from 3.3 for Actavis at the end of September. But Morningstar says the firm's "commitment to deleveraging" and its increasing size and diversity keeps it in investment grade territory. (mike.cherney@wsj.com)

15:48 EST - Although "many investors are growing more positive" on America's biggest banks heading into 2015 on the grounds that regulatory and legal pressures are peaking and trading and investment banking are picking up, Nomura is "incrementally more cautious as we believe investors remain too complacent about the potential for sustained regulatory pressure." The investment bank expects further increases in capital requirements for the biggest banks as well as more pressure on FICC trading revenue--as big banks reduce short-term wholesale funding exposures--and net interest income as banks prepare for rules on liquidity and loss absorbing capital. (saabira.chaudhuri@wsj.com; @SaabiraC)

15:23 EST - The Fed's Board of Governors will hold a closed-door meeting Tuesday to discuss "medium-term monetary-policy issues," according to a notice posted today. That's also the first of the 2-day FOMC policy meeting. Meetings on the subject are becoming routine for the board, which also held them in October, September, July, June and April. It suggests officials are still working on, or at least discussing, the tools they'll eventually use to raise interest rates. (ben.leubsdorf@wsj.com; @BenLeubsdorf)

15:21 EST - Sanctions approved by the US this week on select members of Venezuela's regime come at a choice time, IHS says, as the risk consultancy expects "protests and riots to increase in the 1-year outlook because of an economic crisis." The sanctions won't affect Venezuela's vital oil industry, or any sector of the economy specifically. But that didn't stop President Maduro in a speech this week to lash out against congressional approval of the sanctions bill, which he told supporters were targeting the whole country. IHS says there is risk the government, already grappling with record-low approval ratings, may face instability if widespread protests--like the kind which broke out earlier this year--were to rise up again. (kejal.vyas@wsj.com)

14:52 EST - Investors can't always live with state-run companies and their politicized ways. But in emerging markets, can they always live without them? Wisdom Tree last week brought out the Emerging Markets ex-State-Owned Enterprises Fund, which tracks an index of only private-sector companies. Wisdom Tree advertises this as a way to bet on companies where there are lower risks of governments acting against the interests of minority shareholders. Trouble is, private companies in places like Asia, heavily controlled by families, aren't exactly paragons of investor friendliness. Plus, some investors may care about state firms precisely because they are sensitive to government actions, which matter much more in emerging economies than in richer ones. In India, a new business-friendly leader came to power this year and helped propel State Bank of India shares 75%, compared with 31% for the top 100 stocks. In China, the CSI Central State-owned Enterprises Composite index is up 51% this year, beating the broader market's 39% gain. In many emerging markets, governments do pick winners. (abheek.bhattacharya@wsj.com; @abheekb)

13:19 EST - Peru's central bank will continue to intervene in the forex market to ease volatility but won't affect broader direction, says the bank's chief economist. A good part of Peru's bank loans are in dollars, so big currency swings could hurt companies which have loans in the greenback but revenue in the sol. "Our economy doesn't have the luxury to permit abrupt depreciations," says Armas. "We are going to continue intervening to reduce volatility, but it won't go against the tendency." The sol has fallen some 6% this year against the dollar. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

13:00 EST - Peru's central bank again trims its 2014 economic-growth view, lowering it another half-point to 2.6%. There's been multiple cuts as this year progressed in the wake of weak output at the country's key mining sector. This year's GDP will pale in comparison to 2013's 5.8% advance. Central bank chief economist Adrian Armas says GDP growth should improve next year as commodity output recovers. "We expect a good recovery in the agriculture, fishing and mining sectors." (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1757 GMT As a major oil importer, the euro area should benefit from the slump in oil prices but the positive impact will be limited, Deutsche Bank says. "OPEC's decision to allow oil prices to fall creates a positive growth impact for the euro area, but only enough to broadly balance the weakness we had observed in investment and exports in recent months," the bank says in its European Outlook report for 2015. Lower oil prices should be at least modestly positive for real private consumption, the report says. The danger, however, is that cheaper oil could delay necessary monetary easing and well-designed structural reforms, the bank says. (georgi.kantchev@wsj.com) 


 
Contact us in London. +44-20-7842-9464 
markettalk@wsj.com 

12:27 EST - Argentina's primary fiscal deficit widened sharply in October, with the Finance Ministry saying the shortfall totaled ARS15.2B ($1.8B), versus ARS2.8B a year earlier, as revenues rose ARS17.7B and primary spending jumped ARS30.2B. The primary fiscal deficit, which excludes debt payments, is considered an indicator of the government's ability to finance its spending commitments and meet financial obligations. (robert.kozak@wsj.com; @robertkozak2)

11:50 EST - Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. plans to hike the "guarantee fees" some financial institutions pay to have residential loans backstopped in its MBS program. CMHC, Canada's dominant mortgage insurer, gets a fee in exchange for assurances which cover principal and interest payments. The fee increases, which take effect April 1, vary depending on the term of the MBS pool and are intended to help encourage "the development of alternative funding options in the private market." It's not immediately known what impact the fee increases will have on consumer pricing for mortgages. (rita.trichur@wsj.com; @ritatrichur)

1647 GMT Croatia's GDP is seen contracting 0.2% next year from the year-on-year decline of 0.7% expected in 2014. "Without hard solid evidence of public investment growth, while private investments remain on hold, we see a mild GDP contraction during 2015," says UniCredit analyst Hrvoje Dolenec. Croatian households are focusing on paring their debts, leaving the country's hospitality sector as the main economic driver. With public debts at above 80% of GDP, the country will need cooperating closely with the European Commission on its excessive deficit procedure, or EDP, regime, he adds. (leos.rousek@wsj.com, @LeoRousek)

title: Will MetLife Sue If It's Tabbed a SIFI? -- Market Talk
text:
13:30 EST - MetLife (MET) continued to stay mostly mum during its investor conference call this morning about possibly suing a new federal panel to avert being named a "systemically important financial institution." CEO Steven Kandarian was asked whether the House's passage this week of a bill giving the Fed more flexibility to tailor capital rules to the insurance industry makes suing unlikely. While "delighted" with the bill, he noted the rules have yet to be drafted, so "we don't know what those rules will be even with the flexibility they've been provided." If named a SIFI, "we'll look at the [panel's] reasoning and then we'll make a decision." (leslie.scism@wsj.com)

13:25 EST - The recent plunge in oil prices will have strong lasting positive impacts on many advanced economies including Continental Europe and Japan, Credit Suisse says. Lower oil prices will buoy equities in Europe and act as a tax cut to consumers there, as well as the U.S., the bank says. But the downside to cheaper crude will be disruptions in credit markets and oil company spending cuts that will ripple across energy stocks and hurt employment in the sector. Emerging markets that are big oil exporters -- including Russia and Brazil -- stand out as "major losers," the report said. Even as European equities gain, the U.S. high-yield market has been severely affected and returns are expected to stay down, Credit Suisse says. (lynn.cook@wsj.com; @LynnJCook)

13:24 EST - Duke Energy (DUK) says it has reached a deal with rooftop solar companies for its South Carolina utility customers who install solar panels. More than a dozen states are struggling with rules that require utilities to pay their solar customers for excess power from their panels, over concerns that non-solar customers end up footing the bill. Under the deal, Duke will pay its South Carolina solar customers for their excess electricity at Duke's retail power rate, through 2020. To cover the cost of the payments, Duke will charge its other customers a fee that represents the difference between the retail rate that Duke pays the solar customers and the actual value of their excess power. Duke and the solar firms will revisit the payment scheme in 2020 and potentially make changes that would start Jan. 1, 2021. (cassandra.sweet@wsj.com)

13:19 EST - Peru's central bank will continue to intervene in the forex market to ease volatility but won't affect broader direction, says the bank's chief economist. The sol has fallen some 6% this year against the dollar. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

13:13 EST - As the Dow industrials is looking at its 2nd-biggest percentage drop of 2014--and worst since January--with its current 3.3% decline, performance for the broader S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite both isn't as stark for the year with their 2%-plus slides. The S&P's 2.7% drop would only be the least in 2 months, though also the 2nd worst of 2014, while the Nasdaq's 2% decline only the 6th-biggest of 2014. Meanwhile, this would just be the 7th week this year that the DJIA falls more than 1%. (dan.strumpf@wsj.com)

13:00 EST - Peru's central bank again trims its 2014 economic-growth view, lowering it another half-point to 2.6%. There's been multiple cuts as this year progressed in the wake of weak output at the country's key mining sector. This year's GDP will pale in comparison to 2013's 5.8% advance. Central bank chief economist Adrian Armas says GDP growth should improve next year as commodity output recovers. "We expect a good recovery in the agriculture, fishing and mining sectors." (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

12:49 EST - German lender Commerzbank (CBK.XE) likely having to pay more than $1B to resolve probes examining whether the company violated US economic sanctions and money-laundering laws is a further sign of increased scrutiny on European banks by America. Prosecutors have been extracting massive fines from companies there for sanctions and money-laundering violations the last year, including an $8.9B settlement with BNP Paribas (BNP.FR). The Justice Department, Manhattan DA's office and New York state Superintendent of Financial Services have been investigating Commerzbank's alleged dealing with an Iranian state-sponsored shipping company while the Manhattan US Attorney's office is probing poor money-laundering controls. Shares fell 2.6% in Frankfurt in a broadly weak equities market. (christopher.matthews@wsj.com)

12:45 EST - An appeals court ruling that vacated the 2012 insider trading convictions of two former hedge-fund traders is reverberating through the downtown Manhattan federal court. Later this month, a judge set a hearing date to discuss whether the ruling would affect the guilty pleas of several other insider trading defendants. Some legal specialists are saying that prosecutors might have been wise to quit while they were ahead. Prosecutors continued to press ahead with cases that weren't as clear-cut, involving tippees further removed from the sources of information, and without the benefit of wiretaps that had bolstered the earlier string of convictions and guilty pleas. But alumni of the Manhattan U.S. attorney's office said the criticism is unfair and that the hardest cases were saved for last, and there was always a chance of defeat, a risk worth taking. (christopher.matthews@wsj.com)

12:43 EST - Much is being made of Wall Street's "win" this week on Capitol Hill by securing several long-sought changes to Dodd-Frank, particularly House passage of language which would significantly scale back a requirement that banks spin off certain swaps-trading activities. But the big banks suffered a few big losses this week, too. At the start the week was the Fed unveiling a new capital requirement for the 8 largest banks. There was also the PR damage Citigroup (C) and Wall Street generally sustained in liberal Democrats' fight against the swaps change, which doesn't help an industry that's been desperately trying to regain the public's trust. KBW analyst Brian Gardner tweeted last night, "on net, Wall St lost this week." (victoria.mcgrane@wsj.com; @vgmac)

12:40 EST - Kellogg (K) raised some eyebrows when it reduced the payouts executives would get if K gets acquired. Such a move has sometimes been a precursor to a sale, though it's also something corporate-governance experts advocate for at all companies. The change to K's "change of control" policy, disclosed in an SEC filing Thursday, came as the company has been struggling with persistently declining sales. A spokeswoman says K is simply updating the change-of-control policy "to better align with evolving market practices." Shares, which rebounded 3.6% yesterday amid the SEC filing, are down 1.8% today amid the broader market's slide. (annie.gasparro@wsj.com; @annie_gasparro)

12:31 EST - Sherwin-Williams (SHW) rallied 3% Thursday after announcing its HGTV Home paints will be stocked in Lowe's (LOW) stores starting in March. But during a conference call today, some analysts pressed the paint maker about the risk that such sales will cannibalize business at SHW's stores. CEO Chris Connor insisted that won't happen, adding some professional painters prefer buying supplies at big-box retailers. In a generally weak market, SHW is more than reversing yesterday's gains as shares slide 3.8%. (bob.hagerty@wsj.com)

12:27 EST - Argentina's primary fiscal deficit widened sharply in October, with the Finance Ministry saying the shortfall totaled ARS15.2B ($1.8B), versus ARS2.8B a year earlier, as revenues rose ARS17.7B and primary spending jumped ARS30.2B. The primary fiscal deficit, which excludes debt payments, is considered an indicator of the government's ability to finance its spending commitments and meet financial obligations. (robert.kozak@wsj.com; @robertkozak2)

Both confidence and conditions fell in September and "indicators suggest some reversion is probable," it says. NZD/AUD last at 0.8992. ANZ Bank tips a range of 0.8960 to 0.9060. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com; @FarroHoward)

14:01 EST - Hellman & Friedman is getting by with a little help from its friends. The San Francisco private-equity firm that has backed companies such as Nielsen NV and Getty Images wrapped up its latest mega-buyout fund with $10.9B. The firm raised $10.25B -- hitting its so-called "hard cap" -- from institutional investors including pension funds. Another half billion dollars came from the firm itself, with the rest coming from investors whom the firm termed as "friends and family." With the closing, Hellman & Friedman joins a select group of large-cap firms such as Silver Lake and Apollo Global Management (APO) that have been able to shrug off lingering uncertainty about the viability of large buyout pools and ended up with more interest than they could accommodate. (hillary.canada@wsj.com; @H_Canada)

13:57 EST - Investors traded options at a faster pace in October, pushing contract volume up 22% to 491.4 million from a year earlier, according to research from TABB Group. That's the second-highest monthly volume on record. Options volume in October was driven by a jump in market volatility, according to TABB research. The CBOE Volatility Index on Oct. 15 closed at 26.25, the highest level for the year. (saumya.vaishampayan@wsj.com; @saumvaish)

13:55 EST - The Colombian peso continued to weaken against the US dollar today amid falling crude oil prices and the slowdown of dollars coming into the economy, hitting 2,095.00, from 2,080.00 a week ago. Analysts at Bancolombia said "we see no turning of the tide," and that the peso will likely reach 2,146.00 in 2015. The fall is good news for exporters, and could help cushion any shock to the economy from lower oil prices, the government's biggest source of export revenues. (sara.munoz@wsj.com; @sarasmunoz)

13:53 EST - Farmer's Edge Laboratories is a private company that uses satellite images, computer modeling, soil sampling and weather data to help farmers increase their crop yields and get the most benefit from their land. Offering such products and services puts Farmer's Edge in direct competition with Monsanto (MON), a multinational agriculture biotechnology company that now offers similar big data and analytics products for farmers. The smaller company has a new ally as it squares off against this much-larger rival, however. Silicon Valley venture firm Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers has invested in the company. (timothy.hay@wsj.com)

13:52 EST - Airplane Wi-Fi provider GOGO was down some 7% through midday following its 3Q report, but that red is now green in the wake of AT&T (T) saying it will drop plans to offer a competing service. T disclosing its in-air Wi-Fi intentions in late April sent GOGO shares on a 1-day 29% stock swoon, a decline the company has yet to fully reverse. But with a big potential competitor out of the way and if GOGO can continue to log revenue growth like 3Q's 22%, shares might find an upward trajectory. They're up 1.4% at $16.87, trimming the year's slump to 32%. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com; @kevinkingsbury)

13:46 EST - ECB executive board member Yves Mersch says Germany's economy didn't do significantly better in 3Q after logging a 0.2% drop in 2Q, saying the Ifo and ZEW surveys "confirm this picture." He is speaking at an event in southwestern Germany sponsored by a local savings bank. Germany's statistics office publishes its first estimate on 3Q GDP Friday; forecasters polled by Dow Jones Newswires expect the German economy to have grown by 0.1%. (todd.buell@wsj.com)

13:42 EST - A big start for Alibaba's (BABA) financial-services operation as the 11/11 shopping event in China known as Singles Day--the country's version of Black Friday or Cyber Monday. Gross merchandise volume settled through the Alipay platform topped $1B within 18 minutes, the company says, with mobile accounting for 48%. And it took an hour and 12 seconds to hit $2B. Prior-year data weren't given. The figures, alas, don't include initial activity done through Alibaba itself, which controls some 80% of China's online-shopping market. But the Alipay numbers do give some insight, notably with mobile. BABA said last week that mobile GMV grew to 36% of the company's total last quarter. BABA rises to session highs on the news and is up 2.5% at $117.40. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com; @kevinkingsbury)

13:39 EST - Teck Resources owns 22.5% of Peru's largest copper mine, Antamina, where workers recently launched a strike seeking higher wages. While this disruption shouldn't last more than a few months, says BMO's Aleksandra Bukacheva, a year-long strike would slash the projected 2015 global copper surplus by nearly half to 330,000 metric tons. Teck's copper production would shrink 22% 238,000 tons and its zinc output would fall 8%. As a result, Teck's earnings could fall to CAN$0.69/share from a projected CAN$1.16/share, she adds. TCK shares were recently down 2.5% at $16.17 on NYSE. (tatyana.shumsky@wsj.com; @MissShumsky)

13:35 EST - The San Francisco Fed says in a new paper that the view that changes in the economy point to a lower level of interest rates may be wrong. "Future downward pressure on interest rates may be more muted than indicated by current monetary and fiscal policy projections, which would translate into an upside risk to these longer-term interest rate forecasts," bank economists write. They say economists' forecasts and historical data indicate fears the economy's potential growth rate, and its related level of interest rates, are simply overblown. (michael.derby@wsj.com, @michaelsderby)

13:23 EST - USDA's 2012 move to release market-moving crop reports -- such as today's monthly supply-and-demand estimates -- drew controversy, particularly among old-guard traders who fretted that algorithm-driven firms would get the jump on slower-moving, more fundamental players in the ag markets. Iowa brokerage firm AgriSource today says humans got one over on the machines: Contract prices for wheat, for instance, briefly jumped, but slid after market digested finer points of the lengthy report. "Looks like the High Frequency Traders (HFT) got nailed," AgriSource analysts gloat in a note to clients. (jacob.bunge@wsj.com; @jacobbunge)

title: Peru  Central Bank  Steps In Again to Slow Sol Slide -- Market Talk
text:
14:43 EST - Peru's central bank has stepped up interventions in the foreign exchange market in recent sessions as it looks to slow the depreciation of the sol against the US dollar. The central bank today sold $200M in the spot market, its biggest intervention since Sept. 26. That follows interventions yesterday and Friday, when the central bank sold $185M in each of those sessions. So far this year, the sol has depreciated 4.43% against the dollar. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

14:39 EST - A $1.5B bond sale from Noble Energy (NBL) is causing a bit of a selloff in bonds from other energy companies, one investor says. The firm is selling 10- and 30-year notes, with the latter offering a yield of 2.05 percentage points more than Treasurys, according to S&P Capital IQ LCD. That's cheap compared to its outstanding 2043 bonds, which traded yesterday at a spread of 1.80. Meanwhile, the yield spread on a 2044 Anadarko Petroleum bond rose 15 bps to 1.70 today, and the yield spread on a 2020 Transocean bond rose 27 bps to 4.56, according to MarketAxess. (mike.cherney@wsj.com)

14:36 EST - Two reports due tomorrow may shift expectations about Friday's October payrolls number. Joseph LaVorgna of Deutsche Bank says people concerned about the labor markets--and who isn't?--should pay attention to the ADP private-jobs report and the employment index within the ISM non-manufacturing report. An upside surprise for either could put an upside spin on projections for the payrolls number, says LaVorgna. For now, economists think the US economy added 233K net new jobs in October, a bit less than September's initial reading of 248K. (kathleen.madigan@wsj.com)

14:34 EST - The key message from last night's GlobalDairyTrade auction is that global dairy markets remain well-supplied in the short-term, says ANZ. "There were some signs" a 2Q revival could occur amid "some large improvement in powder prices for the April and May contracts," but that "was the only real ray of light." ANZ notes if weak prices persist through the peak sales period and the revival only occurs in the last quarter of the season, it will be very difficult for Fonterra to achieve its milk-price forecast of NZ$5.30/kilogram for solids. "We are anticipating further downside to the farm-gate price at the next update, which is likely to be in early December." ANZ is tipping a price around NZ$4.85/kg, which "would see further belt tightening from farmers." (rebecca.howard@wsj.com; @FarroHoward)

14:31 EST - Campus Crest's (CCG) plethora of news this morning included what RBC calls "significant and necessary changes which we believe should bring about positive long-term change, both in strategy and in operations." Leading off was the departure of the CEO and CFO, which the investment bank describes "as positive as confidence in prior management had eroded, making change in both leadership and direction necessary." Meanwhile, buying the remaining stakes in 30 properties owned with Copper Beach for $280M "should remove uncertainty, simplify CCG's ownership structure and allow CCG to better manage and dispose of assets as needed." And as the student-housing REITs stops its own construction, RBC says "development made little economic sense" for CCG. Shares bounce 16% to $7.32 after opening at a fresh record low of $6. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com; @kevinkingsbury)

14:30 EST - As TransCanada (TRP TRP.T) moves forward with a slate of multi-year, multi-billion dollar projects, it says it will look to raise money through project finance and joint venture partnerships, but also consider asset sales and common equity financing if needed. "As the balance sheet grows, we'll again chew through the cheaper sources of capital," such as debt, before tapping alternative financing methods, CFO Don Marchard said on a conference call. The Calgary-based company's capital spending program totals $46B, including $24B in oil and other liquids pipelines and $20B in natural gas pipelines. (chester.dawson@wsj.com; @DeleverTheFirm)

14:13 EST - "Despite a lackluster energy trading environment," accelerated cost-cutting at ICE "and an increased capital return are helping to offset these headwinds," says Jefferies in the wake of the exchange operator's 3Q profit beat. ICE last quarter accelerated cost synergies from its NYSE acquisition and has boosted the pace of stock buybacks, going from $350M in 2Q to $449M last quarter. Raymond James notes the earnings outperformance was largely on lower-than-expected compensation costs, coming as ICE again cut 2014 operating-expense guidance today. Shares rise 3.5% to $217.10, halving the year's decline. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com; @kevinkingsbury)

14:03 EST - Even the Eagle Ford Shale, considered one of the top oilfields to drill, has its rough spots. Baird has said the South Texas oilfield can be drilled with US benchmark crude as low as $53-$65 a barrel. But a new analysis by Bernstein shows that while some areas of the Eagle Ford can withstand low prices, a few of the region's counties are uneconomic even when oil is at $100 a barrel. Among the worst are Webb and McMullen counties, where Bernstein analysts say operators "could suffer if lower prices persist." (erin.ailworth@wsj.com; @ailworth)

14:00 EST - Amid Vitamin Shoppe's (VSI) 3Q miss, Sterne Agee downgrades the retailer to hold as it highlights "a sector on very-fragile footing, uncertainty regarding the future of senior management and the company's inability to forecast/control" margins. As consumers potentially move "toward other forms of more "natural" nutrition (i.e., flat out eating healthier) and no signs of a tangible industry response to reignite growth via innovation and/or a large-scale campaign to fight the negative press, visibility into a recovery is hazy at best." Wedbush, which downgrades to neutral, admits its recently lowered views on VSI weren't conservative enough as "multivitamin and fish-oil categories have not yet recovered from negative press" while "increased advertising spend to spur online sales proved ineffective." VSI falls 5.5% to $43.22. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com; @kevinkingsbury)

13:56 EST - Mexican brakes-and-suspension maker Rassini (RASSINI.MX) expects annual sales to reach $1B by late next year or early 2016 from current the $860M, says finance executive Juan Pablo Sanchez, as the company continues to sign new contracts and invests $54M in expansions in Mexico, the US and Brazil. The company this month changed its corporate name from San Luis to Rassini, its better-known brand name, and it will make the brakes for Audi's Q5 when the Volkswagen (VOW.XE) unit starts building those vehicles in Mexico in 2016. RASSINI.MX is up more than fivefold this year. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

13:55 EST - The power and utilities market seems to have recovered from the impact of private equity-backed Energy Future Holdings' collapse. Deal-making volume was up a141% to $11.1B during 3Q from $4.6B the prior year, according to PricewaterhouseCoopers US. The average deal size was also bigger as the same number of deals, 12, was recorded for both periods. The increase was due to strategic acquisitions by corporate players on the demand side, and divestitures of nonregulated power assets on the supply front, PwC says. Going forward, PwC predicts there may be "vertical integration of gas pipeline assets with power utilities." (shasha.dai@wsj.com; @ShashaDai)

13:48 EST - Arguments against current widespread use of antibiotics in meat production include fears that drug-resistant bacteria can spread to humans via meat products, but scientists see a new, six-legged threat: houseflies and other insects that could carry antibiotic-resistant bacteria from farms and wastewater facilities to cities or picnics. Kansas State University researchers tested bacteria found inside flies and roaches near swine and poultry farms and found they carried more drug-resistant bacteria than insects collected several miles away, according to KSU study published earlier this year. (jacob.bunge@wsj.com; @jacobbunge)
