title: Peru Sol Weakens, Even With  Central Bank  Selling Dollars -- Market Talk
text:
17:00 EDT - The Central Reserve Bank of Peruintervened in the foreign-exchange market today to sell US dollars, however the local sol currency still weakened. The central bank sold $95M at an average of PEN2.912 per dollar. That wasn't enough to stem the weakening of the sol, which depreciated to PEN2.912 from PEN2.908 in the previous session. So far this year, the sol has weakened 4% against the greenback. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

16:55 EDT - Pfizer (PFE) board member Suzanne Nora Johnson says the US could benefit from corporate tax reform. "The most important thing here is that we get some kind of tax reform that makes the U.S. [stronger] in a competitive situation and that is critical because if we really do want to be on a level playing field with the rest of the world, then we're going to need to get it right," Johnson says on CNBC. PFE earlier this year dropped a $120B bid for AstraZeneca (AZN) which would've been a so-called inversion. (gillian.tan@wsj.com, @GillianTan)

16:53 EDT - RBC Capital Markets analyst Mark Mahaney expects Twitter (TWTR) to report $332M in revenue for the three months through September, a forecast that is below a consensus of around $352M. While Mr. Mahaney is optimistic TWTR can grow into one of the major consumer tech companies such as social networking rival Facebook (FB), he said the company still needs to prove it can increase its reach with advertisers as well as its user base and engagement metrics. "That said, we'd argue that TWTR's 'mainstreamization' efforts have just recently begun." Mr. Mahaney estimates Twitter's user base will reach 280 million, adding 9 million from the previous quarter. TWTR reports 3Q earnings on Monday after the market closes. (yoree.koh@wsj.com)

16:38 EDT - P&G (PG) has been "a U.S. domiciled company for 177 years so if the past is any indication of the future, we're not going anywhere," CFO Jon Moeller says on CNBC in response to a question about inversions from Perella Weinberg co-founder Peter Weinberg. "When you have an uncompetitive tax rate and an economy that's globalizing, three things are bound to happen relative to domicile and M&A," Moeller said. Companies will move, they'll will get started offshore rather than onshore and "U.S. assets will be purchased by foreign interests simply because of the tax arbitrage that's there to fuel those transactions," he added. Those are among reasons the US should consider tax reform, he says. "I think there are big stakes here, we're talking about American jobs, American industry and American standard of living," he added. (gillian.tan@wsj.com, @GillianTan)

16:24 EDT - When Venezuela earlier this month changed the terms under which it repays China with oil for billions of dollars in loans, speculation soared over what it means for the cash-strapped South American country. Some commentators called it a default. But BofA says it's wrong to do so because there is no change to the loans' face value and "does not alter the financial commitments of Venezuela." The new repayment structure scraps the daily requirement of 330,000 bpd of oil to China. Instead, it allows Venezuela to only send as much oil as necessary to pay for loans, BofA says. For example, high oil prices last year meant Venezuela was sending more barrels than were needed and ended up getting $9.6B back from overpayment, bank notes. (kejal.vyas@wsj.com; @kejalvyas)

16:14 EDT - Remember those edgy days for US stocks last week, when terms like "correction," and even "capitulation," were being tossed around? Feels kind of silly now, doesn't it, after S&P 500 vaults more than 4% higher for the week, Nasdaq Comp up 5.3% and blue chips up a relatively pedestrian 2.6%. All the worries of a global economic slowdown have faded -- though the risks still loom -- and investors are pleased with earnings reports that put companies on track to post roughly the same profit and sales growth they saw in 2Q, up about 7.5% and maybe 4%, respectively. DJIA up 127.51 to 16805.41, and Nasdaq Comp climbs 30.92 to 4483.72. S&P 500 ends 13.76 higher at 1964.58. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

16:07 EDT - Investors grew slightly less bullish on the dollar, and less bearish on the yen, after fears of a slowdown in growth in the world's largest economies erupted on Oct. 15, sending bond yields and stocks plunging as volatility throttled financial markets. The net amount of investor cash betting the dollar would rise slipped 4.3% to $41.4B in the week ended Oct. 21, according to CFTC data. Meanwhile, investors squared some of their yen short wagers versus the greenback, paring net bearish bets to 29% last week to $8.4B. Earlier this week, the dollar-selloff stabilized. Next week's numbers should reflect a moderate recovery in bullish dollar positions on the back of stronger US data. (james.ramage@wsj.com)

15:50 EDT - The Fed's Board of Governors will hold a closed meeting Tuesday, with "Discussion of Medium-Term Monetary Policy Issues" on the agenda, according to a notice posted today. A two-day Federal Open Market Committee meeting starts the same day, and similar board meetings accompanied the central bank's September, July, June and April policy meetings. That suggests Fed officials are continuing to discuss the tools they'll use to eventually raise interest rates, even after releasing a "Policy Normalization Principles and Plans" statement last month. (ben.leubsdorf@wsj.com, @BenLeubsdorf)

15:33 EDT - The USDA's cattle-on-feed report provides new evidence that fewer female animals are entering the food supply chain as ranchers work to increase production by breeding the next generation of beef calves, rather than fattening those cattle for meat. Heifers and heifer calves, which are females that have yet to give birth, in commercial feedyards through Oct 1 totaled 3.55 million head, down 3% from the same time last year, compared with a 1% drop in the number of all cattle on feed. The nation's herd is at its smallest size in decades, contributing to a surge in the price of burgers and steaks. (kelsey.gee@wsj.com; @kelseykgee)

15:30 EDT - Railroad and truck freight broker Hub Group (HUBG) is down 12% at $34.33 after reporting a 76% decrease in 3Q net income amid special charges and tough market conditions. A shortage of truck drivers and traffic-clogged railroads contributed to a 2% decline in revenue from HUBG's intermodal rail business. The company estimates that rail-service problems cost about 7c/share in 3Q profit. Excluding the charges, HUBG reported EPS of 49c vs Street's 53c expectation. CEO David Yeager told analysts that rail service will improve as the railroads add more crews and locomotives, but he doesn't expect normal service to resume before next spring. (robert.tita@wsj.com, @bob_tita)

15:30 EDT - It's a kooky idea, and probably has zero chance of seeing the light of day. So why does Marc Chandler, currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman, raise the possibility that the ECB might buy Treasuries instead of other assets like covered bonds and ABS as it looks to ease monetary policy? Because technically it gets around a key problem the ECB faces--which countries' or companies' bonds it should buy. "The ECB could take a page from the Swiss National Bank's playbook," says Chandler. "It could say that it would like to buy member bonds, but the legal and political hurdles are insurmountable. Instead, it will buy foreign bonds, and for transparency, liquidity and safety, US Treasuries stand out." (pedro.dacosta@wsj.com; @pdacosta)

15:10 EDT - Got a feeling the top people running the company are sometimes out of touch? You're not alone. A survey of 316 executives and managers by a division of the American Management Association finds one-third of those polled said their organization's senior team operates within "a leadership bubble" most of the time. Half indicated this occurs at least occasionally. Asked if they've ever experienced out-of-touch leadership, 90% of respondents said the leadership team usually or sometimes wasn't aware of the problem. Most survey participants blamed poor internal communications or the corporate culture. But only 16% said the problem was due to the CEO's personality. (joann.lublin@wsj.com)

title: Peru  Central Bank  Sells Dollars to Support Sol -- Market Talk
text:
16:30 EDT - Peru's central bankintervenes in the FX market, selling $10M today at PEN2.9051 per US dollar, aiming to support the weakening sol. So far this year the sol has depreciated 3.82% against the greenback, ending today at PEN2.9070. A survey of 21 economic analysts conducted by the central bank recently found expectations that the sol will end this year at PEN2.90 per dollar. (robert.kozak@wsj.com @robertkozak2)

16:02 EDT - Companies shipped 8.3B barrels of oil on US pipelines in 2013, up 11% from a year ago, according to federal data compiled by two industry associations and published today. The surging volume of crude shipments outpaced construction of new pipelines, which increased 6% in 2013 from the previous year, according to the Association of Oil Pipe Lines and the American Petroleum Institute. The data highlight how drillers are tapping oil from shale-rock formations faster than companies can build new pipelines, even as railroads are taking on a much bigger role in carrying crude. (daniel.gilbert@wsj.com; @WSJGilbert)

15:31 EDT - Overnight strength in AUD and JPY saw the respective NZD crosses push toward the bottom end of recent ranges. NZD/AUD is at 0.8895, close to the 2014 low of 0.8860. BNZ FX strategist Raiko Shareef says if Thursday's jobs data out of Australia is robust, the pair may see a short-term break to 0.8800. He expects the pair at 0.8900 by year-end. NZD/JPY is at 84.66, close to the 84.50 level which proved "fairly robust" early in the year. He doesn't expect a sustainable break below 84.00 in the near-term. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com; @FarroHoward)

1924 GMT - NZD/USD is benefiting as markets continue to sell USD, says ANZ Bank. Attention is now on the September FOMC minutes later in the global trading day and "we expect the USD to continue to consolidate implying NZD/USD support," it says. It notes the HSBC China PMI for September will also provide some insight into how the Chinese economy is faring. The pair is at 0.7836 early in New Zealand and ANZ Bank tips a short-term range of 0.7800 to 0.7900. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com; @FarroHoward)

15:09 EDT - New York Fed chief William Dudley says the market's view that the Fed will hold off on rate hikes until mid-2015 looks reasonable. "It still is premature to begin to raise interest rates--the labor market still has too much slack and the inflation rate is too low," he says, adding that policy moves will depend on how data evolve. While he welcomes the current path the economy is on, he sees little risk of an upside surprise, and adds that inflation will likely remain below the Fed's 2% target by 2015-end. Dudley's remarks are a reminder that as much as the heat in the Fed debate centers around raising rate sooner than expected, core officials are still reluctant to end their de facto zero-bound interest-rate stance. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

14:44 EDT - The bond rally is extending as stocks hit fresh session lows, dragging the 30-year yield down to 3.054%, its lowest of 2014. Slumping stocks and concerns about economies overseas are fueling a flight into safer assets. Bond investors, for now, seem to be setting aside concerns about Fed tightening, with shorter-dated notes rallying as well. Still, the long bond is leading the way given a lack of global inflation. That's ironing out the Treasury yield curve. The 2- to 30-year yield gap now just 2.55 percentage points, the smallest this year. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; @cynthialin_dj)

14:22 EDT - Uber-dove Kocherlakota is warning against any push to raise interest rates next year. The Minneapolis Fed chief doesn't expect inflation, as measured by the PCE price index, to rise to the central bank's 2% goal until 2018. Because of that, "it would be inappropriate for the [Federal Open Market Committee] to raise the target range for the Fed-funds rate at any such meeting" that's scheduled for 2015. Kocherlakota also wants the Fed to defend its price target just as strongly from the low side as the high side, and he's worried the current arc of Fed policy won't do that. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

13:57 EDT - In the latest warning sign about Venezuela's precarious financial position, the foreign exchange hoard at Venezuela's central bank shrank by about $1.8B, or 8%, last Friday. Analysts at Barclays bet the cash left the bank's accounts to pay off the government's $1.5B in sovereign debt maturing on Wednesday. Conventional economic policy says countries shouldn't make a habit of tapping their FX backstop to pay down debt. Venezuela, facing a dollar shortage and severe structural issues, is in trouble but widely expected to scrape together the cash to pay off the debt maturing this year. That may be harder in 2015. (matt.day@wsj.com)

13:40 EDT - As U.S. recovery continues and markets price in greater chance of Fed rate hikes, Canadian market rates will also likely rise, tightening domestic financial conditions and raising mortgage costs, Bank of America Merrill Lynch says. This, it says, will cool Canada's housing market, push back the timing of Bank of Canada rate hikes, and reduce the need for hawkish guidance. "Thus, the BOC can sit back, relax and let the Fed take the punchbowl away." BOC deputy governor Tim Lane acknowledged recently that "renormalization" of U.S. monetary policy will tighten Canadian monetary and financial conditions, signaling no hurry to hike rates. (nirmala.menon, @NirmalaMenon)

13:20 EDT - HSBC's 2.1% year-end forecast for the 10-year yield isn't looking so unreasonable with the rate falling another 6 basis points today to 2.361%. The investment bank has maintained its out-of-consensus call all year, arguing that Fed policy and economic uncertainties will prevent the yield from rising to the more-widely expected 3% by year-end. "We believe the US economy cannot take higher yields and that the Fed will adjust policy in response to bond-market moves, as it did with tapering in 2013." And when Fed tightening does come, HSBC sees shallower hikes than the market expects, which should support 3- to 5-year Treasurys. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; @cynthialin_dj)

13:11 EDT - Solid demand at the 3-year auction allows Treasury to pay a borrowing cost of just 0.994%. There were enough bids to cover the $27B sale 3.42 times over, matching 2014's high for 3s. Indirect bidders, often a reflection of overseas appetite, take 35.5% of the supply--above the group's recent 33.5% average--while direct bidders get an on-par 17.4%. Treasurys continue to fly high after the auction results, with prices holding around session highs. Looks like concerns about global growth is trumping concerns about the Fed potentially raising rates next year. Ten-year notes up 17/32 to yield 2.364%. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; @cynthialin_dj)

13:02 EDT - The IMF's latest barometer of global home prices in 50 countries shows they're little changed since 2008, but averages in this case are misleading. The IMF divided those countries into two groups. The first group of 33 "recovering" housing markets had a big property boom before the recession and a crash thereafter. Prices in those countries are around 20% below their 2008 level. That group includes the U.S., Spain, Italy, and Japan. The second group of 17 "rebounded" housing markets had less of a downturn and a much stronger recovery from the 2008 crash. Prices in this group, which includes China, Australia, and Canada, are up 25% since 2008. (nick.timiraos@wsj.com; @NickTimiraos)

The Woodlands, Texas-based retailer announced it was exploring strategic alternatives as its stock continues to suffer from its consumer credit portfolio division. "At this point we're evaluating options; it's too early to say whether one alternative is preferred in particular," Wright says. Likely options include selling the company, splitting up its retail and credit divisions, or slowing down on new store openings. "The announcement wasn't related to any financial distress or lack of available capital," Wright adds. CONN down from $44.83 in late August to close at $28.55 today. (lillian.rizzo@wsj.com)

Boroff, a Massachusetts judge, is stepping in for Judge Bruce A. Harwood, who recused himself. The sapphire screen supplier, which filed for bankruptcy yesterday, has been tight-lipped about its reasons for seeking Chapter 11, saying only in court papers that it was suffering "a severe liquidity crisis due to circumstances that will be more fully described at the hearing." WSJ reported that "liquidity crisis" stems from AAPL withholding a $139M payment. GTAT collapsed 93% Monday following the surprise bankruptcy filing, wiping out roughly $1.4B in market value. Shares bounced 51% to close today at $1.21. (patrick.fitzgerald@wsj.com, @patfitzgerald23)

16:21 EDT - Microsoft (MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella made a personal appeal to the software maker's core business audience during a wide-ranging interview with analysts at the Gartner Symposium IT/xpo Tuesday. "There is no question that we won't exist if we don't serve you well," Mr. Nadella said. "We want to be in tune with... the value we create for customers." Microsoft over the last several months has made some major changes to better address competition from Amazon.com, Google and others in the mobile and cloud technology segments. In March, the company introduced Office productivity software for Apple devices. In July, the company said that it would cut 18,000 jobs and make operations for agile. (clint.boulton@wsj.com)

16:16 EDT - Telecom companies could face an even louder wakeup call as a growing Internet gets too big for some outdated equipment. Some carriers suffered Web outages in August after a blip briefly puffed up the size of the Internet's map of routes, and network research by Dyn suggests the worry isn't over yet. The Internet is set to grow again beyond the so-called 512K route threshold that stresses older gear in mid-November, Dyn researcher Jim Cowie tells an audience at NANOG, the quarterly conference for network engineers. A research note last month from Wells Fargo suggested the threat could spur a small but noticeable uptick in spending on certain network gear. (andrew.fitzgerald@wsj.com; @drewfitzgerald)

16:12 EDT - Dow Industrials 209-point Friday rally proves fleeting as the index coughs up about 290 in the subsequent two sessions. Swirl of data and commentary about weakening global growth -- and perhaps a sense that central bankers have flopped in efforts to fuel a sustainable vigorous pickup -- sends equities tumbling. Crude oil hits its lowest settlement since April 22, 2013, and heating oil -- on the precipice of heating season, no less -- sees its lowest settle since June 2012. Ten-year Treasury yield reaches 4th lowest this year. Not convincing signs of a burgeoning economy. DJIA falls 272.58 to 16719.33, and Nasdaq Comp loses 69.60 to 4385.20. S&P 500 ends 29.72 lower at 1935.10. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

16:02 EDT - Companies shipped 8.3B barrels of oil on US pipelines in 2013, up 11% from a year ago, according to federal data compiled by two industry associations and published today. The data highlight how drillers are tapping oil from shale-rock formations faster than companies can build new pipelines, even as railroads are taking on a much bigger role in carrying crude. (daniel.gilbert@wsj.com; @WSJGilbert)

15:44 EDT - DJIA looks to be headed for its third 200-point-plus move in five sessions (two down, one up), and its 10th triple-digit move in the past 16 sessions. The last time the Dow moved at least 200 points in three out of five sessions was in late November 2011 (also two down, one up) when Europe's debt crisis was really cooking. Top central bankers then unleashed a "coordinated" action that sent stocks ripping higher, with the Dow roaring up 490 points on Nov 30, 2011, culminating a three-gain rally that tacked on more than 800 points. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

15:31 EDT - Overnight strength in AUD and JPY saw the respective NZD crosses push toward the bottom end of recent ranges. NZD/AUD is at 0.8895, close to the 2014 low of 0.8860. BNZ FX strategist Raiko Shareef says if Thursday's jobs data out of Australia is robust, the pair may see a short-term break to 0.8800. He expects the pair at 0.8900 by year-end. NZD/JPY is at 84.66, close to the 84.50 level which proved "fairly robust" early in the year. He doesn't expect a sustainable break below 84.00 in the near-term. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com; @FarroHoward)

15:27 EDT - Sen. Charles Schumer (D., N.Y.) says the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is preparing to implement tougher Ebola screening requirements at US airports this week. Following a call with the health agency's director, Schumer says the measures will go beyond steps announced by the Obama administration yesterday and may reflect recommendations the senator outlined in a letter to the CDC earlier this month. Schumer had called for active screening -- including taking temperatures -- and creation of a passenger database to be shared with hospitals for passengers arriving from Ebola hotspots in Africa. "The CDC has been doing a very good job thus far in combating the threat, but you can't be too careful when it comes to stopping a deadly epidemic," Schumer says. (jeffrey.sparshott@wsj.com)

15:16 EDT - An apparent denial by Interacciones (GFINTERO.MX) CEO Carlos Hank Gonzalez that his family's niche financial institution is poised to merge with Mexican bank Banorte (GFNORTEO.MX) should relieve share-price pressure of the latter, says brokerage Ve por Mas. Shares are down 9% within the past month amid local press reports about a potential combination. GFINTERO.MX said today that Hank is resigning to join GFNORTEO.MX's board, but it's said the decision isn't due to an agreement to merge the firms. GFNORTEO.MX is down 0.8% today and GFINTERO.MX falls 0.9%; that stock has surged 82% this year. (amy.guthrie@wsj.com)

15:09 EDT - New York Fed chief William Dudley says the market's view that the Fed will hold off on rate hikes until mid-2015 looks reasonable. "It still is premature to begin to raise interest rates--the labor market still has too much slack and the inflation rate is too low," he says, adding that policy moves will depend on how data evolve. While he welcomes the current path the economy is on, he sees little risk of an upside surprise, and adds that inflation will likely remain below the Fed's 2% target by 2015-end. Dudley's remarks are a reminder that as much as the heat in the Fed debate centers around raising rate sooner than expected, core officials are still reluctant to end their de facto zero-bound interest-rate stance. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

title: UPDATE 1-Peru's  central bank  sells $10 million, sol ends at new 5-yr low
text:
(Adds context)

LIMA, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Peru's central bank sold $10 million in the local spot market on Tuesday as the sol currency weakened 0.07 percent to finish bidding at 2.905 per dollar, the lowest level in nearly five years.

The sol hit its worst level since November 2009 after the International Monetary Fund cut its forecast for growth in Peru and Latin America this year.

The central bank's intervention was the latest of several in recent weeks as local demand for dollars has surged on the greenback's rise globally. (Reporting by Ursula Scollo; Editing by Meredith Mazzilli and Leslie Adler) 

Released: 2014-10-7T19:55:35.000Z

title: Peru Central Bank Intervenes  Again to Support Sol -- Market Talk
text:
17:10 EDT - Peru's central bank today sold $60M in the foreign exchange market, aiming to support the sol, which closed at PEN2.895 per US dollar, compared with PEN2.888 Friday. The central bank on Friday sold $423M, also aiming to ease depreciation pressures on the local currency. So far this year, the sol has weakened 3.4% against the dollar. (Robert.kozak@wsj.com @robertkozak2)

17:02 EDT - Cocoa butter prices are heating up again, one more factor keeping cocoa-bean futures aloft. In the week ended September 26, cocoa butter, the substance that gives chocolate its creamy texture, was going for $8,542 a ton in the US, according to the Cocoa Merchants Association of America, a trade group. Cocoa-butter prices are up 7.2% over the past two weeks, just as cocoa futures were touching fresh 3 1/2-year highs, fueled by concerns that Ebola could spread into Ivory Coast from Liberia, and hinder the harvest and transport of cocoa from the world's top producer. ICE cocoa ended flat at $3,311/ton. (leslie.josephs@wsj.com; @lesliejosephs)

16:44 EDT - The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says it has the power to go back several years in scrutinizing whether banks mistreated homeowners during the foreclosure crisis. The consumer-finance regulator today reached a $37.5M settlement with Flagstar Bancorp (FBC) over alleged mistreatment of homeowners dating back to 2011. CFPB officials say they have the power to pursue financial firms under tough mortgage-servicing standards that went into effect earlier this year. In addition, CFPB officials say the 2010 Dodd-Frank law allows them to pursue similar allegations for conduct that happened before the mortgage rules went into effect. That aggressive posture from the government's consumer watchdog is likely to unnerve many in the banking industry. (alan.zibel@wsj.com)

16:35 EDT - AUD/NZD is likely to target a move above 1.1310 in the days ahead, which would mark the highest since November 2013, as "the NZD is likely to remain weighed down by the threat of further RBNZ intervention," says Westpaccurrency strategist Imre Speizer. He adds that the highlight of the upcoming session should be the HSBC China manufacturing PMI, although NZ has building permits and monthly business confidence and Australia has credit data and weekly consumer confidence data as well. Speizer adds it seems a multi-year reversal in the cross probably began in January at 1.0493. The pair last at 1.1226. (lucy.craymer@wsj.com; @lucy_craymer)

16:27 EDT - With a pair of U.S. Senate Democrats on one end and the European Union on the other, the Obama administration finds itself in the middle of a tug-of-war over whether exports of oil and natural gas should be included in any trade agreement between the U.S. and the EU. Democratic Sens. Barbara Boxer of California and Edward Markey of Massachusetts are urging against such a move, while the EU has been asking for just that. It's unlikely any trade agreement is imminent, but this tension will only grow alongside the growing U.S. oil and gas production. (amy.harder@wsj.com; @AmyAHarder)

16:26 EDT - NZD/USD has been the worst-performing currency over the past session after the New Zealand central bank's latest FX transaction figures show it sold NZ$521M in August, says BNZ strategist Kymberly Martin. "However, after its precipitous fall, we are wary of a bounce...particularly if the USD uptrend runs out of momentum." Pair down 1.25% at 0.7766. Martin says the upcoming session's domestic focus will be the release of the ANZ business confidence survey for September. She now sees a clear band of support at the mid-2013 lows around 0.7690. (lucy.craymer@wsj.com; @lucy_craymer)

16:23 EDT - Moody's says the declining student-loan default rate that the Department of Education recently posted is a credit positive for US higher education. Improving figures lesson some risks that accompany high default rates, like reputational damage for schools, loss of access to federal financial aid programs and accreditation sanctions, the ratings firm says. Moody's expects default rates to decline during the next few years, though "pockets of risk will persist" at community colleges, for-profit institutions and historically black colleges and university. (melissa.korn@wsj.com; @melissakorn)

16:13 EDT - Moral victory today for bulls, who were able to recover the lion's share of steep opening losses by the closing bell. The Dow Industrials also avoided a sixth straight triple-digit daily move after falling almost 180 points shortly after the open. Some of the nervousness in equities markets gets pinned on pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong, though the lurching moves during the past few sessions shows investors can be fickle when eyeing expensive stock markets. Materials, energy and financials were the biggest laggards, while utilities finish higher. DJIA falls 41.93 to 17071.22, and Nasdaq Comp sheds 6.34 (earlier off about 48) to 4505.85. S&P 500 ends 5.05 lower at 1977.80. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

15:55 EDT - Ford Credit, the finance arm of Ford Motor (F), says today that subprime auto lending has returned to the levels seen in 2007, but loan losses remain consistently healthy. The company says 15% of loans qualify as subprime -- a rate not seen since before the financial crisis. Ford will now begin offering 75-month terms on loans, a new high in terms of length of maturity. (john.stoll@wsj.com)

15:51 EDT - Boutique researcher MoffettNathanson's first ratings on network operators Level 3 (LVLT) and Cogent (CCOI) are a buy. The firm reasons that both telcos, despite very different business models, should see free cash flow "surge" in coming years as they skim more profitable business customers off incumbents providers' base. LVLT could also save hundreds of millions by refinancing debt. Still, fears of network connection disputes and LVLT's unwieldy footprint have kept both companies' multiples relatively low. The firm suggests both are bargains as it pins a $43 price target on CCOI and forecasts $57 for LVLT. Bandwidth discounter CCOI gains 1.8% to $34.23, while much larger LVLT jumps 3% to $45.98. (andrew.fitzgerald@wsj.com; @drewfitzgerald)

15:47 EDT - So much for the Bill Gross-driven selloff. Treasury prices up broadly today as haven demand trump the fallout from Gross's abrupt departure from Pimco, announced Friday. "The Treasury bond market is very large...I am confident that the bond market will move beyond this news as it has so many other noteworthy events," says James Sarni, senior managing partner at Payden & Rygel, which manages about $85B. The 10-year note is 12/32 higher, yielding 2.490%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

15:39 EDT - The dollar store saga over Family Dollar (FDO) is "far from over," Deutsche Bank says, as it calls on investors to be patient over the next couple months as the discount chain decides between being sold to Dollar Tree (DLTR) or Dollar General (DG). FDO needs more "downside protection" before cozying up to DG because should both deals fall apart, FDO would likely trade around $59, more than 23% off current levels. The firm expects DLTR to up its "last & final" offer in the coming weeks, but still is betting on DG to prevail in this fight. FDO nearly flat at $77.52. (paul.ziobro@wsj.com; @pziobro)

Fisher shrugs off the recent round of weak inflation data and says a lot of the softness comes from supply rather than demand-related factors. "Does it worry me that we are not at our 2% intermediate-term target? It does not" because what's being seen now in the data represents "benign price stability," he says. Fisher is an FOMC voter and a long-time opponent of the central bank's easy money policy stance. (michael.derby@wsj.com)

Stocks in Hong Kong sank by nearly 2% overnight and the selling spread to equity markets in Europe and the US as Hong Kong police clash with protesters. "Depending on how the protests advance, the situation in Hong Kong could increasingly become problematic for mainland China and the government's ability to institute reforms while also boosting growth." Ten-year notes up 12/32, yielding 2.490%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

The holdout creditors want the judge to impose a fine of $50,000 a day, and this is not unprecedented: U.S. judges have ordered similar contempt sanctions for Russia and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The problem is that court-ordered sanctions would raise questions about a New York judge setting U.S. foreign policy, and no one can really force Argentina to comply with the sanctions. But if the judge doesn't punish Argentina for circumventing his orders, will that make sovereign nations less likely to comply with U.S. rulings in the future? (nicole.hong@wsj.com)

14:29 EDT - The Fed says it will make interest payments on bank reserves a primary part of its strategy for raising rates in the future, but some observers tell the WSJ that could be a political minefield. As the Fed raises rates, those payments will increase. Since the Fed remits most of its profits to the US Treasury, the higher payments will lower the revenue the Fed sends to taxpayers. As former St. Louis Fed President William Poole tells the Journal, "It's highly likely that some politicians will notice that and given the proclivity of some politicians anyway to demagogue issues, the Fed is going to have some political explaining to do." WSJ's analysis also shows those payments are increasingly going to foreign banks, which could raise eyebrows on Capitol Hill. (ryan.tracy@wsj.com)

Some of the recent drop in the workforce participation rate is due to the retirement of baby boomers, Ms. Stevenson acknowledged. But she added: "Not all of the decline in participation we have seen is the result of natural and good developments. In fact, the long-term trend of declining participation in employment rates for many groups, such as prime-age men, and particularly young black men, is troubling, and merits a policy response," she said. (pedro.dacosta@wsj.com)

17:00 EDT - AUD/USD recovering slightly from an early-week slump, but investors will be watching for comments from RBA Governor Stevens, who is speaking on an economic panel today, says BNZ FX strategist Raiko Shareef. He notes the RBA "came out swinging" against the speculative elements of Australia's housing market in its semi-annual Financial Stability Report, calling the housing market "unbalanced" and flagging it was in discussions with other regulators about further steps to curb pressures. Steven's remarks will be "watched closely for hints as to the types and timing of macro-prudential tools," Shareef says. AUD/USD last at 0.8886, from 0.8925 at the start of the week. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com; @FarroHoward)

16:43 EDT - Commercial paper outstanding from nonbank borrowers totaled $307B as of Sept. 17, Federal Reserve data show, the highest amount since January 2001. The surge is fueled by low interest rates and rising demand by money market funds that are struggling to find higher-yielding investments, said Chris Conetta, head of global CP trading at Barclays. Yields for the shortest-term Treasurys fell below zero after the Fed said it is curbing its overnight-lending program. Companies with the highest ratings were able to borrow from the Fed at 0.04% for seven days as of Tuesday, down from 0.07% on Sept. 17. Conetta observed, "Money in the shortest-term markets is basically free and it's only getting freer." (vipal.monga@wsj.com; @vipalmonga)

16:31 EDT - Forsyth Barr lifts its 12-month target price on the Fonterra Shareholders Fund (FSF.NZ) by NZ$0.30 to NZ$6.80 on increased optimism about long-term growth opportunities in Asia. FSF closed at NZ$6.29. Wednesday. Firm notes that Fonterra reported mixed fiscal 2014 results, with EBIT coming in at the bottom end of the guidance range, so it retains a neutral rating due to short-term capacity risks. However, "in a year of significant headwinds, the Asia division achieved a sound result, with price increases helping partially offset the higher input costs and disrupted sales volumes." Fonterra is "well-leveraged" to the growing Asian dairy market, says Forsyth Barr. (rebecca.howard@wsj.com; @FarroHoward)

16:16 EDT - Today brought a bit of good news and a hint of bad news for Petrobras' (PBR) costly Abreu e Lima refinery project. First, the country's oil regulatory body approved the lifting of crude from the refinery, a small but important step to its operations, which is set to begin in November. But the country's main auditing body says today that it found irregularities concerning the refinery, without elaborating. The refinery has been a sore spot for Petrobras, with delays and financing difficulties. The final cost could eventually balloon to as much as $20B, quite a bit higher than the original $4B price tag. (william.connors@wsj.com)

15:55 EDT - Oil cartel struggles to cope with falling prices--the heart bleeds, surely. Sympathizing aside, OPEC's fiscal health is a big factor in arresting the slide in oil prices, down 15% in three months. In a report published Wednesday, Citigroup estimates oil prices at which various major exporters balance their books. These range from $44 a barrel for Kuwait up to $184 for Libya. Some big producers are squarely in deficit territory. Iran's price is $130, for example, while Venezuela's is $161. Brent's average so far this year--the key metric rather than the current price--is $107. The key country to watch is Saudi Arabia, with an estimated breakeven of $89. That provides comfort in Riyadh, but not for bulls. To stop oil's slide, they need Saudi Arabia to curb supply further. In theory, though, oil could average $39 for the rest of 2014 and still come in at $89 for the year as a whole. Riyadh would obviously react well before prices got anywhere close to that level. Still, this suggests there is room for Brent to fall further before OPEC's kingpin steps in. (liam.denning@wsj.com; @liamdenning)

15:26 EDT - Jobless rates in Canada and the US do not fully capture their labor market slack, says Bank of Canada deputy governor Tim Lane. Like Fed chief Yellen, Lane notes long-term unemployment and 'involuntary' part-time employment remain elevated and wage gains are moderate relative to historical levels. "Our comprehensive measure of labor market slack has shown less slack than in the US, but the gap has been narrowing." (nirmala.menon@wsj.com; @NirmalaMenon)

15:17 EDT - Argentina's black-market peso careened to another record low, closing at 15.83 to the US dollar. Despite a government call to stop buying dollars in the black market, there seems to be no stopping the peso's decline. The gap with the official exchange rate of 8.432 now totals around 88%. Economists say that gap feeds inflation and devaluation expectations. That, in turn, gives exporters such as soybean farmers an incentive to hold onto their goods instead of shipping them abroad. Indeed, last month's exports fell 12% on the year, hurting tax revenue. Exports could continue falling in line with the peso's slide, economists say. (taos.turner@wsj.com; @taos)

14:57 EDT - Another senior Bank of Canada official is signaling that BOC may lag the Fed in hiking rates. BOC deputy governor Tim Lane suggests in a speech that BOC won't have to move in lockstep with Fed. He notes that BOC's key rate of 1% is already higher than the Fed's near zero rate, suggesting BOC can wait longer before pulling the trigger. USD/CAD earlier today hit a 6-month high of 1.1123, now at 1.1067. (nirmala.menon@wsj.com; @NirmalaMenon)

14:44 EDT - Revisions made in the past week to official statistics on the size of the US corporate bond universe have caused that market to contract--in reporting terms--to $7.7T from close to $10T earlier in September. The culprit: an amendment to the Fed's flow of funds data. The Fed changed its methodology for calculating the amount of outstanding non-financial corporate bonds, according to the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association. SIFMA reflected the changes in its own data this month, causing revisions to the bond data from 1995 to now. The data changes mirror a similar shift in calculations for municipal bonds in 2011, when the muni bond market had to be revised by $1T. (katy.burne@wsj.com)

14:32 EDT - US ethanol output fell to a six-month low of 889K barrels/day in the week through September 19, from 931K the prior week, according to federal data. It comes amid softer gasoline demand in the US following summer driving season and weaker export demand for the biofuel, analysts say. Ethanol futures are trading near 11-month lows. Another issue: persistent rail-logistics snarls in the Midwest make it difficult for ethanol processors to transport the corn-based additive. Arlan Suderman, analyst at Water Street Solutions, says he's "fairly optimistic" ethanol makers will "see profitable margins as we go into 2015," but a significant concern is whether "we'll have the locomotives to move the ethanol." Ethanol futures for October delivery slip 0.5% to $1.609/gallon. (david.kesmodel@wsj.com; @davidkesmodel)

title: Peru Central Bank Intervention  May Not Buoy the Sol -- Market Talk
text:
8:24 EST - Weaker copper prices and less abundant global liquidity will cause Peru's sol to depreciate more and to close at PEN2.86 per US dollar this year, even as the central bank continues to actively intervene, Credit Suisse says. The sol closed slightly weaker at PEN2.825 per dollar yesterday, even after the central bank sold $275M. Jefferies meanwhile notes that the central bank has shown little tolerance for foreign exchange weakness on concerns that this "may trigger outflows of the weighty foreign holdings of domestic debt." The sol has depreciated 9.6% in the past year. (robert.kozak@wsj.com)

8:20 EST - Downbeat 4Q results from Arch Coal (ACI) as the company was hit by "a softer pricing environment" and rail disruptions. Cash margin tumbles 40% amid a 10% increase in costs, primarily due to the rail woes. Coal-price softness persisted despite total US output falling below 1B tons for the first time since 1993, which helped power producers' year-end stockpiles be at their lowest since 2006. But ACI is hopeful for what 2014 brings, saying US thermal-coal markets should "tighten further...with favorable weather trends and healthier economic activity driving increased power demand. In addition, elevated natural gas prices compared with prior years should ensure that western coals--as well as most eastern coals--are competitively priced for power generation." ACI is down 2.2% premarket at $3.92 after skidding 5.4% Monday. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

8:15 EST - "With rising inventory, increasing production capacity, and slowing demand, February is shaping up to be an important indicator of the health of the auto industry," Morgan Stanley writes after January's weaker-than-expected sales. Weather "clearly played a materially negative role," MS says, particularly for the Detroit Three as much of their sales are in the Midwest and Northeast. Firm thinks the industry "stands at a cross-road," where "pricing is going to have to keep melting" if US sales are to get to a 17M SAAR in the next 12-18 months. The best of the auto replacement cycle is over, MS thinks, with "the incremental buyer moving from someone who needs to replace their car to one who wants to...making bank willingness to lend and credit availability more important than ever." (john.shipman@wsj.com)

8:11 EST - So JC Penney's (JCP) F4Q same-store sales rose 2%. Congratulations on the first increase in 2 1/2 years. But remember that they crumbled 32% a year earlier during a disastrous holiday which cost supposed savior Ron Johnson his job. Exceedingly low bars make for easy targets to overcome. Now, as the year-earlier sales declines lessen as 2014 progress, JCP needs to show it can log growth over those 2013 levels for investors to really get a sense that the sales hemorrhage is gone. Shares, which hit a fresh 31-year low Monday while falling another 4%, are up 1.9% premarket at $5.79. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

8:01 EST - Nu Skin's (NUS) 4Q results proved even better than the high hopes the multilevel marketer set in October. The update comes as CEO Truman Hunt says, "Given the current review of our business in China and our desire to provide the most-informed guidance possible," NUS is pushing back the release of its full 4Q report to later this month. The company was set to post Thursday, but since setting that date came word Chinese officials would investigate accusations NUS is operating an illegal pyramid scheme. That caused the highflying stock to lose 1/3 of its value, and the stock has marked time the past few weeks. It's up 0.9% premarket at $83.50. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

Sterne Agee notes the "tectonic shift of the technology landscape" has enabled an array of competitors to gain market share against MSFT's customer base and put pressure on its dominant Windows OS business. "The uncertainties of the transition keep us on the sidelines at this point after recent stock outperformance," firm adds. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

7:47 EST - Stout 4Q results and guidance for this quarter and 2014 from Dice Holdings (DHX) as the professional-focused website operator continues to benefit from recent acquisitions. The company's offerings focus on job finding, and DHX says, "Recruitment activity improved in financial services in Europe and Asia while activity was fairly consistent in technology and energy." The company notes profit this year will be held back a bit by "growth investments." Sounds like more M&A is coming. DHX, inactive premarket, fell 4.4% Monday to hit a 4-year low and it's off 28% the past year. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

7:36 EST - After dropping 11% this year, Entegris (ENTG) gives investors some comfort with a nice 4Q beat from the chip-services provider. But what's set to steal the show today is the company's planned acquisition of peer ATMI that will cost ENTG $850M. The deal values ATMI shares at a level last seen in late 2007 as the company recently agreed to sell its lifesciences business to focus on semiconductors. The companies "share a long and successful history of solving some of the most-difficult yield challenges facing the industry," says ENTG CEO Bertrand Loy. Both stocks are inactive premarket. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

7:30 EST - US stock markets look to be bargaining for another oversold bounce after the S&P 500's biggest percentage drop in more than seven months. Stocks in Asia hit hard, Tokyo pounded down into correction territory overnight, but the selling seems to have moderated somewhat in the European session. That helps to lighten the mood a little in the US premarket, but bulls have had a hard time lately maintaining any positive momentum. The early gains signaled by rising futures will no doubt be tested. December factory orders due at 10:00am ET. S&P futures up 6.25; 10-yr note a shade lower, yield at 2.60%. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

7:28 EST - After in-line 4Q results, Boston Scientific (BSX) gives better-than-expected profit views for both this quarter and all of 2014 as the medical-device maker logged a 3rd-straight period of improved results last quarter. The improvement has been making BSX a big stock repurchaser--as many companies have been--with it spending $500M last year, 45% of it in 4Q. Shares rise 1.8% premarket to $13.25, partially offsetting Monday's 3.8% drop. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

7:18 EST - Despite a year-end volume pickup thanks to the FOMC starting the taper and traders taking action in the interest-rate pits, CME's 4Q revenue and profit growth weren't as robust as Wall Street anticipated. Average daily volume remained strong last month, rising 13%, but it would appear the futures-exchange operator isn't mightily benefiting just yet from that increased market action. CME's average rate/contract fell 6% in 4Q from a year earlier. Shares, inactive premarket, are down 6.7% in 2014. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

7:07 EST - Coach's (COH) dour quarterly report 2 weeks ago gave a hint that Michael Kors (KORS) continued to batter the fellow handbag-and-accessories company through the holidays. KORS' F3Q report shows just how much as same-store sales jumped 28% and overall results completely crushed expectations, with quarterly revenue topping $1B for the first time. Top-line gains were led by Europe's 73% SSS surge while North America had 24% growth. That as COH logged a 14% slump in North America last quarter. Unsurprisingly, KORS gives just an in-line 4Q view, which if the past is any indication should be easily surpassed. After falling 4.1% Monday, shares jump 13% premarket to $86.97, which would be a fresh high. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

By Francis Bray, CFTe MSTA

The Australian dollar has been confined in a long-term downtrend, reflected by a three-and-a-half year low at $0.8658 against the US dollar. But technical analysis suggests the Aussie is due for a bounce, albeit a corrective one, with a little help from the Reserve Bank of Australia.

For some time now, the RBA has been on an easing bias with regard to its base interest rate cycle, and bemoaning the fact that its currency is too strong, helping the Aussie lose over 14% in value against USD and over 21% against EUR during 2013.

But the shackles were loosened on Tuesday, when the RBA delivered a much more balanced statement.

The bank left its policy rate on hold at 2.50%, but refrained from commenting about a currency that "remains uncomfortably high". Also in the statement, RBA Governor Glenn Stevens stated that, "on present indications, the most prudent course is likely to be a period of stability in interest rates".

Prior to this, the bank's indications of further rate cuts had sent the AUD/USD spot to a three-and-a-half year low at $0.8658 in January. Also, fears of slower growth in China, Australia's largest export trading partner, has played a role in keeping the Aussie weak.

So will this change of rhetoric from the RBA board prompt a recovery for the ailing Aussie? Technical analysis suggests it can.

Already, the response has been positive. The AUD/USD pushed strongly into two-week highs above $0.8834, and a break above $0.8924 is anticipated in the coming sessions. This would lead to further AUD/USD gains to $0.8950 and the $0.90 level.

But the weekly chart below shows how the Jan. 13 lower high at $0.9087 is the important level to break, because that would lead to the prospect of a more meaningful recovery.

http://www.dowjoneswebservices.com/chart/view/6557

That $0.9087 lower high lies at the junction of the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement level of the three-month decline from $0.9758 to $0.8658.

Additional upside risk to the pivotal $0.9250 area would be signalled on a break above $0.9087, close to the 50% retracement level at $0.9210.

But the powerful long-term downtrend from the July 2011 peak at $1.1083 will remain a dominant force, and the structure of the decline would only be damaged on a break above $0.9568.

The recovery would have to break above the late October lower high at $0.9758 to receive an upgrade.

At 1023 GMT, AUD/USD was trading at $0.8890.

title: Peru  Central Bank  Sells $275M to Support Sol -- Market Talk
text:
14:02 EST - Peru's central bank started the week where it left off Friday, intervening to sell U.S. dollars. The central bank sold $275M, after selling $130M on Friday. From Jan. 22 to Jan. 28 it sold $469M, as turmoil in emerging markets hit Peru. The interventions have helped ease any volatility as the sol has stayed more or less stable, closing Monday at PEN2.825 per U.S. dollar. The central bank has a lot of ammunition, with net international reserves of $65.73B at the end of January. (robert.kozak@wsj.com)

13:15 EST - The IMF suggests, again, that the Canadian government has room to delay its plan to balance the budget in 2015 if there is no "meaningful increase" in economic growth. But according to IMF mission chief to Canada, Roberto Cardarelli, Canada's government may not be comfortable doing so, worried that even delaying it by a year could have negative consquences. Cardarelli says its a "legitimate concern" that a delay could affect consumer confidence. For the Canadian government, it's a "tug of war" between healthier finances and the potential drag that could have on growth, Cardarelli said. Finance Minister Jim Flaherty said recently there would be "no doubt" that the 2014 budget, due Feb. 11, would show the government is on course to return to a surplus in 2015/2016. (nirmala.menon@wsj.com, @NirmalaMenon)

13:06 EST - The IMF says there's a missing piece in Canada's financial system -- a single body with an explicit mandate to take a comprehensive view of systemic risks, or to undertake crisis preparedness. To be sure, Canada's regulatory system and supervisory framework is strong and complemented by a "credible system of safety nets." But according to Aditya Narain, a senior IMF official, there is no forum that brings federal and provincial agencies "in a manner that allows for a discussion of emerging risks" in all parts of the financial system. "Nobody is therefore in a position to have at any one point in time, a very comprehensive view of risks across the system," Narain said. (nirmala.menon@wsj.com; @NirmalaMenon)

UBS economists come in at the higher end of those projections, estimating a 200K gain, partly because weather during the week the survey was conducted (Jan. 12) happened to be a bit better. Firm believes bad weather and statistical one-offs subtracted about 110K from December payrolls, reported at 74K. A full reversal of those anomalies would've put January gains at 240K. "With several weeks of record cold and several large winter storms in January, [a full] reversal might seem unlikely," it says. "However, the unusually cold weeks and the storms bracketed the payroll survey week -- the payroll survey week was neither unusually cold nor unusually stormy." (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; cynthialin_dj)

12:36 EST - Why did the US dollar strengthen against emerging-market currencies after weaker-than-expected manufacturing data earlier this morning? Apparently, investors saw in the January ISM manufacturing numbers another sign that economies across the globe aren't expanding. The weak US report, along with some other recent weaker data, joins evidence of a slowdown in China's economy and troubled emerging-market economies to paint an increasingly uncertain picture for investors. And as uncertainty increases, it prompts more volatile reactions in emerging market currencies, said Clem Miller, an investment strategist at Wilmington Trust Investment Advisors. (james.ramage@wsj.com)

Call us at (212) 416-2181 or john.shipman@dowjones.com

USD/CAD last around 1.1078 from 1.1130 late Friday, according to CQG. CAD has lost about 4.5% of its value to the US dollar since the beginning of the year. (don.curren@wsj.com; @dbcurren)

I think stocks now provide better value than before." (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

Credit Suisse economists say they're "somewhat skeptical that was the only culprit, as ISM and factory activity in general is typically not as weather-sensitive as other sectors, such as construction." Firm says February figures "will be the real test." Hard to believe weather "was the whole or even most of the story, but it's not clear what else triggered the suddenly much slower growth these results point to," Morgan Stanley writes. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

As the Fed sends fewer dollars into the economy, the greenback should be strengthening. That's likely preventing the dollar from falling more than it would've on such a lousy ISM result. title: Peru  Central Bank  Steps Up Dollar Sale -- Market Talk
text:
13:58 EST - Peru's central bank sold $440M, the largest intervention so far this year, as it aims to stem any depreciation of the sol. In the three previous trading sessions, the central bank sold a total of $460M. The heavy intervention seems to be working as the sol has remained stable. The local currency closed Wednesday at PEN2.823 per US dollar, unchanged from the previous session. Still, the sol has depreciated 0.82% so far this year against the greenback. (robert.kozak@wsj.com)

13:54 EST - Because primary dealers took 53% of today's inaugural $15B floating-rate Treasury sale, it's likely many money-market accounts have yet to get their fill of the new notes. The auction offered a 0.045% spread over 3-month T-bills. OppenheimerFunds portfolio manager Christopher Proctor says that spread could even decrease at the next few sales as money funds continue to pile into the market. Proctor said that while he was "very impressed by the initial demand," he didn't put in an order today, wanting to see a yield spread of at least 0.05%. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; cynthialin_dj)

13:53 EST - Marathon Petroleum's (MPC) huge 4Q EPS beat was in notable part thanks to how the turnaround at the Garyville, La., refinery panned out, says Cowen. The facility was fully shut, instead of just some downstream or crude units. As such, the investment bank "overstated the downtime impact in our unit margin and capture-rate forecast." MPC's gross refining margin was $15.69/barrel, some 50% above Cowen's estimate. The stock, the best-performer in the S&P 500 today, climbs 4.6% to $87, nearly halving the month's decline. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com)

13:50 EST - Stocks could stay relatively weak for the next couple months, says Janney technician Dan Wantrobski, but he believes the S&P 500 should bottom before it enters official correction territory. His downside target is 1700, 4.4% below current levels and 8% from Jan. 15's record high of 1848.38. The rule of thumb among technicians is pullbacks turn into corrections when they surpass the 10% threshold. Meanwhile, Wantrobski calls the current pullback a temporary "blip" within a new secular "reflationary bull cycle" that should see stocks and Treasury yields rise and commodities underperform over the very-long term. (tomi.kilgore@dowjones.com)

13:29 EST - Consumer staples are the S&P 500's worst-performing sector, as investors get skittish over the exposure many of these multinationals may have to developing markets, particularly ones in the headlines like Turkey and South Africa as their currencies tumble. A host of food companies and personal products makers -- including Avon (AVP), Kellogg (K), Coke (KO), Mondelez (MDLZ), P&G (PG) and Colgate (CL) -- are among the sector's hardest hit stocks. In general, a stronger US dollar vs the local currencies in developing markets pinches profits. Consumer staples down 1.6%, while S&P 500 slides 0.7%. DJIA down 138, or 0.9%. (john.shipman@wsj.com)

13:13 EST - Any extra sliver of yield on top of what T-bills pay can be attractive for funds which can only invest in the safest short-term assets. But for other short-duration strategies not under strict money-market-fund rules, the new Treasury floaters aren't necessarily the answer to better returns--at least based on today's 0.045% spread. "I see it as a placeholder for cash," says Aberdeen's Kam Poon, who focuses on short-duration mandates. "It's nice to have another asset class to invest in, but I think that's all it is. It's a way of parking your cash." Poon prefers short-term debt sold by high-quality companies. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; cynthialin_dj)

12:52 EST - Treasury yields just hit fresh 2-month lows as stocks slink to their worst levels of the session as investors seek shelter from the market's gyrations and for now appear to show no fear about further tapering in an hour. "Taper is already in the market and accounts are buying before rates fall too far," says Tom di Galoma at ED&F. "Additionally, you have month-end extensions taking place at the same time." The 10-year note is 11/32 higher, yielding 2.706%. (min.zeng@wsj.com; @minzengwsj)

12:50 EST - There's no question the Treasury's first-ever floating-rate auction saw strong demand. Question now is who exactly did the bidding. Market participants believe money-market funds largely drove the demand. Outside that conservative group, some say the 0.045% yield spread may not be so appealing. "It would appear fully priced at this time for investors beyond money-market strategies," says Pimco portfolio manager Jerome Schneider, who oversees short-term markets. "As more supply comes to market, the initial demand fever should subside and valuations should adjust." This adjustment to a juicer yield spread will be key because money funds can only buy so much before reaching their weighted-average life cap of 120 days. (cynthia.lin@wsj.com; cynthialin_dj)

title: ANALYSIS-Peru's steady sol  currency  may defy emerging markets jinx
text:
* Peru currency strengthened most in Latin America in 2011

* Some say Peru's commodities mix makes it recession-proof

By Caroline Stauffer

LIMA, Jan 19 (Reuters) - Peru's sol may not repeat its 2011 performance as Latin America's star currency this year, but strong exports of crisis-proof gold, low currency volatility and growing confidence in the new president could make it a sound emerging market bet.

Local businesses and economists consulted by Reuters mostly see the sol, which gained 4 percent last year, holding stable or strengthening slightly despite the risk of lower commodity prices and fallout from Europe's financial mess.

Peru's currency has been the region's least volatile for years and low volatility makes currencies more attractive for investors looking for less risky bets.

The Mexican and Chilean pesos and the Brazilian real , in contrast, each lost about 10 percent in 2011, lashed in the second half of the year when Europe's debt woes drove risk-shy investors out of many emerging markets.

The sol outperformed mostly on high prices paid for the commodities it exports, including gold, and got a boost when President Ollanta Humala, a one-time radical leftist, pleasantly surprised investors by appointing conservatives to run economic and monetary policy after taking office in July .

"There's a flood of money coming in, both from abroad and internally," said Javier San Miguel, budget manager at Peru's largest consumer goods company Alicorp. "Exports are still quite good even though commodities prices have come down some. We see a favorable outlook."

"Everything Humala has done to date is in line with what the business sector wanted," he added.

San Miguel believes the sol will end 2012 up nearly 2 percent from 2011 at 2.65 per U.S. dollar. Alicorp imports basic food goods like wheat and soy in dollars and sells 75 percent of its finished products domestically in soles.

The sol has been trading around its strongest level in more than a decade so far this year, and is 0.15 percent stronger than its 2011 close of 2.96 per U.S. dollar.

RECESSION-PROOF?

While many economies in Latin America export commodities, Peru is unique. Unlike neighboring Chile, where copper is dominant and accounts for roughly 50 percent of monthly export revenue, Peru is the world's No. 2 copper and silver producer and Latin America's top gold producer.

The dollar value of Peru's monthly gold exports has been nearly equal to that of its copper sales abroad.

Ricardo V. Lago, a former World Bank economist, has said that Peru's role as a gold exporter could mean it is virtually recession-proof in a scenario when precious metals prices leap on safe-haven buying in a global economic meltdown.

Other economists say even though prices for copper and zinc Peru exports may be softer, prices for its gold and fishmeal are still high. It is the world's top fishmeal producer.

"There might be other countries in the region that export gold but it's not as important as in Peru," said Nomura analyst Benito Berber.

Peru, one of the region's most open economies, is also an emerging leader in niche agricultural products like asparagus and it has a growing manufacturing sector, mainly textiles. The government forecasts economic growth of around 5.4 percent in 2012, which could be one of the region's fastest rates.

"The sol doesn't just depend on commodities. Peru has been more successful in exporting value added goods than other countries in the region and is supported by strong macroeconomic fundamentals," said Mariel Koehler, a trader for Peruvian miner Volcan, the world's No. 4 zinc producer.

Koehler sees the currency gaining 3.5 percent in 2012 to end at 2.6 per dollar, barring unexpected global economic trauma.

$50 BILLION IN THE PIPELINE

Others say that while Peru will likely again have the least volatile currency in the region this year, it is not entirely risk free.

Some $50 billion in investment in mining and energy are lined up for the next few years, and some analysts fear the cash will only come through if Humala can avert protests against natural resource extraction in remote areas of the country.

U.S.-based Newmont's $4.8 billion copper and gold project has been on hold since locals started protests in northern Cajamarca, demanding the company stop work on the mine for fear it will disrupt scarce water supplies.

"The risk for the sol is basically a fall in investment if social conflicts break out in mining areas," said Pedro Tuesta, a Peruvian economist with the 4Cast consultancy, who sees the sol trading between 2.68 and 2.72 at year's end.

The sol will likely trade sideways at a time when the Mexican peso could rebound on stronger signs of recovery in the United States, Tuesta said. Barclays Capital says the Mexican peso and Brazil's real could both outperform the sol in 2012.+

But the sol's performance is not entirely determined by market factors. The central bank's ample reserves and frequent interventions have played a role in the sol having a lower volatility. Because Peru is a small market, central bank intervention is much more effective at curbing volatility than in Chile or Mexico.

The central bank intervenes frequently, purchasing $4.7 billion in 2011, because half of all bank accounts in Peru are held in dollars and exchange rate volatility hurts businesses and consumers, who often get paid in soles and owe debts in dollars.

Regardless of how Europe's debt crisis, Chinese demand for minerals and the economic recovery in the United States play out, the sol could well emerge relatively unscathed in 2012.

"It will again be the currency with the lowest volatility," said Nomura's Berber. "And in a scenario in which things continue to complicate in Europe towards mid-year, I see the (sol) depreciating, though less than many other currencies."

(Additional reporting by Ursula Scollo; Editing by Terry Wade and W Simon)

title: Peru's Sol, Ends 2011 Strong, Continues Roll Into 2012
text:
--Sol ended 2011 with 4% appreciation against U.S. dollar

--Sol continues to post gains in new year

--Central bank intervenes to buy dollars to ease sol strength


 
   By Robert Kozak 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's currency, the sol, is continuing last year's trend so far in 2012, appreciating against the U.S. dollar and with the Central Reserve Bank of Peru intervening to ease those gains.

The sol has already appreciated 0.15% against the greenback so far this year, ending Tuesday at PEN2.693. That follows a 4% gain last year.

The sol has appreciated 14% against the U.S. dollar since the end of 2008, as Peru's economic boom shows few signs of abating and investors flock to the Andean nation.

Economists say they expect the sol to retain its strength and to continue to appreciate this year, barring any global downturn that would knock the wind out of commodity prices.

Cesar Perez-Novoa, a managing director with Celfin Capital, noted that waning political risk in Peru coupled with strong commodity prices have helped boost the sol in the shorter term, while robust flows of direct foreign investments in the mining, hydrocarbons and utilities sectors will help support the currency in the medium and longer terms.

The sol should remain relatively stable, with any abrupt gains being met by central bank intervention, he added.

In the past, the central bank has also met any short-term speculative flows into capital markets with measures aimed at making those investments less attractive.

The foreign exchange market intervention however has been continual, with the central bank intervening to buy $3.3 billion in 2011, following the $8.96 billion it bought in 2010.

So far this year, the intervention has also been robust, with the central bank entering to buy $242 million on Tuesday. The interventions have driven up Peru's net international reserves, which ended 2011 at $48.82 billion.

The central bank says it isn't defending any particular exchange rate, only easing volatility.

A recent survey of 24 economic analysts by the central bank, meanwhile, found expectations that the sol will end this year at PEN2.65 to the U.S. dollar and at PEN2.64 to the dollar in 2013.

"We believe that the sol will continue to appreciate but that will be less than in 2011," said Roberto Flores, an economist with brokerage Inteligo.

Michael Henderson, an economist with Capital Economics, sees the sol weakening to around PEN2.80 to the dollar by the end of the second quarter, but then to resume appreciating again over the second half, reaching perhaps PEN2.75 to the dollar by year-end.

He pointed to relatively bearish expectations for global demand over the course of this year which will weaken demand for commodity exports and will likely lead to slowing capital inflows into the region as investors shun risk.

-By Robert Kozak, Dow Jones Newswires; 51-1-99927 7269; peru@dowjones.com [ 11-01-12 1909GMT ]

He has since been embraced by Peru's business community for keeping conservative economic policymakers in their posts.

During periodic bouts of hot-money inflows in the region since 2008, Peru's sol has usually appreciated less than its peers, partly because the central bank has limited the ability of investors to park short-term cash in the country. That means the sol also has less ground to lose during periods of swift outflows.

Peru's economy grew nearly 7 percent this year and is expected to expand more than 5 percent next year as hot domestic demand offsets a potentially softer market for its metals exports.

title: PREVIEW-Peru's key rate seen held steady at 4.25 pct
text:
WHAT: Peru interest rate decision

WHEN: Thursday, Nov. 10, around 6 p.m. EST (2300 GMT)

OUTCOME: 14 of 14 analysts see rate steady at 4.25 percent

REUTERS FORECAST: Economists polled by Reuters unanimously expect Peru's central bank to hold the benchmark interest rate steady at 4.25 percent on Thursday for the sixth straight month citing the ongoing global economic uncertainty.

The central bank added a sentence to its September policy statement implying it would cut the benchmark rate if the global economic outlook deteriorated. Europe is embroiled in a debt crisis and growth is slowing in the United States and China, key markets for Peru's exports.

But inflation rose a higher-than-expected 0.31 percent in October, making a rate cut unlikely this month. All 14 economists surveyed by Reuters said the central bank would maintain the rate at 4.25 percent.

Analysts say a large global economic shock, such as an eventual debt default from Greece, could eventually prompt Peru to cut its interest rate.

In the meantime, the local economy is posting strong growth, and gross domestic product expanded 7.49 percent in August. The economy is expected go grow around 6 around percent this year after accelerating nearly 9 percent in 2010.

MARKET IMPACT: Seen minimal. A higher or lower interest rate could boost or decrease the demand for Peru's currency, the sol, but the sol has strengthened steadily in October and November and is trading around its strongest levels in more than three years even though rates have been on hold.

The sol <PEN=PE> closed bidding flat at 2.703 soles per U.S. dollar on the local spot market on Tuesday, after the central bank purchased $140 million in an intervention.

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's main stock market indexes ended lower on Friday, dragged down by international markets on continued concerns about the health of the global economy.

The broad General Index closed 0.58% weaker at 18,329.10.

The blue-chip Selective Index ended 0.48% lower at 25,552.34.

Stocks saw a high degree of volatility in the third quarter on concerns about a debt crisis in Europe and a slowdown in the U.S. economy.

The Lima Stock Exchange reached a third-quarter high on July 27, a day before President Ollanta Humala took office on improved confidence from investors that the new administration would not make major changes to the economy.

However the bourse tumbled in early August, along with other international markets, after Standard & Poor's downgraded its long-term ratings on U.S. government debt. The Lima Stock Exchange has since continued to be impacted by the outlook for the global economy.

"This isn't an issue of domestic policies, it is basically the international situation," Jose Luis Bustamante, the head trader at brokerage Cartisa SAB, said Friday during a telephone interview.

The mining-heavy exchange has also been impacted by a decrease in metal prices.

On Friday, base metals miner Southern Copper Corp. (SCCO) closed 1.73% lower at $24.96 as copper prices declined. Silver and lead miner Volcan Compania Minera SAA (VOLCABC1.VL) ended 2.30% weaker at 2.55 soles ($0.92).

Going the other way, financial holding Credicorp Ltd. (BAP, BAP.VL) gained 1.65% to end at $92.50.

Meanwhile, the sol also saw volatility in the third-quarter as a result of global economic concerns. During the quarter, the Peruvian currency fluctuated between PEN2.725 per dollar to PEN2.7736.

The weakening of the sol came in the last two weeks of September as investors flocked to the U.S. dollar and copper prices declined.

The weakening of the sol led the Central Reserve Bank of Peru to reverse a trend of intervening in the foreign-exchange market to buy dollars. On Sept. 22, the central bank sold $200 million, which was the first time it intervened to sell dollars since April 27 this year.

The central bank went on to sell a total of $575 million in the final days of September as investor jitters continued to strengthen the greenback.

The total includes an intervention on Friday, when the central bank sold $141 million at an average of PEN2.773 per dollar.

While many economists say short-term volatility for the sol may continue, they also expect the currency to appreciate in the medium term thanks largely to the strength of the nation's external accounts.

On Friday, the sol weakened to PEN2.773 per dollar from PEN2.771 in the previous session. The sol has appreciated 1.21% against the greenback so far this year.

-By Ryan Dube, Dow Jones Newswires; 51-945 043 802; peru@dowjones.com [ 30-09-11 2300GMT ]

title: Peru 's  Central Bank Intervenes  In  Forex  Mkt, Sells $186 Million
Emerging Market  Currencies  Slightly Weaker, Debt Little Changed
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies continued to lose ground in New York trading on Monday, but their losses were less pronounced as investors turned more hopeful that policy makers might be able to engineer a response to the euro-zone's debt problems.

In Latin America, the Brazilian real and Mexican peso lost ground against the dollar, but didn't suffer the kind of deep losses they had been experiencing in recent days. Emerging market debt was little changed, with the risk premium, or spread, on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global two basis points tighter to 460 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, the index was down 0.87%.

"It's primarily due to the external environment.," said Nomura strategist George Lei. "Overall there is some expectation that policy makers will do something on the euro-zone."

The European Central Bank stands ready to provide the debt-troubled euro zone with additional support if necessary, two of its top officials said Monday, even as they put the onus on governments to act quickly to ward off intensifying debt woes in the region.

Still, central banks in growing economies remain concerned about the possible fallouts from a slowdown in the developed world. The Bank of Israel Monday lowered its main interest rate by 25 basis points to 3% to combat the effects of a global slowdown, the latest sign that central banks around the world are shifting to looser monetary policies. The bank pointed to growing expectations that the slowdown in global growth could be worse than expected. The shekel weakened with the dollar rising 0.86% to ILS3.734.

Investors were again faced with weak data from the U.S. New-home sales fell for the fourth-straight month in August to the lowest level in a half-year as the bursting of the housing bubble continues to plague the economy. Mexico's economy is particularly closely linked to that of the U.S. The dollar was up 0.43% against the peso to MXN13.6123. Mexico's spread on the Embig was three basis points tighter to 270 basis points over Treasurys. But in price terms, its index was down 1.2%.

Elsewhere in Latin America, the Central Reserve Bank of Peru intervened in the foreign-exchange market on Monday to sell $186 million at an average of PEN2.7715 per U.S. dollar. The central bank intervenes to smooth out volatility in the exchange market. The peruvian sol was recently up 0.18% to PEN2.772.

title: Peru  sol closes flat after cenbank  intervention
text:
LIMA, Sept 26 (Reuters) - Peru's central bank sold $186 million on Monday and placed 100 million soles ($36 million) as the local currency slipped.

The sol ended up <PEN=PE> closing flat, bidding 2.77 per U.S. dollar on the spot market.

The central bank regularly intervenes in the market because half of all deposits made in Peru are in dollars and volatility hurts businesses and consumers.

Normally it buys dollars to soak up excess liquidity. But the bank began selling dollars last week, when investors started to drop high-yielding emerging market assets on concerns of a new global recession.
