title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real gains after  FX  swap; Latam rebounds
text:
* Brazil c. bank swap sale checks real slide, sets 'limit'

* Mexico, Chile pesos rebound from sharp Thursday declines

* Peru intervenes in currency market; sol erases loss

(Updates prices, adds Brazil, Peru, Colombia comment)

By Jeb Blount

RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's real reversed losses to gain more than 3 percent against the dollar on Friday -- its biggest one-day gain in almost 16 months -- after the central bank's move to bolster the currency a day earlier raised expectations it will act again to limit sharp falls.

Thursday's sale of $2.75 billion of currency swaps effectively put a limit on how far the bank will allow the real to slide, said Mario Battistel, head of trading at Fair Corretora, a Sao Paulo currency brokerage. For more see [ID:nS1E78L0PK].

Currency swaps mimic the sale of dollars and provide investors with insurance against future declines in the real.

The real has lost more than 15 percent of its value since the central bank unexpectedly cut its benchmark interest rate by half a percentage point to 12 percent on Aug. 31. The move was based on the bank's expectation that a world economic slowdown would push down Brazil's 7 percent inflation rate. [ID:nE5E7IM05G] and [ID:nL3E7KN1BZ]

"The central bank swap intervention was a pleasant surprise," Battistel said in a telephone interview. "They're clearly worried about inflation and exporters and our other clients weren't about to start moving their large dollar holdings back into Brazil until they had some idea of when the real's plunge would stop."

Brazil's real <BRBY> gained 3.19 percent to 1.8360 to the U.S. dollar, its first gain in six sessions and its biggest one-day gain since May 27, 2010.

The currency had lost more than 1 percent in early trade and still ended the week down about 5.75 percent against the dollar.

The government is ready to intervene more in the currency market to curb wide swings, or volatility, in the market, Finance Minster Guido Mantega told investors in Washington. [ID:nS1E78M134]

Brazil's central bank targets inflation of 4.5 percent plus or minus 2 percentage points and has long said that inflation, now outside the target range, will come under control soon.

A strong real helps control inflation by cutting the cost of dollar-denominated commodities such as food and the cost of essential imports such as machine-tools for Brazil's industry.

Battistel said the central bank, which as recently as August was working to prevent the real from gaining against the dollar, is signaling that it will act any time the real weakens beyond 1.90 to the dollar or strengthens beyond 1.60.

Other traders said the bank is targeting the first dollar futures contract <DOLc1> on the Sao Paulo BM&FBovespa exchange, moving to weaken the real when it firms beyond 2.01 to the dollar and to strengthen the real when it weakens beyond 1.78.

The real-dollar spot exchange rate's close link to the futures market, where bets can be ramped up using loans or "leverage" is one of the reasons the real lost so much in recent weeks, the government said Wednesday.

In first futures trading, which measure expectations for late September, the real shed 2.16 percent to 1.8585.

Bets on a strong real were a key component in the real's nearly 8 percent rise through late July.

Since then the real has reversed all those gains and is now about 9 percent weaker than it was at the end of 2010.

Elsewhere in Latin America currencies rebounded from steep Thursday declines on expectation losses related to concern about a potential Greek default may be overdone.

Mexico's peso <MXN=D2> jumped 3.63 percent to 13.5584 to the dollar, reversing some of Thursday's losses that took the peso beyond 14 to the dollar for the first time since April 2009. For the week the peso trimmed losses to 3.89 percent.

"I think the market has pushed the currency too far too fast and we may see a bit of retracement in the peso's favor," said Francisco Diez, director of emerging-market trading at RBC Capital Markets in New York.

The next point the peso will test if it begins weakening again is 14.25 to the dollar Diez said.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> gained 0.93 percent to 516.00 to the dollar after plunging more than 5 percent on Thursday.

Colombia's peso <COP2=STFX> gained 0.58 percent to 1,904.

Peru's sol <PEN=PE> trimmed early losses to trade little changed from Thursday at 2.7700 after the country's central bank sold $21 million dollars for pesos, driving up demand for the local currency and helping it firm.

(Additional reporting by Rachel Uranga in Mexico City; Editing by Raymond Colitt and Kenneth Barry)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil, Peru step in to halt  forex  plunge
text:
* Brazil sells swaps, Peru trades soles for dollar debt

* World growth outlook knocks commodities, LatAm currencies

* Brazil swap auction helps trim loss that reached 4.79 pct

(Updates prices)

By Jeb Blount

RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Brazil's real trimmed some of its biggest losses since the 2009 world recession and Peru's sol backed away from three-month lows as the countries' central banks moved to bolster their currencies in the face of deteriorating prospects for world growth.

In the face of a nearly 5 percent plunge in the real, Brazil's central bank sold $2.75 billion in currency swaps, intervening in the futures market to support the currency <BRBY>. This reversed a tactic used as recently as August to use sell swaps to prevent the real from strengthening.

After the swap auction, the currency rebounded, eventually reversing losses. It closed spot market trading at 2 percent weaker than on Wednesday at 1.8946 the real's weakest close in more than two years. [ID:nS1E78L0PK]

"The market got the feeling that the central bank wants to put a range on the real," said Moacir Marcos Junior a currency trader at Interbolsa, a Sao Paulo brokerage. "It's like the bank saying, 'look, 1.60 to the dollar, I don't want, but I don't want 1.90 either and I won't let that happen.'"

Thursday's declines bring the Brazilian real's losses this month to more than 15 percent, turning what was a nearly 8 percent year-to-date gain in July to 1.52, a 12-year high, into a nearly 15 percent loss.

In Peru, after the sol <PEN=PE> fell more than 1 percent to 2.7910, a three-month low, the central bank sold 600 million soles ($216.2 million) of readjustable certificates of deposit, or CDRs.

In the operation, local banks trade soles with the central bank for dollar-denominated bonds a trade the mimics the sale of dollars and puts pressure on the sol to gain. The sol rebounded to 2.7690, trimming losses to 0.4 percent [ID:nS1E78L0U7]

The declines on Thursday came on increasing signs of slowdown in the U.S., Europe and China -- economies responsible for 60 percent of world output. That outlook caused the price of oil, coffee, copper, soybeans and other commodities, which form the bulk of Latin American exports, to fall too. For more information see: [ID:nS1E78L0M6] [ID:nL5E7KM1AQ] [IDnS1E78L0CR]

Adding to the gloom, a decision by the U.S. Federal Reserve late Wednesday to launch "Operation Twist" -- an attempt to cut long-term borrowing rates by shifting Fed holdings of U.S. Treasury debt into longer-term bonds -- was seen as too weak to boost the sluggish U.S. economy.

In Greece, a 24-hour anti-austerity strike raised doubts about passage of a plan to stave off a Greek debt default that could hobble international banks and cut-off credit and growth world-wide. [ID:nL5E7KM2H3]

"We are staring at a possible new global recession and that's pushing investors out of Latin American and other commodities-based currencies and into the dollar," Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist at CM Capital Markets in Sao Paulo.

In times of economic stress investors frequently sell assets in currencies considered high risk, such as Brazil's real and Mexico's peso, and buy assets priced in dollars, the world's most "liquid" or widely negotiated currency.

Mexico's peso <MXN=D2> weakened 2.83 percent to 14.0701, breaking beyond 14 to the dollar for the first time since April 27, 2009. In contrast to Brazil and Peru, Mexico's finance minister Jose Antonio Meade said intervening to protect a level for the peso would unwise. [ID:nS1E78L1NN]

Now that it's weakened beyond 14.0200 to the dollar, it could fall to the 15.59 range, a level last seen at the height of the world recession in March 2009, said Win Thin, an emerging market currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

"Emerging markets are getting killed, and Mexico is going to get killed also," he said. COMMODITY PRICES FALL

Chile, the major regional economy most dependent on a single commodity, also saw its currency plunge. The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> weakened 3.91 percent to 520.80 to the dollar after falling as much as 5.06 percent to 527.20, its weakest level since July 21, 2010.

The world's largest copper producer earned more than half of export earnings from the base metal, an important component in electrical equipment and electronic goods.

Copper <CMCU3> which was already trading at its lowest levels since November after four days of losses plunged for a fifth day, losing 8.19 percent to $7,647.00 a tonne in London, its lowest in more than a year.

The Reuters Jefferies commodities index <.CRB>, a measure of 18 key Latin American energy and agricultural commodities such as oil and soybeans, fell 4.41 percent to 307.24, its lowest level since Dec. 1.

Colombia, a key producer of oil and coffee and a growing producer of coal, saw its peso <COP2=STFX> fall 2.19 percent to 1,916.05 to the dollar.

(Additional reporting by Rachel Uranga in Mexico City and Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo, Editing by Stuart Grudgings and Chizu Nomiyama)

title: Emerging Market Debt,  Currencies  Echo Rebound In Risky Markets
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies and credits took a bit of a break from their recent declines Thursday, as so-called risk assets recovered on news that five major central banks are working together to provide liquidity for crisis-embroiled European banks.

Latin American and Eastern European currencies were slightly stronger against the dollar and euro, while sovereign credit spreads tightened with U.S. Treasury yields rising. The joint announcement from the European Central Bank, the Federal Reserve, and three other key monetary authorities that they are going to coordinate efforts to provide euro-zone banks with dollar funding, lifted investors sentiment.

"People are feeling a little better about Europe from the ECB announcement, so emerging markets are largely up," said Win Thin, senior currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman. "But I'm still skeptical because not much about the underlying dynamic has changed."

The risk premium, or spread, on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global was six basis points tighter to 385 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, the index was down 0.23%.

Emerging-market currencies, which rallied early this year, have fallen sharply in recent days due to worries about global growth and contagion from the euro zone's debt problems. Now central banks in these countries are in the position of having to hold them up rather than find ways to weaken them, as was the case earlier in the year.

"By year-end, all these guys will probably be cutting rates," Thin said.

Chile's central bank rate decision is due later Thursday and it is widely expected to keep its target policy rate unchanged at 5.25%. Its spread on the Embig tightened five basis points to 1.59%, but fell a fraction in price terms.

The Bank of Indonesia was suspected of intervening to shore up its currency. Traders also said that the Philippines central bank appeared to have intervened to support its currency. Peru has been working on extending stimulus from the fiscal side and said Tuesday that it will adopt measures to speed public sector investments.

Indonesia may need to introduce fiscal stimulus next year to help shield its economy from a potential global economic slowdown, senior officials said Thursday. Finance Minister Agus Martowardojo told a parliamentary hearing that the country may need to issue a fiscal stimulus package in the first half of next year.

While growth across Asia appears relatively resilient, the outlook in emerging Europe appears to be headed for a slowdown given its ties to the beleaguered euro-zone bloc. The deteriorating sovereign debt problems there are expected to dent the export demand for goods produced by these highly open economies such as Hungary and the Czech Republic.

The Hungarian currency and credit markets have been coming under excruciating pressure in recent days as investors reel from new government proposals that could hit the country's banks. The forint has fallen particularly hard recently after Prime Minister Viktor Orban announced controversial plans Monday to help struggling households by locking in exchange rates on mortgages denominated in foreign currencies, particularly Swiss francs.

But the forint and Polish zloty recovered ground against the euro Thursday on the coordinated move by the central banks to provide dollar funding to European banks. That alleviates some pressure, for now, that has been mounting for euro-zone banks to raise short-term funding because investors fear their exposure to the region's debt crisis.

The zloty strengthened to PLN4.3284 per euro from PLN4.3809 to start the day, while the forint gained to HUF284.94 a euro from HUF287.06. Emerging Europe's region index on the Embig lost 0.08% in price, while its spread narrowed seven basis points to 3.45%.

By Anjali Cordeiro; Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2200; anjali.cordeiro@dowjones.com

-Clare Connaghan contributed to this article. [ 15-09-11 1830GMT ]

S&P's decision was seen as a surprise, despite Peru's strong macroeconomic indicators, as there is still uncertainty in the new government's microeconomic policies, Banco Continental said Wednesday.

Brokerage Inteligo SAB said the impact of the upgrade on Peru's equity market could last for "some additional time."

"It could lure investors to enter a market with strong fundamentals that have been severely chastised by the bleak external picture and by the worries of a government that has proved to be more pragmatic and market friendly than many initially feared," Inteligo said.

title: EM  Currencies  Lose Ground, Debt Spread Slightly Tighter
text:
Anjali Cordeiro 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Continued worries about global growth held back emerging-market currencies on Monday as investors stayed uneasy about taking on fresh risk.

Emerging-market debt was a notch tighter, but Peruvian assets came under pressure after an election victory for a left-wing candidate. The risk premium, or spread, on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global was three basis points tighter to 309 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms the index was down 0.02%.

The victory in Peru by left-wing nationalist Ollanta Humala in Sunday's runoff vote for president raised jitters that he might push for more government intervention in the economy. Peru's spread on the Embig was 21 basis points wider to 213 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms the index was down 2.22%.

Still, some analysts and investors said it might be some time before Humala makes any radical changes to economic. "He'll be able to do populist things because the economy is doing so well," says John Peta, portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management. "Some of the most extreme things people have been thinking of probably won't crop up for a while."

Early Monday, Peru's sol was a touch weaker after Humala's victory. According to a market observer, the sol was near 2.80 per dollar early Monday, from 2.76 per dollar on Friday. But the market observer said that the central bank appeared to have intervened to prevent too much weakness in the currency.

Elsewhere in Latin America, the Chilean economy continues to grow at a brisk pace on the back of healthy industrial production and domestic demand. The country's monthly economic activity index, or Imacec, grew 6.3% on the year in April, the central bank said Monday. Chile's spread on the Embig was twenty four basis points tighter to 111 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms the index was up 1.49%.

Worries about slowing growth in the U.S. lingered from Friday's weak payrolls data. On Friday, emerging-market currencies like the Mexican peso pulled back after the U.S. jobs data. That weakness lingered on Monday, with the dollar up 0.70% against the peso to MXN11.7621. The Brazilian real was also weaker with the dollar up 0.32% against the real to BRL1.5845. Brazilian financial analysts and economists reduced their 2011 inflation forecasts for the fifth consecutive week, according to a survey by the Brazilian central bank published Monday. Brazil's spread on the Embig was one basis point tighter to 177 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, the index was down 0.10%.

Outside Latin America, South African Trade Minister Rob Davies said the government is discussing what to do about the rand's strength, which he said is overvalued from unstable global markets and quantitative easing in the U.S. The rand lost ground, with the dollar rising to 1.17% to ZAR6.8074.

title: UPDATE 1-EXCLUSIVE-Peru says has economic 'contingency plan'
text:
* Finance minister has plan if markets sell-off

 * Humala economics adviser pledges stability

 * Warns of "speculative attack"

 (Adds quotes, byline)

 By Patricia Velez

 LIMA, June 5 (Reuters) - Peru's government has a "contingency plan" ready to implement if markets sink in the event of a victory by leftist Ollanta Humala in Sunday's presidential election, Finance Minister Ismael Benavides said.

 Humala, a former army officer, has a lead of at least 5 percentage points in three exit polls. He has moderated his anti-capitalist views over the last few years, but many investors still fear he would roll back free-market policies if elected in the fast-growing economy.

 "We have a contingency plan (which aims to) provide liquidity in the market via the Treasury ... to give a hand to the central bank," Benavides told Reuters.

 Benavides stressed that whoever wins the presidency must quickly move to win the confidence of markets.

 Meanwhile, Humala's chief economics adviser said stability would be assured if Humala wins but that the central bank must intervene if the country suffers a speculative attack.

Peru's stocks <.IGRA> and sol currency <PEN=PE> have been highly volatile in recent weeks as investors worry that Humala would pursue an interventionist agenda in Peru's fast-growing economy. Analysts said markets could plunge on Monday if Humala is confirmed.

 "There is no reason to worry, monetary policy will be maintained, responsible fiscal policy will guarantee the sustainability of fiscal accounts," economist Felix Jimenez, who authored Humala's campaign platform, told journalists.

 Peru has investment grade credit ratings and record       international reserves of $44 billion, equal to about one third of annual gross domestic product.

 But Jimenez also warned of potential volatility in financial markets.

 "If there is a speculative attack, I reiterate that I would ask the central bank to do its job. The central bank has the instruments to avert a speculative attack," he said shortly after exit polls gave Humala a narrow lead following voting.

 Peru's central bank has periodically raised deposit requirements on bank accounts, especially those tied to foreign loans, in a bid to limit speculation on the sol and has sold dollars on the local spot market to prop up the sol.

Central Bank President Julio Velarde told Reuters in April that the central bank was studying ways to respond in case confidence undermined markets. [ID:nN01151534]

LIMA, May 30 (Reuters) - Peru's currency weakened the most in nine weeks and the local stock index fell sharply on Monday, with traders citing polls showing right-wing lawmaker Keiko Fujimori's lead over left-wing nationalist Ollanta Humala had narrowed ahead of the June 5 presidential election.

The sol currency <PEN=PE> closed bidding 0.69 percent weaker, its largest fall since March 28, at 2.769 per U.S. dollar, while stocks <.IGRA> closed down 5.16 percent.

Peru's central bank, which frequently intervenes in the local currency market, announced an auction for 250 million soles ($89 million) in deposit certificates to soak up the demand for dollars but did not place any of them.

"The fall in the market is a response to the polls over the weekend," said Edwin Paz, a trader at local stock brokerage Provalor in Lima.

Fujimori leads Humala, who has tried with limited success to campaign as a moderate and distance himself from his former political mentor, Venezuela's socialist President Hugo Chavez. Fujimori's lead ranges between 1 point and 4.6 points in four polls. For more see [ID:nN27173077].

Investors worry Humala would intervene in the economy, one of the world's fastest-growing, and hurt private investment. They trust Fujimori because they credit her father, former President Alberto Fujimori, with opening the economy in the 1990s. He is in jail for corruption and human rights abuse.

Peru's stock index plunged 21 percent between March 24 and April 27 on fears Humala would win. Markets have since recovered as Fujimori surpassed the former army officer in polls but will likely be volatile until the June 5 run-off vote.

With polls showing a small margin between the two candidates, Goldman Sachs wrote in a research note that the election could go to a recount, delaying the results.

"Investors should be prepared for high market volatility as the political system sorts out the vote recount process and manages the ensuing conflicts of interest," the report said.

title: UPDATE: Peru's Markets Bearing Brunt Of Political Worries
text:
(Adds stock market closing figures, and closing and intervention figures for sol.)


 
    By Robert Kozak 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's political uncertainty is undermining the strength of its once robust financial markets, knocking the stock market down from lofty levels, swelling its bond spreads and weakening its currency.

Concerns about the prospects for Peru's policies have increased following the rise in political support for left-leaning nationalist Ollanta Humala, who took the most votes in the April 10 election for president and who is leading in opinion polls before the June 5 runoff.

Humala, 48, and his contender, center-right Congresswoman Keiko Fujimori, 35, both favor placing a windfall tax on mining companies. Humala also hopes to modify Peru's constitution, in part to give the state a greater role in the economy. Fujimori, daughter of jailed ex-president Alberto Fujimori, says she will keep Peru on the same market-friendly policies followed in the last two decades.

The Lima Stock Exchange's broad General Index, which gained 65% last year, has tumbled some 28% so far this year, with a decline of 19% this month to the end of trade on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, the General Index ended 1.09% higher due to bargain hunting and heavy volumes in trade of one blue-chip mining company.

The stock market, which is heavily reliant on mining companies, has weakened despite strong prices for many of the minerals that the companies mine in Peru.

"Peru has become one of the worst performing stock markets in the world and that is because of concerns about Mr. Humala," said Cesar Perez-Novoa, a managing director with Celfin Capital. "You will see a lot of volatility," he added.

A robust economy--gross domestic product expanded by 8.8% last year--and solid government and private sector company finances have helped boost interest in investing in Peru, which has an investment grade debt rating.

The free-floating currency, the sol, which has been on an appreciating trend in the last few years, has depreciated by 0.86% against the U.S. dollar this year, to the end of Wednesday.

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru, which intervened to purchase $8.96 billion last year as inflows of cash strengthened the sol, has changed direction. On April 14, the central bank intervened to sell $91 million, the first intervention to sell since February 2009.

On Wednesday the central bank intervened to sell $492 million, although the sol ended slightly weaker at PEN2.831 per dollar, compared with PEN2.830 per dollar in the previous session.

In addition to the slide in the sol and local stocks, Peruvian bond spreads have been widening.

"With opinion polls suggesting that the second round of voting will be a close call, Peruvian markets have sold off sharply," Capital Economics said in a Wednesday research note. "The principal concern is that if Mr. Humala prevails he will pursue a program of economic nationalism that will squeeze foreign firms, particularly in the mining sector."

Barclays Capital said in a report it was keeping its short position in the sol unless political developments or poll results suggest Fujimori could win the presidency. "Keeping a defensive exposure still pays, in our view," it added.

When Humala ran unsuccessfully for office in 2006 against President Alan Garcia, he was closely tied to Venezuela's socialist firebrand President Hugo Chavez.

In this election Humala has moderated his policies in speeches and press conferences, but his party's official governing plan remains a hard-line manifesto that promises a "Grand Transformation" of Peru's society and economy.

"Our recent baseline assumption had been one of likely political continuity, but the odds have changed in the last month, raising the potential for dramatic political change," Deutsche Bank said in a commentary.

title: ANALYSIS-Peru's sol to shine as cenbank fights inflation
text:
* Central bank seen turning focus to inflation from FX

* Nomura, Barclays see sol at 2.6 per dollar by year end

* Elections not seen affecting financial markets

By Caroline Stauffer

LIMA (Reuters) - Peru's sol could be Latin America's strongest currency performer in 2011, appreciating at double the pace of 2010, as the central bank turns its focus to resurgent inflation rather than the exchange rate.

With Peru's economic growth rate exceeding much of the rest of the world, analysts in Peru and abroad see the sol strengthening to 2.6 or 2.7 per U.S. dollar in 2011, a gain of about 7 percent, as the central bank raises interest rates.

"We believe the sol will outperform the region's currencies over the course of the year," said Alejandro Grisanti of Barclays Capital in New York. "It is a good investment instrument with a strong return and low volatility."

Peru's economy is expected to grow 7 percent this year, propelled by strong domestic demand, foreign investment and the country's adherence to budget discipline. It is a far cry from the 1980s when hyper-inflation battered living standards and violent insurgents scared off investors.

April's presidential elections will not spook markets as all the frontrunners favor policies that emphasize fiscal restraint, free trade and foreign investment, economists say.

Averting currency volatility was long a goal of the central bank as half of all deposits in the country's banking system are in dollars.

Many Peruvians owe loans in dollars but get paid in the local currency, meaning that sharp volatility could hurt consumers and businesses.

Now, the threat of external price shocks from food and oil is threatening to push 2011 inflation beyond the 3 percent ceiling of the central bank's annual inflation target.

That could prompt the bank to rethink its currency interventions as well as raise interest rates.

"When you have food prices going up -- the most important thing to counterbalance that effect is to let the value of the currency rise -- that makes goods cheaper for people," Nomura economist Benito Berber said.

Peru raised its benchmark interest rate twice in two months to 3.5 percent to counter rising food and oil prices after three straight months of holding rates steady.

The central bank has indicated a "neutral" monetary policy would put the rate at 4.5 percent, suggesting more hikes are in store.

"It's already a guideline -- the central bank is prioritizing inflation over the exchange rate," said Mario Guerrero, an analyst at Scotiabank Peru in Lima.

In each of the past two years inflation in Peru was mild or virtually nonexistent, giving the central bank space to focus more attention on limiting gains by the sol.

On Feb. 10, the day after its most recent interest rate decision, Peru's central bank bought $130 million in an intervention to knock the sol back from a 33-month high.

Traders expect the bank to buy between $8 and $9 billion in 2011, similar to the amount purchased in 2010 but not enough to stop the sol from gaining as interest rates rise.

"As the sol strengthens, the central bank will keep intervening," said Gonzalo Navarro, head currency trader at Banco Santander in Lima. "But in the medium term it's not going to change the fundamental tendency of the exchange rate."

The central bank's early and aggressive intervention in 2010 -- when rock-bottom interest rates in the developed world fed demand for higher yielding emerging market assets -- limited the sol's gains to 2.77 percent.

Chile's peso in comparison gained around 8 percent that year as the central bank largely stayed out of the market. But it launched a $12 billion intervention in January and many now expect the peso to weaken. (Additional reporting by Ursula Scollo in Lima and Brad Haynes in Santiago; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latin American  currencies  gain on Mubarak exit
text:
* Chile's peso posts 1.4 pct weekly gain

* Peru cenbank swats down sol from 33-month high

* Speculator bets on Mexican peso rise

* Brazil real up 0.24 pct, Mexico peso 0.37 pct (Adds comments, data on Mexican peso CFTC positions)

By Michael O'Boyle and Silvio Cascione

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Feb 11 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies firmed on Friday after the resignation of Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak eased fears of unrest in the Middle East that had weighed on demand for riskier assets.

Oil and gold prices fell while world stocks rose after Mubarak handed power to the army, curbing concerns that unrest could push up the price of oil and weigh down global growth.

"People came to the conclusion it is not that easy to shut down the Suez Canal," said Dirk Willer, head of Latin America local markets strategy at Citigroup in New York. "If you do not get an oil spike on the back of Egypt developments, since the Suez canal is still open, then it is not a big deal."

Chile's peso closed at its strongest since early January, also helped by the view that the central bank will raise interest rates next week.

Chile's peso <CLP=> bid 0.28 percent firmer at 472.20 per dollar and notched a 1.4 percent gain for the week. The country's central bank is seen raising its benchmark rate to 3.50 percent next week, resuming hikes after pausing last month in part to avoid further appreciation in the peso.

The Chilean peso got a lift earlier this week after the central bank signaled it has no plans to step up dollar purchases. Chile, as well as Brazil and Peru, has been intervening in markets to stem sharp gains in its currency that are hurting local exporters.

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid 0.24 percent firmer at 1.665 per dollar on the local spot market despite two auctions in which the central bank bought dollars. The real firmed 0.54 percent for the week.

SOL INTERVENTION

The new government of President Dilma Rousseff introduced spending cuts this week to bring inflation back under control and minimize the need for aggressive interest rate hikes from the central bank. [ID:nN11131412]

But with Brazil offering among the highest rates in the world, the cuts have not dented appetite for the real.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> firmed 0.33 percent to 12.0325 per dollar, closing the week with a 0.29 percent loss.

Bets by speculators in favor of Mexico's peso edged up to 103,812 contracts in the week ended Feb. 8, according to data from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in Chicago.

The peso has by far the most bets in its favor of the eight major currencies tracked by Reuters. It is up around 4 percent since November on the back of an improving outlook for the economy of the United States, Mexico's main trading partner.

The large amount of bets on the peso could hurt the currency if U.S. stocks pull back and the hoard of speculators run for the exits, analysts said.

"If the S&P were to have a hiccup, then you could see some pressure on the peso," said Willer.

Mexico is the one major economy in the region not facing worsening inflation pressures and it is not expected to hike interest rates for some time.

Peru's sol <PEN=PE> closed flat after the central bank bought $130 million to knock the currency back from a 33-month high.

The country raised its benchmark interest rate for the second straight month late on Thursday to 3.5 percent, boosting the appeal of the sol to yield-hungry global investors. Peru's central bank bought $367 million so far in 2011 to undermine gains in the sol.

The country is expected to keep hiking interest rates, but it may start to rely on other measures to contain credit growth like raising bank capital ratios.

"Currency concerns should prevent rates from rising (in Peru) to their pre-recession levels and the bulk of further monetary tightening is likely to come through more creative channels," wrote Neil Shearing, an economist at Capital Economics. title: DJ  Peru 's  Central Bank  Changes  Intervention  Approach to Buying Dollars
text:
--Central bank changes approach to foreign-exchange interventions

--Aims to increase uncertainty in exchange market

--Central bank may purchase dollars even if sol is weakening 


 
   By Robert Kozak 
 

LIMA, Peru---The Central Reserve Bank of Peru has changed its approach to intervening to buy U.S. dollars, aiming to make it less of a one-way bet.

The central bank may now buy a fixed amount of dollars regardless of whether the dollar is depreciating against the sol, a central bank spokesman said.

The central back has purchased about $10 billion so far this year, mainly by buying varying amounts in each trading session depending on the appreciation pressures on the sol, aiming to reduce volatility.

On Monday, for example, the central bank purchased $40 million, and the sol closed slightly weaker at PEN2.603 to the dollar compared with PEN2.595 on Friday.

Despite the interventions that have helped drive up Peru's net international reserves to a record $60 billion so far this year, the sol has appreciated by 3.5% against the dollar.

Peru's bustling economy--gross domestic product expanded by 7.2% in July--and strong debt ratings, among other factors, have helped boost inflows of capital.

The central bank's aim now is in part to add some uncertainty for those taking out dollar-denominated loans for things like cars or houses, trying to ensure that there is no excessive debt burden in dollars that could hurt borrowers who earn in soles, should the dollar appreciate sharply against the sol.

"I think it is an error for those who earn in soles to be taking out loans in dollars," Central Reserve Bank of Peru President Julio Velarde said at a news conference late last week.

"Before, the sentiment that some [market participants] had is that when it [the sol] starts to depreciate, we stopped buying," he said, adding that, "If we are buying the same amount it will lead to some volatility. We are going to see how it works."

Both the U.S. dollar and the Peruvian sol are legal tender in Peru and are widely used. Most real-estate purchases are made in dollars.

Mr. Velarde added that the office of the Superintendent of Banking, Insurance and AFPs is seeking to turn around the trend of having more and more loans being made in dollars in Peru.

"They are trying to establish some additional provisions and to increase risks in mortgage loans in dollars, and will do the same with vehicle loans afterwards. It is a process," Mr. Velarde said.

Vehicle loans rose 22% in July over the same month last year, with 73% denominated in dollars, a 9-percentage-point increase in dollar-denominated loans over the same month a year earlier.

title: Peru 's  Central Bank Intervenes  in  Forex  Market, Buys $40 Million
Food Prices Seen Pushing Up Peru's Inflation in September -  Central Bank
text:
--Peru's central bank says food prices to keep inflation up in September

--Supply pressures on food prices are seen easing in October

--Central bank says it will continue to intervene in foreign-exchange market


 
   By Ryan Dube 
 

LIMA, Peru--The Central Reserve Bank of Peru said Friday higher food prices are expected to push up Peru's consumer price index in September, however the inflation rate should still converge to the central bank's target range by the end of 2012.

In August, consumer prices in Peru rose 0.51% from the previous month, bringing the 12-month inflation rate to 3.53%. The increase, which was higher-than-expected, was largely due to supply factors that boosted prices for perishable foods, like lemons and onions, the central bank says.

"This increase in the price of foods affected the month of August, and it is also going to affect the month of September," the central bank's chief economist, Adrian Armas, said during a conference call with reporters.

Mr. Armas said that Peru's CPI is forecast to be higher in September than in July, when it rose 0.09%.

Despite the increase, the central bank says it still expects inflation to fall within its annual target of 1.0% to 3.0% by the end of this year.

"Starting in October, there should be better supply conditions," Mr. Armas said.

A survey of 22 analysts released Friday by the central bank showed that the consensus for Peru's inflation this year is 3.0%, compared to a consensus of 3.2% in the prior month.

On Thursday, the central bank's board of directors left its reference interest rate unchanged at 4.25%, where it has stood since May 2011.

BBVA Banco Continental says it expects the central bank to keep its policy rate at 4.25% in the coming months.

"On one hand the central bank communique pointed out that inflation is above its target but because of transitory supply-side factors, while output keeps growing close to its potential," the bank said. "On the other, external risks remain high. We expect the policy rate to be left unchanged over the coming months as economic growth close to potential will limit demand-side pressures on prices, while external risks suggest remaining cautious."

Capital Economics said in a report it sees a "tightening bias" emerging in the next few months. "If global sentiment shows signs of a sustained recovery heading into 2013, the prospect of rate hikes could quickly return to the agenda," the firm said.

Peru's economy is expected to grow by about 6.0% this year. In 2011, it expanded by 6.92%.

Meanwhile, Mr. Armas said the exchange rate between the Peruvian sol and U.S. dollar is expected to continue to depend on global economic factors. So far this year, the sol has strengthened 3.26% against the dollar.

Mr. Armas said the central bank will continue to intervene in the foreign-exchange market to ease volatility. The central bank has intervened to purchase about $9.9 billion so far this year.

title: Emerging-Market  Currencies  and Debt Modestly Up
text:
Emerging-market currencies and debt were firmer for most of the day, though there was some paring of gains toward the end of trading on Tuesday.

Investor confidence rallied on the hope of European leaders resolving the region's debt crisis next month. While there was no statement from the European Central Bank on this, speculation that the ECB may consider capping the yields on weaker euro-zone nations has been making the rounds.

This helped push the euro higher against the dollar, and other higher-yielding assets rallied.

Emerging-market currencies also were buoyed by news that China is weighing stimulus measures to boost domestic consumption in a bid to boost its slowing economy and sliding exports.

"Its full steam ahead for hop-ium (or hope)," said Andrew Busch, global currency and public policy strategist at BMO Capital Markets. "When the biggest unknown out there [Europe] stabilizes, then you are going to get people going back to higher yielding currencies."

However, he expects the positive mood to last only until the meeting this weekend between German Chancellor Angela Merkel and Greek Prime Minister Antonis Samaras, when an extension of Greece's austerity target is likely to be on the agenda.

But such sentiment was absent Tuesday, when the South African rand and the Russian ruble were among the top gainers of the day to the dollar. The rand, however, is not expected to sustain its gains as the country's economic outlook remains bleak on falling demand for commodities, slowing growth and high unemployment. The rand is trading at ZAR8.2649 to the dollar, off from its 8.2124 earlier in the day, according to CQG data.

Just as market participants were waiting for the dollar to edge closer to 2 reais, in sync with a rally in all higher-yielding currencies, the Brazilian central bank announced reverse swap auctions to buy dollars. That indicates the bank's comfortable range for the pair is BRL2-2.10, Citi analysts said. The move is the first dollar-buying intervention since March 26. Brazil, in a bid to boost economic growth, has been weakening its currency, though some analysts have feared doing so would lead to higher inflation. The dollar is currently at BRL2.0178, slightly up from its previous close of BRL2.0173, according to CQG data.

The Central Bank of Peru once again intervened in its currency market to buy $40 million at an average of PEN2.6118 per dollar. The sol closed unchanged at PEN2.613 per dollar.

In Europe, most of the emerging-market currencies strengthened across the board. The Romanian leu benefited from a move by its constitutional court to invalidate the referendum held to impeach its president. The leu has strengthened 0.38% to 4.477 to the euro on the news, and could rally further in the near term.

Emerging-market debt as measured by the Markit CDX.EM index was trading at four basis points firmer at 246, according to Markit data.

India's Axis Bank Ltd. (532215.BY) has priced a $250 million tap of its 5.125% coupon September 2017 dollar bond to yield 390 basis points over comparable Treasurys. The bonds were reoffered at $101.835 per $100 of face value, yielding 4.71%.

--Patrick McGee and Robert Kozak contributed to this article

title: Peru Economists Say Sol to Continue Strengthening Trend
text:
--Peru's sol strengthens more than 3% against U.S. dollar so far this year

--Economists see more room for appreciation

--Central bank expected to continue intervening in foreign-exchange market


 
   By Ryan Dube 
 

LIMA--Peru's sol should maintain its trend of strengthening against the U.S. dollar over the next few years, though short-term volatility in the exchange rate should be expected, economists say.

The Peruvian currency has been gaining against the dollar during the last several years amid strong economic growth in the Andean country. The sol has appreciated more than 3% against the dollar so far this year, while in 2011 it strengthened 3.92%.

Peru's economy has been driven by private-sector investments in recent years. In 2011, Peru's gross domestic product gained 6.9%, while in 2010 it rose 8.8%. In the first half of this year, Peru's economy expanded 6.11%. Economic growth for the full-year 2012 is expected to be about 6%.

The chief economist of BBVA Banco Continental, Hugo Perea, said during an interview the trend for the sol hasn't changed.

"In the medium term, I think that there is still space for the sol to strengthen," Mr. Perea said. "The fundamentals continue to be very strong for Peru."

BBVA Banco Continental (CONTINC1.VL), Peru's second biggest bank, expects the sol to finish 2012 at PEN2.60 per dollar, which would be an appreciation of about 3.6% for the year. By 2015, the bank forecasts that the sol will reach PEN2.50 per dollar.

Mr. Perea said the forecasts consider that the Central Reserve Bank of Peru will continue to intervene in the foreign-exchange market to ease volatility. The central bank has bought about $9 billion this year in the foreign-exchange market, closing in on its 2007 record of $10.3 billion.

The central bank is expected to continue buying dollars while the sol appreciates, Mr. Perea said. "While the economy keeps growing, the central bank can continue to intervene without creating inflationary pressures," Mr. Perea said.

Pedro Pablo Kuczynski, a well-known economist who has served as finance minister and prime minister, said the interventions are necessary to protect local industry that would be hurt by a rapid appreciation of the sol. The sol has been one of Latin America's least volatile currencies thanks to the central bank's interventions.

"We would be swept away if we let the exchange rate move with the natural market," said Mr. Kuczynski. "I think they should intervene more," he added.

Alonso Seguro, the chief economist of Banco de Credito del Peru, the country's largest bank, said that only a major "shock" would reverse the sol's trend of appreciating in the medium-term.

In the short-term, however, volatility should be expected as uncertainty in the global economy continues, the economists say. In May, investor concerns surrounding the euro zone debt crisis resulted in the sol temporarily depreciating against the dollar.

"We are likely going to see some more hiccups that are going to be difficult to anticipate," Mr. Seguro said.

Banco de Credito (CREDITC1.VL) forecasts that the sol will finish 2012 at PEN2.60 per dollar, and to end 2013 at PEN2.55.

Deutsche Bank said that Peru's closely managed currency "still stands as one of the most overvalued currencies in the region."

It added that Moody's recent upgrade of Peru's debt rating will help the appreciation trend to continue. "The observed behavior during August, particularly after the rating upgrade, will only accentuate this trend," it said.

title: DJ Emerging European  Currencies  Gain on Euro-Zone, China Optimism
text:
Emerging European currencies gained, while emerging-market sovereign debt strengthened slightly, as markets pinned their hopes on progress in the euro-zone debt crisis and measures to support China's economy.

Emerging-market currencies largely took cues from European assets, which gained on the back of reports Spain may look to accelerate emergency financial aid for its troubled banking sector. Also Thursday, German Chancellor Angela Merkel also reiterated her country is committed to do what it can to maintain the euro, which help support cheerier market sentiment.

"The market is toying with the idea that Europe is moving toward a more reasonable set of policies," said Jose Wynne, head of North America foreign-exchange strategy at Barclays in New York. "This is one...step in a very long road, which the market is taking well."

Some emerging-market currencies were also encouraged by the prospect of more monetary stimulus in the world's second-largest economy, after China's premier said there is growing room for monetary policy measures.

Emerging-market sovereign debt strengthened slightly, as investors edged out of haven U.S. Treasurys. The cost for protection on this debt, according to the Markit CDX EM index, tightened to 247 basis points from 249 basis points. Venezuela's sovereign debt, which often outpaces wider market moves, outperformed, as the cost to insure this debt through five-year credit default swaps decreased to 868 basis points from 885 basis points.

Among currencies, emerging European and African currencies were the biggest gainers, spurred by euro-zone optimism and hopes for further China easing.

The Polish zloty advanced more than 1% against the dollar and about 0.6% against the euro, which traded at 4.0554 zlotys, according to CQG.

The Turkish lira advanced modestly, even after the country's central bank signaled that it could ease monetary policy in the future. The rate setters, however, kept the interest-rate corridor they use to support the lira and fight inflation unchanged at 5.75% to 11.5%. The lira edged up 0.3% against the dollar, which bought 1.7938 lira late Thursday.

The South African rand and Nigerian naira were also top gainers. South Africa's currency jumped 0.5% against the U.S. currency, which traded at 8.1962 rand, according to CQG.

The naira surged about 1.4% against the dollar, pushed by J.P. Morgan's recent announcement that it would include Nigeria in its benchmark index for emerging-market local currency debt. J.P. Morgan will add Nigeria to its Government Bond-Emerging Markets Index in three phases beginning October, it said in a research note issued this week. Analysts say Nigeria's expected inclusion could likely spur inflows into the African country's local debt market. On Thursday, the dollar bought 156.55 naira from NGN158.78 late Wednesday.

In Latin America, Peru was in focus after Moody's Investors Service upgraded the country's rating further into investment grade, to Baa2 from Baa3. The ratings firm cited Peru's robust economic growth and sound fiscal performance. The Peruvian sol, however, was little changed on the day, with the dollar trading at 2.614 soles from PEN2.615 late Wednesday. Peru's central bankintervened in the foreign-exchange market Thursday to buy $416 million, as part of its regular efforts to smooth out currency volatility.

Brazil's currency advanced slightly on the back of better-than-expected retail sales data, with the dollar falling 0.2% to buy 2.0189 reais.

Chile's central bank will hold its monthly rate-setting meeting later Thursday, but is widely expected to hold its key interest rate at 5%.

--Neelabh Chaturvedi, Graciela Ibanez and Nathalie Tadena contributed to this article.

title: FX  swings may stir debt investors in Mexico, Peru
text:
* Mexico, Peru debt mkts most vulnerable to outflows in Latam

 * Peru acting to curb FX, Mexico avoiding intervention

 * Appetite for emerging mkt debt ebbing after strong inflows 

 By Walter Brandimarte

 SAO PAULO, June 13 (Reuters) - Forex volatility has started to sap foreign investors' appetite for the local-currency bonds issued by emerging economies, adding pressure on countries such as Mexico and Peru to limit sharp swings in their foreign exchange rates.

 Due to their open capital markets, Mexico's and Peru's domestic debt markets are the most vulnerable in Latin America to bouts of capital flight unlike Brazil, whose domestic bond market is much less friendly to foreign investors.

 "When you look at a sudden reversal in capital flows, you have to look at those countries that have the highest percentage of foreign holdings (in their local debt). And that's essentially Mexico and Peru," said Siobhan Morden, head of Latin America strategy at Jefferies & Co.

 "The larger the percentage of foreign holdings, the more that requires policymakers to be responsive and proactive in terms of limiting the forex volatility," she added.  

 So far, both countries have been resilient in the face of  an incipient flight of foreign capital out of emerging markets. But the Peruvian and the Mexican central banks might be forced to become more active in their currency markets if redemptions grow. 

 Latin American central banks have used a variety of methods to support their currencies during the 2009 crisis, from direct sales of dollars in the spot market to the use of derivative contracts that increase the supply of greenbacks in the futures market. None have resorted to raising interest rates at a time when the global economy is slowing and they need to stimulate domestic consumption.

 RECORD INFLOWS REVERSE 

 After attracting record inflows in 2011, emerging market bonds denominated in local currencies lost much of their appeal to foreign investors this year as domestic interest rates dropped and concerns about currency volatility rose.

 So far this year, $8.3 billion have found their way into funds that invest in emerging market hard-currency bonds, while a more modest $2.8 billion have flown into those investing in local-currency debt, according to EPFR Global, a fund flow tracking firm.

 "That's just the opposite story from the previous year," said David Spegel, global head of emerging markets strategy at ING. "Last year, 78 percent of all the inflows into emerging markets debt went into local funds."

 But warning signs have been raised since last month, when those local-currency bond funds started bleeding money. They have lost $721 million in three consecutive weeks of outflows, EPFR data shows.

 "That has a lot to do with the foreign exchange volatility that we've seen spike this year in emerging markets," Spiegel said. "Why hold a local currency bond if you think that the foreign exchange rate might go against you? Certainly it's been more volatile."

 PERU ACTS FIRST

 Peru, with 57 percent of its fixed-rate debt stock in the hands of foreign investors, has so far managed to avoid a potentially disruptive capital flight by actively curbing volatility in its foreign exchange market.

 The Peruvian central bank last month ensured a steady supply of dollars to investors by directly selling the greenback in the spot market, and by offering dollar repurchase agreements for the first time ever.

 As a result, the Peruvian sol erased all the euro-zone related losses it had incurred in May to trade with gains of about 0.8 percent in the year to date.

 Mexico's case is different, though. 

 The Mexican peso has weakened some 10 percent since mid-March as policymakers have limited foreign exchangeinterventions to a minimum. Their official policy has been to offer up to $400 million in auctions in the spot market whenever the peso declines by at least 2 percent against the dollar in a single session.

 Still, the fact that there have been no outflows from Mexico's "bonos" suggests many foreign investors might have been hedging out their exposure to the peso, said Jefferies' Morden.

 Foreigners currently hold a record-high 44.6 percent of Mexico's 1.8 trillion pesos ($128 billion) local-currency debt market. Analysts are unsure how many of them are protected against currency moves, but they say such hedging operations have driven much of the recent volatility in the peso.

 Despite that volatility, Mexican policymakers have brushed aside the chance of more aggressive intervention, with central bank governor Agustin Carstens repeatedly affirming that the bank should let the free-floating currency regime function to the greatest degree possible. 

 "Policymakers are reluctant to be more responsive because Mexico has rules to intervene in the foreign exchange market, but I wonder if those rules need to be reevaluated," said Morden.

 BRAZIL, AN OUTLIER?

 The Latin American country that has been most active in its currency market has not acted to safeguard foreign investors' appetite for its debt, but rather to correct what it has called "distortions" in the market.

 Brazil's central bank has sold more than $7 billion worth of currency swaps to prop up the real since it resumed this type of intervention last month, but the government still imposes a 6 percent financial tax on foreign investors willing to buy its domestic bonds.

 Foreigners hold some 12.3 percent of Brazil's domestic debt, and Finance Minister Guido Mantega, in his fight against "speculative" money, said last month the government does not care about having more foreign capital in its local bond market. 

(Additional reporting by Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City; Editing by Theodore d'Afflisio)

title: Peru Expects Sol To Strengthen Through 2015
text:
--Peru sees sol strengthening to average PEN2.67 per U.S. dollar this year

--Finance Ministry says GDP is expected to expand by 6% in 2012 and 2013

--The ministry says it sees a trade surplus of $8.3 billion in 2012

--Copper production is expected to rise by almost 75% to 2.15 million tons by 2015

By Ryan Dube

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's government expects the sol to strengthen this year to an average of PEN2.67 per U.S. dollar, compared with PEN2.75 in 2011.

The Finance Ministry said Thursday in its multiannual macroeconomic report that the sol's average exchange rate against the greenback is expected to continue to appreciate from 2013 through 2015.

The ministry projects that the sol will average PEN2.64 per dollar in 2013, while in 2014 it is seen at PEN2.62 to the dollar and in 2015 it is forecast to average PEN2.60.

In the first four months of 2012, the sol gained more than 2% against the dollar. The Peruvian currency has since lost those gains as investors seek a safe haven in the dollar due to the euro-zone crisis.

The sudden change in trend has led the Central Reserve Bank of Peru to intervene in the foreign exchange market to sell dollars. On Wednesday, the central bank sold $282 million, which followed the selling of $115 million on Tuesday and $2 million on Friday.

The central bank's president, Julio Velarde, has said he expects volatility in the exchange rate to continue ahead of the June 17 election in Greece.

On Wednesday, the sol closed at PEN2.706 per dollar, which is a depreciation of 0.33% against the dollar so far this year.

In the report, the Finance Ministry also said that it forecasts Peru to maintain solid economic growth over the next few years. The ministry expects the gross domestic product will expand 6% in both 2012 and 2013. Annual economic growth is seen at 6.5% in both 2014 and 2015, the report says. Peru's GDP rose by 6.92% in 2011, and 8.8% in 2012.

The ministry said Peru's economic growth would be harmed if there is a global economic crisis similar to the 2008 financial crisis, a slowdown in private-sector investments and if a number of projects, including those in the country's key mining sector, are not completed.

Private-sector investments are expected to increase 10% in 2012, down from 11.7% last year. Private-sector investments slowed last year from 22.1% growth in 2010 due to uncertainty surrounding the presidential election and the international economy.

The ministry forecasts that private-sector investments will expand by 10% in 2013, 12% in 2014 and 12.5% in 2015.

It said that Peru is expected to have a trade surplus of $8.3 billion in 2012, down from $9.3 billion in 2011. Exports are forecast to total $48.9 billion in 2012, while imports are seen at $40.6 billion.

The government says that exports are expected to reach $63.5 billion in 2015 mainly due to an increase in copper shipments. Imports in 2015 are seen at $55.9 billion.

Peru is the world's second-biggest copper producer, and the red metal is the country's main export. In 2011, the country produced 1.24 million tons of copper.

Copper production in Peru is expected to rise by almost 75% by 2015 thanks to the start-up of new mines and the completion of expansion projects. The ministry sees Peru's copper production totaling 1.33 million tons this year, 1.45 million tons in 2013, 1.69 million tons in 2014 and 2.15 million tons in 2015.

The Finance Ministry also said that it expects Peru to have an average fiscal surplus of 1.2% of GDP between 2012 and 2015, compared with 1.3% from 2006 to 2011.

title: Peru's Main Stock Indexes End Higher; Sol Unchanged

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's main stock market indexes ended higher on Friday, as shares of a number of mining companies moved in opposite directions.

The Lima Stock Exchange's broad General Index rose 0.52% to end at 20,744.49.

The blue-chip Selective Index gained 0.16% to close at 29,969.12.

The intervention Friday was the first time the central bank has sold dollars this year, prompted by the recent weakening of the Peruvian currency compared to the dollar.

The sol closed unchanged Friday at PEN2.698 to the dollar. So far this year, the sol has depreciated 0.04% against the greenback.

title: MARKET TALK: Peru  Central Bank  Could Sell US Dollars -JPMorgan
text:
9:19 (Dow Jones) Peru's central bank, which intervened to buy about $8.0B this year, could sell greenbacks, JPMorgan said. The central bank more recently has added dollar liquidity using other instruments. "Overall, the latest BCRP intervention reaffirms the long-standing view that authorities are more concerned about dampening FX volatility in what is a de facto crawling peg regime, and they smooth both PEN appreciation and depreciation -- the latter in the context of stubbornly high inflation seen so far this year. Indeed, if external pressures intensify, we would expect the BCRP to sell some of the $8.2 billion it acquired in the first part of this year." (robert.kozak@dowjones.com)

9:17 (Dow Jones) US April durable goods orders are mildly disappointing, with non-transportation orders down by 0.6% on the month, says Capital Economics. "The massive 21.5% m/m slump in defence orders illustrates just how big a drag the Federal government already is on the economy, even before we get to the fiscal cliff at the start of next year." (jeffrey.sparshott@dowjones.com)

9:11 (Dow Jones) After a brief spike in euro-Swiss franc, the cross is coming back down toward its CHF1.2010 level that it's been sitting near in recent days. Euro back to CHF1.2024 after jumping up to 1.2052 momentarily early in New York trading. Euro hadn't traded above CHF1.2050 since March 30. Traders say the move was not intervention by the Swiss National Bank. (stephen.bernard@dowjones.com)

9:08 (Dow Jones) Traders say they don't see the Swiss National Bank behind this morning's pop in the EUR/CHF. It seemed to be stops being triggered. The euro rose to CHF1.2052. (matt.walter@dowjones.com)

9:08 (Dow Jones) Brazil's labor market remains tight despite as Latin America's largest economy continues to generate jobs despite slowing activity, Goldman Sachs says. April's unemployment rate retreated to 6.0% from 6.2% in March. Unemployment at near-record lows "remains a source of cost-push pressure on inflation," firm says. Real wage growth has also been accelerating -- thanks to this year's double-digit hike in Brazil's minimum wage -- which will likely "continue to support private consumption growth," Goldman says. Average monthly wages up 6.2% year-on-year in April to BRL1719.50, although down 1.2% from March, data show. (jeff.fick@dowjones.com)

9:03 (Dow Jones) RBC (RY) posted surprisingly higher-than-expected F2Q provisions for credit losses. The reason: two corporate accounts -- a western Canadian real estate project that's been struggling for awhile, and a fraud, says Chief Risk Officer Morten Friis on an earnings call. "Losses are losses but the point is there's nothing systematic about this," he says. RY also had higher PCLs in its C$7B loan book in the Caribbean, which will take another one or two quarters to work through. "Outside of the Caribbean, the portfolio is strong, sound, entirely consistent with our expectations, and I think very encouraging," he says. (caroline.vanhasselt@dowjones.com)

8:59 (Dow Jones) H-P (HPQ) may be progressing in many areas, but it still hasn't reached that corner it needs to turn, Needham says as it stays bearish. HPQ still has "battles on multiple fronts," all while facing a potentially weakening macro picture. Plan to cut 27k jobs is logical, but Needham calls the restructuring more of a reallocation of resources that will take time to have desired effect, given plan to reinvest most of expected savings into new efforts like cloud. Shares, up 8.5% at $22.88 premarket, erase some of the 32% lost in last year through yesterday's close. (joan.solsman@dowjones.com)

8:58 (Dow Jones) Chilean peso trades slightly stronger against the dollar on a more positive external outlook with rising international copper prices and better-than-expected US durable goods orders data. As Chile produces one third of the world's copper, its currency often moves in line with that metal's price, while it also looks at US news for direction. "The world looks better today after yesterday's market losses," said Gloria Soto, head of the currency desk at FXCM Chile. Chilean peso recently trading at CLP506.70 versus Wednesday's four-month low close at CLP507.95, according to Valor Futuro newswire. (graciela.ibanez@dowjones.com)

8:54 (Dow Jones) US dollar briefly dipped but rebounded quickly after weekly jobless claims were little changed, and durable goods orders in April were better than expected. USD was at Y79.43 from Y79.42 before the goods report, according to EBS via CQG. Euro also steady at $1.2570 from $1.2563. The US indicators unlikely to be a driver today, with markets still sensitive to developments in Europe. (matt.walter@dowjones.com)

8:50 (Dow Jones) Don't expect morning data to settle debate on where US economy is headed this summer. Good news: jobless claims keep declining and top-line durable goods posted small gain instead of expected small decline. Bad news: demand for non-defense non-aircraft capital goods tumbled 1.9% last month, hinting businesses are less confident about future. Next up: Kansas City Fed manufacturing report at 11:00am EDT. (kathleen.madigan@dowjones.com)

8:49 (Dow Jones) NetApp's (NTAP) bleak F1Q outlook jolted investors late yesterday, while lack of FY 2013 guidance left analysts miffed. "Demand appears even less firm than it did this time last year," notes Sterne Agee, as the company says there's too much uncertainty in Europe to predict beyond this quarter. NTAP insists macro and cyclical factors, not competitive pressure, are to blame for its weak 1Q view, though Janney calls that claim "debatable," given executive comments implying a slower-than-expected April, elongated sales cycles and smaller deals of late. JPMorgan sees an "element of ultra-conservatism" in the view, especially after a big miss last summer burned the company. NTAP off 15% at $27.96 premarket. (andrew.fitzgerald@dowjones.com)

8:46 (Dow Jones) While top-line durable goods orders come in slightly better than expected--up 0.2% in April--bookings for non-defense capital goods excluding aircraft decreased by 1.9%. That suggests businesses are wary about future demand and are reluctant to invest in more equipment. (kathleen.madigan@dowjones.com)

title: MARKET TALK: Peru's  Central Bank  Used USD Repos For First Time
text:
11:23 (Dow Jones) Central Bank of Peru, which has intervened heavily so far this year to purchase US dollars and help ease appreciation pressures on the sol, yesterday used for the first time a new instrument designed to do just the opposite. With the sol under pressure, central bank sold $50M of one-day dollar-denominated repos, adding greenbacks to the market. So far no sign from the central bank on whether they will repeat the move today. Central bank tightly controls volatility in the currency market, without setting a fixed level for the sol. (robert.kozak@dowjones.com)

11:19 (Dow Jones) The blue chips gathered steam ahead of the 11 o'clock hour, the annointed time for Facebook's trading debut. But so far, said debut is yet to happen, and, amid the anxiety, stocks have slid steadily as the clock ticks. Dow up 10. (michael.driscoll@wsj.com)

11:18 (Dow Jones) The euro's rebound against the dollar gets extended to another high for the day as EU economics chief Olli Rehn says the commission is working on scenarios for Greece staying with the euro, which had been modestly higher already amid some short-covering. The euro traded as high as $1.2737 and is now at $1.2729, according to EBS via CQG. It traded at $1.2697 late Thursday. (stephen.bernard@dowjones.com)

11:13 (Dow Jones) TIM Participacoes SA (TSU, TIMP3.BR), the local unit of Telecom Italia SpA (TIT.MI), reached for the first time ever the leadership position in Brazil's largest city Sao Paulo, in terms mobile-phone market share. In April, TIM reached a market share of 31.30% in Sao Paulo, eclipsing Telefonica Brasil SA (VIV, VIVT4.BR) with a market share of 30.96% in the period. (rogerio.jelmayer@dowjones.com)

11:08 (Dow Jones) Remember those whispers of concern about how the NBA lockout could affect basketball gear sales? Well players eventually hit the courts in a shortened season, though it may not have mattered as new colorful shoes in the fashion-drive category helped drive demand. Still, added exposure couldn't hurt, and Foot Locker (FL) CEO Ken Hicks said key player shoes named after LeBron, Kobe and Durant sold "exceptionally well" in 1Q. He said color was a consistent theme in all athletic categories, a trend Hicks sees continuing. FL's strong F1Q report sends shares up 9.8% to $30.74, while rival Finish Line (FINL) jumped 7%. (john.kell@dowsjones.com)

11:05 (Dow Jones) A bigger risk for ECB than losing money on Greek bonds in the event of a Greece euro-zone exit is a credibility crisis, says Jamie Stuttard, head of international bond portfolio management at Fidelity Investments. "While the ECB's balance sheet can withstand the losses, a key point is the risk of credibility as central banks buying bonds from countries that end up default," he says. With much at stake, the ECB may be prompted to act if the crisis deepens, he says, adding that it's important to check the volatility and velocity of the yield increase, especially in shorter-dated maturities in Spain and Italy, rather just focusing on the actual level of 10-year maturities. (min.zeng@dowjones.com)

11:04 (Dow Jones) Bankrupt Jefferson County, Ala. plans to skip another G.O. debt payment in October, its attorney, Kenneth Klee, says. (The county defaulted on its non-bank owned G.O. debt for the first time last month.) The move is hardly surprising, given that state lawmakers killed a rescue bill for JeffCo this week. Alabama local governments have very limited powers and cannot raise revenue without state permission, so without help, Jefferson County is likely to stay in bankruptcy quite a while and may miss even more debt payments. Klee says under Alabama Supreme Court precedent, the county should provide for the health and welfare of its citizens instead of paying debt holders. (kelly.nolan@dowjones.com)

11:01 (Dow Jones) Chile's GDP isn't likely to continue growing at its current robust pace, Capital Economics says. Chile posted a 5.6% 1Q GDP gain while analysts expected a 5.2% increase. The solid performance of the Chilean economy likely won't last as copper prices, already down 10% so far this month, are expected to continue falling as the global economic turmoil will further intensify, says Capital Economics. Chile produces a third of the world's copper and the metal represents 15% of the country's GDP. (graciela.ibanez@dowjones.com)

11:00 (Dow Jones) After another week of pummelling, Chesapeake (CHK) is climbing along with natural-gas futures. Natural-gas producers are generally higher today amid the broader stock market's modest advance after a string of losses. CHK climbs 6% and Quicksilver gains 3% while Nymex natural-gas futures are up about 2%. (angel.gonzalez@dowjones.com)

11:00 (Dow Jones) Is the hype over Facebook's (FB) IPO warranted? FB is a wonderful wide-moat business, but a choppy growth trajectory will likely send shares lower at some point, offering investors an entry point at a much more attractive valuation than they'll get today, says Morningstar analyst Rick Summer. He sees FB and Google (GOOG) dominating the Internet ad market as FB finds better ways to monetize its massive user base. Its trove of data on users is its ace in the hole as it races to develop new revenue streams, Summer says. (daisy.maxey@dowjones.com)

10:56 (Dow Jones) About 45,000 orders have been entered by TD Ameritrade (AMTD) customers to trade Facebook (FB) shares as of 10:30am EDT Friday, according to Steve Quirk, senior vice president of trading for the firm. About half TD Ameritrade's clients were able to get in on the allocation, says Quirk, who sees the social media giant's debut as a rallying point for individual investors. FB shares not yet trading. (jacob.bunge@dowjones.com; @jacobbunge)

10:51 (Dow Jones) Colombia Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry said today the government will force some banks to boost reserve requirements on consumer credits as past-due loans begin to rise. Rules will only apply to banks with particularly high levels of overdue loans. Bancolombia (CIB), the country's top bank, said in its 1Q earnings report last week it's seeing a rise in delinquent consumer loans, and said it would thus focus more on corporate loans. Bancolombia's share price unchanged in Bogota at COP27,580, but down 6% since it noted the delinquencies. In NY, CIB up a fraction at $62.14. (dan.molinski@dowjones.com)
