title: MARKET TALK: BBVA Says Peru's Sol Will Continue To Strengthen
text:
11:08 (Dow Jones) BBVA Continental expects the strengthening tendency of Peru's sol against the US dollar to continue in coming months and should close this year at about PEN2.60 per dollar. Yesterday, the sol closed at PEN2.652 per dollar, which is an appreciation of 1.7% so far this year. The Central Reserve Bank of Peru regularly intervenes in the forex market by buying dollars to ease volatility. "In this context, the central bank will continue to be active in the exchange market, moderating the pace that the PEN will strengthen," BBVA says. (ryan.dube@dowjones.com)

11:07 (Dow Jones) Ahead of JCPenney's (JCP) F1Q report Tuesday it's anyone's guess how the retailer will do--literally. Of the analysts providing estimates to Thomson Reuters, their bottom-line views range from a 51c loss to a 5c/share profit, a much wider range than has been typical for the company or peers. But JCP hasn't given insight on how it thought the quarter might go, leaving analysts on their own to figure out how JCP's pricing changes have impacted results here in the early going of the shift. Amid that uncertainty, shares have fallen 2.8% this year, trailing rivals Kohl's (KSS) and Macy's (M). (karen.talley@dowjones.com)

11:04 (Dow Jones) JPMorgan's (JPM) credit derivatives-trading losses are punishing finanical stocks, the only sector in the red, as the broader market pushes higher. JPM falls 8.2%, Citi (C) off 3%, Morgan Stanley (MS) loses 4.5%, Goldman (GS) declines 3% and BofA (BAC) gives back 0.5%. The Financial Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLF) is down 0.7%. "This just clouds the whole sector for a long time," says Rick Fier at Conifer Securities. (christopher.dieterich@dowjones.com)

11:03 (Dow Jones) Tucked within the Univ of Michigan prelim May sentiment report are questions about how consumers view the housing market. Economists at Credit Suisse report the average of the readings on home buying and selling conditions are up five of the last six months -- the best stretch without a decline in 15 years. "This move points to higher home sales in coming months," they conclude. (kathleen.madigan@dowjones.com)

10:57 (Dow Jones) Mexico's competitiveness in manufacturing keeps getting stronger, Morgan Stanley says, noting that the country's market share for its principal export destination, the US, is near historic highs even as Mexico gradually diversifies into new markets. (US takes about 78% of Mexican exports, down from 90% a decade ago) An appreciating currency and rapid wage gains in China have benefited Mexican manufacturers. "The greatest threat to the Mexican manufacturing model - China - is likely behind us," the brokerage says. (amy.guthrie@dowjones.com)

10:51 (Dow Jones) JPMorgan (JPM) may have suffered trading losses, but investment manager RegentAtlantic Capital thinks the bank is still in decent shape. "The loss in dollar terms is certainly significant, but the impact on their business we don't expect to be as significant," says its Director of Portfolio Management Greg Allison. Adds Tier 1 ratio still stronger than peers. But says announcement does raise questions over the bank's risk management. "Prior to the announcement, JPMorgan was ahead of its competition in risk control and that's the reason why it came out of 2008 in relatively good shape. The news does raise questions about whether this is a fluke or there's indication they don't have enough risk management." JPM down 8% at $37.45. (amy.or@dowjones.com)

10:49 (Dow Jones) General opinion on JPMorgan's (JPM) trading fiasco seems to concur that perhaps the biggest hit comes to the bank's reputation and trust in its management, something that could eventually prove more costly than a $2B trading loss. "Dimon consistently misrepresented the seriousness of the exposures as soon as the press was onto it," Yves Smith writes at naked capitalism. "Both Bloomberg and the Wall Street Journal were digging, and Dimon was dismissive, calling the concerns a 'tempest in a teapot'." She says Dimon "misled investors, but no one seems to care much about niceties like accurate and timely disclosure these days." JPM down 8.2% at $37.39. (john.shipman@dowjones.com) (http://www.nakedcapitalism.com/2012/05/jamie-dimon-misrepresented-london-whale-risks-admits-to-2-billion-loss-plus-risk-management-black-eye.html("http://www.nakedcapitalism.com/2012/05/jamie-dimon-misrepresented-london-whale-risks-admits-to-2-billion-loss-plus-risk-management-black-eye.html"))

10:45 (Dow Jones) US beef exports slid from a year ago in March as sales to Mexico, South Korea and Japan weakened, according to USDA data compiled by the US Meat Export Federation. Sales for 1Q to the trio was down as well, with South Korea tumbling 56% in March and 36% for the quarter. Multiyear-to-record wholesale-beef prices hit in late February likely slowed buying interest, analysts say. (curt.thacker@dowjones.com)

10:40 (Dow Jones) Short interest for home builders rose in April. While many investors hoped the hard-hit sector had finally struck bottom, contrarian investors are clearly betting some of the stocks have further room to fall. According to JP Morgan, short interest rose 69 bps to 14.3%, led by the smaller-cap players, while the bigger names saw a modest overall rise. Short interest rose the most in Beazer (BZH)--up 955 bps--while Toll (TOL) saw a 195 bps climb. Short interest fell in some of the more troubled names: Hovnanian (HOV) fell 441 bps, while KB Home (KBH) dipped 268 bps. MDC slipped 63 bps. (dawn.wotapka@dowjones.com)

10:40 (Dow Jones) For the commercial-paper market, for now the potential widespread downgrades of banks by Moody's is a bigger worry that JPMorgan's trading losses, says a commercial-paper trader at a primary dealer. "The JPM issue has the market a little bit worried because with controls in place, you don't expect such things to happen." CP trading is already slow as investors are concerned about the potential impact if Moody's does downgrade more than 100 banks, as well as the turmoil in Europe and proposed changes to the way money-market funds operate. (anusha.shrivastava@dowjones.com)

10:38 (Dow Jones) Hovnanian (HOV) shares up 5.4% at $1.95 after UBS upgrades the struggling builder to buy from neutral, citing valuation. Depressed by liquidity concerns, HOV tumbled 23% since Jan 18, while peer group climbed 16%. But UBS notes that HOV is "generating greater operating leverage, through opening new, better located communities." The company is also tackling its financial situation, in part, with a recent equity raise. "While these transactions aren't a panacea, they represent a step in the right direction." (dawn.wotapka@dowjones.com)

10:33 (Dow Jones) Investors were piling into derivatives, to bet, of course, on JPMorgan's (JPM) derivatives bet gone awry. Options activity on the bank's shares surged to more than three-times the daily average volume within the first hour of trading as traders picked up options to protect against additional declines. One trader picked up 20,000 June $35 put options at a cost of $1.9M -- a bet that can hedge two-million JPM shares against an additional 6.5% drop. Shares down 8% at $37.48. (kaitlyn.kiernan@dowjones.com)

text:
(Recasts, adds quotes from Mexico, Peru)

* Mexico's peso off 0.5 pct, Brazil's real gains 0.6 pct

* U.S. services report creates pessimism ahead of Friday's labor report

* Peru raises bank reserve requirements

By Caroline Stauffer

LIMA, May 3 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso weakened on Thursday on disappointing service sector data from the United States, though the real strengthened late in the session after Brazil took a break from market intervention.

Peru's sol weakened slightly as traders digested new bank deposit requirements and Chile's peso closed at its strongest level in more than a month a f ter the country's central bank said it had considered a rate hike at its last board meeting.

The U.S. Institute for Supply Management said on Thursday its services index fell to 53.5 in April from 56.0 in March, missing economists' forecasts for a modest decline to 55.5.

Analysts said the report's employment component pointed to lingering weakness in the recovery of the world's largest economy, leading to investor caution ahead of a highly anticipated April labor data scheduled for release on Friday.

In response, the Mexican peso weakened 0.5 percent to 12.9991 per dollar. The currency is particularly sensitive to U.S. data because Mexico sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to the United States, tying its economy to that of its northern neighbor.

"Given the dependency we have with the U.S. economic cycle, in particular with consumption, these signals of weakness are normally related to a weaker currency," said Delia Paredes, director of Analysis at Mexico City brokerage Banorte-IXE in Mexico City.

"I'm concerned we'll see a contraction of employment in manufacturing in Friday's report," she said.

Peru's sol also weakened, closing down 0.08 percent to bid 2.64 per dollar.

The country's central bank earlier this week moved to curb appreciation of the currency by raising some deposit requirements on banks. The sol has traded around its strongest level in 15 years recently, helped by Peru's swift economic growth.

"The market continues to feel the impacts of the central bank's new measures and one of those is that now dollars are worth more than soles in the bank treasuries," said one trader in Lima who asked not to be named.

Chile's peso meanwhile strengthened 0.48 percent to close bidding 481.8 per dollar.

The Chilean central bank's latest minutes showed that although the bank's governing council voted unanimously to hold the benchmark interest rate at 5.0 percent last month, it considered raising it by 25 basis points.

REAL CHANGES COURSE

After weakening for much of the session, the real closed 0.64 percent stronger to bid 1.9117 per U.S. dollar as traders cheered less central bank intervention in the spot market.

"Two weeks ago we had nearly daily interventions from the central bank, but in the past three days the bank has stayed out of the market, decreasing pressure on the exchange rate," said one trader.

The government and central bank have tried to weaken the currency with taxes on financial transactions and dollar buys in the spot market in a bid to prop up Brazil's manufacturing sector.

The real closed at its weakest level since July 2009 on Wednesday.

Lower interest rates have also made the real, which has weakened nearly 3 percent this year, less attractive for investors.

In the latest sign more rate cuts lie ahead, a draft presidential decree seen by Reuters on Thursday showed President Dilma Rousseff will link returns on some national savings accounts to the central bank's lending rate.

The proposal carries enormous political and economic risks and amounts to a reengineering of one of the basic pillars of Brazil's financial system.

(Additional reporting by Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City, Danielle Fonseca in Sao Paulo and Ursula Scollo in Lima; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: UPDATE 2- Peru  raises deposit rules as sol gains
text:
* Stricter rules complement interventions to soak up inflows

* Economic, credit growth stronger than expected

* Tighter rules follow 11 months of steady interest rates

* Criticism of 'capital controls' resurfaces

(Adds details, quotes)

By Terry Wade

LIMA, April 30 (Reuters) - Peru's central bank said on M onday it was raising deposit requirements on bank accounts in a bid to curb credit expansion and stem appreciation in the local currency, which is at a 15-year high against the U.S. dollar.

Economic growth has been stronger than expected and is forecast to reach 6 percent this year. That has lifted demand for credit, while the sol has firmed about 2 percent since Jan. 1 on heavy inflows of dollars that the central bank has absorbed with frequent interventions on the spot market.

Abrupt fluctuations in the sol have long concerned officials because about half of Peru's bank deposits are held in dollars and many people and companies earn money in one currency but owe debts in the other.

"With this package of measures, the central bank seeks to act preventively to reduce the rate of growth of liquidity in a context of accelerating de-dollarization of deposits, the greater dollar indebtedness of firms, and low interest rates on dollars - a result of high global liquidity," the central bank said in a statement.

Many emerging markets, especially Brazil, have criticized the U.S. Federal Reserve for introducing too much liquidity into the global financial system. Brazil has urged its peers and the IMF to support "defensive" measures designed to fend off excessive appreciation of local currencies.

The measures in Peru also mean the central bank, after holding its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 4.25 percent for 11 straight months, is adopting a more restrictive monetary stance.

Some economists had said the bank was reluctant to raise interest rates to chip away at faster inflation because doing so would have lured in even more hot money.

The tighter measures will increase the average deposit rate on bank accounts denominated in soles and U.S. dollars by 0.5 percentage point and boost the marginal deposit rate to 30 percent from 25 percent on accounts denominated in soles.

In a bid to discourage inflows of speculative capital, the central bank extended to three years from two years the 60 percent deposit requirement that targets short-term credits from abroad. A deposit requirement of 20 percent will also apply to some credits and bonds with terms longer than three years.

It was the first time since last April that the central bank changed deposit requirements. The new rules take effect on Tuesday.

In 2008, Peruvian officials rejected critics who said the central bank was flirting with capital controls when it raised deposit rules and introduced a commission on a type of money market instrument to curb inflows. Those criticisms resurfaced on Monday.

"The measures suggests that Peru's central bank no longer has more ammunition to intervene and is now resorting to capital controls," the 4Cast consultancy said.

(Reporting By Terry Wade, Editing by Leslie Gevirtz and Dan Grebler)

27 Apr 2012 13:22 EDT DJ  Peru Central Bank's Velarde: Sol Appreciation Not 'Dramatic'

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Central Reserve Bank of Peru President Julio Velarde said Friday that the appreciation of the sol so far this year hasn't been that "dramatic."

Velarde reiterated in a conference call sponsored by the Peruvian Business Council that the central bank doesn't have a fixed level for the sol, and added that he wasn't that concerned about the recent appreciation of the sol.

The sol has appreciated by 1.97% so far this year against the U.S. dollar and by 6.57% in the last 12-month period.

The central bank has been intervening heavily to purchase dollars and ease the rate at which the sol has appreciated.

Velarde said that the central bank has been sterilizing the inflows of foreign exchange, and added that there are no short-term limits on the amount of interventions that can be carried out.

He also mentioned that in the past, reserve requirements have been used to help manage inflows and said that the central bank would be able to use that tool again.

He said that anyone who believes that the sol will continue to appreciate indefinitely "will be disappointed" at one time or another.

Velarde said that the central bank's official forecast for economic growth for this year is at 5.7% and that there is an upward bias. He added that if the central bank increases its forecast that could rise to between 6% to 6.2%.

"There are tailwinds that are in our favor," he said, adding that surveys are showing that consumer and investor confidence is returning to levels reached before the general elections held last year.

He also pointed to a strong recovery of public sector investments and added that the construction sector is recovering strongly.

Velarde added that most analysts now expect the reference interest rate will remain on hold to the end of the year. It has been at 4.25% since May last year.

He said that inflation, while still a concern, is expected to end this year within the central bank's target range of 1% to 3%.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  Forex  gains after Dutch debt sale
text:
* Brazil's real gains 0.25 pct, Mexico's peso up 0.15 pct

* Dutch bond sale eases Euro-zone concerns

* Peru sol heads for new 15-year high, intervention eyed

By Caroline Stauffer

Lima, April 24 (Reuters) - Latin America's currencies strengthened on Tuesday after a debt auction in Holland eased concerns over the European crisis and positive news in U.S. consumer confidence and housing reports supported modest gains.

The Mexican peso gained 0.15 percent to 13.1573, recovering from its weakest level in three months. Brazil's real

strengthened 0.25 percent to bid 1.8763 per dollar.

Investors breathed a sigh of relief after the Dutch state raised 2 billion euros by selling two bonds at an auction. The prime minister's resignation over budget cuts on Monday had raised concerns the European debt crisis could be spreading.

"I've seen a strong relationship between the (Mexican) peso and risk sentiment coming from Europe," said Alfredo Puig, a trader at Vector brokerage in Monterrey. "Today's placements helped us, the Dutch auction was very important."

Data from the United States, Mexico's top trading partner, showed new U.S. single-family home sales dropped in March but the reading still beat analysts' expectations.

The S&P/Case-Shiller housing report meanwhile showed U.S. single-family home prices rose in February for the first time in 10 months in a sign the sector is starting to stabilize.

"All of this is supporting U.S. stocks, and Latin American currencies are following that," said Pedro Tuesta, an economist with Washington-based 4Cast.

Signs of recovery in the world's largest economy support assets perceived as risky, like stocks and emerging market currencies.

Farther south, Chile's peso gained 0.28 percent to bid 487 per dollar. Peru's sol gained 0.04 percent to bid 2.65 per dollar, heading for its strongest close in some 15 years, though traders said that level provoked caution.

"Breaking the 2.65 barrier will cause an official intervention, there's hardly any trading," said one Lima-based trader who asked not to be named.

Peru's central bank has bought dollars on the spot market nearly every day in recent weeks amid heavy dollar inflows and strong economic growth in the Andean country.

Though Brazil's real gained on Tuesday, it is the worst performer this month of the world's 36 most-traded currencies tracked by Thomson Reuters. Investors have bet against the currency as the government and central bank tried to weaken it.

But Brown Brothers Harriman said in a report that the currency remains an attractive carry trade investment even though it is not likely to strengthen beyond 1.8 per dollar.

"Hindsight has shown that sell-offs like these have proven excellent medium-term opportunities," the brokerage said.

title: Peru's Sol Seen Appreciating More Than Earlier Forecast
text:
--Economists revise forecasts for stronger sol at end of 2012

--The sol has appreciated 1.56% so far this year, despite heavy central-bank intervention

--Central bank's purchases in the foreign-exchange market close in on record from 2007


 
   By Ryan Dube 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LIMA (Dow Jones)--The strengthening of Peru's sol in the first months of this year has led some economists to revise their forecasts for the currency's year-end exchange rate against the U.S. dollar, projecting that the currency will appreciate more in 2012 than previously anticipated.

Over the last several years, the sol has benefited from strong inflows of foreign direct investments, which have been attracted to the Andean country thanks to its political and fiscal stability. In 2011, the sol strengthened 4% against the dollar, and has appreciated about 14% since the end of 2008.

So far this year, the trend has continued. On Wednesday, the sol closed at PEN2.655 per dollar, 1.56% stronger than its closing rate at the end of last year.

Hedmond Rios, an economist with brokerage Celfin Capital, told Dow Jones Newswires on Wednesday that he recently revised his year-end forecast for the sol and now expects the currency to close 2012 at PEN2.64 per dollar, compared to a previous forecast of PEN2.68 per dollar.

"The currency is going to continue its appreciation trend," Rios said.

Banco de Credito del Peru, the country's largest bank, also recently revised its year-end forecast for the sol. The bank is forecasting that the currency will appreciate 3% in 2012 to finish at PEN2.62, compared to a previous projection of PEN2.64.

Banco de Credito's chief economist, Alonso Segura, said during a meeting with reporters on Tuesday that there is a "downward bias" in the forecast, indicating that the sol could strengthen beyond the bank's official projection.

He said he hasn't seen "anything that changes the tendency" for the sol's appreciation.

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru intervenes in the foreign-exchange market to reduce volatility. So far this year, the central bank has bought about $7 billion, which is more than all of 2011, and is closing in on its 2007 record, when it bought $10.3 billion in the foreign-exchange market.

Mario Guerrero, an economist with Scotiabank Peru, the country's third-largest bank, said the interventions should continue, however with "less intensity" as seasonal factors that affected the exchange rate ease.

Officials from the central bank have said that the sol's appreciation this year has been strongly affected by seasonal factors, including increased demand for the currency by mining companies to pay local taxes.

"We should see the central bank continue to buy dollars, but I think in less intensity than in the first months of this year," said Guerrero. He projects the sol will end 2012 at PEN2.63 per dollar.

title: Emerging Market  Currencies , Debt Weakened By Global Concerns
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market currencies and debt were weaker again as investors' worry about Europe and China escalated. The unexpected decline in U.S. consumer sentiment also weighed on markets.

A softer growth in China held emerging markets in check. The country's first quarter growth rate was at an 8.1% annualized rate, lower than expectations of 8.3%. At the same time, investors were too uncertain about Spain and closed positions ahead of the weekend leading to a weakening of yields on the sovereign's debt again.

The escalation of global concerns has led investors to scale back their exposure to assets with higher risk and higher returns such as emerging market assets. Many investors are taking profits and closing their positions earlier than expected. In sync with this trend is the outflow of $99 million out of emerging market focused funds in the week ended Wednesday, according to flows from EPFR Global.

Much of the outflows were driven by investors exiting local-currency and blended funds. This is the second time so far this year that emerging market funds have seen outflows; the previous time was during the week ended Jan. 18.

"In light of the global rout and price declines, it is somewhat reassuring that investor flows were not more severe," said David Spegel, global head of emerging markets strategy at ING Financial Markets.

"People are starting to kick the tires on their assumptions much earlier in the year," said Cameron Brandt, EPFR's director of research. "Peoples' tendency to sell and go away in May has now just advanced to late March and early April."

Currencies like the South African rand and the Mexican peso were weaker on the day, with the dollar gaining nearly a 1% on each. The dollar-peso was trading at MXN13.1638, up 1.04% on the day. While the dollar-rand pair was at ZAR7.9397, up 0.85% on the day.

Investors, while confident that emerging market economies would fare better than developed markets, expect these currencies to underperform in the next few months. In the short term, the Brazilian real is expected to keep weakening on central bank intervention measures, and the ruble strengthen on technical support and steady oil prices.

Emerging market sovereign bonds were weaker and risk premiums on these bonds widened by five basis points to 360 basis points over comparable Treasury yields on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index Global. Risk premiums on Argentina's bonds widened by 13 basis points after reports of the government taking a majority stake on the country's largest energy producer surfaced. Market participants have been asking how the country plans to finance the acquisition.

Meanwhile, in other parts of Latin America, central banks of Brazil and Peru intervened in the currency market to moderate the pace of their currency appreciation.

Peru's central bank is likely to keep its key rates unchanged, and use its foreign exchange as a tool to tighten monetary policy, said Benito Berber, an analyst at Nomura. The bank held rates at 4.25% Thursday. Since May 2011, the Peruvian sol's real effective exchange rate or inflation-adjusted value against a basket of peers has appreciated by 5%, mostly engineered by the central bank, he said. Peru's inflation pressures have eased, and there's little need to change rates.

That policy, however, could change if the U.S. Fed embarks on another round of economic stimulus measures termed "quantitative easing," or QE3, Berber said.

The dollar-sol pair remains almost unchanged at PEN2.660 on the day after another round of central bank intervention.

-By Prabha Natarajan and Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2468; prabha.natarajan@dowjones.com [ 13-04-12 2016GMT ]

title: Emerging-Market Investors Faced With Fewer 'Carry'  Currencies
text:
--Central bank interventions limit carry-trade options

--Investors continue to seek higher-yielding paper

--Focus turns to Mexican peso and South African rand


 
   By Prabha Natarajan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Investors remain bullish on emerging-market currencies and now that Greece has concluded its debt restructuring, low volatility in global markets offers an ideal time to initiate trades.

The problem, however, is these investors' options are less plentiful now that central banks in emerging markets have built walls to protect their currencies.

One favorite play, selling the dollar and buying Brazilian real assets, lost its luster recently after a rash of central-bank actions to prevent further appreciation of the Brazilian currency. Central banks in Turkey, Colombia and Peru also have intervened either directly or indirectly to stop their currencies from rising too quickly.

The genesis of this "currency war" is the rapid gains among emerging-market currencies in the first two months of the year. Investors, especially those in developed countries like the U.S. and U.K. with a capacity to borrow cash at ultra-low yields, sought out assets in emerging currencies that also offered the added bonus of currency appreciation. This so-called carry trade resulted in emerging-market currencies gaining 5% to 10% in the first six weeks of the year.

Earlier this year, a broad basket of emerging-market currencies including the real, Turkish lira, Indian rupee, and Indonesian rupiah were viewed as the best carry currencies. The purchases were funded either through the dollar or euro.

Now that central banks in many of these countries are resisting, investors are hesitant to go for the same play. After all, no one wants to bet against the central bank. Rather, they are keen on currencies like the rand and Mexican peso, whose central banks don't intervene on a daily basis in the market. Both also offer higher interest rates on local bonds.

"That story of broad risk-on, risk-off way of looking at currencies is changing," said Guillermo Felices, head of European currency strategy at Barclays Capital. "Investors have to be much more discerning in the way one picks carry. Lazy carry will be penalized."

Central banks' protectionism, of course, isn't expected to end carry trades based on the wide yield differentials. Over the medium to long term, emerging-market currencies are expected to gain against the dollar and other developed-world currencies. And as central banks in the U.S., Europe and Japan keep interest rates low and continue with their quantitative-easing policies, investors will be on the lookout for higher-yielding paper.

"There's a competitive nature to this game," said Stephen Jen, partner at SLJ Macro Partners, an investment company that also manages a hedge fund. "Money will go to places where capital flows are welcome, where policy makers are more tolerant."

For many investors that place is Mexico. The currency has gained 10.2% this year, and its central bank hasn't indicated any shift in policy to curb the appreciation. And Mexico's close trade links with the U.S. make it an automatic beneficiary of a recovery here.

In addition, Thanasis Petronikolos, head of emerging-market currency and debt at Baring Asset Management, sees opportunities in dollar-denominated bonds of Chinese companies and so-called dim sum bonds, which are listed in Hong Kong but denominated in Chinese yuan.

But he doesn't recommend backing out of Brazil or Hungary, especially if investors got in early.

"The fundamental story on the strength of the real is still there," he said. "With high-yielding local bonds, investors should be ready to cope with short-term volatility."

-By Prabha Natarajan, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2468; prabha.natarajan@dowjones.com [ 03-13-12 1633ET ]

title: Peru 's Sol Appreciates But Ctrl Bk  Intervention  Limits Gains
text:
--Peru's sol appreciates but central-bank intervention limits gains

--Economists expect the strength of the sol to continue

--Sol appreciation less than in many other Latin American nations

By Robert Kozak

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's sol has appreciated steadily in recent years and that appreciation has continued so far this year, although the Central Reserve Bank of Peru has kept a lid on the local currency's gains.

Economists expect the sol's appreciation trend to continue, with the central bank intervening to purchase U.S. dollars, leaning against the wind for the nominally free-floating currency.

Jefferies & Co . Managing Director Siobhan Morden said in an email that she expects relative stability for the Peruvian sol, reflecting "credit strength and a heavily managed fx rate."

That makes Peru's sol-denominated bonds more attractive.

"On the short list of defensive, low-beta exposure, the Peru Global PEN bonds consistently reaffirm its relative safe-haven status as the lowest beta FX and positive technicals with the onshore investors providing anchor support and valuation the same onshore/offshore," Morden said in a report.

The sol appreciated 4% last year and about 14% against the U.S. dollar since the end of 2008.

The central bank's interventions have capped the appreciation of the sol so far this year at 0.9% as of the end of trade on Wednesday.

That is much less than in other Latin American nations, such as Brazil, where the real has appreciated about 6.2% this year against the U.S. dollar, while in Colombia the peso has gained some 8.9%. The Mexican peso is up about 7.2% against the U.S. dollar so far this year.

"The central bank will continue intervening to moderate the flows in the sol," said Jose Razuri, an economist with Peruvian consulting firm, Maximixe.

The sol has been supported by strong inflows of foreign direct investments, which Moody's recently noted grew 4.5% in 2011.

"The increase is credit positive and came despite the uncertainty that surrounded the election of President Ollanta Humala and the deterioration of the global economy," it said.

Economists noted that Peruvian exporters in the past have complained long and loud when sol appreciation increases too rapidly as many have costs in soles but revenues in dollars.

Central bank officials for their part have said repeatedly that they are concerned about mismatches in domestic loans, between those who have borrowed in soles but who have incomes in dollars.

The ongoing central-bank interventions meanwhile have driven up Peru's net international reserves, to $54 billion as of the end of February.

So far this year, to the end of February, the central bank intervened to purchase $3.6 billion, more than in all of 2011. That compares with purchases of $9.0 billion in 2010.

The central bank has meanwhile left its reference interest rate unchanged at 4.25% since May last year.

-By Robert Kozak, Dow Jones Newswires, 51 99927 7269, peru@dowjones.com [ 03-07-12 1743ET ]

Some market participants worry that continued focus on currency weakness could trigger inflation. Other Latin American countries like Peru also intervened Thursday, to curb its currency's volatility. The dollar recently traded flat at 2.675 soles.

A few analysts are urging investors to get into the Mexican peso now, as that currency once again seems to be at the cusp of a rally. title: Emerging Market  Currencies  Mixed On Weakening Investor Confidence
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market currencies were mixed and lacked direction Thursday as global concerns continued to weigh on investor confidence.

"There are three major global risks to watch and it is likely that global markets will await further clarification about those three before [they] can switch gear away from neutral," said Benoit Anne, head of emerging market strategy at Societe Generale. The events include implementation of Greece's agreement, the second long-term refinancing operation and its impact on global markets, and the recent surge in oil prices on escalation of concerns about Iran.

The blazing rally that led to between 5% and 10% gains across emerging market currencies in the first few weeks of this year has fizzled out, at least for now.

"Investors have switched to a wait-and-see mode, with the result that the momentum has been lost for now," Anne said. Asian currencies were listless through their trading session.

Germany's strong Ifo survey, which indicateded rising confidence in a resilient economy, buoyed investor sentiment some, as did U.S. data that showed no additional workers filed for jobless benefits last week. Currently, the South African rand and emerging European currencies such as the Czech koruna are up, the dollar having lost nearly a 1% against these currencies.

Risk premiums on emerging market debt weakened two basis points to 367 basis points over comparable Treasury yields on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index-Global. Despite the lackluster investor sentiment, some issuers went ahead with new issuance including India's Reliance Industries Ltd. (500325.BY) and Brazil's third-largest bank, Banco Bradesco SA (BBD, BBDC4.BR).

Reliance sold a $500 million tap of its 2022 dollar bond, after a $1 billion bond earlier in the month. The offering by the energy and materials giant--India's largest company by market value--priced at 101.018 to yield 5.267%, and was more than six times oversubscribed.

Bradesco, meanwhile, has a $1 billion bond that is expected to price at a yield of 5.75%, according to sources familiar with the deal.

In currencies, the euro returned to HUF289.90 against the Hungarian forint after hitting a high of HUF290.87 following a surprising poor show at a government bond auction where buyers demanded higher yield for these notes, though they bought more than the planned sale amount. However, continued inaction on the part of Hungary to fix controversial laws and escalating tensions with the European Commission have upset investors.

On the other hand, both the Polish zloty and Czech koruna gained trading at PLN4.1783 and CZK25.064 against the euro, respectively, according to CQG data. The South African rand continued to have a positive run, as its budget showed a deficit of 4.6% vs. 5.5% expected by the market. The dollar weakened to ZAR7.6536 against the rand.

In Latin America, Brazil and Peru saw their central banks intervene again. Market participants suggest that the dollar at BRL1.70 is a critical level for the central bank.

title: Emerging Market  Currencies , Debt Weaker On Lingering Worries
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging market currencies and debt were weaker mostly as investor confidence ebbed on worries that Greece's bailout may not be enough in the long run.

However, some currencies were stronger against the dollar due to local policy action. For instance, South Africa said it plans to embark on its infrastructure action plan as a way to create jobs and tame the country's ballooning 24% unemployment rate. In Latin America, intervention by the central banks of Brazil and Peru helped weaken their respective currencies' gain on the dollar.

Risk premiums on emerging market debt was just a tad firmer at 366 basis points over comparable Treasury yields on the J. P. Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index Global. Risk premiums on Chile and Russia's debt was weaker. Venezuela, once again, was a stronger performer as investors were bullish on the possibility of change in its central administration during the October elections. Risk premiums on its five-year credit default swaps tightened by 15 basis points Wednesday, according to Markit data., while risk premiums on its sovereign debt firmed up 38 basis points to 980 basis points over comparable Treasury yields.

The City of Buenos Aires was back in the market with a $415 million five-year bond at 9.95%, according to a person familiar with the deal. The deal hasn't priced yet.

Last week, the capital city of Argentina backed away from selling this bond as Greece's problems weighed on investor confidence.

On the currencies front, the South African rand managed to stay stronger to the dollar all day long despite the broader market weakness. This is unusual for the rand to buck the broader trend, since it usually is a proxy for risk meaning it is weaker against the dollar when investor confidence is on the wane and stronger when confidence is on the rise. The dollar was at ZAR7.7294, after hitting a low of ZAR7.7018, according to CQG data.

Other currencies that bucked the trend Wednesday were supported by their central banks. For instance, Brazil intervened again in the spot market to buy dollars at BRL1.7083 to the dollar. title: Peru cenbank works to keep Sol stronger than 3/dlr
text:
LIMA, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Peru's central bank intervened in the local foreign exchange market again on Tuesday in what traders said was a move to keep the sol firmer than 3 per dollar.

The monetary authority, which for much of this year was buying dollars to prevent a surging sol <PEN=PE> from overshooting, has since June been selling dollars from its $35 billion in international reserves. Reserves hit a record this year thanks to the central bank's dollar purchases.

The central bank sold $9 million on Tuesday at a preliminary rate of 2.9834, pulling the sol back slightly as it moved close to 3 to the dollar.

On Monday, it made a much larger intervention of $418.6 million as global markets plunged after a $700 billion financial bailout package failed to win a key U.S. congressional vote.

Officials of Peru's central bank have said they want to prevent excessive volatility in the sol, which could drive up inflation during a weakening cycle, or hurt exporters in a strengthening cycle.

The central bank has repeatedly raised interest rates and tightened monetary policy this year in a bid to tame inflation, which has topped 6 percent over the last 12 months -- well above the central bank's target of 2 percent, plus or minus a tolerance band of one percentage point.

During 2008, the central bank has sold $2.3 billion and bought $8.7 billion on the local foreign exchange market. (Reporting by Jean Luis Arce, Writing by Terry Wade; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: Peru Stock Indexes Slide Again; Sol Strengthens Slightly
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's main stock indexes slid again on Thursday, despite higher prices for most base and precious metals and gains on Wall Street.

According to preliminary results, the Lima Stock Exchange's general index fell 2.62% to end at 10,884.43.

"There's definitely a sense of pessimism and more aversion to risk," Gustavo Urrutia, an analyst at brokerage Centura SAB told Dow Jones Newswires. "People are looking for something safe, such as gold, like with Buenaventura."

It wasn't clear when Peru's indexes would recover, said Urrutia, who called the market trend "emotional."

title: UPDATE 1-IMF says Peru outlook good after loan review

 This year, the central bank has been raising interest rates and deposit requirements in an effort to try to ease inflation.

 It also has spent some $9 billion in 2008 intervening in foreign exchange markets to stem the climb of Peru's currency, the sol, which has sharply rallied against the dollar over the last 12 months.

 Peru's economy, one of the fastest growing in the world, expanded some 9 percent last year. title: UPDATE 1-Reuters Summit-Peru  central bank  may clamp down again
text:
(For other news from the Reuters Latin America Investment Summit, click on   http://www.reuters.com/summit/LatinAmericanInvestment08?pid=500  ) (Adds quotes, background)   

By Terry Wade   

LIMA, March 28 (Reuters) - Peru may further tighten monetary policy if inflation speeds up, Central Bank President Julio Velarde said on Friday, adding that the Andean economy could overheat despite a U.S. slowdown.   

Inflation spiked 0.91 percent in February, a four-year high that pushed inflation for the 12 months through February to 4.8 percent. Economists are waiting to see if inflation will ease in March, or get worse.   

"If inflationary pressures start to accelerate, we will take measures, and among those could be the interest rate or bank deposit requirements," said Velarde, who spoke in Lima at the Reuters Latin America Investment Summit. "We aren't ruling anything out."   

To curb inflation, the central bank raised deposit requirements for banks in January and March, and in previous months raised its benchmark rate, now at 5.25 percent.   

The finance ministry has also helped out by slashing tariffs on food imports, lowering fuel taxes, and cutting spending to put a damper on inflation.   

Velarde has lately leaned in favor of raising deposit requirements, rather than interest rates. Higher rates could cause currency appreciation, which in turn would create risks for borrowers and lenders if the Peruvian sol later depreciates. About half of all loans in Peru are in dollars.   

"When we intervene to slow currency volatility, it's in large part because we are worried about what could happen with the financial system," he said. "If the U.S. economy doesn't just slow down but enters a recession that drags down commodities prices, we worry our currency could depreciate."   

GROWTH, OVERHEATING   

Velarde said the Andean economy, which grew 9 percent last year, could overheat if domestic demand continues to surge. Last year, domestic demand led growth, an unusual trend for a country that has long relied on exporting minerals.   

"There is a risk of overheating if internal demand keeps growing at a double-digit pace," he said.   

Velarde said he expects the economy to grow 7.5 percent in 2008, higher than a previous estimate of 7 percent. The central bank also said it expects economic growth of 9.5 percent in February, up from the same month a year ago.   

The central bank's inflation target is 2 percent, plus or minus a 1 percentage-point tolerance band. Last year inflation was nearly 4 percent.   

"Obviously, I'm concerned about inflationary pressure, but I don't think there's any chance we will lose control of it," he said. "I'm convinced that it could take a while to return to the (target) range but we will return to it."   

Most of the recent inflation has come from food imports, for products like wheat.   

"With monetary policy measures, I can't avoid the inflation attack that comes from abroad and the jump in food prices," Velarde said.   

He said a U.S. economic slowdown, trouble with credit markets in major financial centers, and high prices for agricultural commodities are raising doubts.   

"What's happening is that the world has never been so uncertain," he said. (For summit blog:   http://summitnotebook.reuters.com/  ("http://summitnotebook.reuters.com/")) (Additional reporting by Teresa Cespedes, editing by Braden Reddall)

title: FOREX  VIEW: Peru  Central Bank  Moves Cool Hot Flows Into Sol
text:
By Robert Kozak   

A Dow Jones Newswires Column   

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Recent measures implemented by the Central Reserve Bank of Peru have successfully eased speculative pressures on the Peruvian currency, the sol.   

Last month, the sol faced heavy buying from both foreign and local investors, forcing the central bank to adjust how it reacts to smooth out volatility.   

"I think that the effects of the central bank measures are starting to be felt," said Jorge Gonzalez Izquierdo, an economist with the Universidad del Pacifico. Speculative flows into the local currency "have fallen off substantially," he added.   

Speaking to a Congressional commission on Tuesday, Central Bank President Julio Velarde said the market has stabilized after what he called "massive" inflows of speculative capital in January. "In the last few days the market has been quiet, but it (volatility) could return again next week. We don't know," Velarde told Congress, according to newspaper Gestion.   

Intervened Regularly   

Peru allows both the sol and the U.S. dollar as legal tender, and while the central bank says the sol is a free floating currency, it does intervene when needed to avoid volatility.   

The sol has been steadily gaining against the greenback - it appreciated 7.0% against U.S. dollar last year and some 6.4% in 2006, boosted by a number of factors, including strong economic fundamentals, and robust exports.   

But the appreciation pressures took off at the start of this year as the interest rate spread between the U.S. and Peru appeared to be set to widen even more.   

As the sol began to appreciate - it gained 2.1% in January - domestic exporters concerned that the sol was gaining too much began to criticize government policies.   

Still, the Peruvian central bank increased its reference rate 25 basis points in January to 5.25%, concerned about the possibility of rising inflationary pressures.   

Perspectives that the sol would appreciate even more led investors to chase the Peruvian currency and sharply increase purchases of government sol-denominated certificates of deposit.   

Average capital inflows were some $500 million a day in the first half of January, overwhelming a market more used to dealing with volumes closer to half of that.   

The central bank, selling the CDs to sterilize the inflows, first responded to what it called speculative attacks by increasing its open market interventions.   

It purchased $3.27 billion in January, including a single-day record $437.7 million on Jan. 14.   

In all of 2007, interventions totaled $10.31 billion.   

Responds With New Measures   

Reluctant to keep intervening indefinitely, the central bank then responded by with a series of measures, including some to reduce the ease with which investors could dispose of sol-denominated instruments.   

From Monday, for example, the central bank started to sell non-negotiable certificates of deposit.   

On Monday, it placed a series of the non-negotiable CDs, totaling more than $900 million, and followed it up on Tuesday by placing about $1.0 billion worth of the short-term sol-denominated CDs.   

It has also lifted the reserve requirements that banks have with the central bank, called the encaje.   

"This increase in the encaje for the local and foreign currencies reduced liquidity in the market, a measure that also had the advantage of not attracting speculative funds and was the equivalent of a 50 basis point increase in the central bank's reference rate," the central bank said in a statement.   

With the new measures taking effect, the central bank hasn't intervened since Jan. 30, when it purchased $249 million.   

The sol, meanwhile, has continued to strengthen slightly in recent trading sessions, ending Wednesday at a midrate of PEN2.9165 to the U.S. dollar.   

(Robert Kozak is Peru bureau chief for Dow Jones Newswires)

title: Peru  Central Bank  Increases Reserve Requirements
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--The Central Reserve Bank of Peru's board of directors on Wednesday increased reserve requirements on bank deposits, aiming to cut down on speculation in the foreign exchange market. The central bank said that it had lifted the reserve requirements on both the local currency, the sol, and on the U.S. dollar.   

The central bank has intervened heavily in recent trading sessions, buying U.S. dollars, in an attempt to stem the speed at which the sol is appreciating. The central bank decided to increase reserve requirements on dollars in part to restrict the offer of dollars, and to alleviate appreciation pressures on the sol, it said.   

It said that the increased reserve requirements on the sol would help sterilize soles that are injected into the economy when the central bank buys dollars.   

It said that from February the minimum legal reserve requirement would increase to 7% from 6%. The central bank also outlined other measures aimed at easing pressure on the sol.   

Central Bank President Julio Velarde had said earlier Wednesday in a broadcast interview that raising the reserve requirement would make it more difficult to make a profit from speculation. There has been strong demand for the local currency from foreign investors, some of whom are investing in central bank certificates of deposit.   

That demand for the local currency has been joined by local investors, market analysts say. Many investors have been looking at rising interest rates in Peru compared with expectations of declining interest rates in the U.S. The sol ended slightly weaker Wednesday at a midrate of PEN2.9515 to the dollar.   

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru didn't intervene in the foreign exchange market Wednesday after purchasing $478.7 million in the previous session, which was a single-day record high.

title: FOREX  VIEW: Peru Sol's Strength Shows No Sign Of Waning
text:
By Robert Kozak   

A DOW JONES NEWSWIRES COLUMN   

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's fiery sol should continue to appreciate against the U.S. dollar, fueled by a red-hot economic performance, rising interest rates and robust inflows of cash.   

The currency, which appreciated some 7.0% against the dollar in 2007 and 6.4% in 2006, has drawn intense interest, especially from foreign investors. It's up 1.4% so far this month, and closed Monday at PEN2.9435 a dollar.   

In a bid to slow its gains, the Central Reserve Bank of Peru has sharply stepped up its interventions.   

"Beyond any volatility that could be triggered by core market jitters at some point, the appreciation bias of the sol is unlikely to wane this year,"  JPMorgan said in a recent report.   

The investment bank said the sol's gains were due to a combination of strong growth in gross domestic product - expected to have expanded 8.3% last year - persistently high commodity prices, a trade surplus still near the highs for the decade, solid foreign direct investment flows and the continuing de-dollarization of domestic portfolios.   

Over the last few years, a gradual process of greater use of the sol has taken place, particularly in bank loans.   

It forecast a level of PEN2.85 to the dollar at the end of 2008, although that spot level could be reached during the first half of the year, it added.   

Deutsche Bank said it is also bullish on the dollar/sol rate and expects it to "grind lower towards 2.85 (a 2.5% decline from 2.9225 on the Jan. 11 close) over the next couple of months."   

In a recent report, it pointed to the widening interest rate spread between Peru and the U.S. as a reason for the sol's strength against the U.S. unit. Peru's central bank lifted its reference rate 25 basis points to 5.25% last week, due to concerns about increased inflationary expectations tied in good part to imported food prices.   

Some forecasters are saying the central bank could continue to tighten monetary policy this year, perhaps lifting the reference rate to as high as 6.0%.   

That comes about at a time when expectations are high for an easing of monetary policy in the U.S.   

Economists also point to the continuing de-dollarization of the economy. Both dollars and soles are widely used, but the sol is clearly becoming a more favored currency.   

They also point to the likelihood of continued strong foreign direct investment, tied to a recently signed free trade agreement with the U.S. and an expected near-term jump in Peru's credit rating to investment grade.   

Strong remittances by Peruvians living abroad have also supported the sol.   

How Long Will Interventions Last?   

Economists wonder how long the central bank will be willing to assume the cost of intervening.   

The central bank purchased some $10.3 billion last year, aiming to smooth out movements in the market and to avoid undermining the competitiveness of Peru's non-commodity exports, analysts say.   

Just in the last five trading sessions, the central bank has intervened to purchase some $1.68 billion.   

The central bank purchased a record one-day amount of $437.7 million on Monday - in a spot market that  Deutsche Bank estimates normally has average daily volume of around $300 million.   

The interventions have driven Peru's foreign reserves to a record high $28.31 billion as of Jan. 7.   

The central bank sterilizes those inflows by issuing certificates of deposit.   

"While the BCRP will likely maintain its FX purchases to smooth volatility, the increasing cost of sterilization may limit the room to sustain more FX appreciation,"  JP Morgan said.   

It added that the central bank could lean toward accepting greater sol appreciation as a way to ease rising inflation pressures.   

The consumer price index for Lima rose 3.93% in 2007, above the upper range of the central bank's target range of 1.0% to 3.0%.   

Credit Suisse said in a recent report that, "In our view the central bank is not too concerned about the cost of sterilizing its purchases and, like other banks in the region, it may be willing to temporarily have a quasi-fiscal deficit."   

It estimated that the central bank still managed to post a small quasi-fiscal surplus last year, despite the sizable dollar purchases.   

"We think that the central bank will continue with its current policy of interventions in the foreign exchange market. It won't let the exchange rate appreciate rapidly but will maintain the trend throughout the year," Scotiabank said in a report.   

(Robert Kozak is Dow Jones Newswires' Peru bureau chief)

title: Emerging Market Debt Weaker Vs Treasurys Even After Mubarak Exit
text:
Anjali Cordeiro 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Emerging-market debt was weaker versus Treasurys Friday, after Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak resigned from office.

While Mubarak's departure was seen as a generally positive development for emerging-market assets, the inflationary pressures that have sprung up in the developing world have remained a key concern for investors. The worries about inflation have held down emerging-market assets in recent days and have generally overshadowed even positive developments in Egypt.

On Friday, the risk premium, or spread, on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global was 6 basis points wider at 282 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms the index was off 0.23%.

While many emerging currencies and bonds stayed range bound, the South African rand and Turkish lira gained ground against the dollar immediately after news of Mubarak's departure. The Egyptian pound initially weakened against the dollar and then later pared those losses and went on to strengthen against the dollar. The dollar was recently off 0.45% at EGP5.8721 from the previous close. Egypt's spread on the Embig was 5 basis points wider at 304 basis points over Treasurys. The index was up 0.02% in price terms.

Mubarak's departure, while a small positive for emerging markets, is unlikely to drive any "big directional changes" in these assets, said John Peta, an emerging-market portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management. Emerging-market investors are at the moment more focused on global inflation, he said, and particularly on the monetary policy moves of central banks in the developing world.

News out of Asia highlighted the pressures that emerging nations face in managing inflationary pressures and the value of their currencies. Vietnam devalued the dong Friday for the fourth time in 14 months, conceding to a lack of market confidence in its currency as it struggles with a gaping trade deficit. The move is risky, as it could stoke already-strong inflationary pressures and make it more expensive for the country to service its dollar-denominated debt. The State Bank of Vietnam set its exchange rate for the dollar at VND20,693, up 9.3% from VND18,932 Thursday. Vietnam was 3 basis points tighter on the Embig to 373 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms the index was up 0.38%.

News of central bank interventions in foreign-exchange markets continued to trickle in. The Central Reserve Bank of Peru intervened in the market on Friday to buy $130 million at an average rate of 2.7658 soles to the U.S. dollar.

Elsewhere, in Latin America, Mexico's industrial production grew more than expected in December, with manufacturing, mining and construction output all rising from the same month a year ago, bringing full-year 2010 growth to 6.1%, the National Statistics Institute, or Inegi, said Friday. Mexico's spread was 2 basis points wider at 155 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms the index was flat. The peso strengthened against the dollar, with the dollar recently down 0.34% at MXN12.0486.

-By Anjali Cordeiro, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2200; anjali.cordeiro@dowjones.com

--Nguyen Pham Muoi and Anthony Harrup contributed to this article. [ 02-11-11 1551ET ]

title: Chile, Colombia, Peru Finance Ministers Meet To Discuss  Forex
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Finance Ministers of Chile, Colombia and Peru, along with Nobel-prize winning economist Joseph Stiglitz, will discuss the recent appreciation of their respective currencies against the dollar, the ministers said Friday.

The three countries' currencies have appreciated as the region rapidly recovers from last year's global financial crisis, while industrialized nations such as the U.S. and Europe struggle to get back on their feet.

Slow growth in the industrialized nations, and their expansive monetary policies, have helped fuel the strength of the three nations' currencies, Chile's Finance Minister Felipe Larrain told reporters.

"We're going to study the global economic scenario, particularly the situation in industrialized economies," said Larrain. "We're concerned about this because our countries, which are part of the global economy...and despite the strengths we've developed, aren't immune to what's happening abroad."

Chile is one of the remaining countries in the region, however, that hasn't intervened in its local currency market, despite the peso nearing 31-month highs and exporters' demands for a lifeline as the peso's strength hurts the competitiveness of their products.

The Chilean central bank has maintained that intervention is a tool that's always available, but it will only use it if the exchange rate, in real terms, moves out of line with its long-term fundamentals.

The three nations want to compare how they are responding to the challenges presented by their appreciating currencies and see what options they have.

The Central Bank of Peru has maintained a policy of intervening in the foreign-exchange market to smooth out movements of the local currency, although it hasn't intervened to purchase U.S. dollars since Oct. 13.

"We want to see if we can eventually take mutual measures to confront this uncertain situation brought about by developed nations, that we'll be dealing with for a few years to come..what's important is that we share our experiences, because the problem is shared," Peru's Finance Minister Ismael Benavides said.

For its part, Colombia's central bank has been buying $20 million daily in the spot market in a bid to curb the peso's strength.

"There are exchange-rate challenges, and every day we have to react to what's happening. In the meeting we'll discuss what's worked and what hasn't," Colombia's Finance Minister Juan Carlos Echeverry said.

Chile's Larrain added "with humility we can say that if Latin America was the source of problems in the past, today the situation has changed, it is a source of solutions for the world and in that sense we're happy to be working together."

-By Anthony Esposito, Dow Jones Newswires; 56-2-715-8929; anthony.esposito@dowjones.com [ 10-12-10 2219GMT ]

text:
* Central bank to buy at least $20 mln daily

* Dollar purchases to start from Wednesday

* Accumulation of reserves to last at least four months

* Cenbank buys $19.9 mln at its first auction (Recasts; adds peso close, details, comment, byline)

By Jack Kimball and Nelson Bocanegra

BOGOTA, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Colombia's central bank on Wednesday started purchasing what it said would be at least $20 million daily for the next four months to help ease the rise of its currency, becoming the latest Latin American economy to intervene in its market.

The move left the door open for more measures to curb the peso's <COP=RR> appreciation and followed intervention by Brazil to ease the real's climb and Peru's buying dollars to curb the sol. For details, see [ID:nN10255466] [ID:nN14108242]

"The Board of Directors of the Central Bank decided to resume the accumulation of international reserves. To do this, it will purchase daily at least $20 million through competitive auctions for at least four months counting from (Wednesday)," the bank said in a statement on its website.

The peso, one of the region's strongest performing currencies this year, fell 1.43 percent to a low of 1,817 pesos per dollar from Tuesday's close after the bank's announcement. The local unit closed down 0.89 percent at 1,807.1 on Wednesday.

The Colombian peso has soared 12.5 percent against the dollar this year, the sol <PEN=PE> has risen more than 3 percent and the real has rallied 4.5 percent since June. Brazil's currency weakened 1 percent on Wednesday after the government threatened to step up intervention.

Latin America's emerging market economies are struggling with appreciation. Regional powerhouse Brazil is aggressively buying dollars, Peru is tightening deposit requirements and Chile has warned it may also have to intervene.

Peru's central bank purchased $21 million on Wednesday, while on the other side of the world, Japan sold yen to battle an appreciating currency, which risks reducing demand for exports and damaging growth. For more, see: [ID:nTOE68E02W]

The peso's appreciation hurts Colombian exporters, who receive earnings in dollars but pay costs in pesos.

MORE MEASURES TO COME

Colombia has seen foreign investment in oil and mining boom as its decades-long guerrilla conflict ebbs. The Andean country is now Latin America's No. 4 oil producer and an exporter of coal, coffee, flowers and nickel.

Analysts said the dollar purchases would help in the short term but could not rule out the central bank and the government taking more aggressive steps later in the year. For scenarios on possible measures, click on [ID:nN15183902]

Wednesday's "intervention announcement was relatively mild, which shows the authorities are still shying away from more forceful FX market direct or indirect intervention measures," said Alberto Ramos of Goldman Sachs.

Traders said the bank bought $19.9 million at 1,805 pesos per dollar in its first auction on Wednesday after announcing the restart of dollar purchases.

Between March and June, the monetary authority bought $1.6 billion on the foreign exchange market, but stopped greenback purchases at the end of June.

"Surely this announcement will generate volatility and pressures for a rise in the dollar in the short term although it has been shown that this type of action cannot change the structural tendency," Daniel Velandia, manager of economic studies at the brokerage Correval, said in a note.

"However, the uncertainty about the amount of the intervention will prevent an important fall of the dollar in the coming days and we continue thinking that if the dollar restarts its falling tendency strongly in the near future, there will be additional measures."

Colombia's trade minister, Sergio Diaz Granados, said late on Tuesday that after the government pushes through its fiscal plans, the central bank would have room to purchase as much as $9 billion. [ID:nN15156198]

The central bank has other options available to stem the peso's rise, including capital controls on short-term portfolio investment, though such measures would not be favored by investors eyeing a return to investment grade for Colombia.

"History shows that this may be successful in preventing the currency from appreciating further," Capital Economics said in a report. "But it is unlikely to weaken it substantially -- something the authorities are hoping to achieve." (Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: RPT-ANALYSIS-Latam seen stepping up  forex intervention , but risk
text:
(Repeats Tuesday story with no changes to text or headline)

* Central banks seen stepping in to tame currency rally

* Colombia, Chile seen joining concrete action

* Curbing currencies could slow rate up-cycle

By Simon Gardner

SANTIAGO, Aug 17 (Reuters) - South American policymakers will likely step up intervention to stem surging currency gains, but they tread a fine line that risks fueling inflation and could even put the brakes on a regional rate up-cycle.

Lured by higher interest rates and economic growth amid a faltering recovery in the United States and Europe, foreign investors are betting on the region's commodity powerhouses. Dollar inflows are boosting currencies and hurting exporters.

Peru's central bank has aggressively intervened this year to buy nearly $6 billion to soak up excess liquidity, while the finance ministry said last week it would buy $500 million in foreign exchange markets by year-end to temper its sol <PEN=PE> currency, which is at 2-year highs.

Brazil called an auction on Tuesday to buy dollars on the spot market in a bid to boost reserves and limit currency volatility. [ID:nN16270408]

The presidents of Chile and Colombia have both signaled concern about sharp gains in their countries' currencies.

But verbal intervention will likely not be enough.

"I think the central banks will continue to intervene heavily. The central banks that have not yet come in, will. That means Colombia and Chile," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities.

"The problem with intervention is that the global environment is still very fragile." <------------------------------------------------------ For a graphics, see http://link.reuters.com/ged55n  and http://link.reuters.com/wex55n ("http://link.reuters.com/wex55n") For Chile peso scenarios, see [ID:nN17124678] ------------------------------------------------------->

Policymakers could opt to buy dollars to boost international reserves, tax imports or offer incentives to exporters to help counter currency appreciation.

They could also raise deposit requirements to help curb money supply, or raise the overnight rate on interbank loans in dollars.

Analysts say Chile is likely to delay the rate at which it repatriates hundreds of millions of dollars to help fund reconstruction after a massive February earthquake.

RATE UP-CYCLE TO SLOW?

Chile joined a regional rate up-cycle led by Peru and Brazil after keeping its key rate at a record low to help the economy recover from the quake and global crisis. But taming currencies may slow the pace of future hikes in the region.

"By intervening in the foreign exchange market buying dollars you throw pesos into the system (via bonds) and that will eventually generate inflationary pressures," said Alfredo Coutino, Latin America director at Moody's Economy.com.

"I don't see a future for a continuous (rate) heightening cycle in Latin America," he added, saying intervention would likely slow the pace of interest rate increases.

Chilean President Sebastian Pinera said on Thursday he would use all macroeconomic tools to keep the country's peso <CLP=CL> competitive, but after a brief retracement, the currency continued to surge near 7-month highs. For more, see [ID:nN12124343]

The same day, Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos met with the central bank to discuss the strength of the country's peso <COP=RR>, which is up around 10 percent against the dollar year-to-date. [ID:nN12123476]

Peru's central bank this year has sought to squeeze speculative capital out by raising deposit requirements on dollar loans from abroad and local bank accounts denominated in dollars. [ID:nN18173256]

Despite heavy intervention, Peru's sol is up nearly 3 percent so far this year at around 2.8 per dollar, and the market sees it appreciating by another 1.0 to 2.0 percent by year-end.

In neighboring Chile, investors expect the central bank to buy dollars if the peso, which has surged over 3 percent in August alone, firms toward around 480 per dollar. The peso is now 1.0 percent higher year-to-date.

During the 2008 commodity boom that pushed the Chilean currency to 430 pesos per dollar, the central bank began buying dollars on the local market to build up its reserves and the currency weakened sharply by the year-end. It then rebounded by more than 26 percent in 2009.

Chilean exporters are feeling the pinch, and want action.

"Producers are really affected by exchange rate variations and intervention to ensure stability would be positive," said Miguel Montenegro, manager of Chilean berry exporter Blue Valley. Chile is the world's leading copper producer and is also a major fruit, wood pulp and salmon exporter.

The Brazilian real's <BRBY> sharp appreciation has also hit exporters. But traders continue to test 1.75 per dollar, even after the government voiced support for a weaker real.

Doug Smith, head of Latin American research at Standard Chartered in New York, expects more intervention -- whoever wins an Oct. 3 presidential election -- via verbal warnings, double spot auctions or reverse swaps.

However, nothing the central bank will do will come as much of a surprise to major players in the market, says Joao Medeiros, a partner at Pioneer Corretora, one of Brazils biggest currency brokerages.

"The market is like a game of poker but one in which the central bank can see everyones cards," he said. "The central bank could do up to 10 auctions in one day if it needed to but it won't. It has everything under control." (Additional reporting by Samantha Pearson in Sao Paulo, Terry Wade in Lima and Brad Haynes and Alonso Soto in Santiago; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: Peru's  Central Bank  Chief: Dec GDP Growth Could Reach 5%
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's Central Reserve Bank president, Julio Velarde, forecast on Tuesday that December's gross domestic product growth figure could register slightly over 5%, bringing the total 2009 GDP figure to "about 1%."

Speaking at a press conference Tuesday, Velarde also suggested the consumer price index would rise in January, mainly due to recent fuel price increases.

Although Velarde said the bank saw no substantial short-term inflationary pressures, and would maintain its current low reference interest rate, he warned of a possible increase in supply-side prices.

The Central Bank aims to keep inflation at between 1% and 3%. In December, the country's benchmark consumer price index, used to set monetary policy, rose 0.32% from the previous month, bringing the annual increase in the CPI to 0.25%.

Asked if the Central Bank's current interventions to smooth out volatility in the foreign-exchange market would continue, Velarde said yes, "up to a certain limit." He would not specify what the limit is, however.

Since Jan. 8, the Central Bank has purchased about $1.3 billion in interventions.

title: Peruvian Sol's Winning Streak Against Dollar Should Continue
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's sol is on a winning streak and those gains against the greenback are expected to keep going.

The sol has appreciated 1.1% in the early weeks of 2010, and by 9.4% over the last 12 months.

Economists point to strong economic fundamentals, including a positive trade balance and robust investment levels.

"There has been a strong appetite for emerging markets and in particular for the sol, due to expectations of capital inflows," said Roberto Flores, an economist with brokerage Inteligo SAB.

"There is a long list of projects that will get under way in Peru this year," he said.

Strong demand for the sol has led the Central Reserve Bank of Peru to intervene every day for the past week, buying about $830 million in its stated goal of easing movements in the market.

"The fundamentals of the Peruvian economy, as well as a scenario of a global weakening of the dollar, will add to the strengthening trend of the local currency in the coming months, despite interventions by the Central Bank," Banco de Credito said.

Economists point to Peru's investment-grade rating from all the major agencies, and rising demand for its exports, especially minerals.

Peru's exports are expected to rise to $30 billion this year from about $26 billion last year, Trade Minister Martin Perez said at a press conference this week.

After only tepid growth for most of last year, Peru's gross domestic product is starting to show signs of a recovery. GDP in November expanded by a greater-than-expected 4.2%, in part due to a government stimulus program.

The Central Bank forecasts growth of 5.5% in GDP this year after expected full-year 2009 growth of about 1%.

Deutsche Bank said that private domestic investment will easily increase by more than 6% in 2010, adding that public sector investments are also seen posting a "stellar" year.

"We believe fundamentals continue to suggest that the sol should appreciate in the months ahead given that private flows will be more than enough to finance this year's current account deficit, and therefore we hold our short USD/PEN we opened last year. We do expect further Central Bank intervention, but only to moderate the appreciation rate, rather than to modify the trend," Deutsche Bank said.

Financial consultant Macroconsult forecasts trade and current account surpluses this year, "which leads us to expect that the (appreciating) evolution in the foreign exchange market will be seen throughout the year."

title: ANALYSIS-Peru's  currency  likely to extend gains in 2010
text:
* Sol seen ending 2010 at 2.6 to 2.7 per U.S. dollar

* To strengthen on economic rebound; appetite for risk

* Pre-election jitters expected to limit gains

By Ursula Scollo

LIMA, Dec 9 (Reuters) - Peru's currency is likely to strengthen against the U.S. dollar in 2010 as the global and local economies rebound and investors' appetite for risk returns, though the run-up to presidential elections could limit gains.

The sol <PEN=PE>, which is currently hovering at around 2.86 per dollar, is expected to close next year at between 2.60 and 2.70, according to analysts consulted by Reuters. That would be a rally of as much as 10 percent in 2010.

The sol has gained nearly 9.0 percent this year, trailing gains in most other Latin American currencies, which have risen as investors began to bet again on emerging markets.

"The sol may well strengthen next year by about the same amount it did in 2009," said Gonzalo Navarro, head currency trader at Banco Santander in Lima.

Peru's central bank frequently intervenes in the foreign exchange market, buying and selling dollars to smooth out volatility, and is likely to keep doing so in 2010, though it has said it will follow the tendency of the markets.

So far this year, the bank has bought some $910 million to keep the sol from strengthening too fast.

"The central bank is doing a lot so that the dollar does not weaken further. If the bank had not done anything, I think the sol would be under 2.50," or some 14 percent stronger, said Ricardo Lago, an economist who frequently writes about Peru.

2011 ELECTIONS

Though most analysts expect Peru's currency to strengthen next year, they say the gains will be softened by uncertainties surrounding the 2011 presidential elections. Candidates are already jockeying for position in the race, and electioneering could pick up in the middle of next year.

Peru's economy, which is forecast to grow just 1.0 percent this year, is expected to expand by roughly 5.0 percent in 2010 as prices for most of the country's metals exports recover.

"There is a consensus next year will be better for Peru in terms of economics, but it's also a preelection year," said Navarro, with Banco Santander.

In the past, the local currency has tended to weaken ahead of elections as investors weigh possible outcomes.

Peru's President Alan Garcia, who has pushed free-trade and foreign investment, cannot run in the next election and his ruling APRA party has not yet identified a clear candidate.

Lima's Mayor Luis Castaneda and Keiko Fujimori, the daughter of the former President Alberto Fujimori, are currently leading the pack of potential contenders.

Neither would likely make major changes to Garcia's economic model, but in third place is Ollanta Humala, an ultra-nationalist, who spooked investors when he nearly won the last presidential election in 2006. (Reporting by Ursula Scollo; Writing by Dana Ford)
