title: =DJ Peru's  Central Bank  Wants Limits On Banks' Dollar Holdings
text:
(Adds comments from superintendent spokesman and economists, additional comments from Velarde, in sixth through 10th paragraphs; Central Bank moves in last paragraph) 


 
   By Robert Kozak 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LIMA (Dow Jones)--The Central Reserve Bank of Peru wants to have a limit placed on local bank holdings of U.S. dollars, aiming to cut down on exchange market volatility.

The Central Bank wants to reduce to 50% the maximum limit on foreign currencies that local banks can hold in net long positions from the current 100%.

"This is a regulation aimed at a prudent management on the macro level and isn't aimed at any one entity, but rather at ensuring the health of the economy," Central Reserve Bank President Julio Velarde said in a statement released Saturday.

The Central Bank said the current 100% limit contributes to foreign exchange market volatility.

Velarde said setting a limit of 50% would bring that to a level similar to the amount of dollarization in the Peruvian economy. The U.S. dollar is legal tender in Peru and is widely used.

The nation's Superintendent of Banking and Insurance would have to change the limits on bank holdings, a spokesman for the Central Bank said Monday.

Velarde noted that other nations in the region, such as Colombia and Chile, currently have limits on local bank holdings of foreign currencies.

Economists say the proposed measure wouldn't affect Peruvian banks much right now, as for the most part they are reducing U.S. dollar positions.

"It wouldn't be any problem if it were introduced right now," said Hugo Perea, chief economist for BBVA Banco Continental.

The measure could take on greater importance for some banks if the current trend toward a strengthening sol were reduced and in a period of volatility the sol began to weaken, economists pointed out.

Peru's Central Bank also wants to establish a maximum limit of from 40% to 50% in foreign currency holdings, without coverage, for private pension funds.

The Central Bank said this would also reduce foreign exchange risk and volatility in the foreign exchange market.

Currently there is no limit on the investments in foreign currencies for the private pension funds, although those funds are limited in how much they can invest outside of Peru.

Banco BBVA Continental said in a report that as of Sept. 30, the private pension funds had 37.6% of their portfolios in U.S. dollars.

The Central Bank has had to intervene regularly in recent weeks to stem volatility in the exchange market tied to strong demand for the local currency, the sol. In the 2007 to 2009 period, the Central Bank has bought an accumulated $13.17 billion in interventions.

title: Reuters Summit-UPDATE 2-Peru central banker sees aggressive cut
text:
(For other news from the Reuters Latin American Investment Summit, click on http://www.reuters.com/summit/LatinAmericanInvestment09?PID=500) (Adds size of intervention)

By Teresa Cespedes and Terry Wade

LIMA, May 4 (Reuters) - Peruvian interest rates will likely be cut this week if low inflation allows the central bank to implement an "aggressive policy" of reductions, Peru's Central Bank President Julio Velarde said on Monday.

The central bank will meet on Thursday and may trim its benchmark rate, which is now at 5 percent after three months of cuts to help weather the global economic downturn.

"We will continue with an aggressive policy. Aggressive is 50 basis points or more, if inflation keeps falling," Velarde said at the Reuters Latin American Investment Summit in Lima.

The central bank has an annual inflation goal of 2 percent, plus or minus a tolerance band of one percentage point. In the last few months, price increases have slowed sharply.

"We're within the inflationary range," Velarde said. "We don't see inflationary pressures in the short term. This allows us more space for rate reductions, especially in a context in which the Peruvian sol is gaining against the dollar."

The sol <PEN=PE> gained to 2.95 per dollar on Monday, prompting the central bank to buy dollars on the local foreign exchange market for the first time since December. It bought only $2 million, but bigger purchases could be in store.

"It was simply to send signals that the sol wouldn't move sharply," he said. The sol has rallied since March when it was trading at 3.24 per dollar.

IMF AND INTERVENTIONS

Velarde said Peru is "calmly" evaluating whether to tap a new credit line that the International Monetary Fund has created for high-quality emerging markets.

Mexico has already asked to borrow from the IMF, and some analysts speculated Peru might be next after Colombia requested $10.4 billion from the multilateral lender.

"We are sure that if we ask for it (IMF help) that we'd get it," Velarde said.

But Velarde said cash from the IMF might not be needed as Peru's central bank could buy U.S. dollars to build up its reserves further.

"One scenario that we are thinking about, which we haven't ruled out, is that we start to buy dollars," he said.

"If we start to buy dollars, because the tendency is for the sol to keep on strengthening, maybe it won't be necessary to have this credit line (from the IMF)," Velarde said.

Peru's foreign reserves have more than doubled in the past 32 months to $31 billion, and they would hit new records if the central bank were to step up interventions.

"Unfortunately other countries in the region didn't build up ammunition in the good times to face tough times," he said.

GROWTH

Even though economic data has been weak for the past two months, Velarde said growth this year should come in at around 4 percent.

That would be less than last year's pace of nearly 10 percent but still one of the fastest rates in the world. Velarde said the economy appears to have grown a bit less than 3 percent in the first quarter.

He said exporters are reporting that they are receiving solid orders. Some mining projects that were put on hold have been given the green light thanks to better copper prices, and that the credit system is working well.

As a result of an improved outlook, especially for foreign investment, the central bank has narrowed its view for the current account deficit in 2009 to 2.7 percent of GDP from 3.3 percent.

"The signs we are seeing are for a trade balance that is increasingly positive and capital inflows that are maybe higher than we estimated," Velarde said. (For summit blog: http://blogs.reuters.com/summits/("http://blogs.reuters.com/summits/")) (Writing by Terry Wade; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: Peru's Feb 20 Foreign Reserves $17.93 Bln Vs $18.11 Bln
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's net international reserves fell to $17.93 billion as of Feb. 20, compared with $18.11 billion as of Feb. 13, the Central Reserve Bank of Peru said Friday.  

The central bank said the decrease was mainly due to a decline in public sector deposits of $143 million and a foreign debt payment of $60 million, offset to some extent by central bank interventions to purchase U.S. dollars and by other factors.  

Peru's foreign-exchange position was $11.86 billion as of Feb. 20, up $183 million from the end of January.  

The foreign-exchange position doesn't include public sector deposits with the central bank or commercial bank reserves.

title: = Peru's Economy Hits Sweet Spot, Growth Estimates Upped
text:
Sep 01, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

By Robert Kozak  

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES  

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's economy, which has expanded for five straight years, has hit a sweet spot, with inflation low and gross domestic product forecast to grow even more strongly in the short-term.  

Government revenues are robust, while the local stock market is hitting record highs as investors pour cash into local companies.  

A boom in mineral prices has propelled exports to record levels, while confident consumers are opening their wallets to buy cars and other consumer goods.  

"If the external conditions remain favorable, and with our policies of growth in public investments and promotion of economic competitiveness, this nation should be growing between 6.0% and 7.0% in GDP in the coming years," Finance Minister Luiz Carranza said in a meeting with the foreign press this week.  

While economists were earlier forecasting growth of around 5.0% this year, many of those earlier forecasts are now being revised, especially following June's 6.9% gain in GDP. The economy expanded some 6.5% in 2005.  

Banco BBVA Continental recently bumped up its GDP forecast to 6.2% for this year, while consultants Macroconsult now forecast growth of 6.9% for 2006.  

Bear Stearns said in a report that previous 5.5% to 6.0% growth forecasts may be too conservative. "Peru continues to benefit from tremendous growth momentum, something that has taken market confidence in the performance of the economy to three-year highs," it said.  

Meanwhile, the government of President Alan Garcia, which took office in July, has promised to sharply increase public sector spending, in what it calls an "investment shock," while keeping the fiscal deficit modest.  

Despite the vigorous growth, consumer prices remain under control. The 12-month inflation rate to the end of August was 1.87%, at the lower end of the target range set out by the Central Reserve Bank of Peru.  

Raw Materials Boost Exports
  

Despite political volatility, successive governments since the early 1990s have promoted, with some exceptions, free market policies that have cheered investors. Those policies alongside a boom in raw material prices have created growing confidence in the economy.  

Sales of gold, copper, zinc, silver and other minerals have led the export gains. But exports of other products such as fish meal, coffee and textiles have also taken off.  

Overall exports rose to a record $2.3 billion in July, 48.3% higher than in the same month a year earlier, and the highest monthly total on record.  

To take advantage of the strong demand, various mining companies are expanding, such as Sociedad Minera Cerro Verde SAA's (CVERDEC1.VL) $850 million upgrade at its copper mine in southern Peru. Copper miner Southern Copper Corp.(PCU) has a large scale modernization underway.  

Consumer product companies are also pouring cash into the nation, with beverage maker Union de Cervecerias Peruanas Backus & Johnston SAA, controlled by SABMiller PLC, (SAB.JO) recently announcing a $102 million investment. Canada's Bank of Nova Scotia (BNS) recently purchased Peru's third-biggest bank, while HSBC Holdings PLC (HBC) has started the regulatory process to be able to open offices in the Andean nation.  

Consumers and others have also taken heart, a number of indicators show.  

Domestic demand jumped 8.6% in the first six months of this year over the same period a year before. New vehicle sales increased 41% in the first six months of the year.  

Consultants Apoyo Consultoria's index of consumer confidence rose in June to a record high as Peruvians start to sense that the robust economic activity is finally trickling down to benefit them.  

Political Calm Helps
  

Analysts say a return to political calm following the elections earlier this year has helped sway investors.  

Radical nationalist Ollanta Humala, who at one point led in opinion polls, failed to win the presidency, and so far President Alan Garcia's policies have been welcomed by markets.  

The Lima Stock Exchange has posted some of the strongest gains in the world this year, with the broad general index hitting a new record high Thursday. To the end of August, the bolsa's general index has increased 108%, driven in good part by mining company shares.  

The local currency, the sol, has appreciated 5.1% against the U.S. dollar this year, according to Banco Wiese Sudameris.  

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru has had to intervene to buy record amounts of dollars to keep the sol from strengthening too much, purchasing $1.41 billion in August alone.  

Peru's sovereign bonds have also rallied. The country's risk premium on JPMorgan's Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus closed Thursday at 135 basis points over Treasurys, close to the record low of 128 basis points.  

To Post External Surplus
  

The burgeoning economy has also helped lift tax revenues, which posted a real 56% increase in July over the previous year period.  

Finance Minister Carranza, in making his 2007 budget proposal to Congress, said the government will adhere to a target of keeping the fiscal deficit at 1.0% of GDP a year or less. Some forecasts say the Andean nation could even end the year with a small fiscal surplus.  

Meanwhile, the central bank has said Peru's current account surplus in the balance of payments totaled 2.5% of GDP in the second quarter, the highest since 1979.  

Economists note, however, that Peru remains vulnerable to any downturn in commodity prices, although they don't expect this to take place in the near term.  

Ratings agency Fitch Thursday upgraded its foreign-currency credit rating on Peru to double-B-plus from double-B, citing the financial support from the country's buoyant exports. The rating rose to one notch below investment grade, but Fitch noted that Peru still has a narrow economy and export base, and sub-par social development indicators.  

"Further reductions in net external debt, particularly net public external debt, and a broadening of exports and sources of economic growth, would bode well for sovereign creditworthiness, as would further evidence that political shocks will not derail current economic policies and prudent fiscal policy in particular," it added.  

-By Robert Kozak, Dow Jones Newswires; 511-221-7050; peru@dowjones.com
  

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: IMF Approves Review Of Peru's Standby Loan
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday said it had approved the third review of Peru's 26-month Standby loan program, first granted in June 2004.  

The approval makes available some $296 million, although Peru hasn't and doesn't plan to draw on any of the funds. The overall pact was worth about $422.8 million when it was first signed.  

In a letter of intent sent to the IMF Dec. 20 and published Wednesday on the Finance Ministry's Web site, the Peruvian government says "fiscal discipline will continue as the center of a strategy to consolidate macroeconomic stability."  

In the letter, the government says Peru's gross domestic product will grow around 5% in real terms in 2006 and inflation will be 2.5%.  

In 2005, the GDP expanded by 6.3% according to President Alejandro Toledo. The consumer price index rose 1.49% in 2005.  

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru aims to keep consumer inflation within a one percentage point range - with 2.5% serving as the midpoint - into the indefinite future.  

The letter of intent forecasts a fiscal deficit of 1.0% of GDP for 2006.  

In 2005 the fiscal deficit was 0.6% of GDP, according to Finance Minister Fernando Zavala.  

Among other points, the letter said the government will continue to focus on tax reform, seeking to eliminate regional tax exemptions.  

It will also concentrate on reducing tax evasion, it said.  

Peru's tax revenues, excluding certain contributions, reached 28.04 billion soles ($8.15 billion) in 2005, a 14.7% increase in real terms over the previous year.  

Regarding the exchange rate, the letter emphasized that the Central Reserve Bank of Peru will only intervene in the foreign exchange market to control excessive volatility.  

In recent sessions the central bank has been selling dollars in order to shore up the sol as financial markets are affected by political concerns in the run-up to April's general elections.  

Moreover, efforts to de-dollarize the economy will continue.  

For example, 50% of bank loans under a government sponsored housing program in the January - June 2006 period must be granted in the national currency, the government said in its letter of intent.  

Peruvian officials have said they want to discuss an exit strategy from negotiating standby arrangements with the IMF once the current deal ends, arguing that the economy is strong and the fiscal situation is in order.  

The current agreement will expire shortly after a new government takes office July 28.

title: Peru's Sol  Currency  May Suffer Volatile Ride Through 2006
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Uncertainty tied to April's general elections could rattle Peru's local currency in the first half of 2006, but strong economic fundamentals may help calm the sol later in the year.  

The rise of nationalist candidate Ollanta Humala in opinion polls in the later part of 2005 caused volatility in the foreign exchange market, leading to ongoing intervention by the Central Reserve Bank of Peru to calm investors.  

That unrest may continue, economists say.  

"The most probable is that speculation will predominate in the first half the year and then in the second half the fundamentals will be more important," said Banco Wiese Sudameris' chief economist Guillermo Diaz.  

Various elections scheduled in other Latin American nations this year could also create volatility in the Peruvian market.  

Banco Wiese Sudameris forecasts that the sol could average PEN3.42 per dollar in 2006, a depreciation of about 3.7% compared with the 2005 average.  


 
                      Sol Stability Overturned 
   

The sol has been relatively stable for the past five or so years, floating between PEN3.25 per dollar and PEN3.62 per dollar.  

The local currency weakened by some 4.3% in 2005 against the dollar, ending the last trading session of the year at a midrate of PEN3.4185 per dollar.  

That depreciation came about despite Peru's robust exports, tame inflation, and fiscal position well under control.  

The currency actually strengthened in the first part of 2005, reaching an average interbank rate of PEN3.252 per dollar in July.  

Record high prices for minerals have led to a boom in Peruvian exports, particularly in the mining sector, bolstering the sol. Remittances by Peruvians living abroad increased cash flows into the Andean nation.  

The central bank regularly intervened to buy dollars in the first part of the year, helping build the international reserves and ease the appreciation of the local currency.  

But central bank officials say that dollar buying by private pensions funds in Peru in the mid-year started the trend toward a weakening of the local currency.  

Rising short-term interest rates in the U.S. also helped damp interest in Peruvian investments, while Peru's key reference rate, set by the central bank, remained steady.  

The sol also began to weaken alongside poll results that showed presidential hopeful Humala gaining popularity before next April's election for president.  

As the sol weakened, the central bank responded by selling U.S. dollars in October for the first time in about three years. It also began placing certificates of deposit indexed to the exchange rate, which function the same as dollar sales.  

In the last month of the year, the central bank also raised its key reference rate by 25 basis points to 3.25%, citing in part foreign exchange market volatility.  


 
                   Downplay Volatility 
   

Government officials downplay the ability of speculative efforts to seriously weaken the currency before the elections, saying the international reserves are much more than the entire monetary base in soles. The U.S. dollar is also legal tender in Peru and is used for many larger purchases such as real estate and vehicles.  

Central Reserve Bank acting President Oscar Dancourt said in a recent radio interview that the central bank has prepared for any unrest by building the international reserves over the last few years, purchasing a net $998 million in 2003, $1.85 billion in 2004 and $767 million in 2005.  

Peru's net international reserves totaled $14.34 billion as of Dec. 28, while the foreign-exchange position, or the cash available to the central bank, totaled $7.52 billion as of Dec. 28.  

"We have important dollar reserves and can meet any increased demand for dollars caused by the election process, without putting at risk the maintenance of macroeconomic successes," Dancourt said, adding that the exchange rate is one of the toughest variables to forecast.  

The central bank has remained active in easing volatility in the market so far in 2006, intervening to sell U.S. dollars on both Tuesday and Wednesday this week.  


 
                   Fundamentals Remain Solid 
   

Economists continue to point to Peru's solid economic fundamentals as a positive factor, with gross domestic product expected to expand some 5.0% in 2006.  

Although the economy is expected to have expanded by some 6.0% in 2005, inflation has dwindled, with consumer prices rising by only 1.49% in 2005.  

"The fundamentals point out that in 2006 (setting aside the political theme) the Peruvian economy will maintain an important rhythm of growth, with low inflation and a fiscal deficit of around 1.0% of GDP and an important balance in the trade balance that will allow the current account in the balance of payments to remain in surplus," Banco de Credito said.  

That bank expects the sol to weaken by some 1.9% in 2006 against the U.S. dollar. "The depreciation of the sol is expected to be moderate," it said in a recent report.  

(This is the fourth in a series of six stories on the near-term outlooks for major Latin American currencies.)

title: Peru's Ctrl Bk May Lift Reference Interest Rate - Banks
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--The Central Reserve Bank of Peru's board of directors may opt to increase the key reference rate for open market operations when it holds its first meeting of the year on Thursday, economists said.  

They said the central bank could raise the key reference rate to 3.50% from 3.25% in an attempt to ward off volatility in the foreign exchange market.  

"It would mainly be aimed at controlling volatility," said Guillermo Diaz, chief economist at Banco Wiese Sudameris.  

At a press conference Tuesday, Diaz said the central bank could lift the key reference rate by 75 basis points in the first part of this year.  

The central bank last raised the reference rate to 3.25% in December, the first increase since October 2004, aiming to reduce volatility in the foreign exchange market and make speculation more costly.  

Economists say that rising interest rates in the U.S. as well as higher levels of political uncertainty before April's election in Peru are two factors that have undermined the stability of the local currency.  

"Given that episodes of exchange-rate volatility have continued, we can't rule out that the central bank could increase its reference rate," the economic studies service of BBVA Banco Continental said in a report released late Monday.  

In December, the central bank intervened in the market by selling U.S. dollar directly or by offering certificates indexed to the U.S. dollar valued at $644 million, which the central bank calls an "unprecedented" amount of intervention.  

With Peru's inflation rate the lowest in the region, the central bank has little need to increase interest rates to cool price pressures. The consumer price index rose by only 1.49% in 2005, touching the bottom end of the target range set by the central bank.  

The central bank aims to keep consumer inflation within a one percentage point range above or below a midpoint of 2.5% into the indefinite future.  

In 2004 the central bank increased its reference rate twice, in August and in October, as inflation temporarily exceeded the central bank's target range as a result of various supply shocks.  

In 2002, the central bank moved to a system of inflation targeting as its main monetary tool.

title: Peru Markets Rattled By Rise Of Nationalist Pres Hopeful
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--The rapid rise in popularity of nationalist presidential candidate Ollanta Humala has started to rattle Peru's financial markets, with observers expecting more turbulence ahead of the April elections.   

While opinion polls still show the ex-army officer lagging behind in his attempt to become president, with former Congresswoman Lourdes Flores in the lead, Humala appears to be closing the gap.   

A survey by pollster Apoyo Opinion y Mercado SA, published Sunday in newspaper El Comercio, showed the right of center Lourdes with 25% support, down from 28% in November. But public support for populist Humala rose to 22%, a sharp increase from 11% in the previous month and from just 2% in December 2004.   

That was enough to trigger a sell-off in Peruvian soles, leading the Central Reserve Bank of Peru to intervene Monday and sell a $80.5 million in an attempt to ease pressure on the local currency.   

But the sol weakened anyway, closing Monday at a midrate of PEN3.4405 to the dollar compared with a midrate of PEN3.4130 to the dollar in the previous session. In midday trade Tuesday, the sol was almost unchanged at a midrate of 3.4425 to the dollar.   

Market watchers expect the uncertainty surrounding Humala's policies to weaken confidence in the Andean nation. Humala, 43, has tapped into widespread dissatisfaction among Peru's poor with his self-proclaimed goal of "defending national interests against globalization."   

In a research report, Credit Suisse First Boston economist Carola Sandy said: "We think that, in coming months, voters' support for Humala could continue to increase, which would result in volatility of Peruvian asset prices."   

The central bank has been selling dollars since mid-October as the sol has weakened due to large dollar purchases by local pension funds, rising U.S. interest rates and political uncertainty.   

That's in contrast to its pattern of buying dollars in recent years to rein in the sol, which has been boosted by Peru's expanding trade surplus.   

The central bank's most recent dollar sales came about despite strong seasonal demand for soles in December, and the sale of some PEN811 million in sol-denominated local debt last Friday.   

Although the government was able to successfully place the bonds in the local market, the amount issued was below the PEN930 million the government had originally said it would offer. Analysts said that was due partly to nervousness over the elections and weakness in the currency market, which reduced demand for the treasury paper.   

"We estimate that the foreign exchange volatility will continue through this week, and that the central bank will be ready to sell dollars to cut off any speculative attacks against the sol," BBVA Banco Continental said in a report.   

It added that the central bank is also likely to tighten liquidity, leaving the interbank rate above the monetary authority's reference rate of 3.25%. The interbank rate closed Monday at 3.42%.   

Earlier this month, the central bank lifted its key reference rate from 3.0%, the first increase since October 2004, saying it wanted to reduce volatility in the foreign exchange market and to make speculative movements more costly.   

The rising uncertainty tied to Humala's higher popularity ratings could also lead to jitters in the equity market.   

On Tuesday, UBS Investment Research cut its risk exposure to Peru to zero in its model portfolio, selling its holdings of Credicorp Ltd. (BAP), owner of Peru's largest bank, Banco de Credito.   

"Whilst we think Humala's presidential chances are slim, they are nevertheless real, and we do not think the equity market has taken this on-board," said UBS. "Hence, we see short-term downside as the market prices in at least the possibility of a Humala victory."   

Around noon Tuesday, Credicorp's American Depository Receipts were trading down a sharp 4.1% at $26.96.   

The newly elected president will assume office in July for a five-year term.   

President Alejandro Toledo can't run for office again in 2006 as a sitting president is barred from holding a second consecutive term.   

-By Robert Kozak, Dow Jones Newswires; 511-221-7050; peru@dowjones.com [ 13-12-05 1722GMT ]

title: Peru's  Central Bank  Sells $22 Mln To Support Sol
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--The Central Bank of Peru entered into the foreign exchange market Wednesday, selling $22 million to help ease volatility, an official at the central bank said.  

That marks the first time that the central bank has sold U.S. dollars since September 2002, the official added.  

Despite the intervention, Peru's sol ended Wednesday at a midrate of PEN3.3895 on a spread of PEN3.3890-PEN3.3900, weaker than Tuesday's close at PEN3.3600 to the dollar on a spread of PEN3.3590-PEN3.3610.  

The selling of U.S. dollars is a switch for the central bank, which has bought U.S. dollars steadily as the sol gained strength on booming exports.  

It stopped buying U.S. dollars in early September as demand by banks and institutional investors for the greenback increased.  

The sol depreciated by an average of 1.6% in September, the central bank said.  

The sol has weakened due to, among other factors, the decision by the central bank to leave its key reference rate unchanged since late last year.  

Finance Minister Fernando Zavala said Wednesday in a radio interview that the central bank's intervention to sell U.S. dollars was aimed at calming temporary volatility.  

"There aren't any fundamental reasons for a depreciation of the exchange rate," Zavala said, pointing to the nation's strong trade position.  

"We have always said that it is temporary volatility," Zavala added.  

Banco BBV Continental said this week in a report that the weakening trend in the sol has been amplified by low liquidity in the foreign exchange market.  

It added that the weakening of local currency is temporary and will eventually reflect solid economic fundamentals, including Peru's trade surplus and low inflation.  

WestLB Research said in a report Wednesday that Peru's economy could expand by 6.0% this year. It also forecasts a trade surplus of $4.1 billion this year and around $4.4 billion next year, assuming that commodity prices remain close to current levels.

title: Peru's Ctrl Bk Chief Expects Low Inflation, Good Growth
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Any election-related volatility next year shouldn't derail what has so far been a four-year streak of record low inflation and robust economic growth for Peru, according to the nation's top monetary official.  

During a wide-ranging interview with Dow Jones Newswires late Tuesday, the Central Reserve Bank of Peru's acting President, Oscar Dancourt, underlined the bank's commitment to its inflation targeting model, saying that keeping prices under control remains the key mission of the central bank.  

Describing a benign international environment in which Peru's main export buyers - the United States and China - are expected to grow at current levels and in which commodity prices are expected to remain strong, Dancourt said the economy should expand by 5.0% next year, slightly below this year's 5.5% official forecast.  

He said that even with high prices for crude oil, which the central bank budgets at $65 per barrel next year, fiscal, economic and monetary stability should persist well into next year.  

The central bank also forecasts exports reaching $16.1 billion this year and rising to $16.9 billion next year, underscoring the boom in international sales of goods such as minerals, textiles and fish meal.  

"We don't see any negative effects from the election," Dancourt said in the interview in the central bank's art-filled headquarters in Lima's historic center.  

Peru faces general elections early next year and both a new president and a new Congress will take over in July. President Alejandro Toledo can't run for a second term in office in 2006 due to term limits.  

Credit rating agencies have said that any upgrade in Peru's below investment grade rating depends largely on a smooth transition of power.  

Before the campaign starts, however, the central bank has had its hands full dealing with a fast appreciating local currency, the sol, as well as helping to develop a sol-denominated yield curve.  

In the last few years, Peru has increased its issuance of sol-denominated debt in the local market, drawing foreign investors with attractive yields in longer-dated maturities.  

Dancourt said keeping inflation under control is the best way to dampen any possible election-related market concerns among foreign buyers of the sol-denominated debt, some of which Peru placed recently to repay obligations to the Paris Club of private creditors.  

Morgan Stanley said in a market report this week that international investors now hold around three quarters of the longer-term issues.  

"On the back of the substantial rally in local rates, as well as the unexpected bout of foreign exchange volatility, there is concern that international investors could take profits," the investment bank said.  

The sol appreciated by 5.5% against the dollar last year, but Dancourt noted that it remains essentially a free-floating currency. The best approach to allay concerns about its strength, he said, is to keep inflation low.  

However, he also indicated that the central bank remains ready to maintain its policy of interventions if volatility becomes excessive, pointing to Peru's strong international reserves. Reserves totaled $13.70 billion as of Sept. 20.  

"There is a degree of volatility that we consider normal and another that we consider excessive. We have accumulated enough reserves in the last few years to deal with that excessive volatility."  

The central banker added, "The foreign investors that are buying are aware that the interest rate differential is very wide, and they should have some form of hedging."  

He also suggested that the central bank had little impetus to raise its key reference rate from the current 3.0% level, given expectations that prices will remain at current levels.  

"It doesn't make much sense to increase interest rates if we have inflation rates that are below the floor and that should remain like this in the immediate future," he said.  

The central bank aims to keep consumer inflation within a one percentage point range - with 2.5% serving as the midpoint - into the indefinite future.  

Dancourt said Peru's consumer price index could end the year lower than the 1.8% forecast set recently by the central bank and come in closer to the lower end of the central bank's target range.  

He added that inflation in 2006 should also trend in the lower range of the band, ending the year at its 2.5% mid-range level.  

Dancourt noted that over the last four years inflation in Peru has averaged around 2.5%, the lowest levels since the 1930s.  

The consumer price index for Lima rose by 1.22% over the 12-month period to August.  

Dancourt also said efforts to reduce the high levels of the use of the dollar in the economy are taking place on various levels, including promoting efforts to place prices of goods in stores in soles as well as in dollars.  

The central bank has expressed concern that borrowers who have obligations in dollars while receiving income in soles could be caught out by a shift in financial conditions.  

Dancourt also said that any decision by Peru to drop its long-running series of loan programs with the International Monetary Fund will be up to the incoming government. Peruvian officials have expressed the desire for the country to amicably withdraw from its IMF loan programs. In June last year Peru received a 26-month standby loan worth some $422.8 million, but has signaled its intentions to not draw on any of the funds.  

Dancourt, an economist, took over as acting central bank president following the resignation of Javier Silva Ruete in late 2004, who left to work for the IMF.

title: DJ  Peru  Sol Unchanged After Record  Intervention ; Stocks Fall
text:
LIMA, Jul 07, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

Peru's sol ended unchanged Thursday after the Central Reserve Bank of Peru entered the market to purchase a record $150 million.  

The central bank intervention followed strong demand for the local currency as the Finance Ministry held an auction of 12-year treasury bonds to help repurchase Paris Club debt.  

The sol ended unchanged at PEN3.2505 to the dollar on a spread of PEN3.2500-PEN3.2510 in heavy trading.  

The intervention Thursday brought the central bank's purchases of U.S. dollars so far this year to $2.358 billion, above the $2.340 billion it bought in all of 2004, an official said.  

The key average overnight lending rate in the local currency was 3.05% Wednesday.  

The Lima stock exchange, meanwhile, closed lower Thursday as several-blue chip stocks gave up recent gains.  

The stock market's broad general index fell 11.13 points, or 0.27%, to 4050.29, while the selective blue-chip index lost 19.32 points, or 0.29%, to close at 6614.38.  

Beverage producer Union de Cervecerias Peruanas Backus & Johnston SAA (BACKUSI.VL) fell 0.7% to end at 1.40 soles. There has been speculation that the company's controlling shareholder may be the target of a takeover bid.  

Copper miner Sociedad Minera Cerro Verde SAA (CVERDEC1.VL) lost 1.3% to end at $3.93 as copper prices eased.  

-By Robert Kozak, Dow Jones Newswires; 511-221-7050; peru@dowjones.com

title: Peru's Robust Economy Faces Challenges In 2005
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Red-hot metal prices, strong textile exports and development of the fledgling energy sector boosted Peru's economy last year.   

But questions remain about how strongly that momentum will carry over to 2005.   

Protesters may continue to plague the important mining sector, while the approach of the 2006 general elections could add some heat to Peru's volatile politics. Some economists also worry that slower global growth might weaken the Andean nation's vitality.   

Gross domestic product is expected to have grown by about 4.5% last year, a figure that analysts say is solid but not as good as it should be given high raw material prices and low interest rates.   

"Last year was a regular year for growth, since with 4.5% growth we just have the level of job creation needed to meet the number of people entering the labor force. We need growth of seven or eight or even nine percent," said Samuel Gleiser, a businessman and president of the national chamber of commerce, Perucamaras.   

The government forecasts GDP will again grow 4.5% this year, while many private sector economists expect output to be at least 4.0%.   

"It (2005) will be a good year, taking into account what the economy can give. To ask for greater growth, for more than 4.0% or 5.0%, is asking too much in terms in what it can grow without overheating," said Banco BBVA Continental chief economist David Tuesta.   

Banco de Credito forecasts output of 4.5% in 2005, "which would complete seven consecutive years of growth, something that hasn't happened since 1977."   

Both Fitch Ratings and Standard & Poor's lifted Peru's credit rating last year. Nonetheless, Peru is still considered a speculative play for investors, as credit rating agencies keep a close eye on the country's high debt levels and the 2006 elections.   


 
      Resource Sector Helps Boost Growth 
    

Still, the resource sector should continue to lead growth, alongside the awarding of concessions for some highway projects.   

The giant Camisea natural gas project came on stream last year, and officials now point to the second phase, known as Camisea Two, aimed at producing liquefied natural gas for export.   

Peru LNG Co., owned by Hunt Oil Peru and South Korea's SK Corp, (003600.SE) expects to start construction of a $1.6 billion LNG plant in July, although there are still lingering disputes between two regions over ownership of the land where the plant is to be built.   

Fishing sector officials forecast another good year for the anchovy haul, which reached more than 8.0 million metric tons last year. Peru is the world's largest producer of fishmeal from anchovy, used mainly as animal feed.   

In the mining sector, companies last year opposed the imposition of a new royalty on mining company sales, while various community groups led protests, citing environmental concerns. Protesters stopped exploration at Minera Yanacocha SLR's Cerro Quilish gold deposit, run by Newmont Mining Corp. (NEM), and at Buenaventura SAA's (BVN) La Zanja gold deposit.   

Nonetheless, the Energy and Mines Ministry predicts that the mining sector will expand between 3% and 4% in 2005, as several large-scale projects remain on track.   

Among them, Barrick Gold Corp. (ABX) plans to make the first pour at the $340 million Alto Chicama gold project in the third quarter.   

Copper miner Sociedad Minera Cerro Verde SAA (CVERDEC1.VL) expects to start construction of a new concentrator early this year as part of a planned $850 million expansion.   

Swiss-based Xstrata PLC (XTA.LN) plans to start exploring early this year after winning the concession for the Las Bambas copper deposit in 2004, while work to modernize Southern Peru Copper Corp.'s (PCU) facilities will also continue.   


 
            Free Trade Deal Hoped For 
    

The robust mining sector has sharply boosted Peru's exports, which may have reached about $12 billion in 2004 and which are expected to grow by at least 10% this year, Trade and Tourism Minister Alfredo Ferrero said recently.   

Peru, alongside Ecuador and Colombia, will also enter what they hope will be the final phase of talks for a free trade deal with the United States. The government wants that pact to, among other things, extend the special tariff status with the U.S. that helped boost textile and garment exports by 33% in the first eleven months of 2004 compared to a year earlier.   

The lifting of some international quotas on textile and garment quotas from the start of the year could, however, put a crimp in the Peruvian industry as it faces greater competition.   

"There is a sense of gloom and doom until we know the effect of the disappearance of quotas for those products," Perucamaras' Gleiser said.   


 
          Deficit To Remain Under Control 
    

The strong trade accounts have helped boost the local currency, and analysts expect the sol to remain stable in 2005 owing to continued trade surpluses and low inflation.   

The sol appreciated by more than 5% against the U.S. dollar in 2004, prompting the Central Reserve Bank of Peru to intervene to buy a record $2.34 billion, aiming to ease the gains. That in turn helped boost net international reserves to a record high last year.   

Peru is also expected to proceed with plans to prepay some of the $8.18 billion it owes to the Paris Club, issuing debt to ease a scheduled hump in payments over the next few years.   

Economists also expect inflationary pressures to remain under control after supply shocks tied to a drought in Peru and higher energy costs lifted the 2004 consumer price index by 3.48%, just below the higher edge of the central bank's target range.   

Meanwhile, the government forecasts that 2005's fiscal shortfall will narrow to 1.0% of GDP after reaching an expected 1.3% or 1.4% of GDP for 2004.   

Some economists say efforts to reduce the fiscal deficit may weaken if the government increases spending before the elections in an effort to boost its approval ratings. They also point to a perceived lack of political will to eliminate tax exemptions.   

Analysts, moreover, will be watching closely as various politicians position themselves for a run for office in 2006. Peru's constitution prohibits Peru's president, the deeply unpopular Alejandro Toledo, from seeking a second term.   

A series of accusations tied to alleged acts of corruption on the part of several of Toledo's family members has the potential to upset the political order in the new year.   

A group of disgruntled ex-soldiers who took over a police station in a bloody attack in a remote Andean mountain town as the year began also shook the nation.   

"What took place gives the impression that 2005 will be highly volatile year in terms of political and social protests," political analyst Santiago Pedraglio wrote in newspaper Peru21.

title: Peru Exporter Group Calls On Govt To Halt Sol Strength
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's exporters said the sol will likely continue to appreciate in the short run and called on the government to rein in the currency.  

The Exporters' Association, or ADEX, said the sol will strengthen as companies pay a traditional year-end extra monthly salary. An upcoming tax payment period is also seen creating demand for the local currency.  

"The weakening of the dollar is having a detrimental effect for our exporters," the president of ADEX's clothing industry sector, Pedro Gamio, said Tuesday in a telephone interview.  

The sol, which appreciated by 4.8% in November over the previous 12-month period, broke through the important PEN3.30-per-dollar barrier Friday, closing at a midrate of PEN3.2985. It closed Monday unchanged.  

The sol's strength comes despite recent intervention by the Central Reserve Bank of Peru to ease its appreciation. The central bank has purchased about $2.0 billion so far this year, boosting net international reserves to $12.34 billion.  

But economists say that the fact the central bank abstained from intervening in the foreign exchange market on Friday and Monday may signal a change in strategy.  

"This reveals that the central bank is ready to permit a greater appreciation of the sol," the economic studies department of BBVA Banco Continental said in a report late Monday.  

The sol has gained strength due to a number of factors, including a boom in mineral exports.  

Peru posted a trade surplus totaling $284 million in October, compared with $58 million in the same month last year. For the 12-month period to October, the trade surplus totaled $2.38 billion.  

Among other things, the nation's exporters want the government to increase the limits that private pension funds have on investing outside the country, saying this would create demand for dollars.  

-By Robert Kozak, Dow Jones Newswires; 511-221-7050; peru@dowjones.com [ 07-12-04 1608GMT ]

title: Peru's Credicorp sees sol at 3.30/dollar in 2004.
text:
LIMA, Peru, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Peru's largest financial holding, Credicorp. (BAP.LM) (BAP.N), expects the sol to finish the year at around 3.30 to 3.31 to the U.S. dollar, slowing its recent appreciation, an executive said on Tuesday.   

The sol, which closed at 3.306/3.308 to the dollar on Tuesday, strengthened 4.3 percent between January and October due to strong economic growth, rising investor confidence and an export boom.   

"We trust there won't be significant changes; we see exchange rate stability until the end of the year ... at around 3.30 to 3.31 soles to the dollar," Raimundo Morales, Credicorp's chief operating officer, told a news conference.   

Peru's Economy Minister Pedro Pablo Kuczynski last month warned an exchange rate above 3.30 soles to the dollar would be dangerous, putting the country out of sync with the world economy and making its exports too expensive.   

Peru's central bank has spent $1.813 billion intervening in the local currency market so far this year in a bid to prevent the sol from strengthening too fast.   

From this month, the bank now requires commercial banks to place 30 percent of customers' dollar deposits in its vaults, up from 20 percent in October, to help cool the sol's rise.   

The sol averaged 3.50 to the dollar in 2003.

"This is purely psychological and speculative. No one could think this is an economic problem that could affect growth or inflation," President Alan Garcia said at a press conference early Thursday.   

He pointed out that growth in gross domestic product is expected to expand between 7% to 8% this year.   

"The fundamentals of the economy and the companies that trade on the bourse are very strong," stock market president Carmela de Marrou said in one media interview.

title: Peru's Broad General Stock Index Ends 7.59% Lower
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's stock market, one of the best performers in the world so far this year, tumbled sharply Wednesday as nervous investors pulled out their money.   

The main stock indexes were dragged down on heavy trading volume by weakness in mining company shares and to a lesser extent by an earlier slide in stocks in China.   

The decline was so sharp that the stock market halted trading for half an hour late in the morning.   

After declining more than 10% at one point in the session, the stock market's broad general index rebounded a bit to end 1,522.95 points lower, or 7.59%, at 18,543.82.   

The selective blue-chip index fell 2,673.28 points, or 7.67%, to end at 32,171.76.   

"This is herd behavior," said Jorge Luis Rodriquez, with brokerage Centura SAB.   

"One detonator is that the media has been predicting this fall and this has had an impact," he added. "This is one of the biggest falls in the history of the stock exchange."   

Market analysts said that many individual investors, who have piled into the stock market following a 168% increase in the general index last year, decided to sell their shares and their mutual fund holdings.   

"The main factor was internal. It was investors selling their mutual funds, which have had to sell the shares," Gonzalo de la Casas, with private pension fund AFP Integra, said on CPN radio.   

Finance Minister Luis Carranza downplayed the sharp declines, saying Peru's economic fundamentals remain solid.   

Carranza told reporters that the stock market has been affected by speculative behavior.   

"These are speculative movements and aren't affecting the nation's economic fundamentals. We have to be confident that in the long term that business conditions, which sustain dividend payments and the fundamental value of shares, are going to continue to remain very positive," he said.   

Chinese stocks tumbled after the government tripled a tax on securities transactions. That affected confidence in the Lima stock market as well.

title: DJ Peru Stk Indexes Tumble, Tracking Metals Prices; Sol Weakens
text:
LIMA, May 24, 2007 (DJCS via Comtex) --   

Peru's main stock indexes took a tumble Thursday, tracking a fall in metals prices.   

According to preliminary results, the stock market's broad general index fell 428.94 points, or 1.97%, to end at 21,328.24.

According to traders, Peru Copper's shares had risen on rumors that the company is close to obtaining financing for the Toromocho copper project in central Peru.

title: Peru's Main Stock Indexes End Sharply Lower; Sol Stronger
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's main stock indexes ended sharply lower Monday, dragged down mainly by weakness in metals prices that hurt mining companies.   

According to preliminary results, the stock market's broad general index fell 661.07 points, or 2.88%, to end at 22,303.35. The selective blue-chip index ended 1,365.66 points, or 3.42%, lower at 38,593.59.   

"The indexes were correcting for the entire session but took a stronger downturn right at the end on profit-taking. It moved fast," one trader said.   

"The metals prices had a strong influence on the market today. Both the price of zinc and copper fell, and that had a big influence in the session," he said, pointing out that 60% of the trading on the Lima stock exchange is in mining shares.   

Southern Copper Corp. (PCU) and Compania Minera Volcan SAA (VOLCABC1.VL) were among the miners that lost ground over the course of the session.   

Southern Copper dropped 4.4% from Friday's close to end at $86.57, while zinc miner Volcan lost 4.9% to end at 16.41 soles ($5.18).   

Financial holding company  Credicorp Ltd. (BAP) also lost ground, retreating 2.1% to end at $60.50.   

Meanwhile, the sol ended slightly stronger at a midrate of PEN3.1665 to the U.S. dollar on a spread of PEN3.1660 to PEN3.1670, the official said.   

The sol ended the previous session at a midrate of PEN3.1705 to the U.S. dollar on a spread of PEN3.17 to PEN3.1710.   

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru intervened in the foreign exchange market on Monday to purchase $5 million.   

The central bank has been intervening regularly to buy dollars in recent sessions to smooth movements in the foreign exchange market and to build foreign reserves.   

Scotiabank said in a report that it expects the sol to come under some moderate upward pressure due to tax payments.

title: DJ Peru's PM Calls For Probe Into $140 Mln  Forex  Transaction
text:
LIMA, May 08, 2007 (DJCS via Comtex) --   

Peru's Prime Minister Jorge del Castillo called Tuesday for an investigation into a sale late last week of $140 million by a regional government through a private Peruvian bank.   

At a press conference, del Castillo said the operation should have gone through the state-owned Banco de la Nacion, and he raised questions about the propriety of the trade.   

"There were serious irregularities. If the national bank pays more, why go to a private bank. Who gained? The region lost. So who gained, and how much?" he said.   

The large purchase of the local currency, the sol, by the regional government of the department of Ancash took place late Thursday.   

When the private bank turned around and sold those dollars it had bought, mostly on Friday, that added to appreciation pressures on the sol.   

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru responded by intervening to purchase $250 million, to keep the exchange rate from moving too much.   

It was the largest single day purchase of dollars ever for the central bank.   

Since then the regional government, which had received a large transfer payment from the central government tied to mining, has been criticized for not getting the best deal when it bought the soles.   

At a press conference Tuesday, del Castillo lashed out at the regional government, saying it would have received a better exchange rate had it gone to the state's Banco de la Nacion to make the deal.   

Del Castillo said it was likely the comptroller of the nation will look into the movements.   

The central bank intervened last Friday to mop up the U.S. dollars by paying PEN3.1664 per dollar.   

Newspaper El Comercio said in a story Tuesday the government of Ancash received PEN3.1610 per dollar from the private bank it used.   

The sol has been on an appreciating trend in recent years, in part as strong exports, especially of minerals, have boosted inflows of cash into Peru.   

Various regional governments have been criticized recently for not being able to professionally spend the transfer payments they receive from the central government.   

The region of Ancash has received large-scale transfer payments due to presence of some large mines there, including the giant Antamina copper-zinc mine.   

-By Robert Kozak, Dow Jones Newswires; 511-221-7050; peru@dowjones.com   

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Peru's Main Stock Index Rises 3.21% To End At Record
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's main stock indexes roared higher to new records Monday, propelled by widespread strength in all sectors.   

According to preliminary results from the Lima Stock Exchange, the stock market's broad general index gained 691.23 points, or 3.21%, to end at 22,166.68.   

The selective blue-chip index ended 1,206.17 points, or 3.28%, higher at 37,990.37.   

Without taking into account Monday's gains, the general index has risen some 67% so far this year, after gaining 168% in 2006.   

On Monday, mining companies continued to post strong gains.   

Southern Copper Corp.(PCU) rose 1.9% to end at $85.00 on stronger copper prices, while copper miner Sociedad Minera Cerro Verde SAA(CVERDEC1.VL) gained 4.8% at end at $28.40.   

Precious metals miner  Compania de Minas Buenaventura SAA (BVN) gained 0.9% to end at 108.00 soles. ($34.10)   

Financial holding company  Credicorp Ltd (BAP) also continued to rise, ending 0.6% higher to end at $56.31, on confidence about economic growth.   

Peru's gross domestic product is expected to expand some 8.0% this year, after expanding some 8.0% last year.   

"The heaviest traded shares were Credicorp and Volcan. There is a lot of interest in both shares," said one trader.   

Zinc miner Compania Minera Volcan SAA (VOLB.VL) gained 2.8% to end at PEN15.32.   

Meanwhile, the sol ended slightly weaker Monday, at a midrate of PEN3.1670 to the U.S. dollar on a spread of PEN3.1660 to PEN3.1680.   

The sol ended the previous session at a midrate of PEN3.1645 to the U.S. dollar on a spread of PEN3.1640 to PEN3.1650.   

The Central Reserve Bank of Peru intervened Monday in the foreign exchange market to purchase $15 million.   

That followed a purchase of $250 million on Friday, which was the largest single day purchase ever on the part of the central bank.   

The central bank has been intervening regularly in recent sessions to buy dollars to ease movements in the foreign exchange market and to build foreign reserves.   

Analysts say that the sol has appreciated due to strong economic fundamentals, including strong exports.   

They add that some banks that hold large net U.S. dollar positions have also been selling them.   

One local government also recently sold dollars it received in transfer payments tied to resource extraction in the region, market analysts said.   

Flows of dollars into Peru from Peruvians overseas have also risen, while investors are also purchasing soles in order to invest in the stock market, analysts add.

title: UPDATE 1- Peru  cenbank announces new  intervention  instrument.
text:
(Adds Central Bank comments paragraphs 2-3, 5, updates with sol close paragraph 9) 

 LIMA, Peru, July 8 (Reuters) - Peru's Central Bank said on Monday it would launch new certificates of deposit based on fluctuating exchange rates as a new instrument to control volatility in currency markets. 

 "Without (banks) having to enter the spot dollar market or unload their currency positions, this new measure ... helps establish a more stable currency," the Bank's General Manager Henry Barclay told a news conference. 

 "Without a doubt, it helps eliminate volatility," he said. 

 The Central Bank said in a statement in the official gazette that the certificates would be subject to a readjustment based on the change in the exchange rate registered between the placement and expiry dates. 

 Barclay said the new instruments, to be called readjustable certificates of deposit, could be used from now on when the Central Bank saw fit. Market conditions will determine when they are first used. 

 "The average weighted exchange rates of operations conducted via the system Datatec (a foreign exchange trading system) between 9:30 a.m. and 1:30 p.m. will be used," it said, adding that if that information was not available, an average of the exchange rate published by Reuters would be used. 

 "What makes these certificates in local currency different is that they will be readjusted in line with the exchange rate. These operations will help reduce volatility in the price of the sol currency against the dollar," a banking source who requested anonymity told Reuters. 

 The Central Bank periodically offers certificates of deposit as a liquidity-controlling measure in the financial system. Local banks - Peru has 15 - buy the certificates, meaning there is temporarily less money in circulation, and receive interest on the certificates when they come due." 

 Peru's sol slumped last week against the dollar, closing at its lowest level all year against in a falling market riven by speculation ahead of an expected Cabinet reshuffle this month. The sol closed at 3.5320/3.5335 against the dollar.

title: Peru's Sol Gains Respect But Dollar Remains Popular
text:
LIMA -(Dow Jones)- Peru's little-known currency, the sol, is suddenly getting some respect after gaining ground steadily this year against the U.S. dollar. 

 That has forced the Central Reserve Bank of Peru to intervene to buy U.S. dollars on a regular basis in the last few weeks, aiming to keep the sol from strengthening too fast. 

 The free-floating currency has benefited from improved exports, weaker imports and more sol-denominated bond placements. 

 Falling oil prices have left more dollars in Peru, which is a net energy importer. 

 Moreover, lower interest rates have reduced Peru's foreign debt payments, increasing the supply of dollars. An appetite for higher-yielding local instruments has also increased demand for the sol. 

 Still, few expect its recent strength will lead the sol to replace the greenback as the currency of choice for everything from real estate to car purchases. 

 The U.S. dollar makes up almost 70% of total banking deposits, and 81.5% of total domestic credits. 

 "There still isn't any process of de-dollarization. The prices of products of high worth are expressed in dollars in the stores," said Juan Carlos Garcia, head of economic analysis with Banco Wiese Sudameris. 


"We think in dollars. When we stop using the dollar as a reference
currency, that's when we start to have a de-dollarization," he added.
       Pension Funds Buying Debt Instruments



So far this year, the sol has appreciated about 2.46% against the U.S.
dollar, ending Monday at 3.4343 soles per dollar.



To keep it from appreciating even more, the central bank has been a
regular buyer of dollars, purchasing $157 million so far this year up to
Monday.



In 2000 it just bought $3.0 million in total.


Central bank officials have said they have noted a growing confidence
in the local currency.



But, perhaps more importantly, the private pension funds, or AFPs,
have been buying soles.



"For about the last four months there have been few (private sector)
fixed income placements and the money that the AFPs have taken in every
month has been placed with what has been on offer: treasury bonds," said
Gonzalo Tamayo, head of analysis with consulting firm, Macroconsult.



The government has placed PEN1.2 billion in treasury notes on the
local market this year, aiming to build a yield curve and develop the
local markets.



As of the end of September, pension fund investments in Peruvian
treasury bonds tripled to 4.6% of their portfolios from 1.5% in March.
       Portfolio Shifts Seen As Short-Term Move



But fund managers say the portfolio shuffles are likely short-term
moves.



"If the pension funds have invested more in instruments denominated in
soles it's because there have been more sol placements and not from any
deliberate decision to change the weight of investments," said Mariano
Alvarez, chief investment officer for pension fund, Union Vida.



He added that a possible default in Argentina could have a knock-on
effect and "as a long term investor I don't have the luxury of
drastically changing my portfolio for soles."



Another local fund manager echoed those sentiments.



"Despite the fact there is no short-term expectations of a
devaluation, there is always the fear that something will happen locally
or internationally that would negatively affect the exchange rate," said
Credifondo investment manager Ignacio Aguirre.
        Other Factors Weighing Against Sol



Other factors are also weighing against the sol.



Economists forecast a recovery in the economy next year, which should
boost imports and cause a drain on U.S. dollars.



Moreover, many people have strong memories of hyper-inflation. Price
increases hit 7,650% in 1990.



"Peruvians avoid saving in soles despite the fundamentals that
indicate there will be no devaluation because hyperinflation left many
of them deeply traumatized," said Banco Wiese Sudameris' Garcia.



Speaking to reporters late Monday, the general manager of the Central
Reserve Bank of Peru, Henry Barclay, said that the trend towards a
stronger sol could change rapidly.



"It is going to revert soon. The best way to look at this right now is
that the net cost of maintaining dollars, which is basically tied to the
sharp drop in interest rates for dollars. When (interest) rates in soles
start to fall, this will soon allow for a balance to be found that will
return us to a more comfortable situation," Barclay said.



-By Virginia Rey-Sanchez, Dow Jones Newswires; 511-221-7050;
peru@dowjones.com

title: Peru's  Central Bank  Sells Dollars To Bolster Sol
text:
LIMA -(Dow Jones)- The Central Reserve Bank of Peru stepped into the money market Wednesday, selling dollars for the first time in over a year to bolster the sol, a central bank official said. 

 At 0500 GMT the nuevo sol was trading at PEN3.5880 to the dollar on a spread of PEN3.5860 to PEN 3.5900. 

 The nuevo sol had reached levels of PEN3.603 to the dollar in early morning trade on local electoral worries and regional instability led by Argentina, traders said. 

 The nuevo sol had closed Tuesday at a mid-rate of PEN3.5950 a dollar on a spread of PEN3.5940-PEN3.5960, local traders said. 

 "We are in the market and we will continue to sell as much as necessary," a trader said, declining to give a maximum amount of dollars to be sold. 

 Local traders, however, pegged the amount at about $15 million. 

 Peru's local currency has weakened notably after the first round of presidential elections held April 8. No candidate took the majority, and a second round of voting will be held in late May or early June. 

 Managing Director Javier de la Rocha said the central bank would step in to defend the sol if needed, local newspaper Gestion reported Wednesday. 

 "When we think it's opportune, we will intervene," he said. 

 De la Rocha added that Peru's central bank does not control the sol, and only steps into the market to avoid abrupt fluctuations in the local currency. 

 Peru officially has a "dirty float," and the central bank keeps a tight hold on liquidity. 

 The sol's recent depreciation occurred because of the overall Latin American situation and the uncertainty related to any electoral process, de la Rocha added. 

 Finance Minister Javier Silva Ruete said the sol's recent depreciation should not be cause for worry, Gestion reported Wednesday. 

 "There has not been a substantial change in the sol. It will drop again a few cents and settle within the broad range of the dirty float," Silva Ruete said. 

 He added that this system had been highly successful over the last ten years. 

 Although jitters are not likely to subside before the runoff vote, Deutsche Bank analysts see the sol's depreciation "as limited to levels around 3.63/3.64 before the second round." 

 According to the report, Peru's sol is supported by a dollarization rate of nearly 60%, a strong position in reserves, and the central bank's tight hold on liquidity. 

 "Of course, a Garcia victory would trigger further volatility," Deutsche Bank adds in reference to presidential candidate Alan Garcia, whose tumultuous relationship with the financial community is unlikely to soothe market nerves.

title: Peru 's Ctrl Bk Chief Says  Intervention  Possible
text:
LIMA -(Dow Jones)- The Central Reserve Bank of Peru will intervene in Peru's foreign exchange market if conditions make it necessary, the general manager of the central bank, Javier de la Rocha, said Friday. 

 De la Rocha said the central bank would hold a meeting late Friday with representatives of local banks to discuss market jitters, including a sharp increase in interbank lending rates. 

 "There is really no reason for the interbank interest rate to be at about 16%. That is what is worrying us," de la Rocha said. "That interest rate is pure nervousness." 

 Thursday's interbank exchange rate reached 15.72% from 12.59% on Wednesday. 

 De la Rocha added that the central bank wouldn't shy away from using the market mechanisms available to it. 

 "We are going to call them to talk things over, calm them down, and make them see that the central bank obviously holds certain instruments and that will have to be used if to the extent that it is necessary. But of course not in excess," de la Rocha told reporters. 

 No specific trigger rates for the interbank interest rate nor the foreign exchange rate have been fixed, he added. Nevertheless, the absence of transactions could be an indicator for central bankintervention, he said. 

 "We say our floating exchange rate is 'dirty' because the central bank can intervene at any moment despite the fact that it has been two years since we have sold (U.S. dollars) and one year since we have bought them," he said. 

 De la Rocha dismissed sharp exchange rate fluctuations this week in the local currency citing similar volatility in Brazil, Chile, and Mexico and Peru's upcoming run-off elections. 

 "I don't see anything unusual in all this," he said. 

 The local currency market has been shaken by political uncertainty ahead of the presidential run-off election to be held May 27 or June 3. 

 Peru's nuevo sol firmed Friday to PEN3.5700 amid tight liquidity in soles after sliding down to PEN3.5813 per dollar Thursday. 

 Separately, de la Rocha said the change in  Argentina's exchange rate convertibility scheme wouldn't affect the Peruvian market. 

 The bank official also remarked that proposals by presidential candidates to lower minimum reserve requirements for dollar denominated bank deposits, or to change over to a referential interest rate scheme wouldn't have significant impact in the short term. 


"I say if something is working, why change it?" de la Rocha said.

title: Jitters in Peru as Fujimori makes surprise US trip.
text:
LIMA, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's surprise trip to Washington perplexed opposition politicians on Thursday as talk of a coup plot at home sent the sol falling against the dollar to its lowest level this year. 

 Fujimori left for talks with the head of the region's top diplomatic body, the Organisation of American States (OAS), in the early hours of the morning. 

 The State Department said Fujimori had requested a meeting with senior U.S. officials, but no details were available. Fujimori's office said only he would stay until Friday. 

 "(Fujimori's trip) is inexplicable at a time when we need a strong government presence," opposition congressman Valentino Paniagua told local RPP radio. 

 The president, plunged into crisis by a corruption scandal involving his former spy chief, Vladimiro Montesinos, has announced early elections in which he will not run, and last week, appeared to have calmed a volatile situation in which coup fears were rife by rallying the military behind him. 

 However, on Wednesday, a congressmen defecting from his Peru 2000 alliance said the military had urged legislators to break away and form a new group in Congress to sow chaos and pave the way for a coup by pro-Montesinos military within weeks. 

 The army dismissed the talk on Wednesday as "absolutely false", but in the current jittery climate, any talk of military intervention sparked panic. 

 "Peru is down because of people speculating that Fujimori left the country because he had to. I don't believe that rumour. The military denied any kind of coup activity," said one New York bond trader, as Peru Brady bonds prices fell. 

 Some political analysts said that although there were probably divisions in the armed forces, Fujimori appeared to have rallied them behind him and perhaps intended his trip to show he was confident and in control of the situation at home. 

 Montesinos was bundled out of the country to Panama at the weekend after pressure from the United States, the OAS and regional powers. He is awaiting news of his asylum request. 

 Montesinos, who headed Peru's notorious spy service amid allegations of corruption and human rights abuses, was seen in a video aired on television allegedly bribing an opposition legislator $15,000 to switch sides. State prosecutors closed an investigation into the affair before he fled to Panama. 

 Political analysts said it appeared Montesinos, who is still believed to have friends in high places in the military and the judiciary, had cut an impunity deal before leaving. 

 Meanwhile, Fujimori's ruling alliance has begun to splinter. Departures and defections in past days have left him without a majority in Congress for the first time since 1992. 

 FINANCIAL MARKETS WORRIED 

 Nerves - and questions about why Fujimori should suddenly need to travel to Washington - unsettled financial markets. 

 The Peruvian sol sank one percent to 3.5300 to the dollar - its lowest level of the year - at the opening, compared with Wednesday's close of 3.5035 to the dollar. 

 "The market is very nervous about Fujimori leaving for Washington and continued tension over the late interest payment on Peru's Brady bongs," said one foreign exchange dealer. 

 Peru, which is embroiled in a legal battle with one of its U.S. creditors, has until Oct. 7 to pay an $80 million interest bill or be officially declared in default - a move that would weigh on its chances of raising foreign capital. 

 Peru has the money to pay the interest bill but has delayed payment because of a legal ruling that hedge fund Elliott Associates could seize any funds to settle a pending claim. 

 Peru Brady bond prices in New York, which have been under pressure since Fujimori's announcement of elections almost two weeks ago, fell by up to one point while the rest of the market was buoyant. 

 Lima's stock market fell 0.5 percent in scant volume in early trade coloured by the political confusion. 

Foreign exchange dealers did not rule out more drops in the sol. "The talk about military coups is not helping, this will add fuel to the fire," said one foreign exchange dealer, adding the central bank could intervene to prop up the currency. 

 FUJIMORI FLIES ABROAD - BUT WHY NOW? 

 Opposition congressmen were incredulous that Fujimori should have chosen this moment to leave Peru. 

 "Right at the peak of the crisis he goes to Washington to support (OAS Secretary-General Cesar) Gaviria because he's got 23 presidents wondering why (Gaviria) wrote a letter urging asylum for Montesinos," said Luis Solari, spokesman for the Peru Posible party of main opposition leader Alejandro Toledo. 

 Gaviria, backed by other leaders in the hemisphere and the United States, which feared Peruvian democracy was under threat, urged Panama to take in Montesinos to calm a potentially volatile situation. (Additional reporting by Hugh Bronstein in New York).

title: Peru Plans Inflation-Linked Sol Bonds; Mulls Dlr Issue
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru plans to issue inflation-linked bonds denominated in soles within the next few weeks, the chief advisor at the finance ministry said Friday. 

 The issue will be worth 700 million nuevos soles (PEN) ($1=PEN3.3374), and is expected to take place within the next 50 days, the official, Carlos Paredes, said in a speech. 

 The borrower will be Cofide, the government's wholesale lending agency, which channels funds through commercial banks. 

 "This will permit the creation of long-term credits in soles," Paredes said. 

 He later told reporters that officials expect good demand for the bonds with institutional investors such as private pension funds and life insurance companies as well as with the general public. 

 He declined to provide any details about the issue like maturity, referring questions to Cofide. No Cofide spokesperson was immediately available. 

 Peru has also been considering floating a different bond denominated in U.S. dollars in international capital markets, in part to help build a benchmark for local corporate borrowers. 

 The government has also been working to increase liquidity in local markets in order to help Peruvian businesses. 

 Paredes also reaffirmed that Peru will continue with its floating currency regime, and that the Central Reserve Bank of Peru will continue its policy of intervening to soften abrupt movements of the currency when needed. 

 "The exchange rate will float and there will be central bankintervention when needed to avoid speculation," said Paredes.

title: Peru Banks Push Plan For New Aid Program
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's troubled banks need a state-run program that will help keep them above water, Mario Ferrari, the director of the national banking association, Asbanc, said Monday.

title: Peru  Sol Ends -2: Last Ctrl Bank  Intervention  Feb. 4
text:
The Central Bank's move took place after contradictory comments on forex policy by government officials. 

 Early Thursday officials at the Finance ministry told banks in a closed-door meeting that Central Bank would not take any steps to prevent a further weakening of the sol.

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's nuevo sol (PEN) finished weaker against the U.S. dollar Wednesday, as banks and companies continue to buy dollars despite central bank intervention to defend the local currency, traders said. 

 According to local traders, the sol ended trading at mid rate of PEN3.4000 a dollar on a spread of PEN3.3970-3.4000/dollar, compared to Tuesday's close at PEN3.3860 to the dollar on a spread of PEN3.3900-PEN3.3820/ dollar. 

 "Banks and companies were buying dollars, but it seems than many operations were speculative," said a trader at Banco de Credito. He added investors remain a bit nervous following Brazil's currency devaluation last month. 

 Market participants are also watching closely Peru's current account deficit, estimated to have reached 6.4% of gross domestic product at the end of 1998 - still high for regional standards. 

 The Central Reserve Bank Of Peru sold $20 million. Finance minister and other government officials have said the government wouldn't hesitate to intervene in the market against speculators. But the central bank has not acted in the market since Jan. 13, when it sold $10.5 million. 

 The Central Bank also sold PEN46.6 million in four-week certificates of deposit, which gave some support to the sol. 

 The key interbank interest rate stood around 18.0% Wednesday, down from Tuesday's 18.6%. 


In the informal market, the dollar traded at PEN3.42 to the dollar,
weaker than Tuesday's PEN3.39.
