title: Peru Fin Min Confirms Ctrl Bk Sold $10.5M Wed
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--The Peruvian government has announced a series of measures in response to the crisis in Brazil that it says will shield Peru's economy. 

 Finance Minister Victor Joy Way said in a press release late Wednesday that Central Reserve Bank of Peru is prepared to intervene in the foreign exchange market. 

 In an interview with radio station Radioprogramas Thursday, Joy Way confirmed that the central bank sold $10.5 million Wednesday. 

 The press release also said the central bank is prepared to cut the minimum reserve requirement for dollar-denominated deposits. 

 The central bank has been reducing the minimum reserve requirement since July, when it was 45%. The minimum reserve requirement now is 39% for existing dollar-denominated deposits and 20% for new dollar-denominated deposits. 

 The Finance Ministry said the government will use $200 million of a $547 million loan given by Inter-American Development Bank to inject liquidity in the banking system. It didn't specify when the loan could be used. 

 The press release said that Peru is negotiating with the World Bank and IDB for loans to strengthen its foreign reserves. Peru is seeking $500 million from each bank. It is also negotiating a loan from Japan's Export-Import Bank for $300 million. 

 The Finance Ministry said that Peru will sell $600 million of pending state shares in companies already privatized. 

 (END) Dow Jones Newswires  14-01-99

title: Peru cenbank sells dollars, first time in 4 years.
text:
LIMA, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Peru's Central Bank sold dollars Tuesday for the first time in four years in efforts to prop up its depreciating currency amid world market woes spurred by Russia's near economic meltdown. 

 The bank sold $25 million, helping the Peruvian sol to end trading at 3.057/3.060 against the dollar, compared with 3.062/3.065 at the close Monday, but the currency is still well below pre-Russia crisis levels. 

 Peru's free-floating currency typically depreciates only gradually - roughly 0.001 sol within a given session. But since August 26, the sol has slid 0.075 sol/0.076 sol against the dollar when Russia's crisis ignited falls on markets worldwide. 

Peru's central bank said last week it may intervene in the market. Official government policy is only to smooth over sharp changes in the sol's value. 

 The central bank generally influences the exchange rate through controlling liquidity by selling Certificates of Deposits (CDs) or auctioning overnight repurchase agreements, known as repos. 

 The government has also said the central bank would buy an average of more than $90 million per month this year in the foreign exchange market to allow the currency to depreciate gradually. 

 This year's Asia and Russia crises have caused the sol to depreciate more sharply this year as many investors have left Lima's slumping stock exchange and sought a safe haven in dollars, adding to the demand for greenbacks. 

 Still, because Peru's currency is free-floating, meaning its value is not propped up by control mechanisms, the sol is regarded as less sensitive to a risk of devaluation than other regional currencies, which operate within a band system, local macroeconomic analysts said. 

 In its 1998 budget, the government forecast an average exchange rate of 2.90 soles to the dollar and set a formal target that the currency would close the year at 2.95 soles per dollar. 

 As early as July, President Alberto Fujimori predicted the turmoil on global markets would force the currency through the 3.00 soles barrier. 

 In the 1999 budget sent to Congress last month, the government estimated next year's average exchange rate would be 3.10 soles to the dollar. Some economists, however, expect it to fall to an average of 3.25 soles. 

 ((Alistair Scrutton, Lima newsroom, Tel: 511 221-2134, Fax: 511 221-2133, lima.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Peru cenbank says to act if sol falls too sharply.
text:
LIMA, Sep 2 (Reuters) - Peru's currency slide over the last few weeks amid world market woes is only temporary, but the central bank will act to brake particularly sharp movements, the bank's president German Suarez said Wednesday. 

 "We are sure there will be a greater supply of dollars and this (currency fall) is temporary. But if there is too much nervousness, or brusque and speculative changes the bank has to act," Suarez told reporters, in his first public statements after chaos in Russia last month first sparked fears Latin American currencies would be hit. 

 Peru's free-floating currency typically depreciates only gradually - roughly 0.001 sol within a given session - but has seen steep falls in recent weeks. 

 In six sessions since Aug. 26, when an economic crisis in Russia ignited falls on markets worldwide, the sol has fallen 0.69/0.70 sol against the dollar to stand at 3.040/3.044. 

 Since the near Russian economic meltdown last week, Peru's central bank has not intervened in the market while official government policy is only to smooth over sharp changes in the sol's value, according to local traders. 

 The central bank generally influences the exchange rate through controlling liquidity by selling Certificates of Deposits (CDs) or auctioning overnight repurchase agreements, known as repos. 

 The government has also said the central bank would buy an average of more than $90 million per month this year of the sol in the foreign exchange market to allow the currency to depreciate gradually.

 Still, because Peru's currency is free-floating, meaning its value is not propped up by control mechanisms, the sol is regarded as less sensitive to a risk of devaluation than other regional currencies, which operate within a band system, local macroeconomic analysts said.

title: Peru  Ctrl Bk/Defend Sol -2: No  Intervention  Expected
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--The Central Reserve Bank of Peru will consider selling dollars to defend the nuevo sol (PEN) if the sol appears to weaken "irrationally," Central Bank President German Suarez said Wednesday. 

 Suarez, speaking in Congress, said the central bank has not had to intervene in the market to defend the sol in recent months. He also said that he didn't expect the currency to weaken irrationally. 

 "Indications are that the currency will trade within acceptable limits," Suarez said. 

 Suarez said he didn't expect the Colombian peso's devaluation to hurt the sol significantly, since the situations in the countries were different. 

 "This is a very different economy," Suarez said. 

 Analysts said that despite Colombia's problems, the sol should gain against the dollar. 

 "The sol should actually strengthen in the coming sessions, since the supply of dollars is relatively high," a local analyst said. 

 As reported, the sol weakened slightly in early trading Wednesday. But, despite a devaluation of Colombia's peso, the sol was rallying late in the session. 

 The analysts said that the sol was being helped by PEN62 million in central bank certificates of deposit maturing Wednesday. Additionally, the Lima Stock Exchange is showing gains Wednesday, something that normally helps the sol. 

 In recent trading, the sol was trading at PEN3.0452, about the same as Tuesday's close at PEN3.0450. 


(The original item, "Peru Ctrl Bk/Defend Sol -2: No Intervention
Expected," timed about 1713 GMT, attributed some of the analysts
comments to Suarez.)

title: Peru Sol Stronger Ahead Of Approaching Tax Deadline
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's nuevo sol finished stronger for the first time in seven sessions Wednesday, as traders said that private banks bought dollars in anticipation of an approaching tax deadline that must be paid in the local currency. 

 The sol finished the session selling at 2.800 nuevos soles per dollar, higher than Tuesday's close at 2.808 soles per dollar. The buy-rate for the sol Wednesday was 2.796 soles per dollar, stronger than 2.805 soles per dollar Tuesday. 

 "Banks sold dollars preventing further depreciation because the close proximity of a tax payment deadline," a trader at Contibolsa, a local brokerage. "That pushed the sol up." 

 The tax deadline referred to starts for most companies around mid-month. 

 The trader also said that Central Reserve Bank of Peru didn't intervene in the market by buying or selling dollars. 

 But investors who bought 60 million soles in 28-day certificates of deposit on Tuesday paid for them on Wednesday, using up some of the supply of soles. 

 The central bank didn't buy dollars on the market, traders said. The central bank sometimes buys dollars to weaken the sol and make exports more attractive. 

 The 24-hour interbank interest rate, the lending rate between banks, was around 16.3% Wednesday, higher than Tuesday's rate at 16.2%, and higher than the typical rate of 13% to 14%. The official 24-hour rate for one day isn't released until the following day. The trader said the high interest rate reflected the short supply of soles. 


In the informal market, the dollar maintained its value at 2.80 soles.

text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's nuevo sol weakened sharply in moderate trading Thursday, as traders said unconfirmed rumors of possible Central bank intervention hurt the value of the currency.

title: Peru  Nuevo Sol Weaker;Media Reports On Proposed  Intervention
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's nuevo sol weakened slightly Tuesday, but volume was low despite local media reports that the Central Bank could be preparing to intervene in the currency market. 

 The sol weakened to 2.656 per dollar after closing at 2.654 per dollar in each of the last three sessions. 

 The media reports on Central Bank activity seemed to have little effect on the exchange rate. 

 The financial daily Gestion reported that the Central Bank would be buying dollars in coming weeks to help raise $800 million to pay off foreign debt. As reported, the Central Bank bought a five-year high of $425 million in dollars in June, and indications are that it is buying dollars at nearly the same pace so far in July. The Central Bank declined to comment on the report.

text:

title: Peru/ Central Bank  -2: Continued Dollar Buying Expected
text:
The Central Bank periodically buys dollars in order to weaken the sol and make Peruvian exports more attractive. 

 So far, the Central Bank's efforts have had minimal impact, as the sol strengthened Tuesday to 2.624 per dollar, the same as Wednesday's opening level. The sol closed Monday at 2.625 per dollar. 

 The sol has now strengthened or maintained value in 10 of the last 12 sessions since reaching its weakest point on record, 2.651 per dollar, on Feb. 3. 

 Traders contacted Wednesday say they expect the Central Bank to continue buying dollars when the currency markets open Wednesday at 1430 GMT. 

 The Central Bank's periodic interventions are seen as an effort to help Peru curb its trade deficit, which was $1.94 billion in 1996, down slightly from a record $2.14 billion in 1995. But the actions often draw fire from opponents, who say it erodes wages and contributes to inflation.

title: Exotic  Currency / Peru  -2:  Central Bank Interventions  Ebb
text:
The recent slide in the value of the sol has made finance ministry year-end predictions for the sol, normally considered somewhat unrealistic, now seem conservative. 

 In January, the ministry said the year would end with the sol trading at 2.60 per dollar, while most brokerage houses at the time predicted about 2.58 per dollar. 

 The finance ministry hasn't changed its prediction, but brokerage houses such as Flemming's Investment Bank, Interfip Bolsa, Peruval, Hildebrandt and Ferrar and Santander are now predicting a year-end rate in the 2.63-sol to 2.65-sol range. 

 So far in the fourth quarter, the Central Bank has sold only about $8 million worth of soles, mainly to meet standard obligations and not to dampen the sol. 

 That's in considerable contrast to the first three quarters of the year when the central bank, according to its own figures, sold soles for $979.8 million. During that period, the sol weakened to 2.512 sols per dollar from 2.330 sols per dollar. 

 On Wednesday, the nuevo sol weakened slightly to close at 2.591 per dollar. 

 And with the stock market showing little promise of rebounding soon, analysts expect that the Central Bank interventions won't be necessary for most of the rest of this year. 

 'Other forces are weakening the currency,' said Lima economist Jorge Gomes, a former finance ministry official, referring to the declining stock exchange. 'There's no reason for the Central Bank to step in when what they would have happen is happening naturally.'

text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--The Central Bank of Peru plans to spend about $16 million a week to buy dollars on the open market and contain a recent rebound of the nuevo sol, the financial daily Gestion reported Wednesday. 

Currency traders acknowledged Wednesday that new rumors about the planned government intervention in the currency market have been circulating, but haven't been confirmed. 

Central bank officials weren't immediately available to comment on the report. 

 During April and May the government was rumored to have spent as much as $70 million intervening in the market to erode the nuevo sol and curb the country's problematic trade deficit which hit $2.68 billion at the end of May. 

 That central bank action helped to drive the dollar up to 2.455 nuevo sols last week from 2.333 nuevo sols in mid-April. 

 But since last Wednesday, the nuevo sol has gained against the dollar four days out of five, creeping back up to 2.442 nuevo sols. 


In its letter of intent to the International Monetary Fund (IMF)
signed last month, Peru said the nuevo sol would trade at about 2.65
nuevo sols per dollar by year's end, which would show a slight net
depreciation against the dollar when adjusted for anticipated 1996
inflation of about 11.5%.
   -Eric J. Lyman

title: Exotic  Currency /Peru -4: IMF Targets A Consideration
text:
Secada says the government's dollar-buying also reflects a broader change now underway in how the government of President Alberto Fujimori adjusts its economic policy to meet the requirements of its letter of intent with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Secada says. 

 On May 11, the government published a draft of the letter of intent, which spelled out Peru's GDP growth, inflation, fiscal spending and structural reform targets for the next three years. 

 The dollars that Peru accumulates will be an important component in Peru's ability to meet its key fiscal target in 1996, a 1% of GDP primary fiscal surplus, Secada says. 

 But these dollars are being accumulated by the government mainly to make future external debt payments, he says. "This is not a coordinated move to intervene in the foreign exchange market." 

 The Central Bank prefers to concentrate its policy efforts on fine-tuning adjustments in Peru's monetary base, not in large-scale currency intervention, Secada says. 

 Another reason why the government would be unlikely to either allow, or push, the sol to depreciate faster is to protect Peruvian companies and the government from sharp increases in the payments they face on their dollar-denominated debts. 

 "That provides a strong disincentive to devaluing the sol," Secada says. 

 But that doesn't mean that currency traders in London, New York and Lima will be able to rest easy. 

 According to one senior trader in Lima, contradictory currency forecasts by senior economic policy makers "caused a lot of confusion among analysts about where the government sees the sol heading." 

 In February, Peru Central Bank economist Henry Uruga said an overvaluation of the sol was having a negative impact on Peru's trade balance, and added that the sol should trade at about 2.55 soles to the dollar. 

 One month later, Finance Minister Jorge Camet, speaking to reporters in Buenos Aires during a meeting of the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) meeting, roiled Lima markets when he said the sol would drop to 2.65 soles per dollar by year end. 

 "I can't believe (Camet) meant that," the Lima trader says. "We started the year with high inflation due to rising agricultural prices, and there's just not the monetary conditions to support that much depreciation."

title: Peru  Central Bk Declines Comment On Sol  Intervention  Reports
text:
LIMA (DJ-EMR)--Peru's Central Bank declined Wednesday to comment on reports it has been buying soles over the last three months to keep the currency from dropping in value against the dollar. 

 Radio Programas reported Wednesday, citing two unnamed currency traders, that the Central Bank has maintained currency buying activity since mid-November. 

 But a spokesperson for the Central Bank declined to confirm or deny the report, saying it was against policy to discuss the bank's financial activities. 

 The sol, Peru's currency since 1993, dropped sharply in value last October and November. During a five-week span in those two months, the dollar rose to 2.345 soles from 2.222 soles, setting nine all-time highs en route. 

 But since then, the Peruvian currency has stabilized and the dollar was trading at 2.325 soles Wednesday morning.

title: Peru  sol weakens on  Central Bank intervention .
text:
LIMA, Dec 22 (Reuter)- The Peruvian sol weakened slightly on the interbank market to 2.299/2.309 soles to the dollar after opening at 2.298/2.308 on Central Bank purchases of the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 The government's intervention came after the sol had gained strength against the dollar over several weeks due to seasonal factors. At bank counters, the sol ended flat at 2.280/2.340 to the dollar. 

 The parallel market saw the local currency strengthen slightly to close at 2.314/2.316 soles after starting the session at 2.315/2.320 soles, dealers said. 

 According to banking sources, the supply of dollars was high in the morning causing the sol to strengthen until the Central Bank intervened to buy dollars, stabilizing the sol's value. 

 "After the Central Bank intervened, the financial system saw demand on certain speculation," one dealer said. "This caused the currency's (dollar) price to rise." 

 Nonetheless, the market showed little liquidity in soles so, if the bank does not turn around and sell soles, the local currency is likely to continue firm as the banks still have obligations to meet, dealers said. 

 Banking sources said the sol is expected to resume its rise against the dollar unless the Central Bank intervenes again.

title: Peru 's Sol Strengthens Despite  Intervention ; Stocks Rise

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru's sol closed stronger Thursday, despite Central Reserve Bank of Peru intervention to buy a record $83 million.  

The local currency has been gaining ground on strong economic fundamentals and a perception that the dollar could continue weakening.  

On Thursday, the sol closed at a midrate of PEN3.3620 to the dollar on a spread of PEN3.3610-PEN3.3630.

As of Aug. 17, Peru's net international reserves increased $970 million since the year began.  

"There are expectations that the sol will strengthen even more and as long as there these expectations, it will continue to strengthen," a trader at Banco Wiese Sudameris said.  

The government has come under pressure to limit strength in the sol in order to help exporters.  

Silva Ruete, however, pointed out that Peru has been reaching record export levels, which has helped the Andean nation run large trade surpluses.  

Peru's exports in the January to July period totaled $6.52 billion, a 30% rise from the same period a year before.  

The central bank on Thursday also placed PEN80 million in one-year certificates of deposit at an average annual yield of 4.54%, and another PEN80 million in nine-month CDs at an average annual yield of 4.17%.  

The key average overnight lending rate in the local currency was 2.63% on Wednesday.

title: Peru's Foreign Reserves Rise On More Ctrl Bk Dlr Buying
text:
LIMA (Dow Jones)--Peru continues to increase its international reserves, as among other things, the Central Reserve Bank of Peru intervenes to buy U.S. dollars.  

The central bank said late Friday that net international reserves totaled $10.518 billion on March 23, compared with $10.453 billion as of March 16.  

That increase was mainly due to open market purchases of U.S. dollars by the central bank, it said.  

"We buy to make our level of international reserves more robust as part of a preventive policy," central reserve bank President Javier Silva Ruete said in a radio interview on Monday.  

"This will help protect the country from any speculative attacks," he added.  

So far this year, the central bank has bought $632.5 million, aiming to ease appreciation of the local currency.  

To March 23, net international reserves have increased $324 million.  

In a report released Friday, Goldman Sachs (GS) noted that a strong rise in exports, substantial investments in the mining industry, and steady capital market access have allowed for consistent balance of payments surpluses, which the central bank has used to accumulate reserves.  

Peru's foreign-exchange position was $5.144 billion as of March 23, $561 million higher than at the end of the previous year. Those funds don't include public sector deposits with the central bank or commercial bank reserves.  

The strong rise in that foreign exchange position is "an important accomplishment in an economy still heavily dollarized," Goldman Sachs said.  

The sol appreciated by 1.1% in 2003, largely tied to low inflationary expectations and a burgeoning trade surplus.

title: Peru forex  looks set for record 2004  intervention .
text:
LIMA, Peru, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Peru's central bank, which already this year has spent a third of what it did in the whole of 2003 on buying dollars to halt the sol's rise, looks set for a record year of foreign exchange intervention, analysts said.   

Aggressive dollar purchases worth $317 million to date have brought the sol value down to 3.475 to the dollar, from around 3.45 in mid-January, its highest levels this year.   

Peru's currency has risen in recent weeks on solid economic news, including a trade surplus, a rise in regional currencies and progress in the Camisea gas project which is set to come on stream in August.   

The central bank said at the start of January that it expected to spend less intervening to buy dollars this year than the $1.05 billion it did in 2003. Its record was $1.295 billion in interventions in 1997.   

"It's clear that there's upward economic pressure on the sol and the central bank is trying to compensate for that, which makes it very likely that it will make a record amount (of dollar) purchases this year," Jorge Chavez, a former central bank president, told Reuters.   

"If the strong intervention continues, we could be seeing signs of a change in the (flotation regime) monetary policy, with a central bank that tries to fix the exchange rate, and that would be worrying," said Chavez, who heads the private Maximixe consultancy.   

Last year, the sol strengthened 1.2 percent against the dollar, compared with a fall of 2.4 percent in 2002. It ended 2003 at 3.461 against the dollar. Inflation was 2.48 percent last year.   

Some analysts said heavy central bank intervention could also push up interest rates for certificates.   

"The central bank's purchases have been completely balanced out by the issue of paper, but if it keeps intervening, it'll have to offer a better yield for investers since they could seek higher interest rates for certificates (of deposit) that are placed," said Cesar Medina, an analyst at Banco de Credito (CRE.LM).   

RATE FIXING?   

The central bank says it is seeking to avoid brusque changes in the sol's price, not to fix the exchange rate.   

But dealers are not so sure. "Although it denies it, it's fixing an exchange rate," said Medina.   

Other said it was awkward for them having the central bank constantly stepping into the market.   

"The central bank's interventions make us uncomfortable, it's turned into another competitor in the market, with the advantage that it has all the soles to (buy dollars and to) move prices, said one treasury official at a Lima bank who declined to be named.   

Pablo Secada, an analyst at the Peruvian Institute of Economy, said that as long as the country's economic fundamentals remained unchanged, central bank intervention was entirely reasonable, even if it reduced banks' forex profits.   

"The bank has increased the foreign exchange position (of its reserves), it has more dollars to back up the soles which it issues, the government has given it more room to buy dollars and it is in a position to inject liquidity," Secada said.   

The bank's exchange position - which makes up part of its reserves - was $4.583 billion at the end of last year, compared with $3.341 billion at the end of 2002. It was $4.849 billion at January 20 this year.   

Peru has international reserves of $10.561 billion, the highest level since 1998.   

"The central bank should buy and sell dollars at the same time to make it harder for the banks who are speculating against the exchange rate," said Maximixe's Chavez.   

Dealers' forecasts for the sol's exchange rate this year vary between around 3.47 and 3.5 to the dollar. The 2004 budget forecasts a rate of 3.59 soles per dollar - a level that is virtually impossible to reach, analysts say.

title: FOREX  VIEW: Peru's Sol Rock Steady In Oft-Turbulent Zone
text:
By Robert Kozak 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
   

LIMA (Dow Jones)--Latin American currency crashes are a common occurence, leading some countries to even throw in the towel to adopt the U.S. dollar.  

But Peru is moving in the other direction.  

Its local currency, the sol, has shown remarkable stability despite political turbulence that has driven down President Alejandro Toledo's popularity ratings.  

Moreover, authorities are aiming to reduce the nation's heavy reliance on the greenback for buying goods that are seen as a store of value, such as houses.  

Peru's free-floating currency has remained at about 3.5 soles per dollar in the last few years, while so far this year it has appreciated, gaining a nominal accumulated 1.04%, the Central Reserve Bank of Peru said.  

But a number of factors, including rising copper and gold prices, are putting so much pressure on the sol that the central bank has been forced to buy U.S. dollars on an almost daily basis.  

Curiously for a country that a little more than decade ago was rent by hyperinflation, the central bank is now more concerned about consumer prices weakening too much.  

"A big part of the recent stability is tied to the participation of the central bank in the foreign exchange market," said Banco Wiese Sudameris economist Mario Guerrero.  

"If the central bank hadn't intervened in the market and had let the sol gain, inflation would be much lower," he added.  

The local currency closed at 3.4811 per dollar on Monday, after the Central Reserve Bank of Peru again intervened to buy U.S. dollars.  

So far this year, the central bank has stepped into the market to buy $$825.7 million on the foreign exchange market. That's the largest amount since 1997, when a boom in the economy led to large-scale inflows of foreign capital.  

Most of the purchases have been from $3 million to $15 million a day, large enough to sway the small foreign exchange market.  


 
           Trade Surpluses Help Currency

As the mining sector pumps out more minerals, Peru has started to post trade surpluses. That, alongside shifts into sol-denominated portfolio instruments, has helped dampen expectations of a depreciation of the currency.  

Although gross domestic product is seen expanding about 4.0% this year, consumer prices pressures remain weak.  

So weak that observers say the central bank is concerned a stronger sol will propel consumer prices even lower, and push inflation outside the band it has established.  

The central bank has moved to a system of inflation targeting, set at 2.5% within a one percentage point band, for this year and into the near future. Year-over-year inflation of was 1.3% in October.  

Observers say inflation could come in at the lower end of the band this year, or even lower.  

"The central bank will have problems having inflation remains within its range as private consumption is decelerating and there are strong pressures for the currency to appreciate," BBVA Banco Continental said in a report.  

Monetary authorities say they have no target for the sol, but are intervening to "smooth out" its appreciation.  

Still, in a recent review of Peru's economy, the International Monetary Fund, saying a floating exchange rate regime has helped the country adjust to external shocks, also cautioned against too much intervention.  

"In line with the authorities' announced policy, intervention in the foreign exchange market should be limited to smoothing excessive volatility in the exchange rate," the IMF said.  

Moreover, officials hope the sol's stability will help wean the nation from its heavy reliance on the U.S. dollar.  

Many Peruvian have bad memories of the hyperinflation in the late 1980s and early 1990s that robbed the value of their savings. The government of former President Alan Garcia even introduced complicated multiple exchange rates.  

That drove many into the arms of the U.S. dollar, which is legal tender in Peru and which makes up about 80% of all bank loans.  

The IMF, in its report, noted that the high degree of financial dollarization while declining, "remains a source of vulnerability."  

(Robert Kozak is bureau chief in Lima for Dow Jones Newswires)

title: Market uncertain about Peru cenbank's  forex  policy.
text:
LIMA, Peru, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Heavy central bank intervention in Peru's foreign exchange market has slowed an appreciation of the nuevo sol currency and led to market uncertainty over the bank's foreign exchange policy, analysts and traders said on Tuesday.   

The Central Bank's formal policy is to let the currency float freely, buying or selling dollars in the market only to prevent volatility.   

Yet it has dramatically stepped up its purchases of dollars in the market this year, as the currency has firmed 1.0 percent between January and October on an upbeat economic outlook.   

Traders are left wondering who sets the exchange rate - the market or the monetary authority. The bank's purchase of $699.7 million to date this year compared with $95 million last year, when the sol depreciated 2.4 percent and was hit by a financial crisis in Brazil.   

"The Central Bank's intervention causes surprise since there is no volatility in the market. Or is the Central Bank defending a certain level?" said one trader who asked his name be withheld.   

"They're not letting the exchange rate follow the logical trend it would follow, according to market flows," said another trader.   

The Central Bank said its dollar purchases aim only to provide liquidity to the Public Treasury for paying short-term debt.   

"The Central Bank does not have an exchange rate target and its policy is characterized as flotation. It intervenes only to avoid jumps and dramatic falls in the exchange rate or to attend to government operations," a Central Bank official told Reuters.   

One trader said the sol, which has traded recently at around 3.48 soles per dollar, would have strengthened to 3.44 per dollar without the Central Bank intervention.   

"There are several factors making demand for dollars unattractive. If the Central Bank had let the currency float freely, the sol would have strengthened more," said Mario Guerrero, analyst with Banco Wiese Sudameris.   

On Tuesday, the sol traded at 3.478 per dollar at midsession. The government expects the exchange rate to finish 2003 at 3.50 soles and hover around 3.59 soles per dollar in 2004.   

Stability in other regional currencies, advances in the development of Peru's Camisea gas project and domestic support for the government's tax reforms have all helped ease investor demand for safe-haven dollars and bolster the sol.   

The government forecasts economic growth this year of 4 percent and a growing trade surplus.   

Other financial market players suspect the bank wants to prevent the sol from firming to the point where it hurts exporters.   

"The Central Bank is doing what it has always done: avoid an appreciation of the sol that affects the competitiveness of exports in the face of strong pressures to appreciate," said an analyst with Apoyo consultancy.   

Peru is a leading exporter of gold, copper, fishmeal, fish and zinc.
